stem:
A 38-year-old man newly diagnosed with HIV attends his sexual health clinic appointment for review of staging results. He is asymptomatic with no constitutional symptoms, no respiratory symptoms, and no oral candidiasis. His CD4 count is 250 cells/microlitre and HIV viral load 86,000 copies/mL. He has no other medical conditions, no sulfa allergy, and no current medications. He is keen to start antiretroviral therapy and asks about additional prophylaxis given his low CD4 count.

The clinic registrar has called you to clarify the prophylaxis plan.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76/min, blood pressure 120/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Well, no oral thrush; lymphadenopathy minimal in cervical chains; chest clear
data_table.Investigations: CD4 250 cells/microlitre; HIV RNA 86,000 copies/mL; Toxoplasma IgG positive; cryptococcal antigen negative; chest X-ray clear; LFTs and renal function normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate prophylaxis to commence?

options.text: Azithromycin 1200 mg orally once weekly to prevent Mycobacterium avium complex infection.
options.rationale: MAC prophylaxis is recommended when CD4 falls below 50 cells/microlitre, not at 250. (Source: ASHM HIV management guideline)

options.text: Fluconazole 400 mg orally once weekly to prevent invasive cryptococcal meningitis disease.
options.rationale: Cryptococcal prophylaxis is not routinely recommended in Australia; cryptococcal antigen screening is used to drive pre-emptive therapy at lower CD4 thresholds. (Source: ASHM HIV management guideline)

options.text: Pyrimethamine 50 mg plus sulfadiazine 1 g daily for toxoplasmosis prophylaxis given positive IgG.
options.rationale: Routine toxoplasmosis prophylaxis is initiated when CD4 falls below 100 with positive IgG; cotrimoxazole covers both at 250. (Source: ASHM HIV management guideline)

options.text: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg orally once daily for Pneumocystis prophylaxis.
options.rationale: ASHM recommends Pneumocystis prophylaxis with cotrimoxazole when CD4 falls below 200 cells/microlitre or below 14 percent, and at 200 to 250 borderline cases. (Source: ASHM HIV management guideline)

options.text: Isoniazid 300 mg daily for 6 months as latent tuberculosis prophylaxis regardless of QFT result.
options.rationale: Latent TB therapy depends on a positive QuantiFERON or tuberculin test, not on HIV status alone. (Source: ASHM HIV management guideline)

explanation.summary: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis in HIV is indicated when CD4 falls below 200 cells/microlitre, when the CD4 percentage falls below 14, or with a previous PJP episode. First-line is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (cotrimoxazole) 160/800 mg orally daily, with weekly thrice-daily dosing as an alternative. This dose also covers toxoplasmosis prophylaxis (indicated below CD4 100 with positive IgG). Prophylaxis can be stopped once CD4 sustains above 200 for at least 3 to 6 months on antiretroviral therapy. Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis with azithromycin is indicated below CD4 50.
key_points: PJP prophylaxis: cotrimoxazole when CD4 below 200 or below 14 percent.
Toxoplasma prophylaxis (cotrimoxazole) when CD4 below 100 plus IgG positive.
MAC prophylaxis (azithromycin) when CD4 below 50.
explanation.pearls: In sulfa allergy, alternatives include dapsone 100 mg daily after checking G6PD status, or atovaquone 1500 mg daily with food; pentamidine is reserved for cases when oral agents fail.

stem:
A 72-year-old woman presents to the emergency department from her aged care facility with 24 hours of progressive confusion, fever, and reduced oral intake. She has been catheterised long term for retention. She has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and stage 3 chronic kidney disease. She lives in residential aged care and is normally fully ambulant. On arrival she is rousable to voice but disoriented. Her urinalysis shows leukocytes and nitrites, and the urine in the bag is cloudy. Blood cultures have been taken. Her venous blood gas has just come back from the analyser.

The ED team is preparing the immediate resuscitation plan.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 116/min, blood pressure 88/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 38.6°C
data_table.Examination: Rousable to voice, disoriented; warm peripheries with capillary refill 3 seconds; chest clear; suprapubic tenderness
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.31, lactate 4.2 mmol/L; creatinine 145 micromol/L (baseline 110); urine leukocytes and nitrites; blood cultures sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate hour-1 sepsis bundle intervention?

options.text: Give a 250 mL crystalloid fluid challenge and reassess before any further fluid resuscitation begins.
options.rationale: Septic shock with lactate at 4.2 mmol/L requires 30 mL/kg early fluid, not a 250 mL challenge approach. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Defer fluid resuscitation pending CT scan to identify the source of sepsis before resuscitating.
options.rationale: Resuscitation runs in parallel with source identification; imaging must not delay fluids in shock. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Commence noradrenaline 0.05 mcg/kg/min as the very first intervention before any fluid bolus is given.
options.rationale: Vasopressors are started for ongoing hypotension despite adequate fluid resuscitation, not as the first action. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Give an IV stat dose of hydrocortisone 200 mg as first-line therapy for the haemodynamic instability.
options.rationale: Hydrocortisone is reserved for septic shock requiring ongoing noradrenaline at 0.25 mcg/kg/min or more, not first-line. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Give 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid IV; commence broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour; recheck lactate at 2 hours.
options.rationale: Surviving Sepsis hour-1 bundle for septic shock with lactate above 4 mmol/L includes 30 mL/kg fluid, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and lactate clearance reassessment. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

explanation.summary: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle for septic shock comprises: measure lactate (and remeasure if at or above 2 mmol/L), obtain blood cultures before antibiotics, administer broad-spectrum antibiotics, begin rapid fluid resuscitation with 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate at or above 4 mmol/L, and start vasopressors if hypotension persists during or after fluid resuscitation to maintain mean arterial pressure at or above 65 mmHg. Source control is added as soon as feasible.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, fluid 30 mL/kg, vasopressors if needed.
Lactate above 4 mmol/L mandates fluid resuscitation regardless of blood pressure.
Target MAP 65 mmHg; start noradrenaline first-line if hypotension persists after fluids.
explanation.pearls: If lactate has not fallen by at least 10 percent after the initial 30 mL/kg, reassess for source control failure, occult bleeding, or evolving cardiogenic shock from sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy.

stem:
A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents to the emergency department with 36 hours of left calf pain and swelling that started after a minor abrasion at a fishing trip. The pain is now disproportionate to what is visible. He is febrile and rigoring. On examination the left calf is tense, dusky red with a faint dishwater fluid blister proximally, and exquisitely tender beyond the visible margin. There is no obvious crepitus. He has palpable but reduced foot pulses bilaterally. His vital signs and laboratory results are on the trolley.

The ED senior is debating between cellulitis and a surgical emergency.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 122/min, blood pressure 96/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 39.1°C
data_table.Examination: Left calf tense and dusky; pain extends beyond visible erythema; one fluid-filled blister; foot pulses palpable; sensation reduced over the calf
data_table.Investigations: CRP 240 mg/L; WCC 18.5 x10^9/L; Hb 124 g/L; sodium 132 mmol/L; creatinine 130 micromol/L; glucose 14.2 mmol/L; LRINEC score 9

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: MRI of the left calf to confirm fascial involvement before any surgical or antibiotic intervention.
options.rationale: Imaging must not delay theatre or antibiotics when clinical and biochemical features are highly suggestive of necrotising infection. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: antibiotic)

options.text: Urgent surgical debridement plus IV piperacillin-tazobactam, clindamycin, and vancomycin.
options.rationale: LRINEC at or above 8 has a high probability of necrotising fasciitis; surgical debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics including clindamycin for toxin suppression is first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: antibiotic)

options.text: Oral flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily plus rest and elevation as outpatient cellulitis treatment.
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics and outpatient management are inadequate for septic shock with calf pain out of proportion. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: antibiotic)

options.text: Compartment pressure measurement to exclude acute compartment syndrome before surgical debridement.
options.rationale: Compartment syndrome is part of the differential but does not delay debridement when necrotising fasciitis is suspected. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: antibiotic)

options.text: Hyperbaric oxygen as the primary therapy without immediate surgical exploration of the limb.
options.rationale: Hyperbaric oxygen is an adjunct; surgical debridement plus IV antibiotics remain the cornerstone of treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency. Clinical features include pain out of proportion to physical findings, tense oedema, dusky discolouration, haemorrhagic bullae, crepitus, anaesthesia of overlying skin, and rapidly progressive systemic toxicity. The LRINEC score (CRP, WCC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, glucose) stratifies risk: at or above 6 is intermediate, at or above 8 is high. Treatment is urgent surgical debridement with IV piperacillin-tazobactam (or meropenem) plus vancomycin (for MRSA) plus clindamycin (for protein synthesis inhibition and toxin suppression). Imaging is supportive but should not delay theatre.
key_points: LRINEC at or above 8 is high probability of necrotising fasciitis.
Treatment: surgical debridement plus piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin plus clindamycin.
Pain out of proportion and anaesthesia of overlying skin are clinical red flags.
explanation.pearls: Clindamycin earns its place in the regimen by suppressing exotoxin production by Streptococcus pyogenes and Staphylococcus aureus, even if MIC favours another agent for bacterial killing.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman who recently arrived from Vietnam attends a refugee health clinic. She has had 3 weeks of dry cough, low-grade fevers in the evenings, drenching night sweats, and 4 kg of unintentional weight loss. Her QuantiFERON-Gold Plus test is positive. The clinic registrar wants to know whether to treat as latent or active tuberculosis. The chest radiograph shows right upper lobe airspace opacity with a small cavity, and three early-morning sputum samples have been sent for acid-fast smear, culture, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR. HIV testing is negative. The first sputum smear is just back as positive for acid-fast bacilli.

She has no other significant medical history and lives in shared accommodation with one other adult.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 37.8°C
data_table.Examination: Thin; right upper zone fine crackles; no clubbing; no peripheral lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: QFT-Plus positive; CXR right upper lobe airspace opacity with cavity; sputum AFB smear positive; HIV negative; LFTs normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start isoniazid 300 mg daily for 9 months as latent tuberculosis treatment with monthly LFT monitoring.
options.rationale: Cavitating CXR and smear-positive sputum indicate active TB, not latent, and require four-drug therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: antibiotic)

options.text: Defer all treatment until liquid culture confirms drug susceptibility before any therapy commences.
options.rationale: Empirical four-drug therapy should start immediately for smear-positive active TB; cultures and susceptibility refine the regimen later. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: antibiotic)

options.text: Isolate, notify the public health unit, and start four-drug therapy with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol.
options.rationale: Active pulmonary TB with smear-positive disease mandates respiratory isolation, public health notification, and the standard RIPE regimen for 2 months induction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: antibiotic)

options.text: Start rifampicin plus isoniazid for 3 months as a short-course latent tuberculosis regimen now.
options.rationale: Rifampicin plus isoniazid for 3 months is a latent TB regimen and is inadequate for confirmed active disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: antibiotic)

options.text: Start moxifloxacin monotherapy 400 mg daily while awaiting susceptibility testing on the sputum specimen.
options.rationale: Fluoroquinolone monotherapy is contraindicated; it risks rapid resistance and is reserved for multidrug-resistant TB regimens under specialist supervision. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Active pulmonary tuberculosis is diagnosed in any patient with consistent symptoms (cough at least 3 weeks, weight loss, night sweats), abnormal chest radiograph (especially upper lobe airspace disease with cavitation), and positive sputum acid-fast smear or culture. A positive QuantiFERON shows TB infection but cannot distinguish latent from active disease; the clinical and radiological picture does that. Standard induction is rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol (RIPE) for 2 months, then rifampicin and isoniazid for a further 4 months, with directly observed therapy ideally and public health notification mandatory.
key_points: Cavitating CXR plus smear-positive sputum equals active TB regardless of QFT.
RIPE for 2 months then RH for 4 months is standard sensitive-strain therapy.
Notify public health and isolate from the moment active TB is suspected.
explanation.pearls: Add pyridoxine 25 mg daily to any isoniazid-containing regimen to prevent peripheral neuropathy, particularly in malnourished, pregnant, or HIV-positive patients.

stem:
A 68-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 28 hours of fever, dry cough, headache, and myalgia. Her temperature peaked at 38.8°C. She has COPD on tiotropium and salbutamol with one hospital admission in the last year for an exacerbation. She has not received the seasonal influenza vaccine this year and there are confirmed influenza A cases in her residential community. The nasal swab influenza A PCR is positive. Her oxygen saturation is 93% on room air and her chest is clear. She has had no recent overseas travel. CXR shows no consolidation.

The ED team is considering antiviral therapy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 93% on room air, temperature 38.4°C
data_table.Examination: Mild respiratory distress; chest scattered wheeze with no crackles; no oral thrush
data_table.Investigations: Influenza A PCR positive; CXR no consolidation; FBC WCC 9.2 x10^9/L; CRP 42 mg/L; creatinine 78 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Withhold oseltamivir because the 48 hour window from symptom onset has now closed for benefit.
options.rationale: The 48 hour rule applies to low-risk healthy outpatients; high-risk patients benefit even when treatment starts later. (Source: CDNA influenza guidelines)

options.text: Start zanamivir inhaled 10 mg twice daily for 5 days as first-line over oseltamivir for this patient.
options.rationale: Inhaled zanamivir is contraindicated in patients with underlying airway disease such as COPD because it can precipitate bronchospasm. (Source: CDNA influenza guidelines)

options.text: Start amantadine 100 mg twice daily for 5 days targeting influenza A neuraminidase replication.
options.rationale: Amantadine is no longer recommended for seasonal influenza because of widespread resistance and a poor side effect profile. (Source: CDNA influenza guidelines)

options.text: Start oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days because she is high risk despite 28 hours of symptoms.
options.rationale: Oseltamivir is recommended for high-risk groups including COPD even when symptoms have lasted beyond 48 hours, because of mortality benefit. (Source: CDNA influenza guidelines)

options.text: Provide supportive care alone with paracetamol and oral fluids until symptoms resolve over coming days.
options.rationale: Supportive care alone misses the morbidity and mortality benefit of antiviral therapy in high-risk patients. (Source: CDNA influenza guidelines)

explanation.summary: Antiviral therapy for laboratory-confirmed influenza is recommended for high-risk patients (chronic lung disease, chronic cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, diabetes, immunocompromise, pregnancy or postpartum, age 65 or above, severe obesity, Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander adults, residents of aged care) and for any patient with severe illness. Oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days is first-line; treatment within 48 hours is most effective but later treatment still reduces complications in high-risk groups. Inhaled zanamivir is contraindicated in chronic airway disease.
key_points: High-risk groups benefit from oseltamivir even after 48 hours.
Oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days is first-line.
Avoid inhaled zanamivir in COPD or asthma due to bronchospasm risk.
explanation.pearls: Reduce oseltamivir to 30 mg twice daily for an eGFR of 30 to 60 mL/min/1.73m2, and to 30 mg daily for an eGFR of 10 to 30 mL/min/1.73m2; standard dosing risks accumulation toxicity in renal impairment.

stem:
A 42-year-old woman with known Addison's disease maintained on hydrocortisone 20 mg morning and 10 mg afternoon, plus fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily, presents to the emergency department with 24 hours of vomiting, abdominal pain, and lethargy. She has been unable to keep her oral hydrocortisone down. She has not taken her stress dose. She is now drowsy. Her bedside glucose is 3.2 mmol/L and a venous blood gas has just returned. The triage nurse has placed two large-bore IV cannulas and bloods are off to the lab.

The ED registrar is preparing the next interventions.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 128/min, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.6°C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable; dry mucous membranes; capillary refill 3 seconds; abdomen soft, mildly tender
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 128 mmol/L; potassium 5.4 mmol/L; glucose 3.2 mmol/L; creatinine 142 micromol/L; VBG pH 7.31, lactate 2.4 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: Hydrocortisone 20 mg AM and 10 mg PM; fludrocortisone 100 micrograms mane

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Double her oral hydrocortisone dose to 40 mg and observe for 4 hours before discharging home with follow-up.
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis requires parenteral therapy because oral absorption is unreliable in vomiting and shock. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: endocrinology)

options.text: Give dexamethasone 4 mg IV stat alone and wait for cortisol level result before any IV fluid therapy.
options.rationale: Dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity and giving steroid alone without fluids fails to treat the hypovolaemia and hyponatraemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: endocrinology)

options.text: Give 3 percent saline 100 mL to correct hyponatraemia before starting any glucocorticoid replacement therapy.
options.rationale: Hyponatraemia in adrenal crisis is corrected by cortisol replacement and 0.9 percent saline; hypertonic saline risks osmotic demyelination. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: endocrinology)

options.text: Commence fludrocortisone 200 micrograms orally now and hold IV steroids pending early morning cortisol.
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone has no role in the acute resuscitation of adrenal crisis; hydrocortisone IV provides both glucocorticoid and partial mineralocorticoid effect. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: endocrinology)

options.text: Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV stat, commence 0.9 percent saline at 1 L over the first hour, and treat hypoglycaemia.
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis is treated with immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg, rapid saline resuscitation, and glucose correction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a medical emergency in any patient with known adrenal insufficiency who is unwell, vomiting, or shocked. Immediate management is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat followed by 50 mg every 6 hours (or a continuous infusion of 200 mg per 24 hours), rapid 0.9% saline resuscitation 1 L over the first hour, glucose correction with 50 mL of 50% dextrose if hypoglycaemic, and treatment of any precipitant such as infection. High-dose hydrocortisone exerts sufficient mineralocorticoid effect that fludrocortisone is not needed during the acute phase. Sick-day rules: double oral hydrocortisone dose for intercurrent illness; switch to IM hydrocortisone for vomiting.
key_points: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV is the first parenteral dose in adrenal crisis.
Use 0.9 percent saline and glucose correction alongside steroid replacement.
Sick day rule: double oral steroid for intercurrent illness; IM hydrocortisone if vomiting.
explanation.pearls: Every Addison's patient should carry an emergency IM hydrocortisone kit (100 mg) and have a documented sick day plan; failure of community administration is a recurrent driver of preventable crisis admissions.

stem:
A 58-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with 18 hours of fever, severe headache, photophobia, and progressive confusion. He has hypertension and a remote left middle cerebral artery stroke with mild residual right-sided weakness. On arrival he opens his eyes to pain, says inappropriate words, and localises to pain (GCS 11). He has neck stiffness, no rash, and a new right-sided gaze preference. His pupils are 3 mm and reactive bilaterally with no papilloedema. Two large-bore IV cannulas are in. Blood cultures, FBC, U+E, coagulation, glucose, and lactate have been drawn.

The ED registrar is debating LP timing, antibiotic timing, and adjuvant steroid timing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 102/min, blood pressure 168/92 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 39.1°C
data_table.Examination: GCS 11 (E2 V3 M5); meningism; new right gaze preference; pupils 3 mm reactive; no papilloedema; no rash
data_table.Investigations: Blood cultures drawn; WCC 18 x10^9/L; CRP 220 mg/L; INR 1.0; glucose 6.4 mmol/L; lactate 2.0 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next sequence of actions?

options.text: Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV, ceftriaxone 2 g IV, and benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV, then arrange urgent CT brain before LP.
options.rationale: Focal neurology, altered consciousness, or seizure mandates CT before LP; dexamethasone and antibiotics must not wait for imaging, with benzylpenicillin added for Listeria cover above age 50. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: antibiotic)

options.text: Perform immediate lumbar puncture, then give dexamethasone and ceftriaxone after the CSF specimen is in hand.
options.rationale: Focal neurological signs and reduced GCS contraindicate immediate LP because of coning risk; CT must precede LP here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: antibiotic)

options.text: Give ceftriaxone 2 g IV and obtain CT brain first; defer dexamethasone until LP confirms bacterial pathogen.
options.rationale: Dexamethasone benefit in pneumococcal meningitis requires administration before or with the first antibiotic, not later. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: antibiotic)

options.text: Give dexamethasone, ceftriaxone, vancomycin, and aciclovir empirically while waiting for CT and LP results.
options.rationale: Vancomycin is added when penicillin-resistant pneumococcus is suspected (overseas travel, prior antibiotics) and aciclovir if encephalitis is the leading diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: antibiotic)

options.text: Mannitol 1 g/kg IV plus intubation to control intracranial pressure before any antibiotic therapy is delivered.
options.rationale: Antibiotic timing drives mortality in meningitis; intracranial pressure management must run alongside, not delay, antimicrobial therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Adult community-acquired bacterial meningitis is a time-critical emergency. Where altered consciousness, focal neurology, seizure, immunocompromise, or papilloedema is present, CT must precede LP to exclude a mass lesion; however, antibiotics and adjunctive dexamethasone must not wait. Adjuvant dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours for 4 days, given before or with the first antibiotic, reduces mortality and neurological sequelae from pneumococcal meningitis. Australian Therapeutic Guidelines empirical therapy is ceftriaxone 2 g IV plus benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV every 4 hours when age above 50 or immunocompromise to cover Listeria, with vancomycin added if resistant pneumococcus is suspected.
key_points: Empirical adults: ceftriaxone 2 g IV; add benzylpenicillin if age above 50 or immunocompromised.
Dexamethasone 10 mg IV must be given before or with the first antibiotic dose.
CT before LP if focal neurology, GCS below 13, seizures, or papilloedema; antibiotics first.
explanation.pearls: Targeted dexamethasone benefit is greatest in pneumococcal meningitis and uncertain in meningococcal disease; once CSF gram stain shows meningococci, dexamethasone can be withdrawn.

stem: A 58-year-old man with no prosthetic valve presents with four weeks of fevers, night sweats, and fatigue. He has a known bicuspid aortic valve. Today his blood pressure is 124/68 mmHg, pulse 104, temperature 38.4°C. New early diastolic murmur is heard at the left sternal edge. He has splinter haemorrhages and a small embolic stroke on MRI. Three sets of blood cultures have been collected over an hour. Transthoracic echo shows a 9 mm mobile vegetation on the aortic valve with mild aortic regurgitation. He has no penicillin allergy. The microbiology service has been informed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 104, BP 124/68 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 97%, temperature 38.4°C
data_table.Examination: Early diastolic murmur LSE, splinter haemorrhages bilaterally, no Roth spots
data_table.Investigations: Three sets of blood cultures collected; TTE: 9 mm vegetation aortic valve with mild AR; MRI brain: small acute embolic infarct

lead_in: Which empirical antimicrobial regimen is most appropriate while cultures are pending?

options.text: Vancomycin 25-30 mg/kg loading IV with gentamicin 1 mg/kg q8h as adjunct
options.rationale: Empirical vancomycin alone (or with gentamicin) is reserved for severe penicillin allergy or MRSA risk; benzylpenicillin plus flucloxacillin plus gentamicin is the AU first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily monotherapy until cultures speciate the organism
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone monotherapy lacks reliable staphylococcal cover; not first-line empirical. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Benzylpenicillin 1.8 g IV q4h plus flucloxacillin 2 g IV q4h plus gentamicin 1 mg/kg q8h
options.rationale: AU empirical regimen for native-valve infective endocarditis without prosthesis and without severe penicillin allergy covers viridans streptococci, staphylococci, and enterococci pending culture data. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Daptomycin 6 mg/kg daily IV with rifampicin 600 mg orally twice daily
options.rationale: Daptomycin plus rifampicin is a salvage regimen for prosthetic valve MRSA endocarditis; not empirical native valve cover. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Wait for blood culture results before commencing any antibiotic therapy
options.rationale: Delaying antimicrobials in confirmed endocarditis with embolic stroke risk is unsafe; empirical therapy begins immediately after cultures are drawn. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Suspected native-valve infective endocarditis without prosthetic material and without severe penicillin allergy is treated empirically in Australia with benzylpenicillin (viridans streptococci, enterococci) plus flucloxacillin (staphylococci) plus low-dose gentamicin (synergy), pending culture. Severe penicillin allergy or MRSA risk substitutes vancomycin for benzylpenicillin and flucloxacillin. Empirical therapy starts immediately after three sets of blood cultures are drawn.
key_points: AU empirical native valve IE: benzylpenicillin + flucloxacillin + gentamicin
MRSA or severe penicillin allergy: vancomycin substitutes
Antibiotics start immediately after three sets of cultures
explanation.pearls: Synergistic low-dose gentamicin is given for the first 2 weeks then reviewed - renal toxicity is the limiting factor.

stem: A 28-year-old man presents with 10 days of fever, sore throat, generalised rash, and tender cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy. He had condomless receptive anal sex with a new partner three weeks ago. He has not taken HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis. His Monospot test is negative. Throat swab is negative for group A streptococcus. Bloods show mild lymphopenia, normal LFTs, and CRP 38 mg/L. He is asking specifically about HIV testing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99%, temperature 38.4°C
data_table.Examination: Diffuse maculopapular rash on trunk and proximal limbs, tender cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy, pharyngeal injection
data_table.Investigations: WCC 4.2 x10^9/L (lymphocytes 0.9), CRP 38 mg/L, Monospot negative, throat swab GAS negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Defer testing for 6 weeks given symptoms and repeat fourth-generation assay then
options.rationale: Deferring testing during a clinically suggestive seroconversion illness misses the opportunity for early diagnosis and rapid ART initiation. (Source: ASHM HIV testing policy 2023)

options.text: Third-generation HIV antibody assay alone with repeat at 12 weeks if negative
options.rationale: Third-generation antibody assays have a longer window period; fourth-generation combination plus RNA gives best detection during seroconversion. (Source: ASHM HIV testing policy 2023)

options.text: Western blot confirmation as the initial diagnostic test for clarity of result
options.rationale: Western blot is a confirmatory not a screening test; current AU laboratories use immunoblot or HIV-1/2 differentiation assay as confirmation after reactive screen. (Source: ASHM HIV testing policy 2023)

options.text: Fourth-generation HIV antigen/antibody combination assay plus HIV RNA viral load
options.rationale: Acute seroconversion within 2-4 weeks of exposure is best detected by combined fourth-generation antigen/antibody screen plus HIV RNA PCR; either alone may miss the window. ASHM and CDNA recommend the combination during the window period. (Source: ASHM HIV testing policy 2023)

options.text: CD4 count and lymphocyte subset analysis before any other test is requested
options.rationale: CD4 counts are used after diagnosis for staging; they are not a diagnostic test for acute infection. (Source: ASHM HIV testing policy 2023)

explanation.summary: Acute HIV seroconversion presents as a glandular-fever-like illness with rash and pharyngitis 2-4 weeks after exposure. The diagnostic strategy during the window period combines a fourth-generation antigen/antibody assay (detects p24 antigen at about 15 days post-exposure) with HIV RNA PCR (detects RNA from about 10 days). A reactive screen is confirmed with immunoblot or HIV-1/2 differentiation. Early diagnosis allows immediate ART, partner notification, and PrEP counselling for contacts.
key_points: Window period detection: fourth-generation Ag/Ab combination plus HIV RNA PCR
Acute seroconversion: rash plus pharyngitis plus generalised lymphadenopathy
Confirmatory test is immunoblot or HIV-1/2 differentiation assay
explanation.pearls: Immediate ART initiation in acute seroconversion reduces viral reservoir size and transmissibility - same-day start where possible.

sources.label: Australian Commentary on US DHHS HIV

stem: A 32-year-old healthcare worker has migrated to Australia from a high-TB-incidence country two years ago. Pre-employment screening QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus is positive (TB1 1.5 IU/mL, TB2 1.8 IU/mL, nil 0.1 IU/mL). She has no fever, weight loss, night sweats, or cough. Chest X-ray is normal. She has not had a previous TB diagnosis, is not pregnant, is on no immunosuppression, and her LFTs are normal. She is asking what treatment she needs and why.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 118/74 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: No lymphadenopathy, no cough, clear chest, no hepatomegaly
data_table.Investigations: QFT-Plus positive (TB1 1.5, TB2 1.8, nil 0.1 IU/mL); chest X-ray clear; LFTs normal; HIV negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Annual chest X-ray surveillance without antimicrobial therapy
options.rationale: Surveillance does not prevent the 5-10% lifetime reactivation risk; preventive treatment does. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee 2023)

options.text: No treatment is needed because the chest X-ray excludes active disease
options.rationale: A normal chest X-ray excludes active disease but does not negate the latent TB diagnosis or the lifetime reactivation risk of 5-10%. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee 2023)

options.text: Four drug intensive therapy RIPE for two months followed by RH for four
options.rationale: RIPE is the regimen for active TB, not latent infection. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee 2023)

options.text: BCG vaccination repeat dose to prevent reactivation in adulthood
options.rationale: BCG does not prevent reactivation of established latent TB; treatment is the answer. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee 2023)

options.text: Isoniazid 300 mg daily plus pyridoxine 25 mg daily for 6-9 months total
options.rationale: Isoniazid plus pyridoxine for 6-9 months is the established Australian first-line latent TB regimen with the most extensive safety data. Three months of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid (3HP) is an accepted alternative when supervised therapy is available. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee 2023)

explanation.summary: Latent TB infection in an Australian healthcare worker from a high-incidence country with positive QFT-Plus and a clear chest X-ray warrants preventive treatment. Isoniazid 300 mg daily plus pyridoxine 25 mg daily for 6-9 months is the established first-line regimen; three months of weekly rifapentine plus isoniazid (3HP) is an accepted alternative with shorter duration. Baseline LFTs and monitoring are required. RIPE is reserved for active disease.
key_points: Latent TB treatment: isoniazid plus pyridoxine 6-9 months
3HP (rifapentine plus isoniazid weekly for 3 months) is alternative
Lifetime reactivation risk of latent TB is 5-10%
explanation.pearls: Pyridoxine is added with isoniazid to prevent peripheral neuropathy, particularly in those with diabetes, alcohol use, malnutrition, or pregnancy.

stem: A 64-year-old man presents with rigors, confusion, and one day of dysuria. Pulse rate 124, blood pressure 84/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 26, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 39.4°C. Mean arterial pressure is 63 mmHg. Lactate is 4.8 mmol/L. He has received 30 mL/kg of balanced crystalloid over 60 minutes. He has had blood cultures, urine cultures, and piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV within the hour. After fluid resuscitation his blood pressure is 92/56 mmHg (MAP 68 mmHg) and his repeat lactate is 4.2 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 116, BP 92/56 mmHg (MAP 68 mmHg) post-fluids, RR 24, SpO2 96% on 4 L NP, temperature 38.6°C
data_table.Examination: Mottled lower limbs, capillary refill 4 seconds, GCS 14
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.2 mmol/L (down from 4.8), creatinine 168 micromol/L, WCC 18 x10^9/L, urine culture pending
data_table.Medications: 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid given; piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV given

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Commence IV noradrenaline infusion via central venous access to target MAP at least 65 mmHg
options.rationale: Persistent hypoperfusion (MAP under 65 mmHg or persistently elevated lactate above 4 mmol/L) after 30 mL/kg crystalloid is the trigger for vasopressors. Noradrenaline is first-line. Surviving Sepsis 2021 supports this within the first hour. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Administer further 30 mL/kg crystalloid before considering any vasopressor
options.rationale: Beyond 30 mL/kg, further fluid is guided by dynamic assessment; ongoing hypoperfusion needs noradrenaline, not more fluid by default. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Add vancomycin 25 mg/kg IV empirically without an MRSA risk assessment
options.rationale: Vancomycin is added when MRSA risk is present (recent hospitalisation, prior MRSA, healthcare exposure); not all septic shock patients need it. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Give IV hydrocortisone 50 mg six hourly before any vasopressor is started
options.rationale: Hydrocortisone is added when vasopressor requirement persists (often greater than 0.25 mcg/kg/min noradrenaline); not before vasopressors. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

options.text: Transfuse one unit of packed red blood cells targeting haemoglobin at 100 g/L
options.rationale: Transfusion threshold in septic shock is haemoglobin under 70 g/L in most patients; not 100 g/L. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

explanation.summary: Surviving Sepsis 2021 defines hour-1 bundle elements as measuring lactate, taking blood cultures, giving broad-spectrum antibiotics, starting 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate above 4 mmol/L, and starting vasopressors if MAP remains under 65 mmHg or lactate stays elevated after initial fluid. Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor. Hydrocortisone is added when vasopressor requirement persists beyond modest doses. Transfusion targets a haemoglobin of about 70 g/L unless ischaemia is present.
key_points: Vasopressor trigger: MAP under 65 mmHg or lactate above 4 mmol/L after 30 mL/kg crystalloid
Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor
Hydrocortisone added for ongoing high vasopressor requirement
explanation.pearls: Start vasopressors via peripheral large-bore access if a central line is delayed - do not wait for central access while the patient remains hypoperfused.

subtopic_detail: Necrotising soft tissue infection LRINEC intermediate
stem: A 46-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents with 24 hours of left thigh pain disproportionate to a small abrasion sustained gardening. The thigh is tense, dusky, and exquisitely tender beyond the visible erythema, with sensory loss over a 6 cm area and crepitus on palpation. Pulse rate 122, blood pressure 102/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 38.6°C. Bloods: WCC 16 x10^9/L, CRP 180 mg/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, creatinine 154 micromol/L, glucose 16 mmol/L, haemoglobin 132 g/L. LRINEC score totals 6.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 24, SpO2 97%, temperature 38.6°C
data_table.Examination: Left thigh tense dusky tender beyond visible erythema, 6 cm area of sensory loss, crepitus palpable
data_table.Investigations: WCC 16, CRP 180 mg/L, Na 132, creatinine 154 micromol/L, glucose 16 mmol/L, Hb 132 g/L; LRINEC 6 (intermediate)
data_table.Medications: Nil regular; IV access x2 with 500 mL Hartmann's running

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: CT thigh with contrast and admit for observation if no fascial gas is seen
options.rationale: Imaging may help selected stable cases but should NOT delay theatre when bedside hard signs are present; surgical exploration is the gold standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Urgent surgical exploration and debridement plus IV meropenem and clindamycin
options.rationale: Pain disproportionate to examination, sensory loss, crepitus, and rapid progression are clinical hard markers of necrotising soft tissue infection that override an intermediate LRINEC score. Theatre exploration is the diagnosis and treatment combined; empirical IV broad-spectrum cover plus clindamycin (toxin suppression) precedes culture data. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Observe for 6 hours with serial LRINEC scoring before deciding on surgery
options.rationale: Delay of even hours significantly increases mortality; bedside hard signs alone justify theatre. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Treat as severe cellulitis with IV flucloxacillin and elevate the limb only
options.rationale: Cellulitis does not produce crepitus, sensory loss, or pain disproportionate; treating as cellulitis misses NF. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Commence hyperbaric oxygen therapy at the regional centre prior to debridement
options.rationale: Hyperbaric oxygen is adjunctive after surgical source control, never a substitute. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection presents with pain disproportionate to examination, sensory loss, crepitus, dusky skin, and rapid systemic deterioration. The LRINEC score (>=6 intermediate, >=8 high) is supportive but should not be used to rule out NF in the presence of clinical hard signs. Urgent surgical exploration and debridement is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Empirical antibiotics are broad-spectrum (meropenem or piperacillin-tazobactam) plus clindamycin for exotoxin suppression. Hyperbaric oxygen is adjunctive after source control.
key_points: Hard clinical signs override an intermediate LRINEC
Theatre is diagnosis plus treatment in NF
Empirical cover: broad-spectrum beta-lactam plus clindamycin
explanation.pearls: Pain out of proportion plus crepitus plus mottled skin = call theatre before completing imaging; you can debride a clean thigh and apologise, but cannot un-die the patient.

stem: A 31-year-old woman at 28 weeks gestation presents with 36 hours of fever, myalgia, headache, and dry cough during a confirmed influenza A community outbreak. She has not received the seasonal influenza vaccination this year. Pulse rate 102, blood pressure 116/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 38.6°C. She has clear breath sounds and a normal fetal heart rate. Rapid antigen test for influenza A is positive. She has no significant comorbidities.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 102, BP 116/74 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 96%, temperature 38.6°C, FHR 140
data_table.Examination: Clear breath sounds bilaterally, no chest pain, uterus appropriate for dates
data_table.Investigations: Influenza A RAT positive; chest X-ray not yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Zanamivir inhaled twice daily preferred over oseltamivir in pregnancy
options.rationale: Oseltamivir is preferred in pregnancy because of systemic absorption needed for severe disease; zanamivir is reserved for resistance. (Source: ATAGI/CDNA influenza in pregnancy 2023)

options.text: Symptomatic management with paracetamol and review in 48 hours
options.rationale: Pregnant women with influenza are at high risk of severe disease and need antiviral therapy promptly. (Source: ATAGI/CDNA influenza in pregnancy 2023)

options.text: Oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days commenced today
options.rationale: Pregnancy is an independent risk factor for severe influenza. Oseltamivir is recommended at any gestation as soon as influenza is suspected or confirmed, ideally within 48 hours of symptom onset, but late presentations also benefit. (Source: ATAGI/CDNA influenza in pregnancy 2023)

options.text: IV peramivir as the standard parenteral option for outpatient pregnancy
options.rationale: Peramivir is reserved for inpatients unable to tolerate oral therapy; oseltamivir is first-line outpatient. (Source: ATAGI/CDNA influenza in pregnancy 2023)

options.text: Empirical amoxicillin-clavulanate added to cover bacterial co-infection
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics are not indicated without evidence of bacterial co-infection (e.g. pneumonia on imaging, raised inflammatory markers, second deterioration). (Source: ATAGI/CDNA influenza in pregnancy 2023)

explanation.summary: Pregnancy is a Category C risk factor for severe influenza and complications. Oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days should be started as soon as influenza is suspected or confirmed, with no gestational restriction. Treatment within 48 hours of symptom onset gives the greatest benefit, but late initiation still reduces complications. Influenza vaccine is also recommended at any gestation. Bacterial co-infection is treated only when clinical or imaging evidence supports it.
key_points: Oseltamivir is preferred antiviral in pregnancy at any gestation
Start as soon as influenza suspected, ideally within 48 hours
Influenza vaccine offered at any stage of pregnancy
explanation.pearls: Don't withhold oseltamivir past 48 hours - moderate-to-severe disease in pregnancy still benefits from later start.

stem: A 49-year-old man is referred with a 4.5 cm right adrenal mass detected incidentally on CT for renal colic. He gives a history of episodic palpitations, sweating, and headaches over the last 18 months. His 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines are: normetanephrine 8x upper limit of normal, metanephrine 5x upper limit of normal. Plasma metanephrines confirmed elevated. Endocrine surgery has been consulted for laparoscopic adrenalectomy. Current pulse 86 (peaks at 134 during episodes), blood pressure 158/96 mmHg (peaks 220/120).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 86 baseline (peaks 134), BP 158/96 baseline (peaks 220/120), RR 16, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 26, no orthostatic measurement yet, no other abnormality
data_table.Investigations: 24-hour urinary normetanephrine 8x ULN, metanephrine 5x ULN; plasma metanephrines confirmed elevated; CT abdomen right adrenal mass 4.5 cm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate preoperative pharmacological preparation?

options.text: Start oral amlodipine 5 mg daily as the sole agent prior to surgery
options.rationale: Calcium channel blockers are second-line or adjunctive; alpha blockade is the first step. (Source: Endocrine Society phaeochromocytoma 2014)

options.text: Start oral metoprolol 50 mg twice daily and titrate to heart rate under 90
options.rationale: Beta blockade without prior alpha blockade can precipitate unopposed alpha-mediated hypertensive crisis and is contraindicated. (Source: Endocrine Society phaeochromocytoma 2014)

options.text: Proceed directly to laparoscopic adrenalectomy without any pretreatment
options.rationale: Operating without preoperative blockade carries significant haemodynamic instability and mortality risk. (Source: Endocrine Society phaeochromocytoma 2014)

options.text: Start oral phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily and titrate up over 1-2 weeks
options.rationale: Alpha blockade is started first (10-14 days preoperatively) to prevent intraoperative hypertensive crisis. Phenoxybenzamine is the traditional choice. A beta-blocker is added only after alpha blockade is established. Liberal salt and fluid intake support volume expansion. (Source: Endocrine Society phaeochromocytoma 2014)

options.text: Start IV labetalol infusion for combined alpha and beta blockade
options.rationale: Labetalol has a beta:alpha ratio of about 7:1 oral and 3:1 IV, providing inadequate alpha cover for preoperative phaeochromocytoma preparation. (Source: Endocrine Society phaeochromocytoma 2014)

explanation.summary: Preoperative blockade for phaeochromocytoma starts with alpha antagonism (phenoxybenzamine 10 mg BD escalated, or doxazosin 2-4 mg BD as alternative) for 10-14 days before surgery. Beta blockade is added only after alpha blockade for tachycardia or arrhythmia, never before. Liberal salt and fluid intake corrects volume contraction. Operating without this preparation produces severe intraoperative hypertensive crisis and postoperative hypotension. Calcium channel blockers are adjuncts.
key_points: Alpha blockade always before beta blockade in phaeochromocytoma
Phenoxybenzamine 10-14 days preoperative is traditional first-line
Salt loading and fluid expansion mitigate postoperative hypotension
explanation.pearls: If catecholamine surge is severe perioperatively, IV phentolamine (alpha) and magnesium sulfate are the rescue agents - never beta-block first.

stem: A 44-year-old woman has resistant hypertension on three agents (perindopril 10 mg, amlodipine 10 mg, indapamide 2.5 mg). Her blood pressure today is 162/98 mmHg. She has a serum potassium of 3.1 mmol/L without diuretic-induced losses. She is asymptomatic. She is not pregnant. She has no family history of endocrine disease. She has been off spironolactone, beta-blocker, and direct renin inhibitor for at least four weeks. Her morning aldosterone-renin ratio (ARR) on indapamide is markedly elevated at 65 (cut-off 30 for screen positive).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 162/98 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7°C
data_table.Examination: BMI 26, no proximal weakness, no bruit, no abdominal mass
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.1 mmol/L, sodium 142 mmol/L, creatinine 76 micromol/L, ARR 65 (cut-off 30 positive); free metanephrines pending
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 10 mg, amlodipine 10 mg, indapamide 2.5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat ARR after 6 weeks off all antihypertensives including amlodipine
options.rationale: ARR has been performed correctly off interfering agents (excluding indapamide is impractical when BP is uncontrolled); confirmation should now proceed. (Source: Endocrine Society primary aldosteronism 2016)

options.text: Proceed directly to CT adrenal protocol without confirmatory suppression test
options.rationale: CT before confirmation risks chasing an incidentaloma in a patient who has essential hypertension and a false-positive ARR. (Source: Endocrine Society primary aldosteronism 2016)

options.text: Adrenal vein sampling now for lateralisation before any other confirmation
options.rationale: AVS is reserved for confirmed primary aldosteronism in surgical candidates after CT; not the next step. (Source: Endocrine Society primary aldosteronism 2016)

options.text: Empirical spironolactone 25 mg daily with no further investigation
options.rationale: Empirical mineralocorticoid antagonism misses surgically curable adenomas in confirmed primary aldosteronism. (Source: Endocrine Society primary aldosteronism 2016)

options.text: Saline infusion suppression test or oral salt loading with 24-hour urinary aldosterone
options.rationale: A positive ARR is a screening test only; confirmation of primary aldosteronism requires a suppression test (saline infusion, fludrocortisone suppression, or oral sodium loading). Confirmation precedes subtype imaging and adrenal vein sampling. (Source: Endocrine Society primary aldosteronism 2016)

explanation.summary: A markedly elevated aldosterone-renin ratio is a screening result, not a diagnosis. Confirmation of primary aldosteronism requires non-suppression of aldosterone after a salt load (intravenous saline 2 L over 4 hours, fludrocortisone suppression, or oral sodium loading with 24-hour urinary aldosterone). Once confirmed, CT adrenal looks for adenoma versus hyperplasia, and adrenal vein sampling lateralises in surgical candidates. Empirical mineralocorticoid antagonism is reserved for non-surgical candidates.
key_points: ARR is screen only; suppression test confirms primary aldosteronism
CT and AVS follow confirmation
Beta-blockers and MRAs interfere with ARR; ACEi and CCB are acceptable
explanation.pearls: Hypokalaemia is present in only about a third of primary aldosteronism cases - normokalaemia does not exclude it.

stem:
A 64-year-old man presents with sudden tearing interscapular pain radiating to the chest 45 minutes ago. He has uncontrolled hypertension. Examination shows a blood pressure difference of 28 mmHg between arms. There is a faint early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. He has a strong pulse in both groins. Chest X-ray shows a widened mediastinum. ECG shows sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy.

He is haemodynamically stable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 178/108 mmHg right arm, 150/96 mmHg left arm, RR 22, SpO2 96%, temperature 36.8°C
data_table.Examination: Faint early diastolic murmur left sternal edge, equal groin pulses
data_table.Investigations: CXR widened mediastinum; ECG sinus rhythm LVH; troponin pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first investigation?

options.text: Contrast-enhanced CT angiogram chest, abdomen, and pelvis
options.rationale: CT angiography is first-line in stable patients with suspected aortic dissection; it confirms diagnosis, identifies type, and maps branch involvement. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases 2024)

options.text: Transthoracic echocardiogram at the bedside immediately
options.rationale: TTE has limited sensitivity for type B dissection and does not map branch involvement; it is adjunctive. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases 2024)

options.text: Transoesophageal echocardiogram in the emergency department
options.rationale: TOE is reserved for haemodynamically unstable patients who cannot be transported for CT; CT is preferred when stable. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases 2024)

options.text: MR angiogram aorta with non-contrast diffusion sequences
options.rationale: MRA is excellent but slower and less available; CT is first-line in the acute setting. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases 2024)

options.text: D-dimer for risk stratification before any imaging
options.rationale: D-dimer has high sensitivity but is not used to rule out dissection in high pre-test probability; proceed directly to CT. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases 2024)

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection should be suspected with tearing chest or back pain, hypertension, pulse or BP differential between limbs, or a new aortic regurgitation murmur. CT angiography is first-line in stable patients because it confirms diagnosis, classifies type (Stanford A involves ascending; type B does not), and maps branch vessel involvement for surgical or endovascular planning. TOE is the alternative in unstable patients. Immediate management is heart rate control (IV esmolol or labetalol) targeting HR <60 then SBP <120 mmHg.
key_points: Stable patients: CT angiogram first
Unstable: bedside TOE alternative
Heart rate control before blood pressure
explanation.pearls: Stanford type A involves the ascending aorta and is a surgical emergency; type B is initially medically managed unless complicated by ischaemia, rupture, or refractory pain.

stem:
A 42-year-old presents to ED with 12 hours of fever, severe headache, photophobia, and neck stiffness. She is drowsy (GCS 13). There are no focal neurological signs. She has no rash. She has no immunocompromise. CT brain prior to lumbar puncture is normal. Lumbar puncture shows turbid CSF with neutrophil predominance (WCC 2200 x10^6/L, 95% neutrophils), protein 2.4 g/L (0.15-0.40), glucose 1.4 mmol/L with simultaneous serum glucose 6.0 mmol/L.

The ED registrar has IV access established.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 110/70 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 97%, temperature 39.4°C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, GCS 13, neck stiffness, no rash, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: CSF turbid, WCC 2200 x10^6/L 95% neutrophils, protein 2.4 g/L, glucose 1.4 mmol/L (serum 6.0); CT brain normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment now?

options.text: IV dexamethasone with first dose of ceftriaxone 2 g and benzylpenicillin 2.4 g
options.rationale: AU eTG specifies empiric ceftriaxone plus benzylpenicillin (for Listeria cover in age >50, immunocompromised, or pregnant) with dexamethasone given before or with first antibiotic dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Meningitis)

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 2 g alone without any corticosteroid adjunct
options.rationale: Dexamethasone given before or with first antibiotic dose reduces neurological sequelae in S. pneumoniae meningitis; omission is non-standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Meningitis)

options.text: IV vancomycin monotherapy while awaiting susceptibility result
options.rationale: Vancomycin monotherapy does not cover Gram-negative or Listeria; ceftriaxone is the empiric backbone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Meningitis)

options.text: IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg without any antibacterial cover concurrently
options.rationale: CSF neutrophil-predominant with low glucose indicates bacterial meningitis; acyclovir is added if HSV encephalitis suspected, not as monotherapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Meningitis)

options.text: Delay all antibiotics until CSF Gram stain result is available
options.rationale: Empiric antibiotics must be given within 30 minutes of suspicion in bacterial meningitis; Gram stain delay risks death. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Meningitis)

explanation.summary: Suspected bacterial meningitis requires empiric IV antibiotics within 30 minutes. Australian eTG empiric therapy is ceftriaxone 2 g IV plus benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV if age >50, pregnant, or immunocompromised (Listeria cover). Dexamethasone 10 mg IV is given with or before the first antibiotic dose; it reduces neurological sequelae in pneumococcal meningitis. CT brain is required before lumbar puncture only in patients with focal neurology, seizure, immunocompromise, GCS <12, or papilloedema; LP should not delay antibiotics.
key_points: Empiric ceftriaxone +/- benzylpenicillin within 30 minutes
Dexamethasone with or before first antibiotic dose
Listeria cover in age >50, pregnant, immunocompromised
explanation.pearls: Notify public health within 24 hours of suspected meningococcal disease and offer ciprofloxacin 500 mg single dose to close household contacts within the previous 7 days.

stem:
A 32-year-old presents with one episode of haematemesis 12 hours ago after binge drinking and forceful vomiting. He has had no further bleeding. He has no melaena. He has no comorbidities and takes no regular medications. Bloods: haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-180), urea 5.4 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), creatinine 76 micromol/L (60-110), INR 1.0 (0.9-1.2). Examination is unremarkable. His Glasgow-Blatchford score is 0.

He wishes to go home.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 124/76 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.6°C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft, no tenderness, no signs of chronic liver disease, no melaena on PR
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 148 g/L, urea 5.4 mmol/L, creatinine 76 micromol/L, INR 1.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disposition?

options.text: Discharge home with safety netting plus outpatient gastroscopy
options.rationale: Glasgow-Blatchford score of 0 identifies a very low risk group safely managed as outpatient; AU and BSG guidelines support discharge with outpatient endoscopy. (Source: BSG Upper GI Bleeding 2022)

options.text: Admit and perform urgent inpatient gastroscopy within 4 hours
options.rationale: Urgent gastroscopy is for haemodynamic instability or ongoing bleeding; this patient is stable with GBS 0. (Source: BSG Upper GI Bleeding 2022)

options.text: Admit overnight for observation with serial haemoglobin checks
options.rationale: GBS 0 has very low risk of rebleeding; routine admission is not required. (Source: BSG Upper GI Bleeding 2022)

options.text: Start IV pantoprazole 80 mg bolus then infusion 8 mg/hour as inpatient
options.rationale: IV PPI infusion is for confirmed high-risk ulcer post-endoscopy; not indicated empirically in low-risk GBS 0. (Source: BSG Upper GI Bleeding 2022)

options.text: Transfuse 1 unit packed red cells empirically before discharge
options.rationale: Haemoglobin is normal and there is no active bleeding; transfusion has no indication. (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management)

explanation.summary: The Glasgow-Blatchford score uses urea, haemoglobin, blood pressure, pulse, and clinical features to risk-stratify upper GI bleeds. A score of 0 corresponds to a less than 1% rebleeding risk and these patients can be safely discharged with outpatient endoscopy. Higher scores warrant admission and earlier endoscopy. Mallory-Weiss tear is a typical low-risk diagnosis. PPI infusion is reserved for high-risk ulcers identified at endoscopy.
key_points: GBS 0: outpatient gastroscopy is safe
Higher GBS: admit for inpatient endoscopy
IV PPI infusion after endoscopy, not empirically
explanation.pearls: A urea-to-creatinine ratio above 100 (using urea mmol/L and creatinine micromol/L) suggests an upper rather than lower source of GI bleeding due to absorption of digested blood.

stem:
A 38-year-old woman presents with one week of fatigue, bruising, and intermittent confusion. She has no recent infection. Bloods: haemoglobin 78 g/L (115-165), platelets 18 x10^9/L (150-400), reticulocytes 6.2% (0.5-2.5), LDH 1820 U/L (140-280), unconjugated bilirubin 42 micromol/L (3-21), creatinine 138 micromol/L (45-90). Coombs test negative. Blood film shows 8 schistocytes per high power field. ADAMTS13 activity is sent. INR is 1.0.

The haematology team has been called urgently.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 102, BP 128/78 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 99%, temperature 37.4°C
data_table.Examination: Pallor, petechiae, intermittent confusion, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 78 g/L, platelets 18 x10^9/L, retics 6.2%, LDH 1820 U/L, bilirubin 42 micromol/L (unconjugated), creatinine 138 micromol/L; Coombs negative; film 8 schistocytes/hpf; INR 1.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Plasma exchange and pulse methylprednisolone, awaiting ADAMTS13 result
options.rationale: TTP is a haematological emergency with high untreated mortality; plasma exchange must be started on clinical grounds (microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, neurology) before ADAMTS13. (Source: HSANZ TTP Position Statement)

options.text: Platelet transfusion to platelets >100 x10^9/L before any other intervention
options.rationale: Platelet transfusion is contraindicated in TTP unless life-threatening bleeding; it may worsen thrombosis. (Source: HSANZ TTP Position Statement)

options.text: Cyclophosphamide induction prior to any plasma exchange therapy
options.rationale: Cyclophosphamide is not part of TTP induction; the AU pathway is plasma exchange + steroid +/- rituximab/caplacizumab. (Source: HSANZ TTP Position Statement)

options.text: Eculizumab as first-line for presumed atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome
options.rationale: Eculizumab is for atypical HUS not TTP; relatively low creatinine and severe neurology with PLASMIC favours TTP. (Source: HSANZ TTP Position Statement)

options.text: Observation pending ADAMTS13 result before further therapy
options.rationale: ADAMTS13 results take days; waiting risks death. Clinical PLASMIC score guides immediate exchange. (Source: HSANZ TTP Position Statement)

explanation.summary: TTP is a thrombotic microangiopathy driven by ADAMTS13 deficiency causing microvascular platelet thrombi, leading to microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, neurological signs, renal impairment, and fever. The PLASMIC score (platelet count, haemolysis markers, malignancy absence, transplant absence, MCV, INR, creatinine) identifies high-risk cases. Treatment is plasma exchange (PEX) with corticosteroid started before ADAMTS13 confirmation; caplacizumab and rituximab are AU-funded adjuncts. Platelet transfusion is contraindicated unless life-threatening bleeding.
key_points: Clinical diagnosis triggers PEX before ADAMTS13
Platelet transfusion contraindicated in TTP
Adjuncts: caplacizumab, rituximab
explanation.pearls: PLASMIC score 6-7 has a positive predictive value >90% for ADAMTS13 <10%; this threshold supports immediate plasma exchange while awaiting confirmatory testing.

stem:
A 48-year-old man with known Addison disease has had gastroenteritis for two days. He vomited his morning hydrocortisone. He now presents drowsy with abdominal pain. Bloods: sodium 124 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.7 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), glucose 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-7.8), urea 12.4 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), creatinine 142 micromol/L (60-110). He has hyperpigmentation. He is on usual maintenance hydrocortisone 20-10-10 mg daily and fludrocortisone 100 mcg.

IV access has been obtained.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124, BP 86/52 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 98%, temperature 37.0°C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, dry mucous membranes, hyperpigmented buccal mucosa
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 124, potassium 5.7, glucose 3.1, urea 12.4, creatinine 142
data_table.Medications: Hydrocortisone 20-10-10 mg daily, fludrocortisone 100 mcg (missed today)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg and 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L over 30 min
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis is treated with IV hydrocortisone 100 mg plus isotonic crystalloid resuscitation; fludrocortisone is not needed acutely as hydrocortisone provides mineralocorticoid activity at stress dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: IV dexamethasone 8 mg only with maintenance crystalloid fluid
options.rationale: Dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity and is reserved for diagnostic settings where Synacthen testing is planned; hydrocortisone is preferred in crisis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Restart oral hydrocortisone 30 mg and observe in ED short stay
options.rationale: Oral therapy is contraindicated in vomiting and shock; parenteral is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: IV insulin and dextrose infusion to correct hyperkalaemia first
options.rationale: Hyperkalaemia in adrenal crisis corrects with cortisol replacement and fluid; insulin-dextrose risks hypoglycaemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Hypertonic 3% sodium chloride 100 mL over 30 minutes for hyponatraemia
options.rationale: Hyponatraemia in adrenal crisis is corrected by hydrocortisone plus isotonic fluid; hypertonic saline risks osmotic demyelination given chronic hyponatraemia of unknown duration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis presents with hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, and altered mental state. Triggers include intercurrent illness, vomiting of replacement therapy, and surgery. IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus followed by 200 mg/24 hours is the AU standard, with isotonic crystalloid for hypotension. At hydrocortisone doses >=40 mg/day, no separate fludrocortisone is needed. Underlying trigger (gastroenteritis here) must be treated. Patient education and sick-day rules with parenteral hydrocortisone kit at home prevent recurrence.
key_points: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV + 0.9% NaCl is the AU regimen
No fludrocortisone needed at stress doses
Treat trigger and educate sick-day rules
explanation.pearls: Patients with Addison should carry a Medic-Alert bracelet and a parenteral hydrocortisone 100 mg IM kit; instruct partners and family to administer in vomiting or unconsciousness.

stem:
A 58-year-old man presents with three weeks of haemoptysis, fatigue, sinusitis, and progressive dyspnoea. Creatinine has risen from 78 to 312 micromol/L (60-110) over two weeks. Urinalysis shows 3+ blood and 2+ protein with red cell casts. Chest CT shows bilateral nodular and cavitating lesions. PR3-ANCA is strongly positive at 142 U/mL (normal less than 5). MPO-ANCA is negative. He has no fever, no recent infection, no haemodynamic instability, and no overt pulmonary haemorrhage. Renal biopsy shows pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis.

He has consented to immunosuppression.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 138/86 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 95%, temperature 37.0°C
data_table.Examination: Saddle nose deformity, sinus tenderness, bibasal crackles
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 312 micromol/L (rose from 78), urinalysis 3+ blood 2+ protein red cell casts, PR3-ANCA 142 U/mL, MPO-ANCA negative, CT bilateral nodular cavitating lesions, renal biopsy pauci-immune crescentic GN

lead_in: What is the most appropriate induction regimen?

options.text: IV methylprednisolone pulse for 3 days then rituximab weekly induction
options.rationale: ANCA-associated vasculitis with severe organ-threatening disease is induced with rituximab or cyclophosphamide plus high-dose steroids; rituximab is preferred in PR3-ANCA and avoids cyclophosphamide gonadotoxicity. (Source: KDIGO ANCA Vasculitis 2024)

options.text: Methotrexate 25 mg weekly with prednisolone 30 mg daily induction
options.rationale: Methotrexate is reserved for non-organ-threatening disease; severe renal involvement requires rituximab or cyclophosphamide. (Source: KDIGO ANCA Vasculitis 2024)

options.text: Plasma exchange alone without any concurrent immunosuppression
options.rationale: Plasma exchange is adjunctive in pulmonary haemorrhage or dialysis-dependent renal involvement; monotherapy does not address autoantibody production. (Source: KDIGO ANCA Vasculitis 2024)

options.text: Mycophenolate mofetil 1 g twice daily as monotherapy induction
options.rationale: MMF can be used for milder disease or maintenance; severe organ-threatening disease requires rituximab or cyclophosphamide induction. (Source: KDIGO ANCA Vasculitis 2024)

options.text: Hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily with prednisolone 60 mg daily
options.rationale: Hydroxychloroquine has no role in ANCA-associated vasculitis induction; it is used in lupus. (Source: KDIGO ANCA Vasculitis 2024)

explanation.summary: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) commonly presents with upper airway, lower airway, and renal disease; PR3-ANCA is the typical serology. Severe organ-threatening disease is induced with rituximab or cyclophosphamide plus pulse and oral corticosteroids. Rituximab is preferred for PR3-ANCA, women of childbearing age, and to avoid cyclophosphamide toxicity. Plasma exchange is adjunctive in alveolar haemorrhage or severe AKI requiring dialysis. Maintenance is rituximab or azathioprine with low-dose steroid.
key_points: Severe AAV: rituximab or cyclophosphamide + steroid
Rituximab preferred for PR3-ANCA
Plasma exchange adjunctive in haemorrhage or dialysis
explanation.pearls: PEXIVAS trial showed plasma exchange did not improve death or ESRD outcomes overall but a 2024 KDIGO update retains it as an option for diffuse alveolar haemorrhage with hypoxia.

stem:
A 68-year-old presents with two weeks of bone pain, fatigue, and progressive confusion. Bloods: haemoglobin 84 g/L (130-180), creatinine 384 micromol/L (60-110), calcium 3.4 mmol/L corrected (2.10-2.55), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), total protein 96 g/L (60-80). Serum protein electrophoresis shows an IgG kappa M-band of 42 g/L. Serum free light chain ratio kappa/lambda 220 (normal 0.26-1.65). Skeletal survey shows lytic lesions in the skull and pelvis. He is hypovolaemic with mild AKI on dipstick proteinuria 2+.

Haematology and renal teams have been consulted.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 96/62 mmHg, RR 20, SpO2 97%, temperature 36.8°C
data_table.Examination: Pallor, dry mucous membranes, confused (MMSE 22/30)
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 84 g/L, creatinine 384 micromol/L, calcium 3.4 mmol/L corrected, total protein 96 g/L, IgG kappa M-band 42 g/L, kappa/lambda ratio 220, skeletal survey lytic lesions

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management priority?

options.text: IV 0.9% sodium chloride 3 L over 4 hours plus bortezomib regimen
options.rationale: Cast nephropathy AKI in myeloma improves with hydration to reduce light chain delivery and prompt anti-myeloma therapy (typically bortezomib-based); both are needed to preserve renal function. (Source: HSANZ Multiple Myeloma Position Statement)

options.text: IV zoledronic acid 4 mg as the immediate priority for hypercalcaemia
options.rationale: Bisphosphonates require renal function correction first; zoledronic acid is held until creatinine improves and hydration is established. (Source: HSANZ Multiple Myeloma Position Statement)

options.text: Pamidronate 90 mg IV without prior fluid resuscitation hydration
options.rationale: Pamidronate has lower renal toxicity than zoledronate but still requires fluid resuscitation first; hypovolaemia is the immediate threat. (Source: HSANZ Multiple Myeloma Position Statement)

options.text: Plasma exchange as monotherapy for free light chain removal
options.rationale: Plasma exchange does not consistently improve renal outcomes in cast nephropathy and is not a substitute for hydration plus anti-myeloma therapy. (Source: HSANZ Multiple Myeloma Position Statement)

options.text: Urgent haemodialysis with high cut-off filter without chemotherapy
options.rationale: High cut-off dialysis without anti-myeloma therapy does not stop new light chain production; combined treatment is the AU standard. (Source: HSANZ Multiple Myeloma Position Statement)

explanation.summary: Myeloma cast nephropathy is the most common cause of AKI in multiple myeloma. Free kappa light chains co-precipitate with Tamm-Horsfall protein causing tubular casts; hypercalcaemia, dehydration, NSAIDs, and contrast worsen injury. AU management combines aggressive isotonic hydration to lower urinary light chain delivery, treatment of hypercalcaemia (initially with hydration; bisphosphonates after renal recovery), and prompt anti-myeloma therapy (typically bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, dexamethasone) to reduce light chain production. Avoid nephrotoxins.
key_points: Hydration + anti-myeloma therapy together preserve renal function
Bisphosphonates held until renal recovery
Plasma exchange not routine in cast nephropathy
explanation.pearls: A serum free light chain reduction of >=50% within 21 days of bortezomib-based induction predicts renal recovery in approximately 80% of cast nephropathy cases.

stem:
A 62-year-old man presents to ED at 02:00 with 4 hours of central chest tightness radiating to the left jaw. He has hypertension and hyperlipidaemia and smokes 15 cigarettes daily. The pain partially settled with sublingual GTN but has now returned.

The baseline 12-lead ECG shows sinus rhythm with minor T-wave flattening laterally but no ST elevation. The initial high-sensitivity troponin T at 0 hours is 18 ng/L (URL 14 ng/L). A repeat at 1 hour is 32 ng/L. Renal function is normal and there is no recent significant illness or chronic kidney disease.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 138/82 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 98%, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic during pain, dual heart sounds with no murmur, chest clear, no calf swelling
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus rhythm with lateral T-wave flattening, 0-hour hs-cTnT 18 ng/L (<14), 1-hour hs-cTnT 32 ng/L (delta 14 ng/L), eGFR 88 mL/min, electrolytes within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, sublingual GTN PRN

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give intravenous thrombolysis with tenecteplase as he meets ACS criteria with raised troponin
options.rationale: Thrombolysis is for ST elevation MI when timely PCI is not available; NSTEMI is managed by antithrombotic therapy and invasive angiography, not thrombolysis. (Source: CSANZ 2025 Acute Coronary Syndrome Guideline)

options.text: Rule out NSTEMI on these troponin values and discharge home with GP follow-up
options.rationale: The 0/1-hour algorithm rules out only when 0-hour hs-cTnT is below the URL AND 1-hour delta is below threshold; this patient meets neither criterion. (Source: CSANZ 2025 Acute Coronary Syndrome Guideline)

options.text: Plan repeat troponin at 6 hours and admit only if the 6-hour value remains elevated
options.rationale: The conventional 0/3 or 0/6 hour algorithm is superseded by the 0/1 hour high-sensitivity protocol in AU EDs when hs-cTn is available, which already provides the diagnosis. (Source: CSANZ 2025 Acute Coronary Syndrome Guideline)

options.text: Arrange outpatient computed tomography coronary angiography within the next week
options.rationale: CT coronary angiography is for low-risk chest pain after troponin rule-out; once NSTEMI is ruled in, invasive coronary angiography is the procedure of choice. (Source: CSANZ 2025 Acute Coronary Syndrome Guideline)

options.text: Diagnose NSTEMI, give DAPT plus parenteral anticoagulant, and refer for early invasive angiography
options.rationale: ESC/CSANZ 0/1-hour algorithm rules in NSTEMI when the 0-hour hs-cTnT is above the URL with a 1-hour delta ≥5 ng/L; early invasive angiography within 24 hours plus DAPT and parenteral anticoagulation is the AU approach. (Source: CSANZ 2025 Acute Coronary Syndrome Guideline)

explanation.summary: The 0/1-hour high-sensitivity troponin algorithm streamlines acute chest pain triage in Australian EDs. Rule-out requires 0-hour hs-cTnT <5 ng/L if symptom onset >3 hours, or 0-hour <12 ng/L with 1-hour delta <3 ng/L. Rule-in requires 0-hour ≥52 ng/L OR 1-hour delta ≥5 ng/L (men) or ≥3 ng/L (women) above an above-URL baseline. The 'observation zone' between rule-out and rule-in triggers further serial troponin, imaging, or risk stratification. NSTEMI rule-in mandates DAPT, parenteral anticoagulation (heparin or enoxaparin or fondaparinux), and angiography timing by risk class.
key_points: 0/1-hour rule-in: 0-hour above URL plus 1-hour delta ≥5 ng/L.
0/1-hour rule-out: very low 0-hour OR very low + delta <3 ng/L.
NSTEMI: DAPT, parenteral anticoagulant, early invasive within 24 hours for high-risk.
Thrombolysis is for STEMI without timely PCI access, not NSTEMI.
explanation.pearls: hs-cTnT 0/1-hour: delta ≥5 ng/L above an above-URL baseline rules in NSTEMI and triggers early invasive angiography.

stem:
A 35-year-old presents to an outer-suburban GP clinic 15 minutes after eating cashew nuts at a restaurant. He has known peanut allergy and now reports tightness in his throat and difficulty breathing. He has urticarial wheals over his trunk and arms. He is alert but anxious.

He has no diagnosed cardiac disease. He has no regular medications. His weight at his last GP visit was 80 kg. The practice has a single 1 mg/mL adrenaline ampoule and a 1 mL syringe; an EpiPen and EpiPen Jr are also stocked.
