data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124, BP 86/52 mmHg, RR 28 with audible wheeze, SpO2 92% in air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Generalised urticaria, perioral swelling, expiratory wheeze bilaterally, no stridor, alert, capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Bedside only, ECG sinus tachycardia, no other immediate results

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first dose of adrenaline?

options.text: Adrenaline 1:1000 0.3 mg IM (300 mcg) into the mid-anterolateral thigh, repeatable
options.rationale: 0.3 mg is the paediatric EpiPen dose for 20 kg or above; the adult standard ASCIA dose is 0.5 mg of 1:1000 IM. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023

options.text: Adrenaline 1:1000 0.5 mg IM (500 mcg) into the mid-anterolateral thigh, repeatable
options.rationale: ASCIA adult anaphylaxis dose is 0.5 mg (500 mcg) IM 1:1000 into the mid-anterolateral thigh, repeated every 5 minutes if symptoms persist, before considering IV adrenaline infusion. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023

options.text: Adrenaline 1:10 000 1 mg IV (1000 mcg) bolus over 1 minute by intravenous access
options.rationale: Intravenous bolus adrenaline 1 mg is for cardiac arrest, not anaphylaxis; IV adrenaline in anaphylaxis is given by titrated infusion in a monitored setting, after IM has failed. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023

options.text: Hydrocortisone 200 mg IV plus chlorphenamine 10 mg IV before any adrenaline dose
options.rationale: Steroids and antihistamines do not treat acute anaphylaxis cardiorespiratory compromise; adrenaline must be given first and is never delayed by adjuncts. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg with face mask oxygen and admit to the local hospital ward
options.rationale: Nebulised salbutamol is an adjunct for persistent bronchospasm AFTER adrenaline; it does not address hypotension or airway oedema and does not replace adrenaline. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023

explanation.summary: Adult anaphylaxis is treated by ASCIA: IM adrenaline 0.5 mg of 1:1000 (500 mcg) into the mid-anterolateral thigh, repeated every 5 minutes if symptoms persist. Lay the patient flat with legs raised, give high-flow oxygen, and obtain IV access. IV adrenaline infusion (titrated to response, typically starting at 1 mcg/min) is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis. Antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts, not primary treatment, and do not reverse cardiorespiratory compromise. Biphasic reactions occur in approximately 5-20 percent within 4-6 hours; observe for 4 hours minimum.
key_points: Adult ASCIA dose: 0.5 mg (500 mcg) IM 1:1000 into mid-anterolateral thigh.
Repeat every 5 minutes if persistent; lie flat with legs raised.
IV adrenaline infusion only after IM failure in a monitored setting.
Observe minimum 4 hours for biphasic reaction (5-20%).
explanation.pearls: Adult anaphylaxis: 0.5 mg IM adrenaline 1:1000 every 5 minutes if persistent; IV bolus is for arrest, not anaphylaxis.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023

stem:
A 24-year-old presents to ED 6 hours after taking what she states was 30 paracetamol 500 mg tablets in a single ingestion. She is now nauseated but not vomiting. There is no co-ingestion identified on history or urine drug screen, and she takes no regular medications. She weighs 60 kg.

A paracetamol level taken on arrival at 6 hours post-ingestion is 200 mg/L. INR is 1.1. ALT and creatinine are within normal limits. The treating nomogram in your ED is the Australian Rumack-Matthew '150 line' (paracetamol 150 mg/L at 4 hours).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Mildly nauseated, no abdominal tenderness, no jaundice, no encephalopathy, alert and orientated
data_table.Investigations: Paracetamol 200 mg/L at 6 hours, INR 1.1 (0.8-1.2), ALT 28 U/L (5-30), creatinine 70 micromol/L (60-110), urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Withhold N-acetylcysteine because the level is below the standard 200 mg/L 4-hour line
options.rationale: The 200 mg/L line is the 4-hour value of the higher-risk North American nomogram; AU uses the 150 mg/L 4-hour line and at 6 hours the threshold is around 125 mg/L. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Commence intravenous N-acetylcysteine using the 21-hour two-bag Australian protocol
options.rationale: On the Australian Rumack-Matthew 150 mg/L line, the 6-hour threshold is approximately 125 mg/L; this patient's level of 200 mg/L is above the line and requires NAC. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Administer single-dose activated charcoal 50 g orally before any NAC is started
options.rationale: Activated charcoal is considered within 1-2 hours of ingestion; at 6 hours post-ingestion it adds no benefit and delays NAC which is the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Repeat the paracetamol level at 12 hours and start NAC only if the level is still high
options.rationale: NAC efficacy is greatest within 8-10 hours of ingestion; delaying for a further level wastes the protective window when the current level is already above the AU threshold. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Refer immediately for haemodialysis to remove circulating paracetamol from the blood
options.rationale: Haemodialysis for paracetamol is reserved for massive ingestion (>500 mg/kg) with very high levels (>1000 mg/L) or established acidosis with coma; this patient has a single moderate ingestion and is alert. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

explanation.summary: Paracetamol overdose management in Australia uses the 150 mg/L Rumack-Matthew nomogram from 4 to 16 hours post-ingestion; any level above the line triggers N-acetylcysteine. The 21-hour two-bag protocol gives 200 mg/kg over 4 hours, then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours. Earlier NAC (within 8 hours) prevents the majority of hepatotoxicity; later treatment still benefits established disease. Massive ingestion (>30 g or >500 mg/kg) may justify a 3-bag higher-dose protocol. Repeat levels and LFTs at end of NAC determine completion or extension.
key_points: AU nomogram: 150 mg/L 4-hour line; treat any level above.
21-hour 2-bag protocol: 200 mg/kg over 4 hours then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours.
NAC most effective within 8 hours of ingestion.
Massive ingestion (>500 mg/kg) may use 3-bag higher-dose regimen.
explanation.pearls: AU paracetamol nomogram 150 mg/L line at 4 hours = NAC; at 6 hours threshold is approximately 125 mg/L.

sources.label: NSW Poisons Information Centre Paracetamol Guideline

stem:
A 34-year-old healthcare worker presents for review after a routine occupational health screen. She was born in Australia, but worked in a high-prevalence overseas region for 18 months and returned 6 months ago. Her QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus is positive and her chest X-ray is normal. She has no cough, no fever, no weight loss, and no night sweats.

She is otherwise well, with no liver disease, no alcohol overuse, no pregnancy or contraception requirements, and no other medications. Her HIV test is negative. Her baseline LFTs and renal function are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: No lymphadenopathy, chest clear, abdomen soft, no organomegaly, no skin lesions
data_table.Investigations: QFT-Plus positive, chest X-ray normal, FBC and UEC within normal limits, ALT 18 U/L (5-30), bilirubin within normal limits, HIV negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate latent TB treatment regimen?

options.text: Isoniazid plus ethambutol daily for 12 months with monthly visual acuity monitoring
options.rationale: Ethambutol is not used for LTBI; it is part of active TB therapy and adds optic neuropathy risk without benefit in latent infection. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guideline 2017)
source_refs: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guideline 2017

options.text: Isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol daily for 6 months full RIPE course
options.rationale: RIPE quadruple therapy is for ACTIVE TB; LTBI treatment is single or dual agent because the burden of disease is much lower and toxicity must be minimised. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guideline 2017)
source_refs: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guideline 2017

options.text: Rifampicin 600 mg daily monotherapy for 6 months as the single-agent shorter regimen
options.rationale: The AU rifampicin LTBI regimen is 4 months not 6 months; 6 months prolongs hepatotoxicity exposure without added efficacy. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guideline 2017)
source_refs: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guideline 2017

options.text: Isoniazid 300 mg daily plus pyridoxine 25 mg daily for 6 months total duration
options.rationale: Australian guidance lists 6 months of daily isoniazid with pyridoxine as a first-line LTBI regimen; alternative is 3 months of weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine, or 4 months of daily rifampicin. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guideline 2017)
source_refs: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guideline 2017

options.text: No drug treatment; surveillance with annual chest X-ray and symptom review for 2 years
options.rationale: Active surveillance alone is not adequate when QFT-Plus is positive and risk factors (healthcare work, recent return from high-prevalence area) are present; treatment reduces progression to active disease by 60-90%. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guideline 2017)
source_refs: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guideline 2017

explanation.summary: Latent tuberculosis is diagnosed by a positive interferon-gamma release assay (QFT-Plus) or tuberculin skin test in an asymptomatic patient with a normal chest X-ray and no clinical features of active TB. Australian first-line regimens are isoniazid 6 months (with pyridoxine), rifampicin 4 months, or isoniazid plus rifapentine weekly for 12 weeks. Choice is informed by drug interactions, hepatotoxicity risk, pregnancy, and patient preference. Baseline LFTs and renal function are checked and monitored. Treatment reduces progression to active disease by 60-90 percent and is offered to all eligible adults with LTBI plus risk factors.
key_points: AU first-line LTBI regimens: isoniazid 6 m, rifampicin 4 m, or isoniazid + rifapentine 12 weekly doses.
Pyridoxine 25 mg daily with isoniazid prevents peripheral neuropathy.
Baseline and 4-weekly LFT monitoring during isoniazid.
Treatment cuts active TB progression by 60-90%.
explanation.pearls: AU LTBI: 6 m isoniazid + pyridoxine, OR 4 m rifampicin, OR 12-week weekly isoniazid + rifapentine.

sources.label: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee LTBI Guideline 2017

stem:
A 42-year-old with Addison's disease on hydrocortisone 20 mg morning and 10 mg evening, plus fludrocortisone 100 mcg daily, presents 18 hours into a gastroenteritis illness. She has had 8 episodes of vomiting and has not been able to keep down her morning hydrocortisone dose. She did not have her steroid emergency injection at home because the family could not find it.

On arrival to the emergency department she is drowsy but rousable. She is afebrile. Her abdomen is soft. There is no chest or respiratory infection identified clinically.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124, BP 82/48 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 seconds, no peritonism, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.4), sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 12 mmol/L (3.0-8.0), creatinine 110 micromol/L (60-110), VBG pH 7.30 HCO3 18 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg stat followed by 0.9% saline bolus 1 L over 30 minutes
options.rationale: AU adrenal crisis pathway is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat (then 200 mg over 24 hours) plus prompt isotonic saline resuscitation to correct hypovolaemia, hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Oral hydrocortisone 40 mg now and reassess in 2 hours after rehydration with oral fluids
options.rationale: Oral steroids and oral rehydration are inappropriate in adrenal crisis with vomiting and hypotension; absorption is unreliable and the patient needs immediate IV access. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Intravenous fludrocortisone 100 mcg with isotonic saline 500 mL over the first hour
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is not available IV and is unnecessary acutely because high-dose hydrocortisone has sufficient mineralocorticoid activity at 100 mg doses. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Intravenous insulin and dextrose to correct hyperkalaemia before any steroid is given
options.rationale: The hyperkalaemia in adrenal crisis is secondary to cortisol and aldosterone deficiency; it resolves with hydrocortisone and saline, and standard insulin-dextrose risks rebound hypoglycaemia in this already hypoglycaemic patient. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Intravenous calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10% over 10 minutes before fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: Calcium gluconate is used for cardioprotection in life-threatening hyperkalaemia with ECG changes; this patient does not yet have ECG features and steroid plus saline are higher priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is precipitated by intercurrent illness, surgery, missed steroid doses, vomiting, or trauma in patients with primary or secondary adrenal insufficiency. Classic features are hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, and metabolic acidosis. Treatment is immediate IV hydrocortisone (100 mg stat then 200 mg per 24 h as infusion or 50 mg six-hourly), isotonic saline resuscitation, and treatment of any precipitant. After acute recovery, double or triple the regular steroid dose during intercurrent illness ('sick day rules'); ensure the patient has an emergency hydrocortisone injection kit and a Medic-Alert.
key_points: Adrenal crisis: hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia.
IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 200 mg over 24 hours.
Saline resuscitation and dextrose for hypoglycaemia.
Sick day rules: double or triple steroid dose for febrile illness.
explanation.pearls: Adrenal crisis: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat + 0.9% saline bolus before any other intervention; hyperkalaemia self-corrects with steroid replacement.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal insufficiency statement

stem:
A 42-year-old man with type 1 diabetes presents with vomiting, abdominal pain, polyuria, and Kussmaul breathing after running out of insulin 36 hours ago. He weighs 80 kg. He has had no recent diuretic use and no chronic gastrointestinal losses other than the current vomiting.

Venous blood gas shows pH 7.12, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L. Capillary glucose is 24 mmol/L, ketones 5.4 mmol/L. Sodium is 138 mmol/L. Critically, the initial potassium is 2.9 mmol/L and the ECG shows ST depression with a U wave. He is alert and orientated (GCS 15) and has IV access in place. The standard ADS DKA pathway is available.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 96/60 mmHg, RR 32 Kussmaul, SpO2 99% in air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 seconds, alert, mild diffuse abdominal tenderness without peritonism
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.12, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L (22-32), glucose 24 mmol/L, ketones 5.4 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 2.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), corrected anion gap 24, ECG ST depression with U waves
data_table.Medications: Insulin glargine (ran out), insulin aspart (ran out)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: IV saline 1 L plus 40 mmol potassium chloride over 1 hour; hold insulin until K ≥3.5 mmol/L
options.rationale: ADS DKA protocol holds insulin until potassium is at or above 3.5 mmol/L because insulin drives potassium intracellularly and risks fatal hypokalaemia; potassium-replete saline runs first. (Source: ADS Australian Diabetes Society DKA Guideline 2020)
source_refs: ADS Australian Diabetes Society DKA Guideline 2020

options.text: IV insulin infusion 0.1 unit/kg/h commencing immediately at recognition of DKA
options.rationale: Insulin in the setting of potassium <3.3 mmol/L precipitates further intracellular potassium shift and can trigger ventricular arrhythmia; the ADS pathway holds insulin until potassium ≥3.5 mmol/L. (Source: ADS Australian Diabetes Society DKA Guideline 2020)
source_refs: ADS Australian Diabetes Society DKA Guideline 2020

options.text: IV sodium bicarbonate 50 mmol bolus to correct severe acidosis before insulin or fluids
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is only considered for adult DKA with pH <6.9 and persistent shock; routine use worsens intracellular acidosis and aggravates hypokalaemia, which is already critical here. (Source: ADS Australian Diabetes Society DKA Guideline 2020)
source_refs: ADS Australian Diabetes Society DKA Guideline 2020

options.text: IV 0.9% saline 2 L bolus then immediate insulin infusion before any potassium replacement
options.rationale: Aggressive saline without potassium plus immediate insulin will drive potassium even lower from an already 2.9 mmol/L baseline, with ECG changes already present; potassium replacement must come first. (Source: ADS Australian Diabetes Society DKA Guideline 2020)
source_refs: ADS Australian Diabetes Society DKA Guideline 2020

options.text: Subcutaneous insulin aspart 10 units stat plus oral potassium replacement in 200 mL water
options.rationale: Subcutaneous insulin and oral potassium are inappropriate in active DKA with hypokalaemia, vomiting and shock; absorption is unreliable and IV therapy is required. (Source: ADS Australian Diabetes Society DKA Guideline 2020)
source_refs: ADS Australian Diabetes Society DKA Guideline 2020

explanation.summary: Adult DKA management in Australia (ADS protocol) follows fluid, insulin, potassium, glucose, and search for precipitant. Critically, when initial potassium is <3.3 mmol/L, insulin must be HELD until potassium is replaced to at least 3.5 mmol/L, because insulin drives further intracellular shift and causes potentially fatal hypokalaemia. Replace potassium at 20-40 mmol per litre of crystalloid; rates above 10 mmol/h need cardiac monitoring. Once potassium ≥3.5, start fixed-rate insulin 0.1 unit/kg/h. Add 5% dextrose to fluids once glucose ≤14 mmol/L. Bicarbonate reserved for pH <6.9 with shock.
key_points: ADS DKA: hold insulin if K <3.3 mmol/L until replaced to ≥3.5.
Replace K at 20-40 mmol/L in crystalloid; cardiac monitor if >10 mmol/h.
Fixed-rate insulin 0.1 unit/kg/h once potassium safe.
Add 5% dextrose to fluid once glucose ≤14 mmol/L.
explanation.pearls: DKA with potassium <3.3 mmol/L: replace potassium first, hold insulin until K ≥3.5 mmol/L (ADS protocol).

sources.label: ADS Australian Diabetes Society DKA Guideline 2020

stem:
A 48-year-old presents to your endocrinology outpatient clinic for review. She was diagnosed with a unilateral 4 cm right adrenal mass on a CT abdomen done after recurrent panic-like episodes. Plasma metanephrines are markedly elevated, consistent with phaeochromocytoma. Her GP started metoprolol 50 mg twice daily one week ago to control her tachycardia.

Her home BP readings have actually worsened, ranging 165-180 systolic and 100-110 diastolic. She has no history of asthma. She is awaiting surgical planning. She has no other medications and no significant past medical history.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 172/108 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99%, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: No bruits, no thyromegaly, no acanthosis, no orthostatic drop measured today, abdomen soft non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Plasma free normetanephrine 4500 pmol/L (<900), CT abdomen 4 cm right adrenal mass, UEC and FBC within normal limits, ECG sinus rhythm
data_table.Medications: Metoprolol 50 mg twice daily (started 1 week ago)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in pharmacological management?

options.text: Plan immediate surgical adrenalectomy this week without further antihypertensive change
options.rationale: Surgery without adequate alpha blockade for 10-14 days carries a high risk of intraoperative hypertensive crisis, arrhythmia and death; pre-operative blockade is mandatory. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma statement)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma statement

options.text: Continue metoprolol and add phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily, escalating as tolerated
options.rationale: Continuing beta blockade alongside the start of alpha blockade is not safer than the AU recommended sequence of stopping beta first, then starting alpha, then re-introducing beta once alpha is established. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma statement)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma statement

options.text: Increase metoprolol to 100 mg twice daily and add amlodipine 5 mg daily for BP control
options.rationale: Escalating beta blockade in phaeochromocytoma without alpha blockade worsens the unopposed alpha state and accelerated hypertension risk; calcium channel blockers are adjuncts, not the primary fix here. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma statement)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma statement

options.text: Stop metoprolol now and start phenoxybenzamine 10 mg twice daily, titrated to symptoms
options.rationale: Beta blockade without prior alpha blockade in phaeochromocytoma causes unopposed alpha vasoconstriction and worsened hypertension; the AU approach is to STOP metoprolol, start phenoxybenzamine, and only add a beta blocker once alpha blockade is established. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma statement)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma statement

options.text: Substitute hydralazine 25 mg three times daily for metoprolol and continue current plan
options.rationale: Hydralazine causes reflex tachycardia and is not a controlled choice in phaeochromocytoma; phenoxybenzamine is the AU preferred preoperative alpha blocker. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma statement)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma statement

explanation.summary: Phaeochromocytoma requires preoperative alpha-adrenergic blockade for 10-14 days before any beta blockade is added, to prevent unopposed alpha vasoconstriction and hypertensive crisis. The AU first-line agent is phenoxybenzamine (irreversible non-selective alpha blocker); doxazosin is an alternative. Beta blockade is added only AFTER adequate alpha blockade, to control reflex tachycardia. High sodium and fluid intake during the alpha blockade phase prevents volume contraction-related hypotension. Surgery (typically laparoscopic adrenalectomy) is planned when BP and heart rate targets are met.
key_points: Alpha block first, beta block only after alpha block is established.
Phenoxybenzamine first-line; doxazosin alternative.
10-14 days of alpha block before surgery.
Liberal salt and fluid intake during alpha block to prevent hypotension.
explanation.pearls: Phaeochromocytoma preop: stop any premature beta blocker; start phenoxybenzamine for 10-14 days, then re-add beta blocker only once alpha block is established.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma statement

stem:
A 64-year-old woman presents to a metropolitan ED at 0900 with central chest tightness that started at 0700 and has now resolved. She has type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and a 30 pack-year smoking history. Her father had an MI at 55. Initial ECG shows normal sinus rhythm with no ST changes or T-wave inversion.

Her first hs-troponin is back, and a second draw at one hour is now available.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 138/82 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Comfortable, no respiratory distress, chest clear, normal heart sounds with no murmurs, no peripheral oedema, calves soft
data_table.Investigations: ECG: normal sinus rhythm, no ST changes; hs-troponin T at 0 hours 8 ng/L (sex-specific 99th percentile 14 ng/L), 1-hour hs-troponin T 9 ng/L; renal function within normal limits; chest X-ray clear
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1 g BD, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nocte; no aspirin

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Admit for serial troponin testing every 6 hours for 24 hours
options.rationale: 6-hourly serial troponin protocols precede hs-troponin and are no longer the standard. CSANZ accepts the 0/1h hs-troponin algorithm for rule-out, freeing low-risk patients. (Source: Heart Foundation / CSANZ ACS Guidelines)

options.text: Commence dual antiplatelet therapy and admit to coronary care
options.rationale: DAPT for ACS rule-in is not indicated when troponin trajectory rules out NSTEMI; bleeding risk without benefit. (Source: Heart Foundation / CSANZ ACS Guidelines)

options.text: Discharge home for outpatient cardiology with cardiac stress test
options.rationale: The European Society of Cardiology 0/1h hs-troponin T rule-out algorithm (also accepted in AU CSANZ pathways) considers a 0-hour value <5 ng/L OR 0-hour <12 with 1-hour delta <3 ng/L as a rule-out for NSTEMI. Her 0-hour 8 with 1-hour delta of 1 ng/L meets rule-out criteria. Symptoms have resolved and ECG is non-diagnostic so outpatient cardiology review with stress test is appropriate. (Source: Heart Foundation / CSANZ ACS Guidelines)

options.text: Activate the cath lab for urgent coronary angiography now
options.rationale: Urgent coronary angiography is for STEMI, NSTEMI rule-in with high-risk features (haemodynamic instability, dynamic ECG changes, persistent angina), or unstable angina. She has rule-out troponin trajectory and no high-risk features. (Source: Heart Foundation / CSANZ ACS Guidelines)

options.text: Order a CT coronary angiogram before discharge planning
options.rationale: CT coronary angiogram is useful in intermediate-risk patients to refine the diagnosis but is not the standard immediate step after rule-out by 0/1h algorithm; stress testing is preferred for functional assessment in outpatient cardiology pathways. (Source: Heart Foundation / CSANZ ACS Guidelines)

explanation.summary: The CSANZ-endorsed 0/1h hs-troponin algorithm allows rule-out of NSTEMI when 0-hour hs-troponin <5 ng/L OR 0-hour <12 with 1-hour delta <3 ng/L, with non-diagnostic ECG and resolved symptoms. Rule-in is 0-hour ≥52 ng/L OR 1-hour delta ≥5 ng/L. Intermediate values need observation and 3-hour repeat.
key_points: 0/1h hs-troponin algorithm: rule-out <5 at 0h or <12 with delta <3 at 1h
Rule-in: 0h ≥52 ng/L OR 1h delta ≥5 ng/L
Outpatient cardiology stress test or CT coronary angiogram is the post-rule-out pathway
explanation.pearls: The 0/1h algorithm requires assay-specific cut-offs (different for hs-troponin T vs hs-troponin I). Sex-specific 99th percentile cut-offs apply for the rule-in side. Use clinical judgement in patients with renal impairment - the baseline hs-troponin is often above 14 ng/L without acute MI.

subtopic_detail: Community-acquired pneumonia SMART-COP and ICU admission
stem:
A 68-year-old man with COPD on tiotropium presents with a 3-day history of productive cough, fever, and rigors. He is admitted from ED to a general medical ward. Six hours later he becomes more dyspnoeic and the registrar is called.

He has not had any antibiotics in the last 6 months.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124, BP 86/52 mmHg, RR 36, SpO2 88% on 6 L/min via Hudson mask, temperature 38.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Confused (AMTS 4/10), accessory muscle use, right-sided crackles, no wheeze, well-perfused but cool peripheries
data_table.Investigations: Chest X-ray: dense right lower lobe consolidation with small parapneumonic effusion. ABG on 6 L/min: pH 7.32, pO2 56 mmHg, pCO2 38 mmHg, HCO3 19 mmol/L; lactate 4.2; WCC 22 x10^9/L; albumin 26 g/L; sodium 132 mmol/L; urea 10.2 mmol/L; creatinine 102 micromol/L; CRP 318 mg/L
data_table.Medications: Tiotropium 18 micrograms daily; ED ceftriaxone 2 g + azithromycin 500 mg PO given on arrival 6 hours ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Bridge to non-invasive ventilation with BiPAP and reassess in 2 hours
options.rationale: BiPAP is appropriate for COPD-related hypercapnic respiratory failure but he is currently hypoxic and septic with confusion; BiPAP risks aspiration in the obtunded patient and delays intubation. (Source: TSANZ / Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory CAP)

options.text: Continue ceftriaxone monotherapy on the ward with 2 hourly review
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone monotherapy is appropriate empirically only for mild-to-moderate CAP; with SMART-COP 11 and septic shock the patient needs ICU-level care and broader empirical cover (eg piperacillin-tazobactam + azithromycin or as per local antibiogram). (Source: TSANZ / Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory CAP)

options.text: Insert intercostal drain for the small parapneumonic effusion
options.rationale: Small simple parapneumonic effusions are managed with antibiotics; drainage is reserved for empyema or large effusion compromising oxygenation. The dominant issue is sepsis and respiratory failure, not the effusion. (Source: TSANZ / Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory CAP)

options.text: Calculate SMART-COP and refer to ICU for likely intubation and inotropic support
options.rationale: SMART-COP: low Systolic BP (2), Multilobar / large effusion (1), low Albumin (1), high Respiratory rate (1), Tachycardia (1), Confusion (1), low Oxygen (2), low pH (2) = 11. Above 5 predicts >65% need for ventilatory or inotropic support and mandates ICU referral. The AU TSANZ pathway uses SMART-COP for site-of-care decisions in addition to severity-of-illness scoring like APACHE. (Source: TSANZ / Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory CAP)

options.text: Discharge with oral amoxicillin-clavulanate after 24-hour observation
options.rationale: Discharge with oral antibiotics is not an option in septic shock with multilobar pneumonia and respiratory failure. (Source: TSANZ / Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory CAP)

explanation.summary: SMART-COP scores Systolic BP, Multilobar, Albumin, Respiratory rate, Tachycardia, Confusion, Oxygen, pH, and predicts need for intensive respiratory or vasopressor support (IRVS). Above 5 has over 50% positive predictive value for IRVS. AU TSANZ guidelines incorporate this for site-of-care decisions.
key_points: SMART-COP ≥5 predicts ICU need; ≥3 is the typical hospital-admission threshold
Severe CAP requires broad cover: piperacillin-tazobactam + azithromycin or per local antibiogram
BiPAP is contraindicated in obtunded patients with aspiration risk
explanation.pearls: AU TSANZ guidelines emphasise that PSI and CURB-65 underestimate severity in younger patients without comorbidity. SMART-COP is calibrated for IRVS prediction. Add gentamicin for atypicals coverage and Pseudomonas in selected patients.

stem:
A 58-year-old woman with no provoking risk factors presents with mild right-sided chest discomfort. CT pulmonary angiogram (CTPA) reports a single subsegmental pulmonary embolus in the right lower lobe with no proximal involvement. Bilateral leg ultrasound is negative for DVT. She has no haemodynamic compromise, no right heart strain on echocardiogram, and a normal troponin. She has no cancer, no recent surgery, no immobility, and no oestrogen exposure.

The respiratory and vascular teams have reviewed the imaging and discussed treatment options with her.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 124/78 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Comfortable, no respiratory distress, chest clear, calves soft and non-tender, no chest wall tenderness
data_table.Investigations: CTPA: solitary subsegmental PE in right lower lobe, no main pulmonary artery / lobar / segmental PE; lower limb Doppler bilateral negative; D-dimer raised; troponin within normal limits; echocardiogram normal RV function; FBC unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence rivaroxaban 15 mg BD for 21 days then 20 mg daily indefinitely
options.rationale: Indefinite (extended) anticoagulation is reserved for unprovoked proximal PE with low bleeding risk or recurrent VTE. A single subsegmental PE without confirmed VTE elsewhere does not yet warrant indefinite therapy; the 3-month course is the standard initial period. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Commence warfarin with INR target 2 to 3 for at least 6 months
options.rationale: Warfarin is no longer first-line for VTE in AU practice; DOACs are preferred because of fewer monitoring requirements and similar efficacy. Warfarin remains the choice in mechanical valves, antiphospholipid syndrome, and severe renal impairment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Withhold anticoagulation with surveillance lower limb Doppler weekly for 2 weeks
options.rationale: Surveillance without anticoagulation is a CHEST guideline option for subsegmental PE with confirmed absence of proximal DVT, low recurrence risk, and patient preference for not taking anticoagulants; however the AU consensus still favours treating because diagnostic accuracy of subsegmental PE on CTPA is limited and elevated D-dimer here suggests ongoing clot. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Commence apixaban 10 mg BD for 7 days then 5 mg BD for 3 months total
options.rationale: Single subsegmental PE with no proximal DVT, no risk factors, low cancer risk, and no haemodynamic compromise represents an isolated low-risk PE. AU practice supports a 3-month course of anticoagulation as the standard duration for low-risk PE. Apixaban 10 mg BD for 7 days then 5 mg BD is the AU first-line DOAC regimen for VTE; surveillance proximal vein Doppler is an alternative only in selected cases. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Treat with LMWH for 5 days then warfarin for 3 months at INR 2 to 3
options.rationale: LMWH bridging to warfarin is the alternative but DOACs do not require bridging and are preferred for non-cancer-associated VTE in AU. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Subsegmental PE without proximal DVT and without risk factors can be considered for surveillance-only management per CHEST guidelines, but AU practice typically still anticoagulates for 3 months because of false-negative scan rates and elevated D-dimer indicating ongoing clot. Apixaban 10 mg BD for 7 days then 5 mg BD is the first-line DOAC for VTE.
key_points: Apixaban 10 mg BD for 7 days, then 5 mg BD - AU first-line for VTE
Rivaroxaban 15 mg BD for 21 days, then 20 mg daily - alternative DOAC for VTE
Subsegmental PE surveillance is an alternative only in selected patients with confirmed absence of proximal DVT
explanation.pearls: Indefinite anticoagulation is offered for unprovoked proximal PE with low bleeding risk, recurrent VTE, or cancer-associated VTE. LMWH remains first-line for cancer-associated thrombosis in many AU centres, though apixaban and edoxaban now have growing evidence (eviQ guidelines).

subtopic_detail: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes - sequence of management
stem:
A 72-year-old man on hospital ward day 2 of admission for community-acquired pneumonia has a routine 8 am UEC return abnormal. He has chronic kidney disease (eGFR 32) and is on perindopril 10 mg daily and spironolactone 25 mg daily for heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. He feels generally unwell with mild lethargy.

The medical registrar is at the bedside reviewing the ECG.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 58, BP 132/78 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 96% in room air, temperature 37.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Mild lethargy, no proximal weakness, no chest pain
data_table.Investigations: K 6.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 188 micromol/L (60-110, baseline 156), Na 138 mmol/L, HCO3 18 mmol/L, urea 18 mmol/L; ECG: PR 220 ms, peaked T waves in V2-V5, no QRS widening, no LBBB
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 10 mg daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily; ceftriaxone for pneumonia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give 50 mL of 50% dextrose intravenously without insulin cover
options.rationale: Dextrose without insulin does not effectively shift potassium intracellularly. Insulin is the active agent (10 units short-acting IV with 50 mL of 50% dextrose to avoid hypoglycaemia). (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Refer for urgent haemodialysis without further pharmacological measures
options.rationale: Haemodialysis is the definitive treatment for refractory hyperkalaemia but takes time to organise; immediate calcium gluconate plus insulin/dextrose buys that time. Skipping membrane stabilisation risks fatal arrhythmia during set-up. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Give 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate intravenously over 5 minutes
options.rationale: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes (peaked T waves, prolonged PR) is an emergency. The sequence is: stabilise membrane (calcium gluconate 10 mL 10% IV over 5-10 minutes), shift potassium into cells (insulin/dextrose, salbutamol nebs), then remove potassium (resonium, dialysis if refractory). Calcium gluconate is first because the time-critical risk is arrhythmia and cardiac arrest. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Stop perindopril and spironolactone and recheck potassium in 6 hours
options.rationale: Stopping the precipitants is part of management but does not address the immediate ECG-changing hyperkalaemia. Both should be held but acute treatment (calcium then insulin) is the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Commence resonium 15 g orally four times daily for potassium removal
options.rationale: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate (resonium) is for chronic management or as a last-step potassium-remover; it does not address the immediate cardiac membrane risk and has a slow onset. Calcium gluconate must come first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes is an emergency. Sequence: stabilise the cardiac membrane (calcium gluconate 10 mL 10% IV over 5 to 10 minutes; lasts 30 to 60 minutes); shift K into cells (10 units actrapid in 50 mL 50% dextrose, salbutamol nebs); remove K (resonium, dialysis if refractory). Stop precipitants (ACE-I, MRA, NSAIDs, K-sparing diuretics).
key_points: Calcium gluconate stabilises the cardiac membrane but does not lower potassium - bridge to definitive measures
Insulin (10 units short-acting) plus 50 mL 50% dextrose shifts potassium into cells within 15-30 minutes
Dialysis is the definitive treatment for refractory hyperkalaemia (>6.5 with ECG changes despite medical therapy)
explanation.pearls: Calcium chloride is preferred over calcium gluconate via central access (more elemental calcium per volume). Salbutamol nebulisers (10 to 20 mg) add a second shifting mechanism. Bicarbonate is reserved for acidotic patients. Always recheck potassium 1-2 hours after intervention.

stem:
A 38-year-old man with known epilepsy on lamotrigine 200 mg twice daily is brought to ED having had a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure that has been ongoing for 25 minutes. Paramedics gave intramuscular midazolam 10 mg en route (10 minutes ago), with no cessation of seizure. He has not had a seizure in 6 months and his last lamotrigine level was therapeutic.

Intravenous access has been obtained on arrival, and he is being managed in the resuscitation bay with continuous monitoring.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 130, BP 152/96 mmHg, RR 24, SpO2 92% on 8 L/min via Hudson mask, temperature 37.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Generalised tonic-clonic activity ongoing, foaming at mouth, no head trauma, pupils midpoint and reactive, no focal lateralising signs
data_table.Investigations: VBG pH 7.22 lactate 5.8 glucose 6.4 mmol/L; UEC and FBC pending; lamotrigine level pending
data_table.Medications: Lamotrigine 200 mg BD; IM midazolam 10 mg given 10 minutes ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give intravenous levetiracetam 60 mg/kg over 10 minutes
options.rationale: Status epilepticus refractory to first-line benzodiazepines requires a second-line non-benzodiazepine anticonvulsant. The AU TSANZ / ANZAN consensus (post-ESETT trial) is that levetiracetam, valproate and fosphenytoin/phenytoin all show similar response rates (~50%); levetiracetam at 60 mg/kg is often first choice because of fewer interactions, no enzyme induction, and tolerability. He should still get a third line agent if seizure continues past this. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Wait 15 minutes to observe for spontaneous seizure cessation
options.rationale: Status epilepticus is defined as seizure activity lasting more than 5 minutes; waiting risks worsening neurological injury (proportional to duration) and progression to refractory status. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence intravenous fosphenytoin 20 mg/kg phenytoin equivalents
options.rationale: Fosphenytoin/phenytoin is an acceptable second-line per ESETT and AU TSANZ; either levetiracetam, valproate or phenytoin are reasonable choices. Phenytoin requires cardiac monitoring and is contraindicated in heart block, hypotension, and porphyria; levetiracetam is often preferred. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Repeat intravenous midazolam 10 mg and reassess after 5 minutes
options.rationale: Repeat benzodiazepine dose is appropriate at 5 to 10 minutes if first dose has not worked, but past the 20 to 30 minute mark a second-line non-benzodiazepine is added because of receptor internalisation reducing further benzodiazepine response. Excessive benzodiazepines also cause respiratory depression. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Proceed straight to rapid sequence intubation with thiopentone infusion
options.rationale: Thiopentone or propofol infusions are third-line for refractory status epilepticus after second-line non-benzodiazepine has failed. They require intubation and ICU. Skipping second-line escalates aggressively without an evidence basis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Status epilepticus is seizure activity lasting more than 5 minutes. First-line: IV/IM/buccal benzodiazepine (lorazepam 4 mg IV or midazolam 10 mg IM). Second-line at 20 minutes: levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV, valproate 40 mg/kg IV, or phenytoin 20 mg/kg IV (all similar efficacy per ESETT). Third-line: thiopentone or propofol infusion in ICU.
key_points: Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV is AU first-line second-line agent because of safety and few interactions
ESETT trial: levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate equally effective (~50% response rate)
Refractory status epilepticus requires intubation and continuous EEG monitoring in ICU
explanation.pearls: Always check glucose, Na, Mg, Ca, and ammonia (valproate users) in status. Pyridoxine 100 mg IV is added if INH overdose is suspected. Driving cessation rules: minimum 6 months seizure-free in AU under Austroads.

subtopic_detail: Aortic dissection imaging choice with renal impairment
stem:
A 58-year-old man presents with sudden onset tearing inter-scapular chest pain radiating to the back. He has a history of hypertension on irbesartan 300 mg daily, polycystic kidney disease with baseline eGFR 28, and bicuspid aortic valve. He is haemodynamically stable but anxious. He has a 3 cm aneurysm of the ascending aorta on a previous echocardiogram 12 months ago.

The ED registrar has reviewed him and the on-call cardiothoracic surgical team has been contacted. Imaging is being planned.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112, BP 188/108 mmHg right arm / 142/86 mmHg left arm, RR 22, SpO2 97% in room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Distressed with pain, blood pressure differential right arm vs left arm 46 mmHg systolic, diastolic murmur at right upper sternal border, no neurology, calves soft, equal pulses bilaterally on radial and femoral
data_table.Investigations: Bedside transthoracic echocardiogram shows intimal flap visible in ascending aorta and mild aortic regurgitation; creatinine 220 micromol/L (60-110, baseline 188); chest X-ray widened mediastinum; troponin within normal limits; ECG normal sinus rhythm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next imaging step?

options.text: Proceed to MRI angiography of the thoracic and abdominal aorta urgently
options.rationale: MRI is contraindicated by time delay in acute Stanford A dissection. It is reserved for stable Stanford B or follow-up imaging in chronic disease. (Source: Heart Foundation / CSANZ ACS Guidelines)

options.text: Commence intravenous labetalol infusion and admit to cardiology ward for observation
options.rationale: Beta-blockade and BP control are essential bridge therapy but not the definitive management for Stanford A. Type A requires emergency surgery; ward admission is inappropriate. (Source: Heart Foundation / CSANZ ACS Guidelines)

options.text: Proceed directly to operating theatre on the basis of the bedside TTE findings
options.rationale: Stanford type A dissection with confirmed intimal flap on TTE in the ascending aorta plus aortic regurgitation is a surgical emergency. Definitive imaging is helpful but not mandatory if the diagnosis is established and theatre is ready - delays for CT angiography in the setting of confirmed Stanford A worsens outcome. AU and international cardiothoracic practice supports proceeding to theatre with TOE in theatre to further characterise. Renal impairment is a secondary consideration; transoesophageal echocardiogram is the bedside alternative to CT in renal disease. (Source: Heart Foundation / CSANZ ACS Guidelines)

options.text: Insert intraaortic balloon pump as a bridge to definitive surgery now
options.rationale: IABP is contraindicated in aortic regurgitation and aortic dissection because it worsens both. (Source: Heart Foundation / CSANZ ACS Guidelines)

options.text: Proceed to CT angiography of the thoracic and abdominal aorta with iodinated contrast
options.rationale: CT angiography is the gold standard non-invasive imaging but iodinated contrast in eGFR 28 risks contrast-induced nephropathy, especially in stable haemodynamics; the TTE already shows the intimal flap and AR confirming Stanford A. Going to CT first delays surgery for marginal additional information. (Source: Heart Foundation / CSANZ ACS Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Stanford type A (ascending aorta) dissection is a surgical emergency with high mortality (1% per hour untreated); proceeding to theatre on bedside TTE with intimal flap and AR is appropriate when CT contrast risks AKI. Type B (descending aorta) is medically managed in uncomplicated cases. Bedside TOE is the contrast-free imaging alternative.
key_points: Stanford A = ascending aorta involvement, surgical emergency; Stanford B = descending only, medical management for uncomplicated
TTE with intimal flap and AR is sufficient bedside imaging to mobilise theatre when CT contrast risks AKI
Bilateral arm BP differential >20 mmHg with appropriate clinical features is a hallmark
explanation.pearls: Bridge therapy: titrate to systolic BP 100 to 120 mmHg with esmolol or labetalol first, then nicardipine if more BP control is needed (vasodilator without rate response is contraindicated alone). IABP is absolutely contraindicated.

subtopic_detail: Refractory hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state - insulin and fluid choice
stem:
An 84-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin and gliclazide is brought in by his family after 5 days of decreased oral intake from a viral illness. He is now drowsy and oriented only to person. The ED registrar has resuscitated him with 2 L of 0.9% sodium chloride over 2 hours, and a maintenance insulin infusion at 0.05 unit/kg/hour was started 90 minutes ago. His glucose has fallen from 48 to 44 mmol/L. He still has minimal urine output (10 mL/hr).

His paired osmolality is being recalculated and the intensive care team is reviewing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 96/64 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 96% on 4 L/min, temperature 37.4 °C, weight 72 kg
data_table.Examination: Drowsy GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5), dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, no peritonism, no focal neurology, no diabetic foot infection
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 44 mmol/L (3.5-7.8), Na 152 mmol/L (135-145), corrected Na 162 mmol/L, K 4.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), bicarb 22 mmol/L, anion gap 12, ketones 0.4 mmol/L (<0.6), urea 22 mmol/L, creatinine 198 micromol/L (60-110), measured osmolality 348 mOsm/kg (275-295), lactate 2.6
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1g BD, gliclazide MR 60 mg daily; 2L 0.9% saline given; insulin infusion 0.05 unit/kg/hour running

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Double the insulin infusion to 0.1 unit/kg/hour to accelerate glucose decline
options.rationale: Doubling insulin risks dropping glucose too quickly with cerebral oedema risk; HHS is characterised by relative insulin sufficiency to suppress ketogenesis but inadequate for glycaemic control. The slower 0.05 unit/kg/hour rate is standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Stop the insulin infusion and continue saline-only until glucose below 30 mmol/L
options.rationale: Stopping insulin once the diagnosis is confirmed and resuscitation is underway will not adequately lower glucose. The insulin infusion is run alongside fluids, not in isolation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Switch to 5% dextrose / 0.9% sodium chloride and continue insulin infusion at current rate
options.rationale: Switching to dextrose before glucose has dropped below about 14 to 15 mmol/L is premature and would slow glucose correction excessively in someone still at 44. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Give intravenous sodium bicarbonate 50 mmol over 30 minutes for acidosis
options.rationale: There is no significant acidosis (HCO3 22, AG 12, lactate 2.6); bicarbonate is not indicated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Switch to 0.45% sodium chloride and continue insulin at 0.05 unit/kg/hour
options.rationale: HHS with corrected sodium above 150 mmol/L (this patient 162) and an effective osmolality of 348 requires a slow, controlled correction of both glucose and effective osmolality. Lowering osmolality faster than 3 to 8 mOsm/kg/hour and glucose by more than 4 to 5 mmol/L/hour risks cerebral oedema in elderly patients. Hypotonic fluids (0.45% sodium chloride) are switched to once initial volume restoration is achieved AND corrected sodium is rising. AU diabetes society guidelines support this slow correction; the insulin rate is intentionally low (0.05 unit/kg/hour) in HHS, not the 0.1 used in DKA. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: HHS is defined by severe hyperglycaemia (>30 mmol/L), effective osmolality >320 mOsm/kg, dehydration, altered mentation, and only minimal ketosis or acidosis. Fluid resuscitation is the dominant therapy. Switch to 0.45% sodium chloride only once intravascular volume is restored and corrected sodium is rising. Insulin is started low at 0.05 unit/kg/hour with target glucose drop of 4 to 5 mmol/L/hour to avoid cerebral oedema.
key_points: HHS osmolality drop should be no more than 3 to 8 mOsm/kg/hour to avoid cerebral oedema
Insulin rate in HHS is 0.05 unit/kg/hour (half that of DKA)
Switch to 0.45% sodium chloride after volume restoration AND if corrected sodium is rising; otherwise continue isotonic
explanation.pearls: Effective osmolality = 2 x Na + glucose (mmol/L). Mortality is high (5 to 20%), driven by underlying precipitants - sepsis, MI, stroke, drugs (steroids, atypicals). Anti-coagulation is indicated for prevention of arterial thrombosis given hyperviscosity.

stem:
A 71-year-old man is reviewed in general practice. He had an incidental finding of a 4.2 cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm on CT 18 months ago during workup of suspected renal calculi. He has had two surveillance ultrasounds, the most recent today. He has hypertension on perindopril, dyslipidaemia on atorvastatin, type 2 diabetes well-controlled on metformin (HbA1c 6.8%), and a 45 pack-year smoking history; he quit 3 years ago. He has no abdominal pain, no back pain and no syncope.

Today's surveillance ultrasound shows an infrarenal AAA measuring 5.4 cm in maximal anteroposterior diameter, an increase of 0.7 cm from 12 months ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 132/78 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Soft non-tender abdomen, pulsatile mass palpable in upper abdomen, no peritonism, femoral and pedal pulses palpable, no carotid bruit
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, LFTs within normal limits; lipid profile total cholesterol 4.2 mmol/L, LDL 2.4 mmol/L; HbA1c 6.8% (7.4-8.4 individualised target met); recent CT angiogram from 18 months pending re-imaging
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nocte, metformin 1000 mg BD

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue 6-monthly ultrasound surveillance with general practitioner follow-up review
options.rationale: Surveillance is appropriate for AAA between 3.0 and 5.4 cm in men with slow growth, but a maximal diameter of 5.5 cm is the recognised threshold for elective repair (in men); growth rate above 1 cm per year also triggers referral. This case is at threshold AND has accelerated growth (0.7 cm in 12 months is the upper end of normal but combined with diameter approaching threshold warrants surgical assessment). (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Add aspirin 100 mg daily and re-image in 12 months as routine vascular surveillance
options.rationale: Aspirin has not been shown to reduce AAA growth or rupture and antithrombotic decisions in AAA are made on cardiovascular risk grounds, not aneurysm-specific. Delaying definitive vascular assessment is inappropriate when approaching repair threshold. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Arrange immediate emergency department presentation for haemodynamic monitoring now
options.rationale: Rupture is suggested by severe back/abdominal pain, hypotension and a pulsatile abdominal mass. This patient is asymptomatic with normal vital signs; emergency presentation is not warranted. Urgent outpatient referral, however, is. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Refer to vascular surgery for assessment of elective endovascular or open aneurysm repair
options.rationale: Australian and international guidance recommends referral for elective AAA repair consideration when maximal infrarenal diameter reaches 5.5 cm in men (5.0 cm in women), OR when growth exceeds 1 cm per year, OR when the patient becomes symptomatic. A 5.4 cm aneurysm with 0.7 cm growth in 12 months is at the surgical threshold and warrants vascular surgical assessment to discuss endovascular (EVAR) versus open repair and patient-specific anatomy/comorbidity. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Add a beta-blocker to reduce aneurysm growth and review again in 12 months time
options.rationale: Beta-blockers do not reduce AAA growth or rupture rates in randomised trials. BP control is appropriate but does not replace surgical assessment at threshold. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

explanation.summary: Infrarenal AAA referral thresholds for elective repair: 5.5 cm in men, 5.0 cm in women, OR growth above 1 cm per year, OR development of symptoms. Surveillance intervals scale with diameter (24 months for 3.0-3.9 cm, 12 months for 4.0-4.5 cm, 6 months for 4.6-5.4 cm in men). Elective repair (EVAR or open) substantially reduces rupture mortality compared with emergency repair (30 to 50%). Smoking cessation is the most effective modifiable factor; aspirin and beta-blockers do not change AAA growth or rupture rates.
key_points: Repair thresholds: 5.5 cm men, 5.0 cm women, OR growth >1 cm/year, OR symptoms
EVAR vs open: anatomy-dependent; EVAR lower short-term mortality but ongoing surveillance
Smoking cessation is the most effective modifiable risk factor for growth and rupture
explanation.pearls: An expanding AAA with new abdominal or back pain in a haemodynamically stable patient is a contained leak until proven otherwise - never reassure these patients home, image urgently and discuss with vascular on call.

stem:
A 32-year-old G3P2 woman at 28 weeks gestation is reviewed in the emergency department with sudden pleuritic chest pain and breathlessness that began an hour ago while shopping. She has no prior VTE and no thrombophilia. Her two previous pregnancies were uncomplicated. She does not smoke. Her chest X-ray is clear and there is no pneumothorax. Her ECG shows sinus tachycardia. Her lower-limb compression ultrasound is normal.

She remains haemodynamically stable but tachycardic. The obstetric medicine and respiratory registrars are at the bedside.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 116, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 24, SpO2 94% in room air, temperature 36.8 °C, fetal heart rate 145 bpm reactive
data_table.Examination: Mildly distressed, no calf swelling, no asymmetric leg pain, clear chest, no JVP elevation, no parasternal heave, gravid uterus consistent with dates
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia, no S1Q3T3 or RV strain; chest X-ray clear bilateral lung fields; FBC, UEC, LFTs within normal limits; troponin negative; arterial blood gas pH 7.46, PaO2 78 mmHg, PaCO2 30 mmHg, on room air; lower limb compression ultrasound negative bilaterally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Repeat lower-limb compression ultrasound in 7 days and treat empirically if positive
options.rationale: A single negative compression ultrasound does not exclude PE because clot may be confined to the pulmonary or pelvic vasculature. Definitive imaging of the pulmonary vasculature is required when clinical suspicion of PE is moderate-to-high. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan as first-line lung imaging modality in pregnancy
options.rationale: In pregnancy with a clear chest X-ray and no underlying lung disease, ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan is preferred over CTPA because of substantially lower maternal breast radiation dose (V/Q approximately 0.28 mGy maternal breast vs CTPA approximately 10-70 mGy maternal breast). Fetal radiation dose is comparable and within safe limits for either modality. CTPA is reserved for patients with chest X-ray abnormalities, underlying lung disease, or where V/Q is unavailable or non-diagnostic. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: CT pulmonary angiogram as the first-line definitive imaging modality in pregnancy
options.rationale: CTPA exposes maternal breast tissue (highly radiosensitive in young women) to a much higher radiation dose than V/Q. With a clear chest X-ray, V/Q is preferred first-line. CTPA is reserved for abnormal CXR or non-diagnostic V/Q. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Pulmonary angiogram in interventional radiology as the next imaging modality used
options.rationale: Pulmonary angiogram is invasive, carries higher radiation dose than CTPA or V/Q, and is reserved for cases where non-invasive imaging is non-diagnostic and PE confirmation is needed before catheter-directed therapy. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

options.text: Empirical therapeutic anticoagulation with apixaban orally without confirmatory imaging
options.rationale: Direct oral anticoagulants (apixaban, rivaroxaban) are contraindicated in pregnancy because of placental transfer and inadequate safety data. Empirical anticoagulation in pregnancy uses low-molecular-weight heparin (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily). However, imaging should be pursued promptly to confirm and guide duration; empirical treatment without imaging is appropriate only as a bridge if imaging delay is likely. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

explanation.summary: Suspected pulmonary embolism in pregnancy: start with chest X-ray and bilateral compression ultrasound of lower limbs. If CXR clear and CUS negative, V/Q scan is first-line imaging because of lower maternal breast radiation dose. CTPA reserved for abnormal CXR, underlying lung disease, or non-diagnostic V/Q. Empirical anticoagulation with low-molecular-weight heparin (NOT DOACs) is appropriate during imaging delay. D-dimer is not routinely used because it rises physiologically in pregnancy.
key_points: V/Q first-line in pregnancy with normal CXR (lower breast radiation)
CTPA reserved for abnormal CXR, underlying lung disease, non-diagnostic V/Q
Anticoagulation: LMWH only in pregnancy; DOACs contraindicated
explanation.pearls: Iliac vein DVT in pregnancy is missed on standard compression ultrasound (which scans femoral and popliteal); if clinical suspicion is high with negative routine CUS, request specific iliac vein imaging by Doppler or MRI venogram.

stem:
A 68-year-old man with chronic kidney disease stage 4 (baseline creatinine 280 micromol/L, eGFR 22) presents to the emergency department after his nephrology nurse rang him about an out-of-range potassium on a routine blood test. His usual medications include perindopril, spironolactone, frusemide, atorvastatin and a recently started course of trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 5 days (now day 4) for an uncomplicated UTI prescribed by his GP. He feels mildly weak but has no palpitations.

On arrival the triage nurse has placed him on a monitored bed. The medical registrar is at the bedside and the ECG is in front of you.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 56, BP 148/82 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 98% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, mild proximal limb weakness, no fasciculations, no flapping tremor, ECG monitor showing tall peaked T waves and widened QRS
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 7.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 380 micromol/L (45-90, baseline 280), sodium 134 mmol/L, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, calcium 2.32 mmol/L; ECG sinus bradycardia, tall peaked T waves in V2-V5, QRS 142 ms (broadened from baseline 110 ms), no P waves dropping
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, frusemide 40 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nocte, trimethoprim 300 mg daily (day 4)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first step?

options.text: Administer 10 units of intravenous short-acting insulin plus 50 mL of 50% dextrose IV
options.rationale: Insulin-dextrose drives potassium intracellularly and is effective but slower-onset than calcium for myocardial stabilisation. With ECG changes (broadened QRS, peaked T) the FIRST step is calcium for cardiac membrane stabilisation; insulin-dextrose comes immediately after. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Administer sodium bicarbonate 50 mmol intravenously over 5 minutes as first agent
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is most useful in hyperkalaemia with metabolic acidosis but is slow-onset and less effective than insulin-dextrose at lowering potassium. It is not the first step when ECG changes are present. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Administer 10 mL of 10% calcium gluconate intravenously over 5 to 10 minutes now
options.rationale: When hyperkalaemia produces ECG changes (peaked T waves, broadened QRS, loss of P waves, sine-wave pattern), the FIRST step is intravenous calcium gluconate (10 mL of 10% solution, or 30 mL diluted over 5 to 10 minutes) to stabilise the cardiac membrane. It works within 1 to 3 minutes and lasts 30 to 60 minutes. It does NOT lower potassium; insulin-dextrose, salbutamol nebuliser, and definitive removal by dialysis or sodium-binding resin (sodium zirconium cyclosilicate) follow. The trimethoprim is acting as a potassium-sparing agent (functional epithelial sodium channel inhibition like amiloride) on top of ACE inhibitor and spironolactone - withhold these. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Administer nebulised salbutamol 10 mg over 10 minutes as the first medication step
options.rationale: Salbutamol nebuliser drives potassium intracellularly and is a useful adjunct, but is not the FIRST step when ECG changes are present. Calcium first to stabilise the myocardium. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Arrange urgent haemodialysis via the on-call nephrology registrar before other measures
options.rationale: Haemodialysis is the definitive removal of potassium and is required here given CKD 4 with new AKI and severe hyperkalaemia. However, dialysis takes time to set up; calcium gluconate is the immediate first step to stabilise the myocardium while dialysis is arranged. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

explanation.summary: Severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes is a medical emergency. The order is: 1) IV calcium (gluconate or chloride) for cardiac membrane stabilisation, 2) insulin-dextrose and salbutamol nebuliser to shift potassium intracellularly, 3) definitive removal by dialysis (if AKI/severe CKD) or sodium zirconium cyclosilicate orally. Identify and stop precipitating drugs (ACE/ARB, MRA, trimethoprim, NSAIDs, potassium supplements). Trimethoprim functionally inhibits the epithelial sodium channel like amiloride and is a recognised cause of hyperkalaemia, especially with concomitant RAAS blockade.
key_points: Order: Calcium for cardiac stabilisation -> insulin-dextrose + salbutamol -> dialysis or binder
Trimethoprim acts like amiloride at the ENaC; hyperkalaemia risk multiplied with ACE/ARB/MRA
Calcium does NOT lower potassium - it buys time for definitive measures
explanation.pearls: If using calcium chloride instead of gluconate, give via central line because peripheral extravasation causes severe tissue necrosis; calcium gluconate is safer peripherally and provides equivalent membrane stabilisation at three times the volume.

stem:
A 42-year-old woman with a 3-month history of episodic headaches, palpitations and diaphoresis presents to the emergency department with severe headache and chest pain. Her GP referred her two weeks ago to endocrinology for ?phaeochromocytoma after recording a BP of 198/112 mmHg in clinic; 24-hour fractionated plasma metanephrines were markedly elevated (normetanephrine 8.2 nmol/L; reference <0.71). A CT abdomen showed a 4.2 cm right adrenal mass. Her appointment is scheduled in 9 days. She has not yet been started on alpha-blockade.

Her usual medications include ramipril and metoprolol prescribed for the hypertension by her GP. The medical registrar is at the bedside in the resuscitation cubicle.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 232/126 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 98% on 4 L/min via nasal prongs, temperature 37.1 °C
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, anxious, severe pounding headache, no focal neurology, pupils equal and reactive, no papilloedema, cardiac auscultation S1 S2 with a soft systolic flow murmur, no peripheral oedema, GCS 15
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia with no ST changes; troponin pending; FBC, UEC, LFTs within normal limits; CT brain shows no acute haemorrhage; urinalysis no proteinuria
data_table.Medications: Ramipril 10 mg daily, metoprolol 50 mg twice daily (started 4 weeks ago)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Increase metoprolol to 100 mg twice daily and add hydralazine 25 mg orally as an add-on
options.rationale: Beta-blocker monotherapy (or further beta-blockade) in phaeochromocytoma can paradoxically worsen hypertension by leaving alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed. Beta-blockade must NEVER be added before alpha-blockade is established in phaeochromocytoma. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Commence intravenous phentolamine 2 to 5 mg bolus with doses titrated to blood pressure
options.rationale: Phaeochromocytoma hypertensive crisis is managed with non-selective alpha-blockade FIRST. Phentolamine (a short-acting IV non-selective alpha-blocker) is the agent of choice for acute control while transitioning to oral phenoxybenzamine. Sodium nitroprusside or IV nicardipine may be alternative parenteral options where phentolamine is unavailable. Beta-blockade is added LATER, only after alpha-blockade is established and reflex tachycardia emerges. The patient has been on metoprolol without prior alpha-blockade, which is itself a precipitant; this should be paused. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Administer intravenous labetalol 20 mg bolus titrated to blood pressure as first agent
options.rationale: Labetalol is a mixed alpha and beta blocker but its alpha-blocking effect is relatively weak compared with its beta effect, and in phaeochromocytoma the predominant beta effect can worsen hypertension. It is not first-line in phaeochromocytoma crisis. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Administer intravenous amlodipine infusion at 5 mg per hour as a calcium channel blocker
options.rationale: Amlodipine is not available in IV form; it is oral only and has a slow onset (24 to 48 hours). Calcium channel blockers can be used as adjunctive oral therapy in phaeochromocytoma but are not first-line for acute crisis. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Administer intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g bolus then 1 g per hour as primary agent
options.rationale: Magnesium has been used as an adjunct in phaeochromocytoma anaesthesia and crisis but is not first-line; non-selective alpha-blockade with phentolamine is the standard initial agent. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

explanation.summary: Phaeochromocytoma hypertensive crisis is treated with non-selective alpha-blockade first. IV phentolamine is the agent of choice for acute control; sodium nitroprusside is an alternative. Beta-blockade is contraindicated until alpha-blockade is established because unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction worsens hypertension. After acute control, transition to oral phenoxybenzamine titrated against postural BP to a target of mild postural drop, followed by beta-blockade for residual tachycardia, with adequate fluid and sodium replacement before surgical resection at 7 to 14 days.
key_points: Alpha-blockade ALWAYS before beta-blockade in phaeochromocytoma
Phentolamine IV first-line for crisis; phenoxybenzamine oral for chronic preop
Beta-blocker monotherapy precipitates hypertensive crisis (unopposed alpha)
explanation.pearls: Pre-operative preparation needs 7 to 14 days of alpha-blockade with deliberate volume expansion (high sodium diet, IV saline if symptomatic postural drop) to prevent profound post-operative hypotension after tumour removal.

stem:
A 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and chronic venous insufficiency presents to the emergency department with a 36-hour history of rapidly spreading right leg pain and redness. He had a small dog bite on the shin 4 days ago that he managed at home with washing and a bandaid. Now the pain seems out of proportion to what he can see. He has rigors and feels very unwell. He has had no recent travel and no IV drug use.

On arrival the triage nurse fast-tracks him to the resuscitation cubicle. The surgical and medical registrars are at the bedside.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 26, SpO2 96% on 6 L/min via face mask, temperature 39.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Right leg shin to mid-thigh deep dusky erythema with poorly demarcated margins, severe tenderness extending well beyond the area of erythema, areas of grey-blue discolouration with bullae forming, foul-smelling exudate, no crepitus, no femoral or popliteal lymphadenopathy distally
data_table.Investigations: WCC 24 x10^9/L with neutrophilia, CRP 320 mg/L (<5), creatinine 168 micromol/L (45-90, baseline 92), sodium 130 mmol/L, glucose 18 mmol/L, lactate 4.2; CK 1820 U/L (<200); LRINEC score calculated as 9 (high-risk); plain X-ray right leg no gas in tissues; lactate venous 4.2
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1000 mg BD, atorvastatin 40 mg nocte

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Resuscitate, IV piperacillin-tazobactam plus clindamycin plus vancomycin, urgent surgery
options.rationale: The presentation (pain out of proportion, rapid progression, dusky skin with bullae, foul exudate, systemic toxicity, LRINEC 6+ high-risk, deranged renal function, lactate 4) is highly suspicious for necrotising fasciitis. The diagnosis is surgical, not radiological - imaging delays surgery and a normal CT does not exclude. Broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam OR meropenem) PLUS clindamycin (anti-toxin effect against group A streptococcus exotoxins) PLUS vancomycin (MRSA cover) are given immediately, but URGENT operative debridement is the only intervention that changes mortality. Australian guidance supports this combination empirically. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Admit, mark erythema borders, intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g 4-hourly, review in 6 hours
options.rationale: Standard cellulitis management understages this presentation. Pain out of proportion, bullae, dusky skin, lactate 4 and LRINEC 9 indicate necrotising fasciitis - delay of even hours increases mortality from approximately 25% to over 50%. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange urgent CT with contrast of the right lower limb before any surgical referral
options.rationale: Imaging may show fascial thickening, gas or fluid tracking, but the diagnosis is clinical and imaging delays surgery. Urgent surgical referral does not wait for CT in a patient with classic features. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Give intramuscular benzylpenicillin 1.2 g for presumed streptococcal cellulitis only
options.rationale: IM benzylpenicillin is dose-inappropriate for severe sepsis and does not cover Gram-negative or anaerobic flora seen in necrotising fasciitis (especially after a dog bite). Polymicrobial cover is required while awaiting surgical exploration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Give a single dose of oral clindamycin 600 mg with admission for observation overnight
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics are inadequate for septic shock from necrotising fasciitis. IV broad-spectrum antibiotics plus immediate surgery are mandatory. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical diagnosis suggested by pain out of proportion, rapid progression, dusky skin or bullae, systemic toxicity, raised CK, raised lactate and high LRINEC score (6+ high-risk). Empirical antibiotics: piperacillin-tazobactam OR meropenem PLUS clindamycin (anti-toxin) PLUS vancomycin (MRSA). Urgent surgical debridement is the only intervention that reduces mortality. Polymicrobial type I (diabetic, mixed aerobic/anaerobic) and monomicrobial type II (group A strep) are the two main forms.
key_points: Pain out of proportion + systemic toxicity = think necrotising fasciitis
Diagnosis is surgical - do not delay operative debridement for imaging
Clindamycin is essential for anti-toxin effect against group A strep
explanation.pearls: Aeromonas and Vibrio vulnificus necrotising fasciitis follow freshwater and seawater exposure respectively; consider ceftriaxone plus doxycycline or fluoroquinolone in the empirical regimen when the history is consistent with water exposure.

stem:
A 54-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis (anti-AChR positive, on pyridostigmine 60 mg every 4 hours and prednisolone 20 mg daily) is brought to the emergency department by ambulance. Over the last 3 days she has had a productive cough and has been increasing her pyridostigmine dose without medical advice because her weakness has been worse. Today she became more dyspnoeic, diaphoretic and developed abdominal cramps with diarrhoea. Her partner reports increased oral secretions.

On arrival she is fatigued but alert. The neurology and ICU registrars are at the bedside; she has been moved to the resuscitation cubicle and a bedside FVC is being measured.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 56, BP 124/76 mmHg, RR 28, SpO2 92% on 8 L/min via face mask, temperature 37.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, increased oral secretions and lacrimation, miosis with sluggish reaction, generalised muscle weakness MRC 3/5 in all limbs, neck flexion weakness, fasciculations present in upper limbs, abdominal cramps, no rash, no fever above 37.6, no ptosis change documented, FVC 0.85 L (predicted 3.2 L), negative inspiratory force -18 cmH2O (target more negative than -30)
data_table.Investigations: Arterial blood gas pH 7.30, pCO2 56, PaO2 68 mmHg on FiO2 0.5, HCO3 26; CK 320 U/L (<200); chest X-ray small right basal infiltrate; ECG sinus bradycardia with no AV block
data_table.Medications: Pyridostigmine increased from 60 mg every 4 hours to 90 mg every 3 hours by patient over the last 24 hours; prednisolone 20 mg daily, mycophenolate 1 g BD

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Increase pyridostigmine dose to 120 mg every 3 hours and start intravenous plasma exchange
options.rationale: Increasing pyridostigmine in a patient who has been self-titrating, now showing muscarinic features (miosis, secretions, lacrimation, cramps, diarrhoea, bradycardia, fasciculations) along with weakness suggests cholinergic crisis from over-dosing rather than under-treated myasthenic crisis. Increasing the dose worsens the picture. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Administer intravenous neostigmine 0.5 mg as a confirmatory edrophonium-equivalent test
options.rationale: Giving more cholinesterase inhibitor in suspected cholinergic crisis is contraindicated; the historical edrophonium (Tensilon) test has fallen out of practice for this reason. Differentiation of myasthenic from cholinergic crisis is now based on clinical features and response to atropine and cessation of pyridostigmine. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Withhold pyridostigmine, give intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg and prepare for intubation
options.rationale: IVIG is appropriate treatment for myasthenic crisis but does not address the cholinergic component here and the muscarinic features (secretions, bradycardia, miosis, cramps) point to over-treatment. Withholding pyridostigmine is appropriate; IVIG can follow once cholinergic features resolve and pure myasthenic weakness is confirmed. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Withhold pyridostigmine, atropine 0.5 to 1 mg IV for muscarinic features, prepare to intubate
