options.rationale: The combination of weakness with muscarinic excess (miosis, increased oral secretions, lacrimation, bradycardia, abdominal cramps, diarrhoea, fasciculations) in a patient who has been self-escalating pyridostigmine is consistent with cholinergic crisis OR a mixed cholinergic-myasthenic picture. The correct response is to WITHHOLD pyridostigmine, give atropine 0.5 to 1 mg IV titrated for muscarinic features, and intubate given FVC below 1 L, NIF less negative than -20, rising CO2 and clinical respiratory failure. Once intubated and stabilised, treat underlying myasthenic exacerbation with IVIG or plasma exchange, and identify and treat the precipitant (here the chest infection). (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Administer pralidoxime 30 mg/kg intravenously as a cholinesterase reactivator agent
options.rationale: Pralidoxime is used in organophosphate poisoning, not in pyridostigmine-induced cholinergic excess; pyridostigmine causes reversible cholinesterase inhibition that resolves with cessation. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

explanation.summary: Cholinergic crisis from over-treatment with cholinesterase inhibitors produces muscarinic (SLUDGE: salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI cramps, emesis, plus miosis, bradycardia, bronchorrhoea) AND nicotinic (weakness, fasciculations) features. Myasthenic crisis presents with weakness alone without muscarinic features. The historical edrophonium test has been replaced by careful clinical assessment and a trial of cholinesterase withdrawal. Management: withhold pyridostigmine, atropine for muscarinic features, intubation for respiratory failure (FVC under 1 L, NIF less negative than -20, rising pCO2), and treat the underlying exacerbation with IVIG or plasma exchange.
key_points: Cholinergic crisis: muscarinic excess + weakness; myasthenic crisis: weakness only
Respiratory intubation thresholds: FVC <1 L, NIF less negative than -20 cmH2O
Treatment of underlying exacerbation: IVIG or plasma exchange after stabilisation
explanation.pearls: Common precipitants of myasthenic crisis: infections (especially respiratory), aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, beta-blockers, magnesium, neuromuscular blockade and pregnancy/postpartum - always identify and remove the trigger as part of crisis management.

stem:
A 38-year-old woman is admitted to the high-dependency unit with progressive ascending weakness over the last 5 days. She had gastroenteritis 3 weeks ago with documented Campylobacter on stool culture from her GP. Her weakness began as foot tingling, then ankle weakness, climbing proximally. She now cannot stand without assistance. She has not had any cranial nerve involvement until this morning, when she developed mild bilateral facial weakness. She has noticed labile blood pressure and has had two brief episodes of marked tachycardia followed by transient bradycardia today.

Bedside FVC 1.4 L (predicted 3.0 L) and is trending down. The neurology and ICU registrars are at the bedside.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse fluctuates between 50 and 130 over the last hour, BP fluctuates between 168/96 and 92/56 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 96% in room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Lower limb power MRC 2/5 distally and 3/5 proximally, upper limb power 4/5 throughout, bilateral mild facial weakness, areflexia in all four limbs, glove-and-stocking sensory loss to vibration and proprioception, FVC 1.4 L (down from 2.0 L 8 hours ago), no cough impairment yet, no swallowing difficulty
data_table.Investigations: Lumbar puncture protein 1.8 g/L (<0.45) with cell count 4/microL (albuminocytologic dissociation); MRI lumbar spine shows enhancement of cauda equina nerve roots; nerve conduction studies pending; FBC, UEC, LFTs within normal limits; ECG bradycardia at present without AV block

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily and observe with serial neurological examination
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are NOT effective in Guillain-Barre syndrome (multiple trials have shown no benefit). Steroids are used in chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP), not in GBS. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Intubate immediately and commence mechanical ventilation regardless of vital capacity
options.rationale: Intubation is required when FVC falls below approximately 20 mL/kg (about 1.0 to 1.2 L in adults), MIP less negative than -30, MEP under 40, or there is bulbar dysfunction with aspiration risk (the so-called 20-30-40 rule). At FVC 1.4 L with downward trend, immediate intubation is premature; close monitoring with intubation when criteria met is appropriate, alongside specific therapy. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Administer atropine 0.5 mg intravenously and start a continuous noradrenaline infusion
options.rationale: Treating individual autonomic events symptomatically may be necessary but does not address the underlying disease; autonomic instability resolves with treatment of the GBS itself. The fundamental treatment is IVIG or plasma exchange, with cardiac monitoring for arrhythmia. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Commence plasma exchange of 5 sessions over 2 weeks as the disease-modifying therapy
options.rationale: Plasma exchange is an equally effective treatment to IVIG in GBS but is less practical in many Australian centres, requires central venous access and is generally reserved for patients in whom IVIG is contraindicated or fails. IVIG is the more commonly used first-line. Either is acceptable; the key point is that disease-modifying therapy is needed now. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

options.text: Commence intravenous immunoglobulin 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days with HDU cardiac monitoring
options.rationale: Guillain-Barre syndrome with progressive weakness, autonomic instability and falling FVC warrants prompt disease-modifying therapy with IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days (total 2 g/kg). Plasma exchange is an equivalent alternative. Concurrent management includes HDU/ICU level monitoring for autonomic instability (cardiac telemetry), serial FVC and NIF every 2 to 4 hours, DVT prophylaxis, and intubation criteria readiness. Steroids are not effective. Autonomic instability (labile BP, tachy-brady) is a major cause of mortality and necessitates HDU/ICU. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

explanation.summary: Guillain-Barre syndrome is treated with IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days (or plasma exchange 5 sessions over 2 weeks - equivalent efficacy). Corticosteroids are NOT effective. Monitor for respiratory failure (FVC, NIF, MIP/MEP - 20-30-40 rule: FVC less than 20 mL/kg, MIP less negative than -30, MEP less than 40 triggers intubation) and autonomic dysfunction (cardiac arrhythmia, labile BP) - both are major causes of mortality. Common precipitants: Campylobacter jejuni, CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma, vaccinations (rare). Recovery over weeks to months; residual disability in 20%.
key_points: IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day x 5 days OR plasma exchange; steroids ineffective
20-30-40 rule for ventilatory support thresholds
Autonomic dysfunction is a major mortality contributor - HDU monitoring mandatory
explanation.pearls: The Miller Fisher variant of GBS presents with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia without prominent limb weakness; anti-GQ1b antibody is positive in over 85% and is the diagnostic test of choice when this triad is seen.

stem:
A 56-year-old man presents to your general practice with a 2-day history of a red, painful, hot patch on the medial aspect of his right shin. He recalls a minor abrasion gardening 4 days ago. He has type 2 diabetes managed with metformin (HbA1c 6.8% last month), no prior MRSA, and no penicillin allergy. He is systemically well, afebrile, and has a clear margin on the cellulitis that you outline with a marker.

On examination there is a 12 cm by 8 cm area of warmth, erythema, and tenderness on the medial right shin without lymphangitic streaking, abscess, or crepitus. Distal pulses are intact and sensation is preserved. There is no necrosis, bullae, or pain disproportionate to examination.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, BP 134/82 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: 12 x 8 cm area of warmth and erythema medial right shin, marker outlined, no abscess, no crepitus, intact pulses, normal sensation, no lymphangitic streaking
data_table.Investigations: Capillary glucose 8.2 mmol/L, recent HbA1c 6.8% (4.0-6.0 normal); no bloods done today

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral cefalexin 500 mg four times daily for 5 days as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Cefalexin is reasonable but at 500 mg QID covers streptococci adequately but has weaker beta-lactamase stability against community methicillin-susceptible S. aureus than flucloxacillin in AU practice. eTG prefers flucloxacillin first-line for non-purulent cellulitis without MRSA risk factors. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily via hospital in the home for 5 days
options.rationale: IV antibiotics are indicated when systemic sepsis features are present (sepsis criteria, rapid progression, failure of oral therapy), in immunosuppressed patients, or for facial cellulitis; this patient is systemically well with limited disease and well-controlled diabetes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral clindamycin 450 mg three times daily for 7 days as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Clindamycin is reserved for non-severe penicillin allergy or where MRSA cover is needed. It is not first-line in non-purulent cellulitis without MRSA risk factors. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg twice daily for 7 days
options.rationale: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is used when MRSA is suspected or confirmed and is not standard first-line cover for streptococcal cellulitis where streptococci are the predominant organism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral flucloxacillin 500 mg four times daily for 5 days for this patient
options.rationale: eTG recommends oral flucloxacillin 500 mg every 6 hours for 5 days as first-line for non-purulent cellulitis in an adult without MRSA risk factors or severe sepsis; it covers Streptococcus pyogenes and methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus, the predominant causative organisms. Mark the erythema border and reassess at 48 hours. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: eTG first-line for non-purulent cellulitis in an adult without MRSA risk factors and without severe sepsis is oral flucloxacillin 500 mg every 6 hours for 5 days. Mark the margin and reassess at 48 hours; escalate to IV if no improvement, sepsis develops, or rapid progression. Clindamycin or TMP-SMX is for non-severe penicillin allergy or MRSA cover. IV therapy is reserved for systemic illness or facial/orbital cellulitis.
key_points: First-line non-purulent cellulitis: flucloxacillin 500 mg QID 5 days
Cefalexin is reasonable but second-choice in AU practice
TMP-SMX or clindamycin if MRSA risk or non-severe penicillin allergy
IV therapy: systemic illness, rapid progression, facial cellulitis
explanation.pearls: Marking the erythema border with a marker and reassessing at 48 hours is an underused practical bedside test that tells you whether the antibiotic is working before changing therapy.

stem:
A 68-year-old woman attends your GP clinic for review after a minimal-trauma distal radius fracture sustained 6 weeks ago. She is otherwise well, post-menopausal since age 51, with no fragility fractures previously. Her mother had a hip fracture at age 72. She is on no regular medications. Her renal function is normal (eGFR 88 mL/min/1.73 m^2), serum calcium 2.36 mmol/L, vitamin D 78 nmol/L, and PTH within normal limits.

DEXA scan shows lumbar spine T-score -2.7 and femoral neck T-score -2.5. FRAX 10-year hip fracture probability is 6.2% and major osteoporotic fracture 14.5%. She has good dental health with no upcoming invasive dental procedures. She prefers oral therapy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 132/82 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Well-healed distal radius scar, no kyphosis, no spinal tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Calcium corrected 2.36 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), phosphate 1.05 mmol/L, vitamin D 78 nmol/L, PTH 4.6 pmol/L (1.6-6.9), eGFR 88 mL/min/1.73 m^2, TSH 1.8 mIU/L, DEXA L-spine T -2.7, F-neck T -2.5
data_table.Medications: Calcium 600 mg + vitamin D 800 IU daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence oral alendronate 70 mg once weekly with calcium and vitamin D, falls assessment, and rebook DEXA in 2 years
options.rationale: Postmenopausal woman with a minimal-trauma fracture plus DEXA T-score ≤-2.5 meets PBS-funded criteria for anti-resorptive therapy. Oral alendronate 70 mg weekly is first-line in patients with normal renal function and no high-risk dental procedures or oesophageal contraindication; calcium and vitamin D are maintained; falls assessment is added. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis)

options.text: Commence denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously every 6 months with the proposed clinical action
options.rationale: Denosumab is an alternative anti-resorptive and is preferred for renal impairment (eGFR <35) or oral bisphosphonate intolerance. With normal renal function and patient preference for oral therapy, oral alendronate is first-line. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis)

options.text: Commence teriparatide 20 mcg subcutaneously daily for 18 months with the proposed clinical action
options.rationale: Teriparatide is an anabolic agent reserved for severe osteoporosis with multiple vertebral fractures, very low T-score, or failure of anti-resorptive therapy; it is not first-line in this case. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis)

options.text: Continue calcium and vitamin D only and recheck DEXA in 12 months as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Calcium and vitamin D alone are insufficient when osteoporosis is established with a recent minimal-trauma fracture; PBS-funded pharmacotherapy is indicated and delay increases re-fracture risk. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis)

options.text: Commence menopausal hormone therapy with conjugated oestrogens and medroxyprogesterone as the proposed approach
options.rationale: MHT is no longer first-line for osteoporosis given thromboembolic, stroke, and breast cancer risks in older postmenopausal women, particularly more than 10 years from menopause as in this case. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis)

explanation.summary: A postmenopausal woman with minimal-trauma fracture plus DEXA T-score ≤-2.5 meets PBS criteria for anti-resorptive therapy. Oral alendronate 70 mg weekly is first-line in normal renal function with no dental contraindication. Denosumab is preferred for renal impairment or oral intolerance. Teriparatide is for severe disease. MHT is no longer first-line for osteoporosis in older women.
key_points: Minimal-trauma fracture + T ≤-2.5 = anti-resorptive eligible
First-line: alendronate 70 mg weekly if eGFR ≥35 and no dental contraindication
Denosumab if renal impairment or oral intolerance
Calcium 1000 mg/day + vitamin D 800-1000 IU/day
explanation.pearls: PBS osteoporosis criteria in AU include minimal-trauma fragility fracture in adults aged 70+ OR DEXA T-score ≤-2.5; either alone meets the eligibility threshold.

stem:
A 28-year-old woman presents to your neurology clinic 3 weeks after acute onset of blurred vision and pain on movement of her right eye lasting 10 days, now resolving. There is no preceding viral illness, no recent travel, and no family history of demyelinating disease. She has a 6-month-old breastfed child and is otherwise well.

On examination today her visual acuity is 6/9 right and 6/6 left with a relative afferent pupillary defect on the right. Fundoscopy shows mild right optic disc pallor. Neurological examination is otherwise normal. MRI brain demonstrates three periventricular and one juxtacortical T2 hyperintense lesion with no enhancement on gadolinium; MRI cervical spine shows one short-segment lesion. CSF reveals oligoclonal bands positive in CSF, absent in serum.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 14, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5 °C
data_table.Examination: Right visual acuity 6/9, left 6/6, right RAPD positive, mild right disc pallor, no internuclear ophthalmoplegia, no nystagmus, motor and sensory examination normal, no cerebellar signs
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain: 3 periventricular + 1 juxtacortical T2 lesions, no gadolinium enhancement; MRI cervical spine: 1 short-segment T2 lesion; CSF: oligoclonal bands positive in CSF (negative in serum), normal cell count, glucose, protein; aquaporin-4 IgG and MOG-IgG negative

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency myelopathy with subacute combined degeneration
options.rationale: Subacute combined degeneration causes dorsal column and corticospinal tract signs, often peripheral neuropathy and megaloblastic anaemia. It does not cause optic neuritis with periventricular MRI lesions and OCBs. (Source: BMJ Best Practice MS)

options.text: Clinically isolated syndrome alone, not yet meeting MS criteria
options.rationale: CIS describes a first clinical event without dissemination in time evidence; here CSF oligoclonal bands plus DIS substitute for DIT under the 2017 McDonald criteria, making this MS rather than isolated CIS. (Source: 2017 McDonald Criteria)

options.text: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) as the proposed approach
options.rationale: NMOSD typically presents with longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (3+ vertebral segments) or severe optic neuritis with aquaporin-4 IgG positivity; AQP4-IgG is negative here and lesion patterns are consistent with MS. (Source: International NMOSD Criteria)

options.text: MOG antibody disease with the proposed clinical action
options.rationale: MOG-IgG is negative; MOGAD typically presents with bilateral optic neuritis, ADEM-like episodes, or longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, with a different MRI pattern. (Source: MOGAD Criteria)

options.text: Multiple sclerosis (relapsing-remitting) by 2017 McDonald criteria
options.rationale: Dissemination in space is met by typical MRI lesions in two or more CNS locations (here periventricular and juxtacortical plus spinal). Dissemination in time is met by CSF-specific oligoclonal bands (acceptable substitute for a second clinical attack or enhancing lesion under 2017 McDonald criteria). The clinical syndrome of optic neuritis with positive lesion and OCBs supports RRMS diagnosis. (Source: 2017 McDonald Criteria)

explanation.summary: The 2017 McDonald criteria allow CSF-specific oligoclonal bands to substitute for dissemination in time. With one clinical attack (optic neuritis) and DIS demonstrated on MRI plus CSF OCBs, the diagnosis advances from CIS to relapsing-remitting MS, allowing earlier initiation of disease-modifying therapy. AQP4 and MOG antibody testing are mandatory in atypical presentations to exclude NMOSD and MOGAD respectively.
key_points: 2017 McDonald: OCBs substitute for DIT
DIS: lesions in ≥2 of 4 typical locations (periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial, spinal)
Test AQP4 and MOG to exclude alternatives
Earlier diagnosis = earlier DMT = better long-term outcome
explanation.pearls: The 2017 McDonald update shifted OCBs from a supportive feature to an accepted substitute for DIT, enabling MS diagnosis at the first clinical event in many patients and earlier DMT initiation.

stem:
A 52-year-old woman with established AChR antibody-positive myasthenia gravis on pyridostigmine 60 mg six times daily and prednisolone 20 mg daily is brought to the emergency department with worsening dyspnoea, dysphagia, and bilateral ptosis. She had a mild upper respiratory infection 5 days ago, and her treating neurologist increased her pyridostigmine from 4 to 6 doses daily 2 days ago.

In the emergency department she is anxious and breathless with shallow respirations. She has bilateral ptosis, weak shoulder abduction, and difficulty swallowing her saliva. Her pupils are 3 mm and reactive, mucous membranes are dry, and bowel sounds are normal. Arterial blood gas shows pH 7.32, pCO2 56 mmHg, pO2 78 mmHg on room air, with bedside FVC measured at 1.0 L (predicted 3.4 L).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 132/86 mmHg, RR 28, SpO2 92% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Bilateral ptosis, fatigable shoulder abduction, dysarthria, pooling secretions, paradoxical abdominal breathing, no fasciculations, pupils 3 mm reactive, dry mucous membranes
data_table.Investigations: ABG pH 7.32, pCO2 56 mmHg, pO2 78 mmHg, HCO3 28; FVC 1.0 L (predicted 3.4 L), single breath count 12; sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, urea 5 mmol/L, troponin <5 ng/L, viral swab pending
data_table.Medications: Pyridostigmine 60 mg 6x daily (recently increased from 4x), prednisolone 20 mg daily, calcium and vitamin D

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Pulmonary embolism; commence therapeutic enoxaparin and arrange CTPA as the proposed approach with the proposed clinical action
options.rationale: Pyrexia, normal troponin, and clinical features of bulbar weakness with ptosis are characteristic of myasthenic crisis, not PE; ABG shows hypercapnia (PE typically hypocapnia with type 1 respiratory failure). (Source: BMJ Best Practice MG)

options.text: Cholinergic crisis; administer atropine 0.6 mg IV and continue pyridostigmine as the proposed approach with the proposed clinical action
options.rationale: Cholinergic crisis presents with miosis, fasciculations, hypersalivation, lacrimation, diarrhoea, and bradycardia (SLUDGE/miosis), which are absent here. Dry mucous membranes and normal pupil size point to myasthenic, not cholinergic, crisis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Neurology)

options.text: Myasthenic crisis; arrange ICU admission for non-invasive ventilation or intubation, withhold pyridostigmine temporarily, and commence plasmapheresis or IVIG
options.rationale: Bilateral ptosis with bulbar weakness, paradoxical breathing, hypercapnia (pCO2 56 mmHg) and FVC under 1 L (or 15 mL/kg) define myasthenic crisis. Initial trigger here was viral illness. Distinguishing from cholinergic crisis: pupils normal-sized, mucous membranes dry (not wet), no fasciculations, bowel sounds normal - all favouring myasthenic rather than cholinergic crisis. Treatment is airway protection (NIV or intubation), withholding pyridostigmine to remove ambiguity, and immunomodulation with plasmapheresis or IVIG. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Neurology)

options.text: Asthma exacerbation; administer nebulised salbutamol and IV hydrocortisone as the proposed approach with the proposed clinical action
options.rationale: Asthma exacerbation does not cause bilateral ptosis, dysphagia, or fatigable shoulder weakness, and the respiratory failure here is from neuromuscular weakness not bronchoconstriction. Wheeze is absent. (Source: BMJ Best Practice MG)

options.text: Anxiety hyperventilation; reassure and arrange anxiolytic as the proposed approach with the proposed clinical action as the proposed clinical action
options.rationale: Hyperventilation would cause hypocapnia, not hypercapnia, and would not produce bilateral ptosis or bulbar features. The objective ABG and FVC exclude anxiety as cause. (Source: BMJ Best Practice MG)

explanation.summary: Myasthenic crisis: FVC <15 mL/kg or <1 L, weak cough, respiratory failure, often triggered by infection or medication. Cholinergic crisis (excess pyridostigmine): SLUDGE/miosis with fasciculations and bronchorrhoea. Pupil size and secretions are the bedside discriminators. Management of myasthenic crisis is airway/ventilation support, withholding pyridostigmine temporarily, and plasmapheresis or IVIG to remove circulating antibodies.
key_points: Myasthenic: normal pupils, dry membranes, no fasciculations
Cholinergic: miosis, fasciculations, SLUDGE
FVC <1 L or <15 mL/kg is crisis threshold
Withhold pyridostigmine, IVIG or plasmapheresis, ICU
explanation.pearls: Cholinergic crisis is rare in modern practice as pyridostigmine doses are usually conservative; assume myasthenic crisis until cholinergic features (miosis, fasciculations, bronchorrhoea) prove otherwise.

stem:
A 62-year-old man with long-standing hypertension and a 30-pack-year smoking history presents to the emergency department with sudden severe interscapular and chest pain that began 90 minutes ago while gardening. He describes it as tearing in quality, peaking immediately at onset. He has no nausea, no diaphoresis, and no exertional component. He has no known prior cardiovascular event.

In the resuscitation bay, his right arm BP is 168/96 mmHg and left arm BP is 132/82 mmHg. Pulse 88, regular. Chest auscultation reveals a soft early diastolic murmur best heard at the left sternal edge. ECG shows sinus rhythm with non-specific lateral T-wave flattening. Bedside troponin is below the rule-in threshold. Chest X-ray shows widening of the upper mediastinum. He is hypertensive, alert, and orientated.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP right arm 168/96 mmHg, left arm 132/82 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Soft early diastolic murmur left sternal edge, no carotid bruit, peripheral pulses intact bilaterally, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus, non-specific lateral T flattening; troponin <5 ng/L; chest X-ray widened mediastinum; D-dimer pending; FBC and creatinine within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 8 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for urgent coronary angiogram for suspected NSTEMI as the proposed approach with the proposed clinical action
options.rationale: Coronary angiography with anticoagulation in dissection causes catastrophic bleeding; dissection must be excluded before any invasive coronary procedure even when troponin rises (which can occur with coronary ostia involvement in dissection). (Source: ESC Aortic Dissection)

options.text: Administer aspirin 300 mg, ticagrelor 180 mg, and IV heparin while awaiting troponin trend as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Dual antiplatelet therapy and anticoagulation in suspected aortic dissection cause catastrophic bleeding into the false lumen and pericardial space; ACS treatment is contraindicated until dissection is excluded. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular)

options.text: Bolus IV glyceryl trinitrate without rate control to lower blood pressure rapidly as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Vasodilators alone increase reflex tachycardia and aortic wall stress; beta-blockade must precede or accompany any vasodilator therapy to control rate and dP/dt before reducing BP. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular)

options.text: Arrange transthoracic echocardiogram and discharge pending outpatient follow-up as the proposed approach
options.rationale: TTE sensitivity for aortic dissection is limited (especially descending dissection) and discharge of a patient with classical dissection features is unsafe; CT aortogram or TOE is required urgently. (Source: ESC Aortic Dissection)

options.text: Urgent contrast-enhanced CT aortogram and immediate IV labetalol infusion targeting systolic BP 100-120 mmHg and heart rate under 60
options.rationale: Sudden tearing interscapular pain, blood pressure differential between arms over 20 mmHg, aortic regurgitation murmur and widened mediastinum strongly suggest acute aortic dissection. Urgent CT aortogram is the diagnostic modality of choice in the haemodynamically stable patient; meanwhile rapid IV beta-blockade (labetalol or esmolol) targeting heart rate under 60 and systolic BP 100-120 mmHg reduces aortic wall shear stress. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection is suggested by sudden severe tearing chest/back pain, inter-arm BP differential over 20 mmHg, aortic regurgitation murmur, and widened mediastinum. CT aortogram is the diagnostic standard. Treatment targets rate first (HR under 60 with beta-blockade) then BP (systolic 100-120 mmHg). ACS therapy is contraindicated until dissection is excluded. Type A dissections require emergency cardiothoracic surgery; type B is medical unless complicated.
key_points: Pain quality + BP differential + AR murmur + widened mediastinum
CT aortogram is diagnostic standard
Beta-blocker first (rate, dP/dt), then vasodilator
Avoid ACS treatment until dissection excluded
explanation.pearls: Treating dissection like ACS with antiplatelets and anticoagulants is the high-yield exam disconfirming step; the inter-arm BP differential >20 mmHg with an early diastolic murmur in a hypertensive smoker is the picture that must override the ACS reflex.

stem:
A 28-year-old tall thin man is brought into the emergency department after sudden onset right-sided chest pain and shortness of breath 30 minutes ago while playing basketball. He has no past history. On arrival he is alert but pale and diaphoretic. His trachea is shifted to the left, the right hemithorax is hyperresonant with absent breath sounds, and his jugular venous pressure is markedly elevated.

He rapidly deteriorates with hypotension and worsening hypoxia. Pulse 138, BP 84/52 mmHg, RR 32, SpO2 88% on 15 L non-rebreather. A bedside lung ultrasound shows absent lung sliding and a 'barcode sign' on the right.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138, BP 84/52 mmHg, RR 32, SpO2 88% on 15 L non-rebreather, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Trachea deviated to left, right hemithorax hyperresonant with absent breath sounds, JVP elevated, peripheral cool, no surgical emphysema
data_table.Investigations: Bedside lung ultrasound: absent lung sliding right, barcode sign right; ECG sinus tachycardia; chest X-ray deferred for time-critical management

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Pericardiocentesis under ultrasound guidance as the proposed approach with the proposed clinical action
options.rationale: Cardiac tamponade produces muffled heart sounds, equal breath sounds bilaterally, and pulsus paradoxus; the clinical picture and ultrasound here are pneumothorax, not tamponade. (Source: ATLS 10th Edition)

options.text: Urgent chest X-ray before any intervention as the proposed approach with the proposed clinical action as the proposed clinical action
options.rationale: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis; waiting for imaging delays life-saving decompression and risks cardiac arrest. Bedside ultrasound has already confirmed pneumothorax (absent sliding, barcode sign). (Source: ATLS 10th Edition)

options.text: Endotracheal intubation and positive-pressure ventilation to improve oxygenation as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Positive-pressure ventilation in tension pneumothorax can convert a simple pneumothorax to tension and rapidly worsens haemodynamics; decompression must precede intubation when tension is suspected. (Source: ATLS 10th Edition)

options.text: IV fluids and noradrenaline to support BP while awaiting cardiothoracic surgery as the proposed approach
options.rationale: Fluids and vasopressors do not address the obstructive cause of shock; chest decompression is the only effective intervention. (Source: ATLS 10th Edition)

options.text: Needle decompression of the right hemithorax in the 4th-5th intercostal space, anterior axillary line, followed by intercostal catheter
options.rationale: Tension pneumothorax with haemodynamic compromise requires immediate decompression. AU and ATLS now recommend the 4th-5th intercostal space anterior or mid-axillary line as the preferred site in adults (replacing the 2nd ICS midclavicular site for higher reliability in adult chest wall thickness), followed by formal intercostal catheter for definitive drainage. (Source: ATLS 10th Edition)

explanation.summary: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis identified by haemodynamic compromise with tracheal deviation, ipsilateral hyperresonance and absent breath sounds, raised JVP, and hypoxia. Immediate needle decompression in the 4th-5th ICS anterior or mid-axillary line is followed by formal intercostal catheter. Positive-pressure ventilation before decompression can precipitate cardiac arrest. Lung ultrasound (absent sliding, barcode sign) confirms the diagnosis at the bedside.
key_points: Clinical diagnosis - decompress before imaging
4th-5th ICS anterior/mid-axillary line preferred in adults (ATLS 10)
Avoid positive-pressure ventilation pre-decompression
Formal intercostal catheter follows needle decompression
explanation.pearls: ATLS 10th edition moved adult needle decompression from 2nd ICS midclavicular to 4th-5th ICS anterior/mid-axillary because the lateral chest wall is consistently thinner and the needle more reliably reaches the pleural space.

stem:
A 58-year-old woman is referred to your respiratory clinic with progressive right-sided pleural effusion. She had a thoracic spine T8-T10 fusion 6 weeks ago for traumatic vertebral compression after a motor vehicle accident. She has lost 4 kg since surgery and is mildly breathless on exertion. Diagnostic pleural aspiration today yields 60 mL of milky white fluid.

Fluid biochemistry returns later: pleural total protein 38 g/L (serum 65 g/L), pleural LDH 280 U/L (serum 220 U/L, upper normal 250), pleural pH 7.42, glucose 5.1 mmol/L, cell count 1900 cells/microL with 92% lymphocytes. Pleural cholesterol 1.8 mmol/L. Cytology shows mature lymphocytes with no malignant cells.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 86, BP 122/76 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Stony dull right base with reduced breath sounds and decreased tactile fremitus, no clubbing, no peripheral oedema, no palpable lymphadenopathy, thoracic spine surgical scar healing
data_table.Investigations: Pleural fluid: milky white, total protein 38 g/L (serum 65 g/L), LDH 280 U/L (serum 220), pH 7.42, glucose 5.1 mmol/L, cell count 1900 cells/microL with 92% lymphocytes; cholesterol 1.8 mmol/L; cytology mature lymphocytes; CT thorax pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate confirmatory investigation?

options.text: Pleural fluid amylase; raised amylase confirms pancreatic pleural fistula
options.rationale: Raised pleural amylase suggests pancreatic effusion or oesophageal rupture, neither of which is supported by the post-thoracic-surgery context with milky lymphocytic fluid. (Source: BTS Pleural Disease)

options.text: Pleural fluid cholesterol confirms chylothorax if above 5.18 mmol/L
options.rationale: High cholesterol with low triglyceride is the signature of pseudochylothorax (chronic effusions from RA, TB, old empyema), not true chylothorax. Triglyceride is the discriminator for chylothorax. (Source: BTS Pleural Disease)

options.text: Pleural fluid ADA level; above 40 U/L confirms tuberculous pleurisy
options.rationale: ADA is useful in suspected TB pleural effusion but the milky appearance and post-thoracic-surgery context point to chylothorax; ADA does not confirm chylothorax. (Source: BTS Pleural Disease)

options.text: Pleural fluid Gram stain and culture; positive culture confirms empyema
options.rationale: Empyema fluid is purulent with pH below 7.20, glucose below 2.2 mmol/L, and high neutrophils; this fluid has normal pH, normal glucose, and lymphocyte predominance, excluding empyema. (Source: BTS Pleural Disease)

options.text: Send pleural fluid triglyceride; a level above 1.24 mmol/L confirms chylothorax
options.rationale: Milky pleural fluid with high lymphocyte count after thoracic surgery is highly suspicious for chylothorax from thoracic duct injury. Pleural fluid triglyceride above 1.24 mmol/L (110 mg/dL) confirms chylothorax; below 0.56 mmol/L (50 mg/dL) excludes it. The intermediate range requires lipoprotein electrophoresis for chylomicrons. Cholesterol level differentiates pseudochylothorax (cholesterol >5.18 mmol/L with low triglyceride) from true chylothorax. (Source: BTS Pleural Disease)

explanation.summary: Chylothorax presents as milky pleural fluid from thoracic duct injury, often after thoracic, oesophageal, or cardiac surgery. Diagnosis is by pleural fluid triglyceride: above 1.24 mmol/L confirms; below 0.56 mmol/L excludes; intermediate requires chylomicron electrophoresis. Pseudochylothorax (cholesterol >5.18 mmol/L, low triglyceride) is seen in chronic inflammatory effusions. Management is dietary fat restriction with medium-chain triglycerides, octreotide, and thoracic duct ligation or embolisation for refractory cases.
key_points: Pleural triglyceride >1.24 mmol/L = chylothorax
Cholesterol >5.18 mmol/L + low triglyceride = pseudochylothorax
Post-thoracic surgery is a classic chylothorax setting
Treatment: MCT diet, octreotide, then duct ligation/embolisation
explanation.pearls: Pleural cholesterol >5.18 mmol/L with low triglyceride distinguishes pseudochylothorax from true chylothorax - the two milky-effusion entities that look identical at the bedside but have entirely different aetiologies and management.

stem:
A 64-year-old man presents to your emergency department with 3 days of productive cough, fever, and pleuritic right-sided chest pain. He says 'I get out of breath just walking from the kitchen to the toilet now'. He has well-controlled hypertension and is an ex-smoker (40 pack-years, quit 6 years ago). He has had no recent travel, no aspiration risk, no immunosuppression, and no prior pneumonia.

On examination he is alert. The chest has right basal crackles with bronchial breathing and dullness to percussion. There is no asterixis. Chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation without effusion. Investigations: WBC 16 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), CRP 220 mg/L (<5), albumin 36 g/L, urea 8.5 mmol/L, sodium 135 mmol/L, creatinine 102 micromol/L, arterial pH 7.42, PaO2 65 mmHg on room air, PaCO2 38 mmHg. SMART-COP score is 3 (low albumin, multilobar nil; respiratory rate, tachycardia, confusion nil; oxygen, pH).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108, BP 124/76 mmHg, RR 26, SpO2 92% on room air, temperature 38.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Right basal crackles with bronchial breathing, dullness to percussion, no peripheral oedema, no confusion
data_table.Investigations: WBC 16 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), CRP 220 mg/L (<5), albumin 36 g/L, urea 8.5 mmol/L, sodium 135 mmol/L, creatinine 102 micromol/L; ABG pH 7.42, PaO2 65 mmHg, PaCO2 38 mmHg on room air; chest X-ray right lower lobe consolidation, no effusion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily and oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily as an outpatient course of treatment
options.rationale: Oral monotherapy or oral combination is appropriate for low-severity CAP (SMART-COP 0-2) without admission; SMART-COP 3 in this patient (low SpO2, low pH-neutral with low PaO2 less than 70 mmHg, plus low albumin) is moderate severity warranting admission and intravenous therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g 6-hourly plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily as the ward regimen
options.rationale: Moderate-severity CAP (SMART-COP 3-4, admitted to ward) is treated with AU first-line intravenous benzylpenicillin plus oral doxycycline (or oral azithromycin) to cover Streptococcus pneumoniae and atypicals (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila). Step-down to oral amoxicillin when stable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g 6-hourly plus intravenous azithromycin and intensive care admission
options.rationale: Anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam plus macrolide combination is reserved for severe CAP (SMART-COP 5+), severe sepsis, or specific risk factors for resistant organisms (structural lung disease, recent broad-spectrum antibiotics); SMART-COP 3 with ward admission does not need this. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus intravenous vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading dose and ward admission today
options.rationale: Vancomycin empirical cover is reserved for MRSA-suspected pneumonia (severe necrotising, post-influenza secondary bacterial, intravenous drug use, or community MRSA prevalence high); none apply here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous moxifloxacin 400 mg daily monotherapy and discharge home on completion with general practitioner review
options.rationale: Fluoroquinolone monotherapy in CAP is reserved for penicillin allergy with anaphylaxis or other contraindication; AU stewardship discourages fluoroquinolone first-line because of resistance and tendinopathy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; AMH)

explanation.summary: SMART-COP stratifies community-acquired pneumonia by need for intensive respiratory or vasopressor support. Score 0-2: low severity, outpatient amoxicillin plus doxycycline. Score 3-4: moderate severity, ward admission with IV benzylpenicillin plus oral doxycycline. Score 5+: severe, ICU consideration with IV ceftriaxone plus IV azithromycin (and anti-pseudomonal cover if structural lung disease). Step-down to oral amoxicillin or doxycycline when clinically stable; total duration 5-7 days.
key_points: SMART-COP 0-2 outpatient, 3-4 ward, 5+ ICU consideration
Ward AU first-line: IV benzylpenicillin + oral doxycycline (or azithromycin)
ICU CAP: IV ceftriaxone + IV azithromycin; add anti-pseudomonal if at risk
Total duration 5-7 days; step down when clinically stable
explanation.pearls: SMART-COP gives 2 points for systolic BP under 90 mmHg, multilobar CXR, low albumin under 35 g/L, RR raised, tachycardia over 125 bpm; and 2 points for confusion, oxygen low, low pH - a score of 3 or 4 is moderate severity requiring admission.

subtopic_detail: Iron deficiency anaemia in older adult
stem:
A 67-year-old man attends your general practice clinic with 4 months of progressive fatigue and dyspnoea on exertion. He says 'I get puffed bringing in the shopping now, when last winter I was still walking the dog up the hill'. He has not noticed any rectal bleeding, melaena, change in bowel habit, abdominal pain, or weight loss. He has no past gastrointestinal disease. He is a non-smoker, drinks 4 standard drinks weekly, and his diet is balanced.

On examination he is pale with no signs of heart failure. Per-rectal examination reveals no mass and faecal occult blood is positive on point-of-care testing. FBC shows haemoglobin 88 g/L (130-180), MCV 72 fL (80-100), MCH 24 pg (27-32). Ferritin 8 micrograms/L (30-300), transferrin saturation 7% (16-45%). LFTs and UEC are within normal limits. He is haemodynamically stable. His grandparents were Mediterranean but he has never been investigated for haemoglobinopathy; his haemoglobin 3 years ago was 142 g/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84, BP 132/78 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, no signs of heart failure, abdomen soft non-tender, no organomegaly, per-rectal no mass, faecal occult blood positive
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 88 g/L (130-180), MCV 72 fL (80-100), MCH 24 pg (27-32), ferritin 8 micrograms/L (30-300), transferrin saturation 7% (16-45%); LFTs and UEC within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Empirical oral iron supplementation for 12 weeks and arrange repeat FBC and ferritin assessment then
options.rationale: Empirical iron treatment without investigating the source of loss in an adult over 50 (and any postmenopausal woman) is unsafe; colorectal malignancy must be excluded. (Source: GESA Iron Deficiency Guidelines; NHMRC NBCSP)

options.text: Test for haemoglobin electrophoresis and HbA2 for beta-thalassaemia trait given his Mediterranean family history
options.rationale: Inherited haemoglobinopathy is unlikely in an adult whose haemoglobin was 142 g/L three years ago; ferritin of 8 micrograms/L is diagnostic of iron deficiency. (Source: GESA Iron Deficiency Guidelines)

options.text: Refer for upper endoscopy and colonoscopy under one anaesthetic session for source of blood loss
options.rationale: Iron-deficiency anaemia in an adult over 50 (or any postmenopausal woman) is colorectal cancer until proven otherwise. AU practice is dual upper endoscopy and colonoscopy on the same anaesthetic to identify upper gastrointestinal pathology (peptic ulcer, malignancy) and lower gastrointestinal cancer or angiodysplasia. Empirical iron without endoscopy delays diagnosis. (Source: GESA Iron Deficiency Guidelines; NHMRC NBCSP)

options.text: Order CT colonography with intravenous contrast as the only screening investigation needed at this stage
options.rationale: CT colonography misses small adenomas and cannot biopsy or treat; colonoscopy is preferred when the index of suspicion for malignancy is high. Upper endoscopy is also needed. (Source: GESA Iron Deficiency Guidelines)

options.text: Send urea breath test for Helicobacter pylori and treat empirically with eradication if positive on testing
options.rationale: H. pylori may contribute to iron deficiency via gastritis but does not exclude malignancy; endoscopy with biopsy is required. (Source: GESA Iron Deficiency Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Iron-deficiency anaemia in adults over 50 (any sex), or in postmenopausal women, mandates urgent gastrointestinal investigation for occult malignancy. Combined upper endoscopy and colonoscopy under one anaesthetic is the AU standard. Premenopausal women with menstrual losses can be treated empirically with iron, but those with persistent or severe deficiency, family history of colorectal cancer, or other red flags warrant endoscopic workup. Once a cause is found, treat with oral iron (or IV iron if oral intolerant) and recheck at 6-12 weeks.
key_points: Adults over 50 with iron deficiency: dual endoscopy until proven otherwise
Premenopausal: treat empirically with iron unless red flags
Oral iron first-line; IV iron if oral failed or intolerant
Recheck Hb and ferritin at 6-12 weeks of treatment
explanation.pearls: Oral iron is best absorbed when taken second-daily on an empty stomach (the hepcidin rebound from daily dosing reduces absorption), often with vitamin C; treat for 3 to 6 months past haemoglobin normalisation to refill stores.

subtopic_detail: New atrial fibrillation rate control and anticoagulation
stem:
A 73-year-old woman attends your general practice clinic with 3 days of palpitations and exertional breathlessness. She says 'my heart has been racing on and off, and the chemist found my pulse was all over the shop'. She has a history of hypertension treated with amlodipine, type 2 diabetes treated with metformin, and previous transient ischaemic attack 5 years ago that was managed conservatively. She has no chest pain, no syncope, and no symptoms suggesting heart failure.

On examination her pulse is irregularly irregular at 124 bpm. Heart sounds are dual with no murmurs. Chest is clear. There is no peripheral oedema. ECG confirms atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 124 bpm, no ischaemic ST changes, and QRS 90 ms. TSH 2.0 mIU/L; electrolytes, renal and liver function within normal limits; haemoglobin 132 g/L. Bedside echocardiogram shows preserved left ventricular function with no significant valvular disease. CHA2DS2-VA score is calculated.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124 irregularly irregular, BP 138/86 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Irregularly irregular pulse, no murmur, no signs of heart failure, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: ECG atrial fibrillation HR 124 bpm, no ST changes; TSH 2.0 mIU/L; UEC and LFTs within normal limits; haemoglobin 132 g/L; bedside echo preserved LV function, no significant valvular disease
data_table.Medications: Amlodipine 10 mg daily, metformin 1 g twice daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Electrical cardioversion this admission and discharge home on aspirin alone for the long-term stroke prophylaxis
options.rationale: Aspirin is not adequate stroke prophylaxis in atrial fibrillation; CHA2DS2-VA score over 1 in this patient (age, hypertension, diabetes, prior TIA) mandates oral anticoagulation. Cardioversion in unscreened AF over 48 hours requires either transoesophageal echo to exclude thrombus or 3-4 weeks of anticoagulation first. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Commence intravenous heparin infusion and refer for transoesophageal-guided cardioversion within 24 hours
options.rationale: TOE-guided cardioversion is a reasonable strategy when prompt rhythm control is needed, but rate control with oral anticoagulation is the AU first-line for newly diagnosed AF of uncertain duration; rhythm strategy is decided at outpatient follow-up. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline)

options.text: Refer urgently for pulmonary vein isolation ablation procedure and commence aspirin pending the catheter laboratory date
options.rationale: Ablation is reserved for symptomatic paroxysmal or persistent AF refractory to medical therapy; first-line is rate or rhythm control and oral anticoagulation. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline)

options.text: Add bisoprolol 2.5 mg daily for rhythm control and arrange repeat ECG and routine review in 6 weeks without other therapy
options.rationale: Bisoprolol is for rate control, not rhythm control; anticoagulation is missing from this option and is the priority for stroke prevention. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline)

options.text: Commence apixaban 5 mg twice daily, bisoprolol 2.5 mg daily for rate control, and refer cardiology for outpatient rhythm decision
options.rationale: CHA2DS2-VA score of 5 (age, hypertension, diabetes, prior TIA - the VA scheme drops sex; under AU practice this score mandates anticoagulation). Apixaban is AU first-line DOAC, well-tolerated, no INR monitoring required. Bisoprolol provides rate control. Cardiology decides on rhythm vs rate strategy at outpatient review; if rhythm control is desired and AF is over 48 hours, anticoagulation precedes cardioversion. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline; AMH)

explanation.summary: New atrial fibrillation is managed with stroke prophylaxis (CHA2DS2-VA-based anticoagulation) and either rate or rhythm control. Direct oral anticoagulants (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, edoxaban) are AU first-line; warfarin is reserved for mechanical valves or moderate-severe mitral stenosis. Rate control (beta-blocker first, calcium channel blocker if beta-blocker contraindicated) targets resting heart rate under 110 bpm (lenient) or 80 bpm (strict). Cardioversion in unscreened AF over 48 hours requires either TOE-guided or 3-4 weeks of anticoagulation first.
key_points: CHA2DS2-VA replaces CHA2DS2-VASc in AU - drops sex points
DOAC first-line; warfarin only for mechanical valve / moderate-severe MS
Rate control: bisoprolol first, target HR under 110 bpm
Cardioversion in AF over 48 hours: TOE-guided or 3-4 weeks anticoagulation first
explanation.pearls: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily is the AU first-line DOAC for stroke prevention in non-valvular AF; reduce to 2.5 mg twice daily if any two of age over 80, weight under 60 kg, or creatinine over 133 micromol/L are present.

stem:
A 54-year-old woman is brought to your emergency department resuscitation bay by ambulance with sudden-onset dyspnoea and pre-syncope. Her partner says 'she just stood up after the long flight home this morning and went pale and dizzy'. She had a knee arthroplasty 3 weeks ago. She has no history of bleeding, no stroke, no recent surgery within 2 weeks, and no malignancy. She is currently taking enoxaparin prophylactic dose at home.

On examination she is dyspnoeic. There is no leg swelling. JVP is raised at 7 cm. Cardiac auscultation reveals a loud P2 and right ventricular heave. Chest is clear. Bedside echocardiogram shows right ventricular dilatation with septal flattening and a McConnell sign of preserved apical contractility with akinetic basal-mid right ventricular free wall. ECG shows sinus tachycardia, S1Q3T3 pattern, and right axis deviation. A point-of-care CT pulmonary angiogram, completed within 10 minutes of arrival, confirms saddle pulmonary embolus.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132, BP 84/56 mmHg, RR 32, SpO2 88% on room air rising to 94% on 10 L oxygen, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Dyspnoeic, JVP 7 cm, loud P2, right ventricular heave, no leg swelling, no calf tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Bedside echo: RV dilatation, septal flattening, McConnell sign; ECG sinus tachycardia, S1Q3T3, right axis deviation; CTPA saddle PE; troponin 0.4 microgram/L (under 0.04); haemoglobin 128 g/L; platelets 220 x10^9/L; INR 1.0

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Administer intravenous alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours as systemic thrombolysis for haemodynamically unstable PE
options.rationale: Haemodynamically unstable PE (systolic BP under 90 mmHg or vasopressor requirement) with confirmed embolus and no absolute contraindication is treated with systemic thrombolysis. The AU regimen is alteplase 100 mg intravenously over 2 hours, then anticoagulation. Reduced dose or catheter-directed thrombolysis is considered in high bleeding-risk patients. Surgical embolectomy is reserved for failed thrombolysis or absolute contraindications. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ VTE Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Commence intravenous unfractionated heparin infusion at therapeutic rate and admit to the high-dependency unit
options.rationale: Heparin alone is the standard for haemodynamically stable PE; with shock (systolic BP under 90 mmHg), thrombolysis or thrombectomy is the AU intervention; heparin is given alongside but is not sufficient on its own. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ VTE Guideline)

options.text: Refer for inferior vena cava filter placement before any antithrombotic therapy is administered to this patient
options.rationale: IVC filters are reserved for absolute contraindication to anticoagulation or recurrent PE despite therapeutic anticoagulation; they do not treat the embolus already in situ. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ VTE Guideline)

options.text: Increase enoxaparin to 1 mg/kg subcutaneously twice daily and admit for haemodynamic monitoring overnight
options.rationale: Therapeutic-dose LMWH is appropriate for haemodynamically stable PE; shock features (hypotension, low SpO2 needing oxygen) place this in the high-risk category requiring thrombolysis. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ VTE Guideline)

options.text: Trial fluid resuscitation alone with 2 L normal saline and reassess haemodynamic and respiratory status in 60 minutes
options.rationale: Aggressive fluid loading in obstructive shock from PE can worsen right ventricular overload and reduce cardiac output; small judicious volume is acceptable while reperfusion therapy is given, not as primary treatment. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ VTE Guideline)

explanation.summary: Pulmonary embolism is risk-stratified by haemodynamic status, right ventricular strain, and cardiac biomarker elevation. High-risk (massive) PE - shock or sustained hypotension - is treated with systemic thrombolysis unless absolute contraindication, in which case catheter-directed thrombolysis or surgical embolectomy is considered. Intermediate-risk PE - normotensive with RV strain - is treated with anticoagulation alone, with close monitoring; rescue thrombolysis if deterioration occurs. Low-risk PE is treated outpatient with DOAC in selected patients.
key_points: Massive PE (shock): systemic thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours
Intermediate-risk PE: anticoagulation, monitor for deterioration
Avoid fluid overload in RV failure; small judicious bolus only
Catheter-directed lysis or surgical embolectomy if thrombolysis contraindicated
explanation.pearls: Alteplase 100 mg intravenously over 2 hours is the AU thrombolytic regimen for massive PE; followed by unfractionated heparin infusion once thrombin time or APTT confirms adequate clearance.

stem:
A 47-year-old woman is brought to your emergency department by her partner after 3 days of vomiting, abdominal pain, and increasing weakness. He says 'she's been getting darker on her hands and her gums all winter, but she didn't want to bother the doctor'. She has no past psychiatric history. She has been losing weight, feeling weak, and has had postural symptoms. She has no diarrhoea, no fever, and no recent travel.

On examination she is drowsy but rousable. She has hyperpigmentation in her palmar creases and gums, with skin tanning over light-exposed areas. There is no goitre. Her abdomen is soft, mildly tender, and there are no signs of peritonism. Bloods show sodium 122 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 6.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 12 mmol/L, creatinine 110 micromol/L, glucose 3.0 mmol/L (3.5-6.0), and pH 7.30 on a venous blood gas with bicarbonate 19 mmol/L. She has had no morning cortisol or ACTH check before. Septic screen is sent.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124, BP 84/52 mmHg supine and 70/40 mmHg standing, RR 22, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, hyperpigmentation palmar creases and buccal mucosa, postural drop, soft mildly tender abdomen, no focal signs
data_table.Investigations: Na 122 mmol/L (135-145), K 6.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urea 12 mmol/L, creatinine 110 micromol/L, glucose 3.0 mmol/L (3.5-6.0), VBG pH 7.30, HCO3 19 mmol/L; FBC, septic screen, paired random cortisol and ACTH samples sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Wait for the morning cortisol level to return before any glucocorticoid is administered to confirm diagnosis first
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis is life-threatening and treatment must not wait for biochemical confirmation; the paired sample can be drawn before steroid administration but treatment proceeds. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology; AMH)

options.text: Commence intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg as the immediate steroid choice, followed by intravenous saline resuscitation
options.rationale: Dexamethasone has no mineralocorticoid effect (important in primary adrenal failure) and is less preferred in established crisis where mineralocorticoid replacement is needed; hydrocortisone is the AU first-line. Dexamethasone is acceptable only when needing to preserve cortisol assay for short ACTH stimulation. (Source: AMH)

options.text: Administer intravenous 50% dextrose 50 mL for the hypoglycaemia and review the haemodynamics after that single bolus
options.rationale: Glucose correction alone does not address adrenal failure and the patient remains in crisis; steroid is the priority intervention alongside fluid and glucose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Administer intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg stat with intravenous normal saline resuscitation and glucose correction
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis (hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, hypotension, hyperpigmentation suggesting primary adrenal failure) is treated empirically with intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg stat, followed by 50-100 mg every 6 hours, alongside isotonic saline resuscitation and glucose correction. Paired cortisol and ACTH can be drawn before the first dose. Mineralocorticoid is not needed acutely at hydrocortisone doses of 50 mg or more (sufficient mineralocorticoid activity). (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology; AMH)

options.text: Refer urgently for adrenalectomy after CT imaging today and arrange intensive care admission before any pharmacological treatment
options.rationale: Surgical referral is irrelevant in acute adrenal crisis from primary adrenal failure; immediate steroid is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a medical emergency. Empirical hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenously stat, followed by 50-100 mg every 6 hours, is the AU first-line - given before biochemical confirmation when crisis is clinically suspected. Paired cortisol and ACTH samples can be drawn beforehand for later interpretation. Aggressive isotonic saline (1-2 L initially) and glucose correction address hypovolaemia and hypoglycaemia. Hyperpigmentation in light-exposed areas plus hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia points to primary adrenal failure (Addison disease); secondary adrenal insufficiency lacks hyperpigmentation and hyperkalaemia.
key_points: Treat first, confirm second - hydrocortisone 100 mg IV stat
Paired cortisol and ACTH before first dose if feasible
Hyperpigmentation + hyperkalaemia = primary (Addison); think autoimmune adrenalitis in AU
Sick-day rules: triple hydrocortisone dose for febrile illness or major stress
explanation.pearls: Hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenously stat then 50-100 mg every 6 hours covers both glucocorticoid and adequate mineralocorticoid receptor activity in acute crisis; fludrocortisone is added on transition to maintenance oral therapy.

stem:
A 22-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus presents to your emergency department with 24 hours of nausea, vomiting, and breathlessness. She says 'my insulin pump alarmed yesterday afternoon, and I thought I'd just put a new line in this morning, but I haven't been able to eat'. She has no chest pain, no infection symptoms, and no recent surgery. She is alert and oriented.

On examination she has Kussmaul breathing and dry mucous membranes. There is no focal neurological deficit. Bloods show glucose 24 mmol/L, ketones 5.4 mmol/L (under 0.6), pH 7.18, bicarbonate 8 mmol/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), corrected sodium 138 mmol/L, anion gap 24, creatinine 105 micromol/L, urea 8 mmol/L. ECG sinus tachycardia 116 bpm, no T-wave changes. Septic screen sent; chest X-ray clear. Urinary HCG negative. She has had no insulin in 18 hours since the pump failure.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 116, BP 102/64 mmHg, RR 28 with Kussmaul pattern, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Kussmaul breathing, dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, capillary refill 3 seconds, soft non-tender abdomen, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 24 mmol/L, ketones 5.4 mmol/L (under 0.6), pH 7.18, HCO3 8 mmol/L, Na 134 mmol/L, K 4.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), corrected Na 138 mmol/L, anion gap 24, creatinine 105 micromol/L, urea 8 mmol/L; ECG sinus tachycardia, no T-wave changes; CXR clear; urinary HCG negative
data_table.Medications: Continuous subcutaneous insulin pump (failed 18 hours ago)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first intervention?

options.text: Intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hour as a single first intervention prior to fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: Starting insulin before adequate fluid resuscitation worsens hypovolaemia (osmotic diuresis is the primary driver of dehydration) and can precipitate hypoglycaemia and hypokalaemia faster; AU pathways open with fluid first then insulin within the first hour. (Source: ADS/ADIPS DKA Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L over the first hour while preparing insulin infusion and potassium replacement
options.rationale: Adult DKA management opens with intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L over the first hour to restore intravascular volume. Insulin infusion 0.1 unit/kg/hour is started within the first hour once potassium is known (over 3.5 mmol/L can give insulin without potassium replacement first; under 3.5 mmol/L withhold insulin and replace potassium). Potassium is added to the second litre of fluid unless K is over 5.5 mmol/L. Add 5% dextrose when glucose reaches 14 mmol/L while continuing insulin to clear ketones. (Source: ADS/ADIPS DKA Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin 0.3 unit/kg bolus immediately and arrange admission to the high-dependency unit
options.rationale: Subcutaneous insulin in established DKA is unreliable due to peripheral vasoconstriction; intravenous infusion is the AU first-line. (Source: ADS/ADIPS DKA Guideline)

options.text: Administer intravenous 8.4% sodium bicarbonate 50 mL stat to correct the venous acidaemia she has on the gas today
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is reserved for pH under 6.9 with shock or hyperkalaemia-related cardiac instability; routine use in DKA worsens intracellular acidosis and prolongs ketosis. (Source: ADS/ADIPS DKA Guideline)

options.text: Empirical intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily as antibiotic cover given the prevalence of infection as a DKA trigger
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics are not part of the DKA bundle unless infection is clinically suspected; the trigger here is pump failure. (Source: ADS/ADIPS DKA Guideline)

explanation.summary: Diabetic ketoacidosis in adults is treated with fluid first, insulin second, and aggressive potassium replacement. Open with intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L over the first hour. Start insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hour once potassium is known; withhold if under 3.5 mmol/L and replace potassium first. Add 5% dextrose to the fluid when glucose falls to around 14 mmol/L (continue insulin until ketones cleared). Treat the precipitant and convert to subcutaneous insulin only when acidosis and ketones have resolved and the patient can eat.
key_points: Fluid first, insulin within the first hour, potassium replacement priority
Withhold insulin if potassium under 3.5 mmol/L until replaced
Add 5% dextrose when glucose under 14 mmol/L while continuing insulin to clear ketones
Bicarbonate reserved for pH under 6.9 with shock or hyperkalaemic instability
explanation.pearls: AU DKA pathway: insulin infusion 0.1 unit/kg/hour without bolus; the priority is volume restoration and potassium replacement, not rapid glucose correction.

stem:
A 78-year-old man presents to your emergency department with sudden right-sided weakness and headache that started 60 minutes ago. He has atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and a mechanical mitral valve replacement 5 years ago. He says 'the room started spinning, then I couldn't lift the right arm at all'. His regular medications are warfarin (target INR 2.5-3.5 for the mitral mechanical valve), bisoprolol, and ramipril. His most recent INR 1 week ago was 2.8.

On examination GCS is 14 (E4 V4 M6). Right-sided hemiparesis power 1/5 upper and 2/5 lower, with right facial droop and dysarthria. Non-contrast CT head shows a 25 mL left basal ganglia haemorrhage with no midline shift and no intraventricular extension. INR returns at 7.0. Platelet count 180 x10^9/L. There is no clinical evidence of mechanical valve thrombosis, no fever, and no recent infection. He has had no falls or trauma. He has had no procedures or surgery recently.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 178/96 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: GCS 14 (E4 V4 M6), right hemiparesis power 1/5 arm and 2/5 leg, right facial droop, dysarthria, no neck stiffness
data_table.Investigations: Non-contrast CT head 25 mL left basal ganglia haemorrhage, no midline shift, no intraventricular extension; INR 7.0; platelets 180 x10^9/L; haemoglobin 138 g/L; UEC normal; troponin negative
data_table.Medications: Warfarin (target INR 2.5-3.5), bisoprolol 5 mg daily, ramipril 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate haemostatic intervention?

options.text: Administer fresh frozen plasma 4 units intravenously as the only haemostatic intervention for the elevated INR today
options.rationale: Fresh frozen plasma reverses warfarin slowly (large-volume infusion limits rate), provides incomplete factor replacement, and risks transfusion-associated circulatory overload in the elderly; AU guidelines prefer prothrombin complex concentrate. (Source: NBA Warfarin Reversal Consensus; HSANZ)

options.text: Administer intravenous vitamin K 10 mg as the only intervention given the high INR and the clear ICH on imaging today
options.rationale: Intravenous vitamin K alone takes 6 to 12 hours for full effect, far too slow for ongoing intracerebral haemorrhage; rapid factor replacement is required first. (Source: NBA Warfarin Reversal Consensus)

options.text: Withhold warfarin alone and recheck the INR in 6 hours before administering any further haemostatic interventions then
options.rationale: Watchful waiting in major bleeding with INR over 4 is contraindicated; rapid reversal is the AU standard. (Source: NBA Warfarin Reversal Consensus)

options.text: Administer recombinant activated factor VII 90 micrograms/kg intravenously as the immediate haemostatic intervention
options.rationale: Recombinant factor VIIa is not the AU first-line for warfarin-associated ICH and carries arterial thrombosis risk; prothrombin complex concentrate is preferred for warfarin reversal. (Source: NBA Warfarin Reversal Consensus)

options.text: Administer intravenous prothrombin complex concentrate 50 IU/kg plus intravenous vitamin K 10 mg as the immediate combined reversal
options.rationale: Warfarin-associated major bleeding (intracerebral haemorrhage is the highest-risk category) is reversed with three- or four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (Prothrombinex-VF in AU) at 50 IU/kg plus intravenous vitamin K 10 mg. Prothrombinex restores factors II, IX, and X within minutes; vitamin K provides sustained factor synthesis to prevent rebound coagulopathy as the prothrombin complex concentrate clears. Mechanical mitral valve thrombosis risk in the short term is acceptable in the context of active ICH; restart anticoagulation when imaging stabilises (typically 1 to 4 weeks). (Source: NBA Warfarin Reversal Consensus; HSANZ; ANZSBT)

explanation.summary: Warfarin-associated major bleeding (intracerebral haemorrhage, ongoing major bleeding, or pre-emergency surgery) requires rapid reversal with prothrombin complex concentrate plus intravenous vitamin K. The AU agent (Prothrombinex-VF) contains factors II, IX, and X and works within minutes; vitamin K provides sustained factor synthesis as prothrombin complex clears. Fresh frozen plasma is second-line due to slow speed, large volume, and incomplete factor profile. In mechanical valve patients, recommencement of anticoagulation is balanced against rebleed risk; typically restart at 1 to 4 weeks based on imaging stability and valve type.
key_points: Major bleed on warfarin: prothrombin complex concentrate 50 IU/kg + IV vitamin K 10 mg
Prothrombinex-VF is the AU agent (3-factor: II, IX, X) - works within minutes
FFP is second-line: slow, volume burden, incomplete factor coverage
Mechanical mitral valve: restart anticoagulation at 1 to 4 weeks based on bleed stability
explanation.pearls: Prothrombinex-VF 50 IU/kg combined with intravenous vitamin K 10 mg restores warfarin-suppressed factors II, IX, and X within minutes while vitamin K secures sustained correction - the AU rapid-reversal pair for warfarin-associated intracerebral haemorrhage.

stem:
A 68-year-old man is brought to your emergency department by ambulance with 6 hours of confusion and rigors. His wife says 'he was shivering, then he went pale and floppy on the couch and stopped making sense'. He has a background of type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease (baseline creatinine 140 micromol/L). He has not had recent surgery. He has had increasing urinary frequency and dysuria over the past 3 days.

On examination he is drowsy and disoriented to time and place, with mottled peripheries, a capillary refill of 4 seconds, and warm core. There is no neck stiffness. Abdomen is soft with left renal angle tenderness. Bedside lactate is 4.6 mmol/L (under 2.0). VBG shows pH 7.30 (7.35-7.45), HCO3 18 mmol/L (22-26). FBC shows WCC 18.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), neutrophils 16.2 (2.0-7.5), platelets 96 x10^9/L (150-450). Creatinine 220 micromol/L (45-90), CRP 240 mg/L (under 5). Urinalysis: nitrites positive, leukocyte 3+. He has received 250 mL of normal saline en route.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122 regular, BP 84/52 mmHg (MAP 63 mmHg), RR 28, SpO2 94% on room air, temperature 38.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, disoriented x2, mottled peripheries, CRT 4 seconds, left renal angle tenderness, no rash, no neck stiffness
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.6 mmol/L (under 2.0); VBG pH 7.30 bicarbonate 18 mmol/L; WCC 18.4 with neutrophilia, platelets 96 x10^9/L; creatinine 220 micromol/L (baseline 140); CRP 240 mg/L; urine nitrites positive leukocyte 3+
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1 g BD; gliclazide MR 60 mg daily; perindopril 4 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Send blood cultures, give IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg single dose plus IV ampicillin, and 1 L crystalloid fluid bolus
options.rationale: Crystalloid resuscitation for sepsis-induced hypotension or lactate above 4 mmol/L targets 30 mL/kg within 3 hours, not a single 1 L bolus; gentamicin dose is reasonable but needs review in CKD and is paired with a broader-spectrum agent for urosepsis with shock. (Source: ANZICS Surviving Sepsis Adaptation; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Give intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg as first-line therapy for the septic shock physiology immediately
options.rationale: Hydrocortisone is added when shock persists despite adequate fluid resuscitation and vasopressor therapy; it is not the first-line step. (Source: ANZICS Surviving Sepsis Adaptation)

options.text: Take blood cultures, give 30 mL/kg crystalloid over the first 3 hours, IV piperacillin-tazobactam, lactate trend, and call ICU
options.rationale: Surviving Sepsis adapted hour-1 bundle: measure lactate, take blood cultures before antibiotics if no delay, administer broad-spectrum empirical antibiotics within 1 hour (piperacillin-tazobactam covers Gram-negative urosepsis), give 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate over 4 mmol/L, repeat lactate, start vasopressors to maintain MAP at least 65 mmHg if hypotension persists after fluids. Early ICU communication is part of escalation. (Source: ANZICS Surviving Sepsis Adaptation; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Hold antibiotics until urine culture returns a positive organism and titrate fluid by hourly central venous pressure
options.rationale: Antibiotic delay in septic shock increases mortality by approximately 7% per hour; empirical broad-spectrum therapy is given before culture results. CVP-guided resuscitation has been superseded by dynamic measures. (Source: ANZICS Surviving Sepsis Adaptation)

options.text: Commence noradrenaline immediately before any fluid resuscitation to restore mean arterial pressure to 65 mmHg
options.rationale: Noradrenaline is initiated when fluid resuscitation has been inadequate to restore MAP to 65 mmHg, not before initial fluid loading; in undifferentiated shock, fluid resuscitation precedes vasopressor in the first hour. (Source: ANZICS Surviving Sepsis Adaptation)

explanation.summary: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign 1-hour bundle (adapted in Australia by ANZICS) includes measuring lactate, blood cultures before antibiotics if no delay, broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate over 4 mmol/L, and vasopressor (noradrenaline) to maintain MAP at least 65 mmHg if fluid-refractory. Repeat lactate guides response. Empirical antibiotic choice is by source. Urinary tract sepsis is treated with piperacillin-tazobactam or third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone or cefotaxime), with gentamicin added when severity warrants and renal function permits. Source control (drainage, removal of foreign material) is essential.
key_points: Lactate, cultures, antibiotics, 30 mL/kg fluid, vasopressor if refractory - the hour-1 elements
Antibiotic delay raises mortality - empirical cover starts immediately
Source control completes the bundle
Noradrenaline first-line vasopressor; vasopressin second
explanation.pearls: Noradrenaline is the first-line vasopressor in septic shock targeting MAP 65 mmHg; vasopressin 0.03 IU/min is added to reduce noradrenaline requirements when high doses are needed.

stem:
A 52-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents to your emergency department with 36 hours of severe left thigh pain and erythema, having scraped his shin on a metal gate at work 2 days ago. He says 'the pain is way worse than the redness looks, paracetamol does nothing, and now my whole leg feels numb in patches'. He has had a fever overnight and one episode of vomiting this morning. His diabetes is managed with metformin and an SGLT2 inhibitor.

On examination he is pale and unwell. The left thigh is erythematous, swollen, exquisitely tender, with patchy dusky areas and a single haemorrhagic blister on the antero-medial surface. Crepitus is palpable along the medial thigh. Sensation is reduced over the medial aspect of the thigh. There is no inguinal lymphadenopathy. WCC 21 x10^9/L (4-11), CRP 280 mg/L (under 5), sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 156 micromol/L (45-90), glucose 16.4 mmol/L, lactate 3.8 mmol/L, haemoglobin 122 g/L. LRINEC score is 9.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124 regular, BP 96/58 mmHg, RR 26, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 38.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Erythematous swollen left thigh with patchy duskiness, haemorrhagic blister antero-medially, palpable crepitus medially, reduced sensation over medial thigh
data_table.Investigations: WCC 21 x10^9/L, CRP 280 mg/L, sodium 132 mmol/L, creatinine 156 micromol/L, glucose 16.4 mmol/L, lactate 3.8 mmol/L, Hb 122 g/L; LRINEC 9
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1 g BD; dapagliflozin 10 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Computed tomography of the thigh with intravenous contrast to delineate the extent of fascial gas before referral
options.rationale: Imaging is supportive but should not delay surgical referral and exploration when clinical features are characteristic; the operating theatre is the diagnostic and therapeutic destination. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin and gentamicin and admit under general medicine for serial limb examinations
options.rationale: Empirical cover for necrotising fasciitis requires broad spectrum including anaerobic and protein synthesis inhibitor for toxin suppression; surgical debridement is the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Urgent surgical referral for theatre debridement, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics including clindamycin, and fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: Necrotising soft tissue infection (LRINEC over 6, pain out of proportion, dusky skin, haemorrhagic blisters, crepitus, systemic toxicity) is a surgical emergency. Empirical broad-spectrum cover (meropenem or piperacillin-tazobactam) plus clindamycin (for streptococcal and clostridial toxin suppression) and fluid resuscitation accompany urgent surgical debridement. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; ANZBA Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection)

options.text: Outline the erythema and discharge home on oral cephalexin with review by general practitioner in 24 hours
