Urine culture from this morning has just been called as growing gram negative rods.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, BP 84/52 mmHg, RR 28/min, SpO2 94% room air, temperature 38.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but orientated; CRT 4 sec, cool peripheries; clear chest; mild suprapubic tenderness; IDC draining cloudy urine
data_table.Investigations: VBG: lactate 4.8 mmol/L (<2), pH 7.30, BE -5; urine MCS gram negative rods on Gram stain

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management bundle?

options.text: Hour-1 bundle: blood cultures, IV ceftriaxone plus gentamicin, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, ICU for vasopressors
options.rationale: This is septic shock (sepsis plus lactate >2 mmol/L despite resuscitation OR hypotension requiring vasopressors). The Surviving Sepsis hour-1 bundle and ANZICS recommendation are: measure lactate, take cultures, give broad spectrum antibiotics, give 30 mL/kg crystalloid, start vasopressors if MAP <65 despite fluids; antibiotics for urosepsis with gram-negative growth follow eTG sepsis empirical pathway. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis; eTG Antibiotic; Surviving Sepsis Campaign)

options.text: Administer IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g and arrange CT abdomen before fluids or cultures are taken
options.rationale: Tazocin is an acceptable empirical agent for complicated urosepsis but should follow cultures and accompany fluid resuscitation; imaging must not delay the hour-1 bundle. (Source: eTG Antibiotic; ANZICS Sepsis)

options.text: Give 250 mL balanced crystalloid bolus and reassess at 30 minutes before considering further fluid
options.rationale: A 250 mL bolus undertreats septic shock; the hour-1 bundle calls for 30 mL/kg of balanced crystalloid as the initial resuscitation in adults. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis)

options.text: Start IV adrenaline 0.05 mcg/kg/min via peripheral line before any crystalloid fluid resuscitation today
options.rationale: Vasopressors are escalated after fluid resuscitation has failed to restore MAP; starting vasopressors first does not address the relative hypovolaemia and is not the bundle sequence. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis)

options.text: Withhold empiric antibiotics until full microbiology sensitivities return and focus on fluid resuscitation
options.rationale: Time to antibiotics is the strongest modifiable predictor of mortality in septic shock; empiric therapy starts within the first hour. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis)

explanation.summary: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response to infection. Septic shock is the subset with circulatory and cellular metabolic dysfunction requiring vasopressors and lactate above 2 mmol/L. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle is: measure lactate (repeat if initial >2), take blood cultures before antibiotics, administer broad spectrum antibiotics within an hour, give 30 mL/kg crystalloid (balanced solution preferred over saline) for hypotension or lactate above 4, and start vasopressors (noradrenaline first-line) if MAP remains under 65 after fluid resuscitation. Source control follows. Norepinephrine is initiated through a central line ideally but may be started peripherally if needed.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, vasopressors if MAP <65
Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor; adrenaline second
Empirical antibiotics within 1 hour; source control follows
Mortality rises about 7% per hour of antibiotic delay in septic shock
explanation.pearls: Each hour of delay in antibiotic administration in septic shock raises mortality by approximately 7%; the hour-1 bundle is the most evidence-supported intervention package in adult sepsis care.

subtopic_detail: Type B aortic dissection BP control
stem:
You are the medical registrar called urgently to ED for a 58-year-old man with sudden tearing chest pain radiating to his back that started 90 minutes ago. He has a history of poorly controlled hypertension and is a current smoker. ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 112/min with no acute ischaemic changes. Troponin is within normal limits. CT aortogram has just been completed and reports an uncomplicated type B aortic dissection arising distal to the left subclavian artery with no end-organ malperfusion, no rupture and no aortic diameter above 5.5 cm. He is talking in full sentences.

On arrival his BP is 192/104 mmHg in the right arm and 188/100 mmHg in the left arm. He has equal radial pulses. His chest is clear, abdomen is soft and non tender, and lower limb pulses are present and symmetric. He has had paracetamol 1 g and fentanyl 50 mcg with mild improvement in pain. The interventional radiologist and the cardiothoracic surgeon are in handover and they ask you to commence BP control. He has no asthma, no heart failure and no known allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112/min, BP 192/104 mmHg right arm, 188/100 mmHg left arm, RR 22/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Equal radial pulses; clear chest; soft non tender abdomen; symmetric lower limb pulses
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia 112/min no ischaemic changes; troponin within normal limits; CT aortogram: uncomplicated type B dissection distal to left subclavian, no malperfusion, no rupture, max diameter <5.5 cm

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line BP/HR target and agent?

options.text: Intravenous frusemide 40 mg bolus to reduce afterload via brisk diuresis and improve perfusion
options.rationale: Frusemide does not provide acute BP or rate control; it has no role in acute aortic syndrome management. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Acute Aortic Syndromes)

options.text: Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion targeting systolic BP 100-120 mmHg without rate control
options.rationale: Vasodilator without prior beta-blockade triggers reflex tachycardia which increases shear stress on the dissection flap; beta-blockade must precede or accompany vasodilatation. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Acute Aortic Syndromes)

options.text: Oral perindopril 5 mg with planned reassessment of blood pressure and heart rate in 30 minutes
options.rationale: Oral antihypertensives do not titrate fast enough for acute dissection; IV infusion that can be adjusted minute-to-minute is required. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Acute Aortic Syndromes)

options.text: Intravenous labetalol infusion titrated to systolic BP 100-120 mmHg and heart rate <60/min
options.rationale: Uncomplicated type B dissection management is medical anti-impulse therapy: lower shear stress (dP/dt) by first achieving HR <60/min with beta-blockade, then add vasodilator if SBP remains >120; IV labetalol's combined alpha and beta blockade achieves both in one agent and is the Australian first-line. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Acute Aortic Syndromes; eTG Cardiovascular)

options.text: Urgent endovascular stent graft regardless of complication status or current haemodynamic stability
options.rationale: Uncomplicated type B dissection is managed medically with optimal anti-impulse therapy and surveillance; TEVAR is reserved for malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain, or rapid aortic expansion. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Acute Aortic Syndromes)

explanation.summary: Acute aortic syndrome encompasses dissection (type A: ascending; type B: descending), intramural haematoma and penetrating aortic ulcer. Type A is a surgical emergency. Uncomplicated type B is managed medically with anti-impulse therapy targeting HR <60/min and SBP 100-120 mmHg, achieved with IV beta-blockade (labetalol or esmolol) plus vasodilator (sodium nitroprusside or GTN) if needed after HR is controlled. TEVAR is indicated for complicated type B (malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain, rapid expansion, persistent hypertension on maximum medical therapy, or aortic diameter >5.5 cm). Pain control with opioids, calm environment, transfer to monitored bed and arterial line placement complete the acute management.
key_points: Type B uncomplicated: medical anti-impulse therapy
Targets: HR <60/min, SBP 100-120 mmHg
Labetalol IV combines alpha and beta blockade (Australian first-line)
TEVAR for malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain, expansion
explanation.pearls: Beta-blockade must precede any vasodilator in aortic dissection - reflex tachycardia from unopposed vasodilatation raises wall shear (dP/dt) and can extend the dissection.

stem:
You are the surgical registrar called to the ED for a 62-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin and gliclazide who has presented with 36 hours of progressive right lower limb redness, swelling and pain. He recalls a minor superficial scratch from gardening four days ago. He has had a fever of 38.5 °C at home and felt increasingly unwell over the last 12 hours.

On examination he is unwell, with a pulse of 116/min, BP 102/68 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 38.7 °C. Erythema extends from the ankle to the mid-calf with poorly defined borders. The skin is tense and there is severe pain on light palpation that he reports as out of proportion to the visible signs. There are no obvious skin blisters, no crepitus and no necrotic patches. Bloods this morning: WCC 22.4 x10^9/L (4-11), CRP 280 mg/L (<5), sodium 131 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 142 micromol/L (60-110), glucose 14.8 mmol/L, haemoglobin 138 g/L. He has no warfarin and no immunosuppression.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 116/min, BP 102/68 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 38.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Right lower limb erythema ankle to mid-calf with poorly defined borders; tense skin; pain out of proportion to visible signs; no blisters, crepitus or necrosis
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.4 x10^9/L; CRP 280 mg/L; sodium 131 mmol/L; creatinine 142 micromol/L; glucose 14.8 mmol/L; Hb 138 g/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Order an urgent MRI of the right lower limb before any antibiotic escalation or surgical referral decision
options.rationale: MRI can show fascial enhancement and gas but is not specific and must not delay urgent surgical exploration when the clinical picture is concerning. (Source: ANZSA Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection)

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g six hourly and reassess clinical progress and inflammatory markers in 24 hours
options.rationale: Flucloxacillin alone is appropriate for uncomplicated cellulitis but inadequate for necrotising soft tissue infection which is polymicrobial or group A streptococcal; the syndrome requires both surgery and broad spectrum cover. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

options.text: Outline the erythema in marker pen, elevate the limb and repeat inflammatory blood markers in 12 hours
options.rationale: Conservative observation is appropriate for stable uncomplicated cellulitis; with systemic toxicity, hyponatraemia and disproportionate pain, delay is dangerous. (Source: ANZSA Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection)

options.text: Urgent surgical exploration with on-call team plus IV piperacillin-tazobactam, clindamycin and vancomycin
options.rationale: Pain out of proportion to visible signs, systemic toxicity, hyponatraemia and high LRINEC score (>=6 here) are the bedside red flags for necrotising fasciitis; the LRINEC score is supportive but should not delay surgical exploration which is both diagnostic and therapeutic. (Source: ANZSA Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection; eTG Antibiotic; LRINEC score)

options.text: Discharge home on oral cephalexin 500 mg six hourly with general practitioner review in 48 hours
options.rationale: Discharge home with oral antibiotics in a systemically unwell diabetic with red flags is unsafe; admission is mandatory. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency with a mortality of 20-40%. The LRINEC score uses CRP, WCC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine and glucose; scores >=6 suggest probable necrotising fasciitis, >=8 makes it highly likely. The score is supportive only - clinical features (pain out of proportion, systemic toxicity, rapid progression, skin signs evolving over hours, gas, crepitus, necrosis) drive decisions and should not be overridden by a low score. Empirical antibiotics are broad: piperacillin-tazobactam (or meropenem) plus clindamycin (anti-toxin effect at the ribosome reducing streptococcal exotoxin production) plus vancomycin for MRSA cover. IVIG is considered for streptococcal toxic shock. Surgical debridement is mandatory, with relooks every 24 hours until source-controlled.
key_points: Pain out of proportion + systemic toxicity = NSTI until proven otherwise
LRINEC >=6 probable, >=8 highly likely (supportive only)
Empirical: piperacillin-tazobactam + clindamycin + vancomycin
Surgical debridement must not be delayed for imaging
explanation.pearls: Hyponatraemia (sodium <135) plus tachycardia plus pain out of proportion in a limb cellulitis is the classic triad that should trigger surgical referral for necrotising fasciitis exclusion regardless of LRINEC score.

stem:
You are the GP registrar at a sexual health clinic seeing a 28-year-old man who reports a flu-like illness with fever, sore throat, generalised lymphadenopathy and a transient truncal maculopapular rash that began 14 days ago and lasted 7 days. He has now fully recovered. He is a man who has sex with men and reports a single condomless receptive anal intercourse encounter with a new partner 35 days ago. He did not start HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis. He last tested HIV-negative 6 months ago.

On examination he is well, with normal observations and no rash today. Mild residual cervical lymphadenopathy is present. He has had no recent travel and no other risk exposures. His past medical history is unremarkable and he takes no medications. He has had a recent gonorrhoea/chlamydia panel (negative one month ago) and the practice has 4th generation HIV antigen/antibody immunoassay (HIV Ag/Ab combo) available, as well as HIV viral load and rapid antibody testing.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Well; mild residual cervical lymphadenopathy; no rash today
data_table.History: MSM, condomless receptive anal intercourse 35 days ago; flu-like illness 14 days ago lasting 7 days; HIV negative 6 months prior; no PrEP

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnostic test today?

options.text: HIV-1 RNA viral load assay alone as the sole diagnostic test without any immunoassay today
options.rationale: Viral load testing detects HIV earlier than immunoassays (window approximately 10 days) and is reserved for suspected acute infection when 4th-gen is negative or for confirming acute primary HIV in selected cases. (Source: ASHM Acute HIV)

options.text: Fourth-generation HIV antigen/antibody combination immunoassay (HIV Ag/Ab combo)
options.rationale: At 35 days post-exposure with prior clinical seroconversion features, the 4th generation HIV Ag/Ab assay has a window period of approximately 18-45 days and reliably detects p24 antigen plus IgM/IgG antibodies; ASHM recommends 4th-gen as first-line and a reactive result triggers confirmatory testing. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Policy; ASHM Acute HIV)

options.text: Rapid point-of-care HIV antibody test only (third generation rapid antibody assay)
options.rationale: Third generation rapid antibody tests have a longer window period (approximately 23-90 days) and miss acute primary HIV with high antigen load but low antibody titre; 4th generation is preferred. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Policy)

options.text: Repeat HIV testing in three months without performing any laboratory tests on her samples today
options.rationale: Three-month deferral misses the diagnostic window where antiretroviral initiation reduces transmission and disease progression; testing now identifies acute infection. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Policy)

options.text: Lymph node biopsy of the cervical lymphadenopathy to characterise the underlying pathology
options.rationale: Reactive lymphadenopathy in this context does not require biopsy; serological and virological HIV diagnosis is non-invasive and definitive. (Source: ASHM HIV Testing Policy)

explanation.summary: Fourth generation HIV assays detect both p24 antigen and HIV-1/2 IgM/IgG antibodies, with a window period of approximately 18-45 days from infection. This is the Australian first-line HIV test per ASHM. HIV-1 RNA viral load can detect infection earlier (approximately 10 days post-exposure) and is reserved for high index of suspicion when 4th-gen is negative, suspected acute primary HIV, or seroconversion illness. Confirmatory testing of any reactive screening assay uses HIV-1/2 antibody differentiation and Western blot. Early diagnosis enables prompt antiretroviral initiation which reduces transmission (treatment-as-prevention) and disease progression. Notification to the public health unit is mandatory.
key_points: 4th gen HIV Ag/Ab combo: window approximately 18-45 days, first-line
HIV RNA viral load: window approximately 10 days, for suspected acute primary HIV
Rapid 3rd-gen tests miss acute infection
Notify to public health unit on confirmed diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Suspected HIV seroconversion illness presenting at day 35 post-exposure: 4th generation Ag/Ab combo is first line and HIV-1 RNA is added when the immunoassay is negative or equivocal but suspicion remains high.

stem:
You are the inpatient medical registrar reviewing a 54-year-old woman admitted 72 hours ago with community-acquired pneumonia. She presented with five days of cough, fever and pleuritic chest pain. She was assessed in ED as SMART-COP score 3 (BP 102/68, RR 28, SpO2 91% room air, multilobar infiltrate), commenced on IV benzylpenicillin 1.2 g 6-hourly plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily and admitted to the ward.

On day 3 of treatment she is no better. Her temperature has continued spiking to 38.8 °C twice daily. Her oxygen requirement has risen from 2 to 4 L/min nasal prongs. She has a new mild confusion that her family confirms is out of character. She has developed loose stools twice in the last 12 hours but no abdominal pain. Sodium has fallen from 138 to 128 mmol/L, ALT is now 220 U/L (was 32 U/L) and CRP has risen from 184 to 256 mg/L. Repeat chest radiograph shows progression of the right lower zone consolidation with a small new left mid zone infiltrate. Sputum cultures are negative. She returned a week ago from a hot springs holiday in the Northern Territory. Urinary Legionella antigen has not yet been sent.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, BP 108/68 mmHg, RR 26/min, SpO2 91% on 4 L nasal prongs, temperature 38.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Mild confusion (new); right lower zone crackles plus new left mid zone crackles; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 128 mmol/L (was 138, ref 135-145); ALT 220 U/L (was 32, ref <40); CRP 256 mg/L (was 184); chest radiograph: progression right lower + new left mid zone; sputum culture negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Bronchoscopy with BAL today to obtain definitive microbiological diagnosis before changing antibiotics
options.rationale: Bronchoscopy is useful in non resolving pneumonia but should not delay empiric escalation when clinical and biochemical clues already strongly suggest Legionella; urinary antigen and BAL can be sent in parallel. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

options.text: Escalate to IV piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin for nosocomial pneumonia
options.rationale: She has community acquired pneumonia (presented from home) and there is no evidence of pseudomonal or MRSA risk; broad spectrum nosocomial cover does not address suspected atypical Legionella infection. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

options.text: Continue current therapy and add IV hydrocortisone 50 mg 6-hourly for severe CAP
options.rationale: Corticosteroids may have benefit in severe CAP but do not substitute for adequate antimicrobial cover when an atypical pathogen is being missed by the current regimen. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

options.text: Send urinary Legionella antigen and switch to IV azithromycin 500 mg daily plus continue beta-lactam cover
options.rationale: The triad of hyponatraemia, transaminitis and gastrointestinal symptoms in a patient with progressive multifocal pneumonia and recent exposure to a warm-water source is highly suggestive of Legionella pneumophila, which requires azithromycin (or a fluoroquinolone such as moxifloxacin) for adequate coverage; doxycycline has weaker activity against severe Legionella infection and the urinary antigen test should be sent immediately to confirm. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Community-acquired pneumonia; CDNA Legionellosis SoNG)

options.text: Transfer to ICU for non invasive ventilation without changing antibiotic regimen
options.rationale: Oxygen requirements may indeed warrant higher level care, but escalation of respiratory support without addressing the inadequately covered pathogen perpetuates clinical failure. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis)

explanation.summary: Treatment failure in community acquired pneumonia at 72 hours is defined as worsening clinical status or absence of improvement and prompts re-evaluation. Causes include inadequate antimicrobial cover (atypical pathogens such as Legionella, Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila), resistant organism, complication (empyema, abscess), wrong diagnosis (PE, vasculitis, eosinophilic pneumonia, malignancy) or host factor (immunosuppression). Legionnaires disease classically presents with hyponatraemia, transaminitis, diarrhoea, relative bradycardia and progressive multilobar consolidation; the urinary antigen is sensitive for serogroup 1 (most common). First-line therapy in Australia is azithromycin or a respiratory fluoroquinolone (moxifloxacin); doxycycline has less activity against severe Legionella. Source identification (cooling towers, spa pools, warm water systems) triggers public health notification.
key_points: CAP non-response at 72 h: rethink pathogen, complication, diagnosis, host
Legionella triad: hyponatraemia + transaminitis + diarrhoea
Urinary antigen sensitive for serogroup 1
First-line: azithromycin IV or moxifloxacin; doxycycline weaker
explanation.pearls: The classic Legionella signature in an otherwise typical-looking CAP is the combination of hyponatraemia under 130 mmol/L, ALT above 100 U/L and gastrointestinal symptoms; presence of a warm-water exposure (cooling tower, spa, hot tub) clinches the suspicion even before urinary antigen returns.

stem:
A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus on metformin and a body mass index of 32 kg/m2 presents to your general practice with sudden onset severe pain, redness and swelling of the first metatarsophalangeal joint of the right foot that woke him at 4am. This is his first such episode and there is no preceding trauma. He has a history of a duodenal ulcer 3 years ago managed with proton pump inhibitor and is reluctant to take any NSAID; ibuprofen tried for this episode caused immediate epigastric pain.

On examination he is afebrile. The first metatarsophalangeal joint is exquisitely tender with overlying erythema, warmth and swelling extending to the dorsum of the foot. He cannot bear weight. There is no skin breach and no extension proximally. There are no tophi and no other inflamed joints. His estimated glomerular filtration rate is 65 mL/min/1.73 m2 with a normal urinary albumin to creatinine ratio. Serum urate today is 0.48 mmol/L. CRP is 84 mg/L; FBC and LFTs are within normal limits. He is on no medications other than metformin 500 mg twice daily.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, BP 132/82 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Right first MTP joint exquisitely tender, erythematous, warm, swollen; cannot weight bear; no tophi or other inflamed joints
data_table.Investigations: eGFR 65 mL/min/1.73 m2; urate 0.48 mmol/L; CRP 84 mg/L; FBC and LFTs within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: Probenecid 500 mg twice daily orally as a uricosuric agent to lower serum urate concentration
options.rationale: Probenecid is a urate lowering agent for chronic management, not acute flare treatment, and is contraindicated in the acute flare and in moderate renal impairment. (Source: AMH)

options.text: Intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g pulse infusion over 60 minutes for severe inflammatory flare control
options.rationale: Pulse intravenous steroid is excessive; a short oral prednisolone course or intra-articular steroid is appropriate when colchicine is unsuitable. (Source: eTG: Rheumatology)

options.text: Indomethacin 50 mg three times daily orally with a proton pump inhibitor cover for gastric protection
options.rationale: NSAIDs are first-line in many but contraindicated by his recent ibuprofen reaction and his duodenal ulcer history; colchicine or intra-articular steroid is preferred here. (Source: eTG: Rheumatology)

options.text: Oral colchicine 1 mg now then 500 micrograms 1 hour later, with maximum 1.5 mg in 24 hours
options.rationale: Low-dose colchicine 1 mg followed by 500 mcg 1 hour later is the recommended first-line in acute gout when NSAIDs are contraindicated or not tolerated, with eGFR over 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 supporting safe use. (Source: AMH; eTG: Rheumatology)

options.text: Allopurinol 100 mg orally daily commenced today as urate lowering therapy for prevention
options.rationale: Urate lowering therapy is initiated AFTER the acute flare settles, not during it; starting urate lowering during a flare can precipitate further gout attacks. (Source: AMH; eTG: Rheumatology)

explanation.summary: Acute gout is treated with NSAIDs (first-line if no contraindication), low-dose colchicine, or short course corticosteroid (oral 30 mg prednisolone for 5 days, or intra-articular if mono articular). Low-dose colchicine 1 mg now followed by 500 mcg 1 hour later (maximum 1.5 mg in 24 hours) is preferred over the historical high-dose regimen, which caused unacceptable diarrhoea. Colchicine is safe at this dose in eGFR over 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 but contraindicated with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin) and P-glycoprotein inhibitors (ciclosporin). Urate lowering therapy (allopurinol or febuxostat) is started 2 to 4 weeks after the flare settles with colchicine 500 mcg daily prophylaxis for 6 months to prevent flare from urate mobilisation. Target serum urate is under 0.36 mmol/L (under 0.30 mmol/L if tophaceous or recurrent).
key_points: Acute gout first-line: NSAID, low-dose colchicine, or short steroid
Colchicine 1 mg + 500 mcg in 1 hour, max 1.5 mg/24 hours
Start urate lowering 2 to 4 weeks after flare with colchicine cover
Target serum urate under 0.36 mmol/L (under 0.30 if tophaceous)
explanation.pearls: Colchicine has narrow therapeutic index and interacts with CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin, diltiazem) and P-glycoprotein inhibitors; check for these in elderly patients before prescribing per AMH.

stem:
A 65-year-old man with established stable angina diagnosed 3 years ago by exercise stress echocardiogram (single vessel left circumflex disease, non revascularisation candidate) reviews you for ongoing symptom control. He takes bisoprolol 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg, aspirin 100 mg and perindopril 4 mg. He is a former smoker (quit 4 years ago), is normotensive, and walks his dog daily but reports two episodes of central chest tightness per week on inclines that settle within 3 minutes of rest and use of glyceryl trinitrate spray.

On examination he is comfortable. Resting heart rate 58 beats per minute, blood pressure 124/72 mmHg. Heart sounds are dual with no murmur and the chest is clear. There is no peripheral oedema. He is in sinus rhythm on a recent ECG with no Q waves. A recent transthoracic echocardiogram shows preserved left ventricular ejection fraction 60% with no valvular disease. A repeat exercise stress echocardiogram 3 months ago shows the same single vessel disease without progression. He is keen to remain functional and prefers to add medication rather than undergo angiography.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 58/min, BP 124/72 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Heart sounds dual, no murmur; chest clear; no peripheral oedema; sinus rhythm
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiogram: LVEF 60%, no valvular disease; recent stress echo: single vessel left circumflex disease without progression
data_table.Medications: Bisoprolol 5 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, aspirin 100 mg, perindopril 4 mg, GTN spray PRN

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next addition?

options.text: Add nicorandil 10 mg orally twice daily as a potassium channel opener with nitrate like action
options.rationale: Nicorandil is a third-line agent reserved for patients intolerant of beta blockers or calcium channel blockers; it is not first dual therapy. (Source: eTG: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Add diltiazem 60 mg orally three times daily as a non dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker
options.rationale: Non dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are contraindicated with beta blockers due to AV node conduction block and risk of bradycardia or asystole. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Stable Angina; AMH)

options.text: Refer for coronary angiography with consideration of percutaneous coronary intervention for revascularisation
options.rationale: He has already been assessed as a non revascularisation candidate; medical therapy optimisation is the agreed pathway and dual antianginal therapy has not been tried yet. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Stable Angina)

options.text: Add ranolazine 500 mg orally twice daily as a late sodium current inhibitor for refractory symptoms
options.rationale: Ranolazine is a third-line agent on PBS authority for refractory angina; it is added after first-line dual therapy fails, not before. (Source: PBS)

options.text: Add amlodipine 5 mg orally daily as a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker for anti anginal benefit
options.rationale: Beta blocker plus dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (amlodipine) is the recommended dual antianginal therapy in stable angina with inadequate symptom control on monotherapy. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Stable Angina; eTG: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Stable angina is managed with both prognostic therapy (aspirin, high-intensity statin, ACE inhibitor in selected patients) and antianginal therapy (beta blocker or non dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker first-line). When monotherapy is inadequate, dual antianginal therapy with a beta blocker and a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (amlodipine or felodipine) is preferred; non dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are NOT combined with beta blockers due to AV node block. Refractory symptoms may justify addition of nicorandil, ivabradine (sinus rhythm only), or ranolazine. Revascularisation is considered for symptoms refractory to optimal medical therapy or for prognostic indications (left main, three vessel disease with reduced left ventricular function). All patients receive cardiovascular risk factor optimisation.
key_points: Dual antianginal: beta blocker + DHP-CCB (amlodipine)
AVOID non-DHP-CCB (diltiazem, verapamil) with beta blocker
Third-line: nicorandil, ivabradine (SR), ranolazine
Revascularisation for refractory symptoms or prognostic indications
explanation.pearls: Ivabradine 5 mg twice daily is an alternative third-line antianginal in patients with sinus rhythm and heart rate over 70 beats per minute on maximally tolerated beta blockade; it has no effect on blood pressure unlike calcium channel blockers per NHFA guidance.

stem:
A 45-year-old woman with newly diagnosed primary hypothyroidism reviews you in your general practice 8 weeks after starting levothyroxine 50 mcg daily. Her diagnosis was made on a TSH of 28 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0) and a free T4 of 7 pmol/L (10 to 22), with positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies. She weighs 65 kg, has no cardiovascular disease, and is not pregnant. Initial fatigue and cold intolerance have improved but she still notes mild fatigue at the end of the day.

She has been taking her levothyroxine each morning on an empty stomach 30 minutes before breakfast and coffee, with no calcium, iron, or proton pump inhibitor co administration. Compliance has been complete according to the pharmacy records. She is on no other regular medications. Today's blood pressure is 122/74 mmHg, pulse is 68 in sinus rhythm and she is clinically euthyroid on examination. The latest thyroid panel reports TSH 12.5 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), free T4 12 pmol/L (10 to 22) and free T3 within normal limits. Other biochemistry is within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 68/min, BP 122/74 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Clinically euthyroid; no goitre; no tremor
data_table.Investigations: TSH 12.5 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); free T4 12 pmol/L (10-22); free T3 within normal limits; weight 65 kg
data_table.Medications: Levothyroxine 50 mcg daily for 8 weeks taken correctly on empty stomach

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase levothyroxine to 75 mcg orally each morning and repeat the TSH in 6 to 8 weeks
options.rationale: Full replacement for primary hypothyroidism is approximately 1.6 mcg/kg/day (around 100 mcg for this patient at 65 kg); titrate in 25 mcg increments every 6 to 8 weeks until TSH is in the lower half of the reference range. (Source: AMH; eTG: Endocrinology)

options.text: Add liothyronine 10 mcg orally daily as combination therapy for residual fatigue symptoms
options.rationale: Combination T4 plus T3 is not first-line because trials show no consistent symptom benefit; adequate levothyroxine titration should be tried first. (Source: AMH; eTG: Endocrinology)

options.text: Continue current 50 mcg dose and repeat thyroid function tests in 6 months as a stable dose
options.rationale: TSH 12.5 mIU/L is above target; under-replacement should not be left for 6 months because it perpetuates symptoms and adverse effects on lipids and cardiac function. (Source: eTG: Endocrinology)

options.text: Increase to 100 mcg orally each morning and repeat thyroid function tests in 4 weeks
options.rationale: A large dose increment of 50 mcg risks overshoot to subclinical hyperthyroidism; 25 mcg titration with 6 to 8 week re-check is the standard. (Source: eTG: Endocrinology)

options.text: Switch to natural desiccated thyroid extract 60 mg orally daily as an alternative replacement formulation
options.rationale: Desiccated thyroid extract has variable hormone content batch to batch and is not recommended over levothyroxine in evidence-based practice. (Source: AMH; eTG: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Primary hypothyroidism is treated with once daily oral levothyroxine taken on an empty stomach to minimise food and calcium or iron interaction. Full replacement is approximately 1.6 mcg/kg/day; lower starting doses (25 to 50 mcg) are used in elderly or coronary artery disease patients. TSH is the marker of replacement adequacy: target lower half of the reference range (0.4 to 2.5 mIU/L). Dose adjustments are made in 25 mcg increments every 6 to 8 weeks because the half-life of levothyroxine is 7 days. Persistent fatigue with adequate TSH suggests a parallel diagnosis (depression, vitamin D deficiency, anaemia) rather than under-replacement. Pregnancy or planned pregnancy requires a 25 to 50% dose increase to maintain TSH under 2.5 mIU/L.
key_points: Full replacement approximately 1.6 mcg/kg/day
TSH target lower half reference range (0.4 to 2.5 mIU/L)
Dose adjust in 25 mcg increments every 6 to 8 weeks
Pregnancy: increase dose 25 to 50%, target TSH under 2.5
explanation.pearls: In pregnancy, levothyroxine dose typically needs to rise by 25 to 50% from preconception baseline; women on stable therapy should add 2 extra tablets per week as soon as pregnancy is confirmed per RANZCOG and Endocrine Society guidance, until the trimester-specific TSH is checked.

stem:
A 48-year-old plumber is referred to the endocrinology clinic by his general practitioner with a 12 month history of progressive change in his appearance. He has noticed that his wedding ring no longer fits, his shoes have gone from size 10 to size 12, and his glove size has gone up. He has new daily frontal headaches, oily skin and sweating that disturbs his sleep. His wife noted his lower jaw has become more prominent in a recent family photograph compared with one from 5 years ago.

On examination he has coarse facial features with prominent supraorbital ridges and prognathism. His tongue is enlarged. Hand examination reveals spade-like fingers with skin tag development. Blood pressure is 158/95 mmHg. There is no visual field defect on confrontation. Cardiac and respiratory examination are unremarkable. Random growth hormone concentration done by the referring doctor was 6 mcg/L (under 1 in healthy adults); insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) is markedly elevated for his age and sex. Renal function is normal and HbA1c is 7.2%. A pituitary MRI has been requested but not yet performed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, BP 158/95 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Coarse facial features with prominent supraorbital ridges and prognathism; enlarged tongue; spade-like fingers; visual fields full on confrontation
data_table.Investigations: Random GH 6 mcg/L (<1 healthy); IGF-1 markedly elevated for age and sex; HbA1c 7.2%; renal function within normal limits; MRI pituitary not yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Random morning cortisol and TSH to screen for combined pituitary hormone abnormalities first
options.rationale: Pituitary hormone screening is appropriate as part of workup after diagnosis but does not confirm acromegaly itself; the diagnostic step is OGTT-GH suppression. (Source: Endocrine Society Acromegaly)

options.text: Oral glucose tolerance test with serial growth hormone measurements at 0, 30, 60, 90 and 120 minutes
options.rationale: Failure of growth hormone to suppress below 1 mcg/L during a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test confirms acromegaly biochemically; IGF-1 plus failed OGTT suppression is the diagnostic gold standard. (Source: Endocrine Society Acromegaly; eTG: Endocrinology)

options.text: 24-hour urinary insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) measurement to confirm overproduction objectively
options.rationale: Urinary IGF-1 is not part of the diagnostic algorithm; serum IGF-1 already screened is the standard measure of growth hormone exposure. (Source: Endocrine Society Acromegaly)

options.text: Insulin tolerance test with serial growth hormone measurements during induced hypoglycaemia
options.rationale: Insulin tolerance test is used to confirm growth hormone DEFICIENCY (lack of rise); it is not the test for growth hormone excess in acromegaly. (Source: Endocrine Society Acromegaly)

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary with contrast as the first definitive confirmatory investigation
options.rationale: MRI confirms the anatomical lesion but does not confirm hormonal hypersecretion biochemically; OGTT with serial growth hormone is the biochemical confirmation that defines active disease. (Source: Endocrine Society Acromegaly; eTG: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Acromegaly is caused by a growth hormone secreting pituitary adenoma in over 95% of cases, with insidious onset and average diagnostic delay of 7 to 10 years. Cardinal features include coarse facial features, prognathism, macroglossia, soft tissue and acral enlargement, hyperhidrosis, headache, sleep apnoea, hypertension, glucose intolerance, and arthropathy. Biochemical diagnosis is by raised serum IGF-1 for age and sex plus failure of growth hormone to suppress below 1 mcg/L during a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test. After biochemical confirmation, MRI pituitary defines the adenoma (microadenoma under 10 mm or macroadenoma 10 mm and over), and the rest of pituitary function is assessed. First-line treatment is transsphenoidal surgery for microadenomas and most macroadenomas; medical therapy (somatostatin analogues, pegvisomant, dopamine agonists) and radiotherapy are second and third line.
key_points: Screen with IGF-1 for age and sex; random GH alone is unreliable
Confirm with OGTT-GH suppression below 1 mcg/L failure
MRI pituitary defines anatomy AFTER biochemical confirmation
First-line treatment: transsphenoidal surgery
explanation.pearls: Cardiovascular disease drives excess mortality in acromegaly (heart failure, hypertension, coronary disease); standardised mortality ratio falls from approximately 1.7 in untreated disease to 1.0 with adequate biochemical control of IGF-1 and growth hormone.

stem:
A 68-year-old man is referred to your acute medical clinic with 6 months of progressive mid-thoracic back pain, intermittent fatigue and 4 kg of unintentional weight loss. He has no fever, night sweats or lymphadenopathy. He worked as a builder until retirement 3 years ago. There has been no recent travel and no obvious infective history. He has been managing the back pain with paracetamol with limited benefit and the general practitioner has organised initial bloods.

On examination he is pale. Cardiac and respiratory examination is unremarkable. There is tenderness over the thoracic spine at T8 with no neurological deficit in the lower limbs. There is no hepatosplenomegaly. Initial bloodwork shows haemoglobin 92 g/L, white cell count 6.2 x10^9/L with normal differential, platelets 218 x10^9/L. Creatinine has risen from 90 (3 years ago) to 168 micromol/L. Corrected calcium is 2.85 mmol/L (2.10 to 2.60). Albumin is 32 g/L. ESR is 110 mm/hour. LFTs and TSH are within normal limits. The general practitioner has organised a thoracic spine X-ray which shows multiple lytic lesions in T7 and T8 vertebral bodies.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 80/min, BP 132/80 mmHg, RR 14/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Pale, T8 thoracic tenderness, no neurological deficit; no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: Hb 92 g/L, WCC 6.2 x10^9/L with normal differential, platelets 218 x10^9/L; creatinine 168 micromol/L (was 90 three years ago); corrected calcium 2.85 mmol/L; albumin 32 g/L; ESR 110 mm/hour; LFTs and TSH within normal limits; thoracic spine: lytic lesions T7 and T8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Whole body PET-CT to exclude other haematological malignancies and solid organ neoplasm as differential
options.rationale: PET-CT is more useful in solitary plasmacytoma and treatment response monitoring than in initial diagnosis of suspected myeloma; serum and urine paraprotein detection are the first step. (Source: HSANZ Myeloma)

options.text: Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy with flow cytometry as the first diagnostic procedure today
options.rationale: Bone marrow is part of myeloma workup but follows demonstration of paraprotein; jumping to marrow without paraprotein screen is not standard. (Source: HSANZ Myeloma)

options.text: Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation, serum free light chains and urinary Bence Jones protein
options.rationale: In CRAB-pattern clinical picture (hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia, bone lesions), the diagnostic step is to detect monoclonal protein with SPEP plus immunofixation, serum free light chain assay and Bence Jones protein in urine; bone marrow follows. (Source: HSANZ Myeloma; MSAG Clinical Practice Guidelines)

options.text: Renal biopsy to identify the cause of acute kidney injury and proteinuria before any further workup
options.rationale: Renal biopsy is reserved for cases where paraprotein workup is negative or the cause of kidney injury remains uncertain; in classic CRAB the paraprotein screen comes first. (Source: HSANZ Myeloma)

options.text: Whole body magnetic resonance imaging to characterise the extent of skeletal disease across the axial skeleton
options.rationale: Imaging staging follows biochemical confirmation; serum protein electrophoresis, free light chains and Bence Jones are the initial diagnostic step for suspected myeloma. (Source: HSANZ Myeloma; MSAG Clinical Practice Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Multiple myeloma is suspected when CRAB features (hypercalcaemia over 2.75 mmol/L, renal impairment, anaemia, lytic bone disease) are present in an older patient with normochromic normocytic anaemia and raised ESR or rouleaux on film. Initial workup is serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) with immunofixation, serum free light chain assay, and 24-hour urine for Bence Jones protein. Approximately 97% of myelomas have a detectable paraprotein. Confirmation requires bone marrow showing clonal plasma cells over 10% plus end-organ damage (CRAB) or biomarkers of malignancy (clonal plasma cells over 60%, light chain ratio over 100, MRI focal lesions over 1). Whole body low-dose CT or PET-CT or whole body MRI staging follows. Treatment depends on transplant eligibility but typically involves bortezomib-based induction with dexamethasone plus lenalidomide.
key_points: CRAB: hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia, bone lesions
First test: SPEP + immunofixation + serum free light chains + urine Bence Jones
Confirm with marrow plus CRAB or biomarkers (SLiM-CRAB)
Stage with whole body low-dose CT, PET-CT, or whole body MRI
explanation.pearls: In Australia, low-dose whole body CT has largely replaced traditional skeletal survey for myeloma staging because it detects more lytic lesions at lower radiation dose; whole body MRI is the more sensitive alternative for marrow involvement when CT is equivocal per HSANZ guidance.

subtopic_detail: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis disease modifying therapy
stem:
A 70-year-old retired farmer is referred to your respiratory clinic with 18 months of progressive exertional breathlessness and a daily dry cough. He has been previously well, is a never smoker, and has no occupational asbestos history despite his farming background. He has no current bird exposure, no humidifier use, and a recent normal echocardiogram with no pulmonary hypertension. He has no joint or skin features of connective tissue disease, and the rheumatology screen ordered by his general practitioner including ANA, ENA, RF, anti-CCP and myositis panel is negative.

On examination he is comfortable at rest with no clubbing. There are bilateral basal fine end-inspiratory velcro crackles to mid zone on auscultation. Cardiovascular examination is unremarkable. High resolution computed tomography of the chest is reported by the multidisciplinary meeting as showing peripheral and basal predominant honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis, and reticulation; no ground glass, no nodules and no mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Pulmonary function tests show FVC 65% predicted, FEV1/FVC 80%, DLCO 50% predicted. The MDM has reached a confident diagnosis of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, BP 132/78 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Comfortable at rest, no clubbing; bilateral basal fine end-inspiratory crackles
data_table.Investigations: HRCT: peripheral basal honeycombing, traction bronchiectasis, reticulation, no ground glass; PFT: FVC 65% predicted, DLCO 50% predicted; rheumatology screen negative; echocardiogram no PH
data_table.MDM: Multidisciplinary diagnosis: idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (definite UIP pattern)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate disease modifying treatment?

options.text: Oral N-acetylcysteine 600 mg three times daily as a mucolytic and antioxidant for disease modification
options.rationale: N-acetylcysteine monotherapy showed no benefit over placebo in the PANTHER-IPF and INSTAGE trials and is not standard care. (Source: TSANZ IPF Position Statement)

options.text: Pulse intravenous cyclophosphamide 600 mg/m2 monthly as immunosuppressive induction for 6 months
options.rationale: Cyclophosphamide is used in severe connective tissue disease ILD (scleroderma ILD) but is not recommended in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. (Source: TSANZ IPF Position Statement)

options.text: Mycophenolate mofetil 1 g orally twice daily with regular full blood count and LFT monitoring
options.rationale: Mycophenolate is reserved for connective tissue disease-associated ILD which has been excluded by negative rheumatology screen; it is not the recommended IPF therapy. (Source: TSANZ IPF Position Statement)

options.text: Oral pirfenidone titrated to 801 mg three times daily with photosensitivity precautions and LFT monitoring
options.rationale: Antifibrotic therapy with pirfenidone (or nintedanib) is the recommended disease modifying therapy in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis; it slows decline in forced vital capacity and reduces mortality. (Source: TSANZ IPF Position Statement; ATS/ERS IPF Guidelines)

options.text: Long-term oral prednisolone 30 mg daily with calcium and vitamin D for bone protection and azithromycin prophylaxis
options.rationale: Long-term steroids are NOT recommended in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis because the PANTHER-IPF trial demonstrated harm with prednisolone, azathioprine and N-acetylcysteine combination. (Source: TSANZ IPF Position Statement; ATS/ERS Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is the most common idiopathic interstitial pneumonia, characterised by progressive fibrosis with a usual interstitial pneumonia pattern on HRCT. Diagnosis requires exclusion of known causes (connective tissue disease, asbestos, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, drug induced) and a definite UIP HRCT pattern confirmed at multidisciplinary meeting. Antifibrotic therapy with pirfenidone or nintedanib slows annual FVC decline by approximately half and reduces mortality; both are subsidised on the PBS for definite IPF with FVC 50 to 90% predicted. Long-term steroids are harmful in IPF per the PANTHER-IPF trial and N-acetylcysteine monotherapy is not effective. Supportive care includes pulmonary rehabilitation, supplemental oxygen, GORD treatment, vaccination, and consideration of lung transplantation in eligible candidates.
key_points: Definite UIP HRCT + exclusion of secondary causes = IPF
Antifibrotic: pirfenidone or nintedanib slows FVC decline approximately 50%
Long-term steroids are HARMFUL in IPF (PANTHER-IPF)
Supportive: oxygen, pulmonary rehab, transplantation, palliative care
explanation.pearls: PBS subsidy for pirfenidone and nintedanib in Australia requires definite IPF on multidisciplinary review, FVC 50 to 90% predicted, and DLCO 30 to 79% predicted at initiation; FVC threshold for ongoing PBS subsidy requires demonstrated stabilisation or decline less than 10% per year on therapy.

stem:
A 56-year-old woman is referred to your general medicine clinic with a 4-month history of episodic flushing of the upper chest and neck, watery diarrhoea up to 8 times daily, and audible wheeze with intermittent dyspnoea during the flushing attacks. She has lost 5 kg of weight. Her primary care general practitioner organised a transthoracic echocardiogram for the wheeze; it shows tricuspid valve leaflet thickening with severe regurgitation and pulmonary stenosis, with preserved left ventricular function.

On examination she has a slightly cyanotic facial complexion. There is no telangiectasia. JVP is mildly elevated with a giant V wave. There is a pansystolic murmur at the lower left sternal edge augmenting with inspiration. Abdomen is soft with mild right upper quadrant fullness; bowel sounds are active. There is no obvious lymphadenopathy. CT abdomen and pelvis ordered as part of her weight loss workup shows a 2 cm enhancing mass in the terminal ileum, multiple bilobar liver lesions and mild mesenteric desmoplastic reaction. Liver function tests are within normal limits today; renal function and electrolytes are unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, BP 122/74 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Mild facial cyanosis; JVP elevated with giant V wave; lower left sternal edge pansystolic murmur augmenting with inspiration; RUQ fullness
data_table.Investigations: Echocardiogram: tricuspid leaflet thickening with severe regurgitation, pulmonary stenosis, preserved LV function; CT abdomen: 2 cm enhancing terminal ileal mass, multiple bilobar liver lesions, mesenteric desmoplasia; LFTs, renal function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

options.text: Plasma chromogranin A measurement and serum serotonin measurement as ambulatory screening biomarkers
options.rationale: Plasma chromogranin A is supportive but non specific and serum serotonin is not a primary diagnostic test in Australia; 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA on a low amine diet is the established Australian biochemical confirmation. (Source: AGS Neuroendocrine Tumour Guidelines; eviQ Cancer Treatments)

options.text: Image guided percutaneous liver biopsy of the largest lesion under ultrasound guidance for histology
options.rationale: Liver biopsy carries risk of carcinoid crisis from serotonin release and requires somatostatin analogue cover; biochemical confirmation should precede biopsy. (Source: AGS Neuroendocrine Tumour Guidelines)

options.text: Iodine-131 metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scan for catecholamine-secreting tumour imaging
options.rationale: MIBG imaging is used in phaeochromocytoma and neuroblastoma diagnosis; it is not the test of choice for serotonin-secreting carcinoid tumours. (Source: AGS Neuroendocrine Tumour Guidelines)

options.text: 68-Ga DOTATATE positron emission tomography for tumour somatostatin receptor expression mapping
options.rationale: DOTATATE PET is the staging imaging of choice in neuroendocrine tumour after biochemical confirmation; it identifies somatostatin receptor expression but does not establish the diagnosis. (Source: AGS Neuroendocrine Tumour Guidelines)

options.text: 24-hour urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid measurement on a low amine diet for 2 consecutive collections
options.rationale: 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA on a low amine diet (no banana, walnut, tomato, avocado, kiwifruit, pineapple, paracetamol, caffeine) for 2 consecutive collections is the diagnostic standard for carcinoid syndrome; serotonin metabolism via 5-HIAA correlates with tumour load. (Source: AGS Neuroendocrine Tumour Guidelines; eviQ Cancer Treatments)

explanation.summary: Carcinoid syndrome occurs in approximately 20% of patients with midgut neuroendocrine tumours when serotonin and vasoactive metabolites reach the systemic circulation - usually after liver metastases bypass first-pass hepatic clearance. The classic triad is episodic flushing, watery diarrhoea and bronchospasm; right heart valve fibrosis (tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonary stenosis) is the late carcinoid heart disease. Biochemical confirmation is 24-hour urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) on a low amine diet for 2 consecutive collections; sensitivity over 75% and specificity over 90%. Imaging staging is 68-Ga DOTATATE PET. Treatment of carcinoid syndrome is somatostatin analogue (octreotide LAR or lanreotide) for symptoms, liver-directed therapy (resection, embolisation, radiofrequency ablation, Y-90 radioembolisation) for liver burden, and peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (177-Lu DOTATATE) for refractory disease. Carcinoid crisis is precipitated by anaesthesia, biopsy or tumour manipulation and is prevented with peri-procedure octreotide infusion.
key_points: Classic triad: flushing, watery diarrhoea, bronchospasm
Tricuspid regurgitation plus pulmonary stenosis = carcinoid heart disease
Confirm with 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA on low amine diet x 2
Stage with 68-Ga DOTATATE PET; treat with somatostatin analogue
explanation.pearls: Carcinoid crisis (severe flushing, hypotension, bronchospasm, arrhythmia) is precipitated by anaesthetic induction, biopsy or tumour manipulation; peri-procedural octreotide 500 mcg subcutaneous before induction and 100 mcg/hour intra-operative infusion is recommended by eviQ to prevent crisis.

subtopic_detail: Type B aortic dissection rate control before vasodilator
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a tertiary ED. A 58-year-old previously well man presents with sudden severe interscapular pain radiating to his lower back that began 90 minutes ago while walking. He is on no regular medications and has no past medical history beyond untreated hypertension. He smokes 20 per day. CT aortogram has confirmed a type B aortic dissection beginning distal to the left subclavian artery with no end-organ ischaemia and no rupture.

On examination he is restless and uncomfortable but cooperating. He has equal radial pulses, neurologically intact lower limbs, and a soft non-tender abdomen. He has no clinical signs of cardiac tamponade. The vascular surgeon has been consulted and recommends initial medical management. The intensive care team is preparing a bed and the consultant cardiologist has been informed.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 105/min, BP 196/118 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Restless, cooperating; equal radial pulses; abdomen soft, non-tender; lower limbs warm with intact pulses and sensation
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia, no ischaemic changes; troponin 8 ng/L (under 14); creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110); lactate 1.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial intravenous therapy?

options.text: Intravenous labetalol infusion alone targeting mean arterial pressure under 80
options.rationale: Labetalol alone is acceptable as both rate and BP control but the target MAP is too low and would risk end-organ ischaemia; usual target is SBP 100-120 with HR 60-80, not aggressively low MAP. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Intravenous sodium nitroprusside infusion immediately to drop systolic BP under 120
options.rationale: Pure vasodilator without prior rate control causes reflex tachycardia and increased aortic shear stress, propagating the dissection; rate control with beta-blocker must precede vasodilator. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion as the first-line vasodilator titrated to BP
options.rationale: GTN without prior beta-blockade causes reflex tachycardia and propagates dissection; rate control comes first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: IV esmolol or labetalol to HR <60 first, then add IV vasodilator (GTN or nicardipine) for BP
options.rationale: AU and international guidance for type B aortic dissection is rate control with beta-blocker first (esmolol or labetalol) to a heart rate under 60, then add a vasodilator if BP remains elevated; this sequence prevents reflex tachycardia and dissection propagation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Oral metoprolol 50 mg plus oral amlodipine 5 mg as adequate initial control
options.rationale: Oral therapy lacks the titration speed and reliability required in acute dissection; IV titratable agents are mandatory in the initial hours. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection management aims to reduce aortic shear stress (dP/dt) by first controlling heart rate with a beta-blocker, then adding a vasodilator if BP remains above target. Starting with vasodilator alone causes reflex tachycardia and propagates the dissection. Targets are heart rate under 60 and systolic BP 100-120 mmHg with adequate organ perfusion.
key_points: First beta-blocker (esmolol, labetalol), then vasodilator (GTN, nicardipine).
Heart rate target under 60; systolic BP 100-120 mmHg.
Type A dissection (proximal) is a surgical emergency; type B is initially medical unless complicated.
Avoid pure vasodilator without prior beta-blockade due to reflex tachycardia.
explanation.pearls: The sequence in aortic dissection BP control is rate first, pressure second; the order matters because reflex tachycardia accelerates the tear.

subtopic_detail: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes acute management
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a tertiary ED reviewing a 72-year-old woman with heart failure on lisinopril 10 mg daily and spironolactone 25 mg daily who has presented with generalised weakness and palpitations. She has been less active over the past week with reduced oral intake. Her baseline eGFR was 45 mL/min and her last potassium 2 weeks ago was 5.0 mmol/L. She has no diabetes and is on no insulin.

On arrival she is alert but feels weak. The ECG shows tall peaked T waves in the precordial leads, a PR interval of 220 ms, and a QRS duration of 110 ms. She has no chest pain and no focal neurology. Her potassium has just returned at 7.3 mmol/L. The renal registrar has been informed and a HDU bed is being arranged.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 56/min, BP 122/78 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.6 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert; mild proximal weakness lower limbs; abdomen soft non-tender; no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: K 7.3 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); creatinine 215 micromol/L (45-90), eGFR 28 mL/min; HCO3 18 mmol/L (22-26); ECG peaked T waves, PR 220 ms, QRS 110 ms; venous gas pH 7.30

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate first intervention?

options.text: Intravenous insulin 10 units plus 50 mL of 50% dextrose over 15 minutes
options.rationale: Insulin-dextrose shifts potassium but does not protect the myocardium; calcium for membrane stabilisation must come first when ECG changes are present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 10 mg by mask as first-line treatment of hyperkalaemia
options.rationale: Salbutamol shifts potassium intracellularly but does not stabilise the myocardium; calcium gluconate is given first when ECG changes are present. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol bolus to correct acidosis and shift potassium
options.rationale: Bicarbonate is reserved for severe metabolic acidosis as adjunct; its effect on potassium is modest and slower than calcium. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Oral resonium 30 g (sodium polystyrene sulfonate) with sorbitol as binder
options.rationale: Resin binders act over hours, are slow, and do not address acute cardiac membrane risk; they are an adjunct after stabilisation and shifting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: IV calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL over 5 min for cardiac membrane stabilisation
options.rationale: When hyperkalaemia produces ECG changes (peaked T waves, PR prolongation, QRS widening), calcium gluconate is the first intervention to stabilise the cardiac membrane, followed by potassium-shifting (insulin-dextrose, salbutamol) and removal (resin, dialysis). (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes is managed in three sequential steps: stabilise (calcium gluconate or chloride), shift (insulin-dextrose, salbutamol), and remove (resin binder or dialysis). The first step prevents arrhythmic death; the second buys time; the third corrects the total body potassium. ACE inhibitor plus aldosterone antagonist plus declining renal function is a common precipitant.
key_points: Stabilise: IV calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL over 5 min (or calcium chloride 10% 10 mL via central line).
Shift: IV insulin 10 units + 50% dextrose 50 mL; nebulised salbutamol 10 mg.
Remove: cation exchange resin or dialysis depending on burden.
Cease the precipitating ACE inhibitor, ARB, or potassium-sparing diuretic.
explanation.pearls: Peaked T waves with a potassium above 6 mmol/L on an ACE inhibitor plus spironolactone gets calcium gluconate first; insulin-dextrose alone does not protect the heart in the next 5 minutes.

subtopic_detail: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia hypertonic saline bolus
stem:
You are the medical registrar in a tertiary ED reviewing a 78-year-old woman commenced on sertraline 50 mg daily and amitriptyline 25 mg nocte 2 weeks ago for depression and chronic pain. She was found by her daughter having a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 90 seconds with post-ictal drowsiness. She has no other medical history of note and was previously well. She has not been drinking excessive fluid.

On examination she is post-ictal but rousable to voice. She is clinically euvolaemic with normal jugular venous pressure, no peripheral oedema, and warm peripheries. Cortisol and TSH are within range. She has no clinical evidence of heart failure, cirrhosis, or hypovolaemia. The renal team and intensive care team are aware and a HDU bed is being prepared.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, BP 120/70 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Post-ictal but rousable; euvolaemic; chest clear; abdomen soft; no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Na 112 mmol/L (135-145), K 3.8 mmol/L; urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg, plasma osmolality 248 mOsm/kg; urine Na 65 mmol/L; cortisol within range; TSH 2.1 mIU/L (0.4-4.0); creatinine within normal limits

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: IV 3% hypertonic saline 150 mL bolus over 10 minutes, repeat to raise Na 4-6 mmol/L
options.rationale: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizure, coma) is treated with bolus 3% hypertonic saline 150 mL over 10 minutes, repeated to raise sodium 4-6 mmol/L in the first hour, with strict caution not to exceed 8-10 mmol/L in 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination; the SSRI is a likely precipitant. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Intravenous 0.9% saline at 250 mL/hour with daily sodium monitoring
options.rationale: Isotonic saline corrects too slowly for symptomatic severe hyponatraemia with seizure and can worsen SIADH-driven hyponatraemia; bolus hypertonic is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Fluid restriction to 500 mL/day alone with repeat sodium in 12 hours
options.rationale: Fluid restriction is for chronic asymptomatic SIADH; severe acute symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizure mandates immediate hypertonic saline. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Intravenous tolvaptan 30 mg as a vasopressin receptor antagonist infusion
options.rationale: Tolvaptan is oral, not IV; it is reserved for sub-acute SIADH management, not acute symptomatic severe hyponatraemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Intravenous mannitol 25 g infusion for presumed cerebral oedema management
options.rationale: Mannitol is not used for hyponatraemia-related cerebral oedema; the specific treatment is hypertonic saline to raise serum sodium directly. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizure, coma, vomiting) is treated with bolus 3% hypertonic saline 150 mL over 10 minutes, repeated up to 3 times if needed, aiming to raise serum sodium 4-6 mmol/L in the first hour. Overcorrection above 8-10 mmol/L in 24 hours risks osmotic demyelination syndrome. SSRIs and TCAs are common precipitants of SIADH in older adults.
key_points: Hypertonic saline bolus dose: 150 mL of 3% saline over 10 min, up to 3 doses.
Target sodium rise: 4-6 mmol/L in the first hour, then a maximum of 8-10 mmol/L per 24 hours.
SSRIs, TCAs, thiazides, and carbamazepine are common medication precipitants.
Overcorrection risk: osmotic demyelination syndrome (former central pontine myelinolysis).
explanation.pearls: Seizure plus sodium of 112 mmol/L on a new SSRI gets 3% saline bolus 150 mL now, not 0.9% saline maintenance; the target is up by 5 in the first hour, then slow.

sources.label: European Society of Endocrinology Hyponatraemia Guideline

stem:
You are the medical registrar in a regional ED reviewing a 52-year-old woman with long-standing primary adrenal insufficiency on hydrocortisone 10 mg morning, 5 mg lunch, 5 mg evening, and fludrocortisone 100 mcg daily. She has had 24 hours of vomiting from a presumed gastroenteritis and was unable to keep her medications down today. She has presented to the ED feeling weak, dizzy, and confused.

On examination she is drowsy with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 13. Her peripheries are cool and her capillary refill is 3 seconds. She has no fever and no focal infection on examination. She has had no recent surgery or other intercurrent illness. The endocrine team is on the way but you are managing the acute resuscitation. The HDU bed has been requested.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122/min, BP 84/52 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy GCS 13; cool peripheries; capillary refill 3 seconds; mucous membranes dry; abdomen soft non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Na 126 mmol/L (135-145), K 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); glucose 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-7.8); creatinine 132 micromol/L (45-90); cortisol pending; venous gas pH 7.30

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous ondansetron 4 mg and oral rehydration salt trial over 2 hours
options.rationale: Anti-emetics and oral rehydration alone do not address adrenal crisis; immediate IV hydrocortisone and saline are required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg plus 0.9% saline 1 L bolus and dextrose if hypoglycaemic
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis is treated with IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat (then 50 mg every 6 hours or infusion), 0.9% saline 1 L bolus for hypovolaemia, and dextrose if hypoglycaemic; this is the AU first-hour bundle and should not wait for the cortisol result. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Intravenous fludrocortisone 200 mcg as the primary mineralocorticoid replacement
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is for chronic mineralocorticoid replacement; high-dose IV hydrocortisone has sufficient mineralocorticoid activity in the acute phase, and oral fludrocortisone is irrelevant when vomiting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Oral hydrocortisone 50 mg with intravenous fluids only and no IV glucocorticoid
options.rationale: Oral therapy is unreliable in a vomiting patient with adrenal crisis; IV hydrocortisone is mandatory. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg as preferred glucocorticoid in adrenal crisis
options.rationale: Dexamethasone has no mineralocorticoid activity and is reserved for when biochemical confirmation of adrenal insufficiency is required (will not interfere with cortisol assay); in known adrenal insufficiency, hydrocortisone is preferred. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is treated with immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg, IV 0.9% saline 1 L bolus, and IV dextrose if hypoglycaemic. Hydrocortisone has both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity at high dose, sufficient for the acute phase. Dexamethasone is reserved for when biochemical confirmation is needed (it does not interfere with cortisol assay) but hydrocortisone is the preferred treatment in known adrenal insufficiency.
key_points: First hour: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat + IV 0.9% saline 1 L + dextrose if hypoglycaemic.
Maintenance: IV hydrocortisone 50 mg every 6 hours or 200 mg/24 h infusion until oral tolerated.
Do not delay treatment for cortisol or ACTH result.
Dexamethasone is used when biochemical confirmation pending; otherwise hydrocortisone.
explanation.pearls: A vomiting patient on long-term hydrocortisone gets 100 mg IV in resus before bloods come back, not after; the sick-day rules trump the cortisol level.

stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 30-year-old woman in your suburban clinic after she was stung by a bee on her arm 8 minutes ago in the waiting room. She has no prior allergy history but has developed generalised urticaria, marked lip and tongue swelling, hoarse voice, audible stridor, and an audible wheeze over the past 5 minutes. She feels dizzy on standing.

On examination she is anxious and unable to complete sentences. The practice nurse has placed her supine on the floor, has cannulated her, and has the emergency drug box open. An ambulance has been called and is 8 minutes away. The practice has IM and IV adrenaline available in standard ampoules of 1:1000 strength. There is no anaphylaxis action plan on file.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138/min, BP 80/52 mmHg, RR 28/min, SpO2 91% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Anxious, sentence fragments only; generalised urticaria; lip and tongue swelling; stridor at rest; bilateral wheeze; capillary refill 3 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 6.4 mmol/L; no other bedside investigations available; cannula in situ

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Intravenous adrenaline 100 mcg bolus given via the peripheral cannula
options.rationale: IV adrenaline boluses are reserved for refractory anaphylaxis after IM doses fail and only by clinicians with critical care familiarity due to arrhythmia and myocardial ischaemia risk; IM is first-line. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 as the primary therapy for stridor
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is an adjunct for upper airway oedema after IM dosing; it is not first-line treatment for systemic anaphylaxis. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1:1000) into the anterolateral mid-thigh
options.rationale: Adult anaphylaxis with hypotension, airway, and circulatory features is treated with IM adrenaline 0.5 mg into the anterolateral mid-thigh as the first action; repeat every 5 minutes if no improvement. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg first while preparing adrenaline
options.rationale: Steroids do not act in time and are an adjunct, not first-line; their use as primary therapy delays the only proven life-saving step. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis

options.text: Intravenous promethazine 25 mg to reduce histamine-mediated effects
options.rationale: Promethazine causes vasodilation and sedation in anaphylaxis and is contraindicated; antihistamines treat skin symptoms only and have no primary role. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis

explanation.summary: Adult anaphylaxis is treated with IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1:1000) into the anterolateral mid-thigh as the first action, repeated every 5 minutes if no improvement. IV adrenaline boluses are reserved for refractory anaphylaxis. Steroids and antihistamines are adjuncts that do not act in time and must not delay adrenaline.
key_points: Adult IM adrenaline dose: 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1:1000) into anterolateral mid-thigh.
Repeat every 5 minutes if no improvement; move to IV infusion if multiple IM doses fail.
Steroids and antihistamines are adjuncts only; they do not act fast enough as primary therapy.
Promethazine is contraindicated due to vasodilation and sedation.
explanation.pearls: The needle should be in the anterolateral thigh within 30 seconds of recognising adult anaphylaxis; IV access can come after the IM dose.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis

subtopic_detail: Massive transfusion protocol activation with TXA timing
stem:
You are the trauma team registrar in a tertiary trauma centre when a 28-year-old man arrives 90 minutes after a high-speed motor vehicle collision. He is hypotensive despite 1 L of crystalloid given by ambulance, with a rigid abdomen on examination and a clinically unstable pelvic fracture. His Glasgow Coma Scale is 12. FAST scan is positive in the right upper quadrant and pelvis.

On arrival the airway is intact and he is breathing spontaneously. He has 2 large bore cannulae and a third intraosseous in his left tibia. Group and hold has been sent and the blood bank has been called. The general surgery and orthopaedics teams have been activated and theatre is being prepared. The trauma consultant is leading the resuscitation and asks you to direct the next blood product and pharmacological intervention.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132/min, BP 78/40 mmHg, RR 28/min, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 35.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Pale, cool peripheries; rigid abdomen; clinically unstable pelvis on gentle compression (no springing); GCS 12 (E3 V4 M5)
data_table.Investigations: Hb 78 g/L (130-170); lactate 5.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); base excess -8 mmol/L; INR 1.4; fibrinogen 1.5 g/L (1.5-4.0); platelets 110 x10^9/L; FAST positive RUQ and pelvis

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: 4 units of packed red blood cells plus 4 units of fresh frozen plasma given over 2 hours
options.rationale: Slow ratio transfusion in active haemorrhage worsens dilutional coagulopathy and hypothermia; massive transfusion protocol with rapid 1:1:1 ratio is the standard. (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management Guidelines)

options.text: Packed red blood cells alone plus crystalloid until INR confirms coagulopathy
options.rationale: Crystalloid worsens dilutional coagulopathy in trauma haemorrhage and is restricted to a minimum; FFP and platelets are given empirically as part of the MTP. (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management Guidelines)

options.text: Whole blood transfusion 4 units only as sole product, without ratio mix or TXA
options.rationale: Whole blood is an option where available but is not the universal standard; the MTP fixed ratio with TXA addresses both shock and coagulopathy. (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management Guidelines)

options.text: Activate MTP at 1:1:1 ratio of PRBC:FFP:platelets plus IV tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 min
options.rationale: Trauma haemorrhage at 90 minutes from injury still falls within the 3 hour TXA window where CRASH-2 demonstrated mortality benefit; MTP with 1:1:1 ratio plus TXA is the AU NBA standard. (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management Guidelines, CRASH-2)

options.text: Recombinant factor VIIa 90 micrograms/kg as initial haemostatic adjunct
options.rationale: Recombinant factor VIIa is not first-line in trauma haemorrhage, raises thrombosis risk, and is reserved for selected refractory cases; MTP and TXA come first. (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Trauma haemorrhage with shock and a positive FAST scan triggers Massive Transfusion Protocol activation with fixed 1:1:1 ratio of red cells, FFP, and platelets, plus IV tranexamic acid 1 g within 3 hours of injury (and a further 1 g infusion over 8 hours). TXA mortality benefit was established by the CRASH-2 trial and is sustained when given inside the window. Crystalloid is minimised to limit dilutional coagulopathy.
key_points: TXA mortality benefit window: within 3 hours of trauma; loading dose 1 g IV over 10 minutes.
MTP fixed ratio 1:1:1 PRBC:FFP:platelets reduces dilutional coagulopathy.
Crystalloid is restricted (no more than 1 L) once MTP active.
