Cease MTP when haemodynamically stable, surgical control achieved, and lactate trending down.
explanation.pearls: TXA mortality benefit in trauma is preserved up to 3 hours from injury; this patient at 90 minutes is well within the window and gets 1 g IV alongside the first MTP pack.

stem:
You are the ED registrar in a tertiary trauma centre as a 24-year-old man arrives 20 minutes after a high-speed motorbike crash. He has blunt right-sided chest trauma and is in extreme respiratory distress on arrival. The paramedics report decreasing oxygen saturations and a falling blood pressure in transit. His airway is patent but he is using accessory muscles markedly.

On examination his trachea is deviated to the left, there are no breath sounds over the right hemithorax, and his right hemithorax is hyper-resonant to percussion. His jugular venous pressure is raised at 8 cm. He is becoming progressively obtunded. There is no obvious open chest wound. A finger thoracostomy kit is at the bedside and the trauma consultant has just arrived.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 138/min, BP 80/40 mmHg, RR 38/min, SpO2 89% on 15 L non-rebreather, temperature 36.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Distressed, drowsy; tracheal deviation to left; absent right-sided breath sounds; hyper-resonant right hemithorax; JVP raised at 8 cm
data_table.Investigations: No imaging performed (no time); ECG sinus tachycardia; no other bedside investigations

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate decompression site and follow-up?

options.text: 14G needle in 2nd ICS mid-clavicular line right, no follow-up tube needed
options.rationale: The 2nd ICS mid-clavicular line is the historical landmark but adult chest wall thickness commonly exceeds the needle length; ATLS 10th edition and AU practice now prefer the 4th-5th ICS in the anterior or mid-axillary line, and a chest tube must follow needle decompression. (Source: ATLS 10th Edition; Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: 14 gauge needle in the xiphisternum for pericardiocentesis as primary intervention
options.rationale: Pericardiocentesis treats tamponade, not tension pneumothorax; the clinical picture is decompensated lung collapse, not cardiac tamponade. (Source: ATLS 10th Edition)

options.text: Intercostal catheter at 5th ICS mid-axillary line first, before needle decompression
options.rationale: Definitive chest drain is the end-point but in true tension pneumothorax with cardiovascular collapse, immediate needle or finger thoracostomy is performed first to relieve the pressure, then the formal drain is inserted. (Source: ATLS 10th Edition)

options.text: Bag-mask ventilation with high-flow oxygen for 5 minutes then reassess thoracic
options.rationale: Bag-mask ventilation worsens tension pneumothorax by adding positive pressure through a non-intact pleura; immediate decompression is mandatory. (Source: ATLS 10th Edition)

options.text: 14G needle at 4th-5th ICS anterior axillary line right, then intercostal catheter
options.rationale: ATLS 10th edition and AU practice updated the recommended needle decompression site to the 4th-5th intercostal space anterior or mid-axillary line because adult chest wall thickness at the 2nd ICS often exceeds the needle length; needle decompression must be followed by definitive chest drain insertion. (Source: ATLS 10th Edition; Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

explanation.summary: ATLS 10th edition updated the recommended adult tension pneumothorax needle decompression site from the 2nd intercostal space mid-clavicular line to the 4th-5th intercostal space anterior or mid-axillary line, reflecting evidence that adult chest wall thickness at the 2nd ICS frequently exceeds standard cannula length. Needle decompression is a temporising measure that must be followed by definitive intercostal catheter insertion. Finger thoracostomy is an alternative in intubated patients.
key_points: ATLS 10e adult site: 4th-5th ICS anterior or mid-axillary line, not 2nd ICS mid-clavicular line.
Paediatric site is still 2nd ICS mid-clavicular line.
Needle decompression is temporising; intercostal catheter follows.
Finger thoracostomy is an alternative, especially in intubated patients.
explanation.pearls: If you teach the 2nd ICS mid-clavicular line as the only adult site, you risk the needle not reaching pleura; ATLS 10e moved adults to the 4th-5th ICS anterior axillary line.

stem:
A 64-year-old man is reviewed in the orthopaedic ward 3 days after right total knee replacement. He has been on enoxaparin 40 mg daily as prophylaxis. He develops sudden dyspnoea and pleuritic right-sided chest pain over the past 30 minutes. He has no history of bleeding, no recent stroke, and no relevant family history.

On examination he is alert and oriented. He has tachypnoea, oxygen saturations of 88% on room air improving to 95% on 4 L by nasal prong. There are no signs of haemodynamic shock. The CTPA performed urgently shows a large saddle embolus with right ventricular dilation and a right-to-left ventricle diameter ratio greater than 1.0. There is no signs of overt cardiogenic shock and he remains awake and conversing throughout assessment.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, BP 105/72 mmHg, RR 28/min, SpO2 95% on 4 L nasal prong, temperature 36.9 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert; mild respiratory distress; clear chest auscultation; cardiac dual heart sounds no murmur; right calf swelling 2 cm greater than left circumference; no overt cardiogenic shock signs
data_table.Investigations: Troponin I 95 ng/L (<14), BNP 850 pg/mL (<100); CTPA large saddle PE with RV dilation, RV:LV ratio >1.0; eGFR 55 mL/min/1.73 m²; INR 1.0, platelets 195 x10⁹/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous unfractionated heparin infusion with HDU admission for close haemodynamic monitoring and cardiology and respiratory input, reserving systemic thrombolysis for haemodynamic deterioration
options.rationale: Intermediate-risk (submassive) PE with normal BP is treated with anticoagulation alone and close monitoring; systemic thrombolysis is reserved for haemodynamic decompensation (PEITHO showed thrombolysis prevents deterioration but increases major bleeding). UFH preferred over LMWH in renal impairment and possible bleeding need. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Acute PE position statement)

options.text: Systemic thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg infused over 2 hours immediately given the size of the saddle embolus and right ventricular dilation seen on the CT pulmonary angiogram performed in radiology
options.rationale: Routine thrombolysis in intermediate-risk PE (without shock) increases major bleeding (PEITHO) without improving mortality; reserved for haemodynamic deterioration on heparin. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Acute PE position statement)

options.text: Therapeutic enoxaparin 1 mg per kg subcutaneously twice daily and ward admission for ongoing observation and serial troponin and BNP monitoring while continuing standard nursing observations
options.rationale: LMWH at therapeutic dose is acceptable in low-risk PE but in intermediate-risk PE with renal impairment and possible need to switch to thrombolysis, IV UFH (rapidly reversible) is preferred in HDU. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Acute PE position statement)

options.text: Catheter-directed mechanical thrombectomy as definitive first-line therapy in the cath lab today, followed by therapeutic warfarin from day 1 with bridging heparin until INR is therapeutic over the next week
options.rationale: Catheter-directed therapies are reserved for high-risk PE with shock or contraindication to thrombolysis; not first-line in intermediate-risk PE. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Acute PE position statement)

options.text: Insertion of inferior vena cava filter alone without anticoagulation given the recent surgery and possible bleeding concerns, with reassessment for anticoagulation start in 7 days postoperatively
options.rationale: IVC filter without anticoagulation in established PE has no role unless absolute contraindication to anticoagulation; this patient has none, and bleeding risk from a knee replacement at day 3 is acceptable for UFH. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Acute PE position statement)

explanation.summary: Pulmonary embolism is risk-stratified into high (shock or sustained hypotension), intermediate (RV dysfunction by imaging or biomarkers without shock), and low (no RV dysfunction, no biomarker rise) categories. Intermediate-risk PE is further divided into intermediate-high (both imaging RV dysfunction AND biomarker rise) and intermediate-low (one or other). Anticoagulation with IV UFH or LMWH or DOAC is the foundation; systemic thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg over 2 h or weight-based 0.6 mg/kg) is RESERVED for high-risk PE (with shock) or intermediate-risk PE that deteriorates haemodynamically on anticoagulation. The PEITHO trial showed routine thrombolysis in intermediate-risk PE prevented haemodynamic decompensation but doubled major bleeding without mortality benefit. Catheter-directed therapies are an alternative when systemic thrombolysis is contraindicated or fails.
key_points: Risk stratify: high (shock), intermediate (RV dysfunction), low.
Anticoagulation foundation: UFH, LMWH, or DOAC.
Systemic thrombolysis reserved for high-risk PE or intermediate that decompensates.
PEITHO: routine thrombolysis in intermediate-risk doubles major bleeding.
UFH preferred when bleeding risk uncertain (reversible with protamine).
explanation.pearls: PEITHO trial: routine alteplase in intermediate-risk PE doubles major bleeding without reducing mortality - reserve thrombolysis for the patient who actually decompensates on heparin.

sources.label: ESC Guidelines for Acute Pulmonary Embolism 2019

subtopic_detail: Adult DKA - fluid first then insulin with potassium-led delay
stem:
A 24-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus (diagnosed age 11) presents to the emergency department with 12 hours of vomiting, polyuria, polydipsia and abdominal pain following a gastrointestinal viral illness. Her insulin pump dislodged 48 hours ago and she has not replaced the cannula. She weighs 65 kg.

On examination she is alert with Kussmaul respiration. Her mucous membranes are dry and capillary refill is 3 seconds. There is no focal abdominal tenderness or peritonism. Her bedside glucose is 28 mmol/L with serum ketones of 5.8 mmol/L. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.10, HCO3 10 mmol/L. Serum potassium is 5.4 mmol/L. She is haemodynamically compensated. She is fully oriented and her speech is coherent throughout the assessment.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122/min, BP 95/60 mmHg, RR 28/min with Kussmaul respiration, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert and oriented; Kussmaul respiration; dry mucous membranes; capillary refill 3 seconds; soft abdomen with mild diffuse tenderness; no peritonism; pump site erythematous
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 28 mmol/L (4-7); ketones 5.8 mmol/L (<0.6); pH 7.10, HCO3 10 mmol/L (22-26), anion gap 24; Na 134 mmol/L (135-145), K 5.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 110 micromol/L (45-90)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management plan?

options.text: Commence intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 unit per kilogram per hour immediately as the first intervention and add intravenous fluid resuscitation simultaneously as bicarbonate measurement results come back
options.rationale: Insulin before fluid resuscitation in DKA can precipitate cardiovascular collapse and worsen intracellular potassium shift; fluid is started first per Australian DKA guidelines. (Source: ADIPS / RACP Diabetes Australia: Adult DKA Management)
source_refs: ADIPS / RACP Diabetes Australia: Adult DKA Management

options.text: Commence sodium chloride 0.9% 1 L over 1 hour as initial fluid resuscitation, then add intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 unit per kilogram per hour, with hourly potassium monitoring and replacement once below 5.5
options.rationale: AU adult DKA protocol: 1 L 0.9% saline over 1 h first, then insulin infusion 0.1 U/kg/h; K replacement only when serum K <5.5 (high risk of arrhythmia from hypokalaemia as insulin drives K intracellularly). (Source: ADIPS / RACP Diabetes Australia: Adult DKA Management)
source_refs: ADIPS / RACP Diabetes Australia: Adult DKA Management

options.text: Administer a bicarbonate infusion 100 mmol over 1 hour to correct the acidosis as the priority first intervention, followed by fluid resuscitation and insulin therapy once the pH normalises
options.rationale: Bicarbonate in DKA does not improve outcomes and may worsen hypokalaemia and paradoxical CSF acidosis; reserved for pH <6.9 only. (Source: ADIPS / RACP Diabetes Australia: Adult DKA Management)
source_refs: ADIPS / RACP Diabetes Australia: Adult DKA Management

options.text: Commence 10% dextrose infusion with subcutaneous intermediate acting insulin twice daily to address dehydration and provide background insulin while continuing oral rehydration with dietary salt
options.rationale: Dextrose is added only when glucose falls below 14 mmol/L during DKA treatment; SC intermediate insulin is not appropriate for acute DKA management. (Source: ADIPS / RACP Diabetes Australia: Adult DKA Management)
source_refs: ADIPS / RACP Diabetes Australia: Adult DKA Management

options.text: Trial of oral rehydration solution with subcutaneous rapid acting insulin 0.2 unit per kilogram and review in 4 hours given haemodynamic stability and ability to tolerate oral intake during this presentation
options.rationale: Oral rehydration and SC insulin alone is inadequate for established DKA with pH 7.10 and significant ketonaemia; IV protocol is required. (Source: ADIPS / RACP Diabetes Australia: Adult DKA Management)
source_refs: ADIPS / RACP Diabetes Australia: Adult DKA Management

explanation.summary: Adult diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is defined by hyperglycaemia (>11 mmol/L), ketonaemia (>3 mmol/L) or ketonuria, and metabolic acidosis (pH <7.30 or HCO3 <15). Management has 4 pillars: (1) fluid first - 1 L 0.9% sodium chloride over 1 h, then 1 L over 2 h, then 1 L over 4 h with adjustments for haemodynamic state; (2) insulin infusion at 0.1 U/kg/h started AFTER first fluid bag; (3) potassium replacement guided by serum K - K <3.3 hold insulin and replace K first, K 3.3-5.5 add KCl to fluid (40 mmol/L), K >5.5 no replacement; (4) dextrose added when glucose <14 mmol/L. Bicarbonate only if pH <6.9. Hourly bloods until anion gap resolves. Look for precipitant (infection, pump failure, non-adherence, MI). Transition to subcut insulin only when anion gap resolved and patient eating.
key_points: Fluid first (1 L 0.9% saline over 1 h), then insulin infusion 0.1 U/kg/h.
K <3.3 hold insulin; 3.3-5.5 replace; >5.5 no replacement.
Add 10% dextrose when glucose <14 mmol/L.
Bicarbonate only for pH <6.9.
Look for precipitant: infection, pump failure, non-adherence, MI.
explanation.pearls: In adult DKA, fluid comes first, insulin second, and potassium replacement waits until serum K drops below 5.5 - the insulin infusion will drop K within 2 hours.

sources.label: ADIPS / RACP Diabetes Australia: Adult DKA Management

subtopic_detail: NSTEMI high GRACE score - early invasive within 24 hours
stem:
A 68-year-old man with hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus and ex-smoker (20 pack-years) presents to the emergency department 4 hours after an episode of substernal chest discomfort lasting 30 minutes at rest, now resolved. He drove himself to hospital. He has no prior history of acute coronary syndrome and is on metformin, perindopril and atorvastatin.

On examination he is comfortable and pain free. There are no signs of heart failure or new murmur. His ECG on arrival shows 1 mm of ST depression in leads V4 to V6 with T wave inversion in I, aVL, V5 and V6. Troponin I drawn on arrival is 65 ng/L; repeat at 1 hour is 95 ng/L. His GRACE risk score in ED is 145. There is no history of bleeding and his estimated GFR is 65 mL/min/1.73 m².

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, BP 135/85 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Comfortable, pain free; no signs of heart failure; cardiac dual heart sounds no murmur; chest auscultation clear; peripheral pulses normal; no signs of bleeding diathesis
data_table.Investigations: Troponin I 0 h 65 ng/L (<14), 1 h 95 ng/L; ECG ST depression V4-V6 plus T-wave inversion I/aVL/V5-V6; eGFR 65 mL/min/1.73 m²; haemoglobin 138 g/L (130-180); HbA1c 8.0%

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Conservative ischaemia-guided management with discharge after 24 hours of telemetry observation if asymptomatic and serial troponins down trending, with outpatient stress test arranged within 2 weeks
options.rationale: GRACE score >140 categorises as high risk; conservative ischaemia-guided strategy is for low-risk NSTEMI; high risk warrants early invasive within 24 hours. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guideline)

options.text: Immediate primary percutaneous coronary intervention within 90 minutes of arrival as if this were ST elevation myocardial infarction given the troponin rise and chest pain history at rest in this patient
options.rationale: Primary PCI within 90 min is for STEMI (or NSTE-ACS with refractory chest pain, electrical/haemodynamic instability, mechanical complication, or VT/VF). NSTEMI with high GRACE without these features is invasive within 24 hours. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guideline)

options.text: Aspirin 300 mg loading dose plus ticagrelor 180 mg loading dose plus fondaparinux 2.5 mg subcutaneously plus cardiology admission with invasive coronary angiography within 24 hours of arrival
options.rationale: GRACE >140 = high-risk NSTEMI; AU protocol is dual antiplatelet loading (aspirin 300 mg + ticagrelor 180 mg) plus parenteral anticoagulant (fondaparinux preferred over enoxaparin in stable AU practice unless undergoing immediate PCI) and invasive angiography within 24 hours. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guideline)

options.text: Thrombolysis with tenecteplase weight adjusted intravenous bolus dose given immediately as if this were ST elevation infarction, with subsequent transfer to a tertiary cardiology centre for ongoing care
options.rationale: Thrombolysis is contraindicated in NSTE-ACS (no transmural occlusion to lyse); inappropriate and would increase bleeding without benefit. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guideline)

options.text: Outpatient CT coronary angiography in 4 weeks with cardiology clinic review, with discharge today on aspirin only given the chest pain has resolved and ECG changes are non-specific in their distribution
options.rationale: Discharge of a high-risk NSTEMI (GRACE >140) for outpatient CT-CA risks recurrent infarction and death; inpatient invasive workup is mandatory. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guideline)

explanation.summary: NSTE-ACS is risk-stratified by GRACE score (or TIMI) into very high, high, intermediate, and low risk. Invasive timing: VERY HIGH risk (haemodynamic instability, refractory chest pain, life-threatening arrhythmia, mechanical complication) - immediate angiography (<2 hours). HIGH risk (GRACE >140, dynamic ST/T changes, troponin rise) - early invasive (<24 hours). INTERMEDIATE risk (diabetes, renal dysfunction, EF <40%, prior PCI/CABG, GRACE 109-140) - delayed invasive (<72 hours). LOW risk - ischaemia-guided strategy with non-invasive testing. All NSTE-ACS get dual antiplatelet loading (aspirin + ticagrelor or prasugrel or clopidogrel), parenteral anticoagulation (fondaparinux for non-immediate PCI, UFH or enoxaparin for PCI), statin, beta-blocker, ACEI.
key_points: GRACE >140 = high-risk NSTEMI, early invasive within 24 hours.
Aspirin 300 mg + ticagrelor 180 mg dual antiplatelet loading.
Fondaparinux 2.5 mg SC preferred when PCI not immediate.
Thrombolysis CONTRAINDICATED in NSTE-ACS (no transmural occlusion).
Very high risk (instability) needs immediate angiography <2 hours.
explanation.pearls: GRACE over 140 is the 24 hour gate to the cath lab for NSTEMI - ticagrelor 180 mg load is preferred over clopidogrel unless oral anticoagulant on board or high bleeding risk.

subtopic_detail: Tumour lysis syndrome - rasburicase and hypocalcaemia management
stem:
A 32-year-old man newly diagnosed with Burkitt lymphoma was admitted 36 hours ago to commence chemotherapy. Pre-chemotherapy bloods (baseline) were: K 4.0 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urate 480 micromol/L (200-420), phosphate 1.4 mmol/L (0.8-1.5), calcium 2.30 mmol/L (2.10-2.55) corrected, creatinine 95 micromol/L (45-90), LDH 1200 U/L (<250), estimated GFR 75 mL/min/1.73 m². He was started on allopurinol 300 mg orally daily and IV maintenance fluids 24 hours before chemotherapy.

12 hours after first dose of rituximab plus cyclophosphamide: K 6.1 mmol/L, urate 720 micromol/L, phosphate 2.1 mmol/L (0.8-1.5), corrected calcium 1.85 mmol/L, creatinine 145 micromol/L, LDH 2400 U/L. Urine output is 30 mL/h. ECG shows no peaked T waves and no QRS widening. G6PD assay sent 24 hours ago is still pending. He is asymptomatic.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, BP 130/80 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 37.0 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, comfortable; no Chvostek or Trousseau; no arrhythmia on monitor; no peripheral oedema; urine output 30 mL/h over past 4 hours
data_table.Investigations: K 6.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), urate 720 micromol/L (200-420), phosphate 2.1 mmol/L (0.8-1.5), corrected calcium 1.85 mmol/L (2.10-2.55), creatinine 145 micromol/L (45-90), LDH 2400 U/L (<250); G6PD assay pending; ECG no peaked T or QRS widening

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Maintenance fluids and oral allopurinol 300 mg daily with biochemistry recheck after 24 hours of chemotherapy completion and dietary phosphate restriction overnight on the haematology ward
options.rationale: Maintenance fluids alone are inadequate in established TLS (Cairo-Bishop criteria met); rasburicase, aggressive hydration to UO 100 mL/h, and dialysis criteria review are required. (Source: HSANZ TLS prevention and management)

options.text: Intravenous calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10% to correct hypocalcaemia immediately with continued intravenous maintenance fluids and oral allopurinol therapy and recheck in 6 hours overnight
options.rationale: Asymptomatic hypocalcaemia in TLS should NOT be corrected with calcium - it precipitates as calcium phosphate causing AKI and worsens metastatic calcification; treat the hyperphosphataemia instead. (Source: HSANZ TLS prevention and management)

options.text: Sodium bicarbonate infusion to alkalinise urine and oral allopurinol 600 mg daily with maintenance fluids and dietary potassium restriction to prevent further potassium rise overnight on the ward
options.rationale: Urinary alkalinisation is no longer recommended in TLS - it worsens calcium phosphate precipitation when phosphate is high; rasburicase is the AU first-line in established TLS. (Source: HSANZ TLS prevention and management)

options.text: IV 0.9% sodium chloride targeting urine output 100 mL per hour, single dose rasburicase 0.2 mg per kg IV, frequent biochemistry, and renal-replacement therapy if refractory to medical management
options.rationale: Established TLS in high-risk haematological malignancy: aggressive hydration (UO 100 mL/h), rasburicase (recombinant urate oxidase) drops urate within hours; dialysis for refractory hyperkalaemia, oliguria, or fluid overload. G6PD result not required to give first dose if otherwise indicated and the patient is not in a known G6PD-deficient demographic. (Source: HSANZ TLS prevention and management)

options.text: Withhold rasburicase pending G6PD assay result, continue allopurinol 600 mg daily, start sodium bicarbonate infusion to aid uric acid clearance and continue regular monitoring overnight on the haematology ward
options.rationale: Waiting for G6PD result delays critical urate lowering; in emergent TLS, give first dose of rasburicase and accept the small risk if G6PD-deficient (haemolysis), particularly in non-African/Mediterranean ancestry; alkalinisation harms calcium-phosphate handling. (Source: HSANZ TLS prevention and management)

explanation.summary: Tumour lysis syndrome is defined by Cairo-Bishop criteria: any 2 of K >6.0, urate >476 micromol/L, phosphate >1.45 mmol/L, calcium <1.75 mmol/L, OR a 25% change from baseline, within 3 days before or 7 days after chemotherapy commencement. CLINICAL TLS adds creatinine >1.5x ULN, arrhythmia, seizure, or sudden death. High-risk malignancies: Burkitt lymphoma, T-cell ALL, blastic phase CML, AML with high WBC. Prevention in high-risk: rasburicase prophylaxis, aggressive hydration. Established TLS: aggressive IV hydration targeting UO 100 mL/h, rasburicase 0.2 mg/kg IV (drops urate within hours by enzymatic oxidation to soluble allantoin), correction of hyperkalaemia (calcium gluconate, insulin/dextrose, salbutamol), do NOT correct asymptomatic hypocalcaemia (causes calcium phosphate precipitation), urinary alkalinisation NO LONGER recommended. Dialysis for refractory hyperkalaemia, oliguria, or fluid overload.
key_points: Cairo-Bishop: any 2 of K/urate/PO4/Ca derangement.
Rasburicase 0.2 mg/kg IV - drops urate within hours.
Do NOT correct asymptomatic hypocalcaemia (precipitates calcium phosphate).
Urinary alkalinisation no longer recommended (worsens Ca-PO4 precipitation).
Dialysis for refractory hyperK, oliguria, or fluid overload.
explanation.pearls: Asymptomatic hypocalcaemia in TLS gets the phosphate treated, not the calcium - injecting calcium gluconate into a high-phosphate state precipitates calcium phosphate in the kidneys and worsens the AKI.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Tumour lysis syndrome

stem:
A 41-year-old woman is seen in the endocrine outpatient clinic with an 18-month history of progressive central weight gain (12 kg), facial fullness with persistent facial redness, easy bruising on her forearms, oligomenorrhoea, and proximal muscle weakness with difficulty climbing stairs. Two months ago she was newly diagnosed with hypertension (BP 165/100) and type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 8.2%). She is on no glucocorticoids and has no exogenous steroid exposure including inhaled, topical, or intra-articular.

On examination she has wide (2 cm) purple abdominal striae, supraclavicular fullness, and proximal muscle weakness (Medical Research Council grade 4/5 hip flexion bilaterally). Her potassium is 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.0) and her random morning serum cortisol is 920 nmol/L (50-550 morning). She has not yet had any other endocrine investigations.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min, BP 165/100 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Cushingoid appearance; central obesity, facial fullness with plethora; supraclavicular fullness; wide purple abdominal striae 2 cm; proximal weakness MRC 4 of 5 hip flexion bilaterally
data_table.Investigations: K 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), HbA1c 8.2%, random AM cortisol 920 nmol/L (morning 50-550); FBC, LFTs, TSH within normal limits; pregnancy test negative; no exogenous steroid exposure

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line investigation strategy?

options.text: Pituitary MRI with contrast immediately as the first investigation, then proceed to biochemical workup only if a pituitary mass is identified on the imaging study and refer to neurosurgery
options.rationale: Pituitary incidentalomas occur in 10-20%; imaging before biochemical confirmation cannot distinguish hormone-secreting from non-secreting lesions. Biochemistry first to confirm hypercortisolism is the AU standard. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)

options.text: Short Synacthen test 250 mcg with serum cortisol at baseline 30 minutes and 60 minutes to assess adrenal cortisol production response capacity over the standard testing interval used clinically
options.rationale: Short Synacthen tests for adrenal INsufficiency (Addison's), not Cushing syndrome (hypercortisolism); inappropriate test for the clinical question. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)

options.text: Random serum ACTH alone with serum cortisol at the time of sampling, taken at a single time point in the morning of clinic review, for interpretation against a normal range provided by the laboratory
options.rationale: Random ACTH alone cannot diagnose or differentiate Cushing syndrome aetiologies; it has a role AFTER hypercortisolism is biochemically confirmed to differentiate ACTH-dependent vs independent disease. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)

options.text: Plasma renin to aldosterone ratio and saline suppression test for primary hyperaldosteronism workup as the priority investigation given the hypertension and hypokalaemia features that have developed recently
options.rationale: Renin-aldosterone workup investigates Conn's syndrome; the clinical phenotype here (wide striae, central obesity, proximal weakness, glucose intolerance) is Cushing syndrome and demands cortisol-axis workup. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)

options.text: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test and 24 hour urinary free cortisol as first-line screening, with plasma ACTH measurement once two of three screening tests confirm hypercortisolism over the next week
options.rationale: Endocrine Society first-line: any 2 of 3 (1 mg overnight DST, 24 h UFC, late-night salivary cortisol) positive to confirm hypercortisolism; ACTH then differentiates ACTH-dependent (pituitary, ectopic) vs ACTH-independent (adrenal) disease. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)

explanation.summary: Cushing syndrome workup proceeds in 3 stages: (1) BIOCHEMICAL CONFIRMATION of hypercortisolism using ANY 2 of 3 first-line tests (1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression, 24-hour urinary free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol); single test has insufficient specificity. (2) ACTH-DEPENDENT vs ACTH-INDEPENDENT differentiation by plasma ACTH (low <2 pmol/L = adrenal cause, normal/high = pituitary or ectopic). (3) LOCALISATION by pituitary MRI (Cushing disease), inferior petrosal sinus sampling if discordant, CT chest/abdomen for ectopic ACTH or adrenal mass. Pseudo-Cushing causes (obesity, depression, alcoholism, pregnancy) may give false positives; exogenous steroid use is the most common false positive cause overall. Skipping straight to imaging causes misdiagnosis from incidentalomas.
key_points: Confirm hypercortisolism FIRST with 2 of 3: DST, UFC, salivary cortisol.
Then ACTH to differentiate ACTH-dependent vs independent.
Pituitary MRI for ACTH-dependent; CT abdomen for ACTH-independent.
Inferior petrosal sinus sampling if pituitary MRI normal but ACTH-dependent.
Exclude exogenous steroid use as the most common false positive cause.
explanation.pearls: 2-of-3 screening (1 mg DST, 24 h UFC, late-night salivary cortisol) confirms Cushing biochemically before any imaging - pituitary incidentalomas in 10-20% mean MRI-first invites misdiagnosis.

subtopic_detail: Atrial fibrillation DOAC choice with renal impairment
stem:
A 78-year-old woman is reviewed by her GP for ongoing care of newly diagnosed non-valvular atrial fibrillation. She has a history of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and stage 3b chronic kidney disease. She weighs 58 kg. She has had no falls or significant bleeding. She lives independently with her husband and remains mobile. Her HAS-BLED score is 2 and her CHA2DS2-VASc score is 5 (age, hypertension, diabetes, female sex, T2DM).

She is currently on metformin 500 mg twice daily, perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, and gliclazide 60 mg modified release daily. She has no documented mitral stenosis, no mechanical valve, and her recent transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated normal left ventricular function with mild mitral annular calcification. She is reviewed for choice of stroke prevention. Her eGFR has been stable at 32-34 mL/min/1.73m2 over the past 6 months.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88/min irregular, BP 138/82 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Irregularly irregular pulse, no carotid bruit, no lower limb oedema; weight 58 kg; mental state intact, normal gait, no recent falls
data_table.Investigations: ECG atrial fibrillation; creatinine 138 micromol/L (50-90), eGFR 32 mL/min/1.73m2; haemoglobin 124 g/L, platelets 198 x10^9/L; INR 1.0; transthoracic echo normal LV function with mild MAC; CHA2DS2-VASc 5, HAS-BLED 2

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line anticoagulation choice for this patient?

options.text: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily orally as direct oral anticoagulation for non-valvular atrial fibrillation given her CHA2DS2-VASc score is 5 and HAS-BLED is acceptable at 2
options.rationale: She meets 2 of the 3 dose-reduction criteria (weight 58 kg and creatinine 138 micromol/L); the correct dose is 2.5 mg twice daily, not the standard 5 mg twice daily. (Source: AMH)

options.text: Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily orally as direct oral anticoagulation for non-valvular atrial fibrillation given her renal function and age and weight profile
options.rationale: Apixaban reduced dose criteria require 2 of: age 80 or older, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 micromol/L or higher; she meets weight and creatinine criteria, so 2.5 mg twice daily is correct. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular; AMH; NHFA/CSANZ Atrial Fibrillation Guideline)

options.text: Dabigatran 110 mg twice daily orally as direct oral anticoagulation for non-valvular atrial fibrillation given her chronic kidney disease and age and stable eGFR
options.rationale: Dabigatran is 80% renally cleared and is contraindicated in CrCl below 30 mL/min and used with caution in 30-50 mL/min; apixaban (less renal clearance) is preferred at her eGFR of 32. (Source: AMH)

options.text: Warfarin titrated to INR 2 to 3 with weekly monitoring during initiation and monthly INR monitoring thereafter via a community pharmacy or general practice clinic
options.rationale: Warfarin is reserved for mechanical valves, moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis, and ESRF on dialysis; DOACs are first-line in non-valvular AF including with stage 3b CKD per AU guidance. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Atrial Fibrillation Guideline)

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg daily as antiplatelet therapy for stroke prevention given her age and concerns about bleeding risk on full anticoagulation given her chronic kidney disease today
options.rationale: Aspirin is NOT recommended for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation - the benefit is small and bleeding risk approaches that of full anticoagulation. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Atrial Fibrillation Guideline)

explanation.summary: NHFA/CSANZ recommends direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) as first-line stroke prevention in non-valvular atrial fibrillation with CHA2DS2-VASc 2 or higher (women) or 1 or higher (men). Apixaban is preferred in elderly patients with renal impairment because of its lower renal clearance. The apixaban dose reduction criteria require 2 of: age 80 years or older, weight 60 kg or less, serum creatinine 133 micromol/L or higher. Dabigatran is contraindicated below CrCl 30 mL/min. Warfarin is reserved for mechanical valves and moderate-severe mitral stenosis. Aspirin is NOT recommended for stroke prevention. HAS-BLED informs bleeding-risk modification (BP control, alcohol, drugs) rather than withholding anticoagulation.
key_points: DOACs are first-line for non-valvular AF in Australia
Apixaban dose reduction: 2 of age 80+, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133+ micromol/L
Dabigatran contraindicated below CrCl 30 mL/min
Warfarin reserved for mechanical valves and moderate-severe MS
Aspirin not recommended for AF stroke prevention
explanation.pearls: Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily is the AU standard dose when any 2 of 3 criteria are met (age 80+, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 micromol/L or higher); under-dosing without meeting criteria reduces stroke protection without lowering bleeding.

subtopic_detail: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes immediate management
stem:
A 67-year-old man with stage 4 CKD attends the emergency department with one day of muscle weakness and palpitations. His regular medications include enalapril 20 mg daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, frusemide 40 mg daily, and a recent 5 day course of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole started 4 days ago by his GP for a presumed UTI. He has not changed his diet but his urine output has decreased over the last 48 hours.

On arrival he is alert but feels generally weak. Bedside ECG shows sinus rhythm at 56/min with peaked T waves in the chest leads, broadened QRS at 124 ms, and absent P waves in lead II. A point-of-care blood gas confirms severe hyperkalaemia. Calcium gluconate has been drawn up by the nurse. He has been put on continuous cardiac monitoring and 2 large-bore intravenous cannulae have been sited. He is haemodynamically stable. There is no chest pain.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 56/min, BP 132/78 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert, generalised weakness, no focal neurology, no ascites; no pitting oedema; abdomen soft non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Point of care VBG potassium 7.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), sodium 132 mmol/L, pH 7.28, bicarbonate 16 mmol/L; creatinine 396 micromol/L (baseline 220), eGFR 14 mL/min/1.73m2; venous glucose 6.4 mmol/L; ECG sinus bradycardia 56/min, peaked T waves V2-V5, QRS 124 ms, absent P waves lead II

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate next intervention?

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 10 mg via mask in 4 mL of normal saline as a beta-2 agonist to shift potassium intracellularly via stimulation of the sodium potassium ATPase pump
options.rationale: Nebulised salbutamol is an adjunct to insulin-dextrose for potassium shifting but is not the first step when ECG changes are present; membrane stabilisation precedes shifting. (Source: UpToDate Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Intravenous insulin 10 units in 50 mL of 50% dextrose over 15 minutes to shift potassium intracellularly with bedside glucose monitoring every 30 minutes for 4 hours
options.rationale: Insulin-dextrose shifts potassium effectively but takes 15-30 minutes to start working; calcium gluconate must precede it when ECG changes are present to stabilise the myocyte membrane. (Source: UpToDate Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Intravenous calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL slow push over 2 minutes to stabilise the cardiac myocyte membrane with cardiac monitoring during administration of the bolus
options.rationale: Hyperkalaemia with broadened QRS and peaked T waves requires immediate myocyte membrane stabilisation with calcium gluconate before insulin-dextrose; calcium stabilises within 1-3 minutes and lasts 30-60 minutes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology; UpToDate Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Resonium) 30 g now and repeat every 4 hours until normokalaemia is achieved with daily monitoring of his electrolytes and renal function
options.rationale: Resonium removes potassium slowly (hours) and has GI side effects including necrosis; it has no role in immediate management of life-threatening hyperkalaemia with ECG changes. (Source: UpToDate Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Urgent renal replacement therapy via temporary central venous access at the nearest tertiary centre and ICU transfer with nephrology consultation before any pharmacological intervention
options.rationale: Dialysis is the definitive treatment in refractory hyperkalaemia or CKD/AKI without rapid response; immediate calcium gluconate plus insulin-dextrose precedes dialysis preparation and bridges to RRT. (Source: UpToDate Hyperkalaemia)

explanation.summary: Hyperkalaemia management proceeds in 3 sequential steps when ECG changes are present: (1) membrane stabilisation with calcium gluconate (10 mL 10% IV over 2 minutes; works in 1-3 min, lasts 30-60 min); (2) intracellular shift with insulin 10 units in 50 mL of 50% dextrose IV over 15 min plus nebulised salbutamol 10 mg plus sodium bicarbonate 50 mmol IV (if metabolic acidosis); (3) total body removal via loop diuretic (with intact kidney function), patiromer or zirconium cyclosilicate, or dialysis. Identify and stop the precipitant: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone, NSAIDs, trimethoprim, beta-blockers, heparin. Calcium chloride is more potent than calcium gluconate but requires central access.
key_points: Sequence: stabilise (calcium), shift (insulin-dextrose, salbutamol, bicarbonate), remove (loop, binder, dialysis)
Calcium gluconate works within 1-3 minutes and lasts 30-60 minutes
Trimethoprim plus ACE inhibitor plus spironolactone is a classical pharmacological triad of hyperkalaemia
Resonium and patiromer are slow GI removers (hours), not for immediate use
Dialysis is definitive in refractory or CKD/AKI cases
explanation.pearls: Trimethoprim added to background ACE inhibitor plus spironolactone in CKD is a classical hyperkalaemia precipitant; the trimethoprim blocks the renal tubular ENaC channel similarly to amiloride and can raise serum potassium by 1-2 mmol/L within days.

subtopic_detail: Severe community acquired pneumonia AU empirical antibiotics
stem:
A 58-year-old man presents to a metropolitan emergency department with 3 days of progressively worsening productive cough, pleuritic right-sided chest pain, fever, and breathlessness. He is normally well, drinks 20 standard drinks per week, and smokes 15 cigarettes per day. He has not travelled recently and has no specific occupational exposures. He has no penicillin allergy.

On arrival he is alert but tachypnoeic with confusion to time on the AMTS (8 of 10). Bronchial breathing is heard at the right base with reduced expansion. Crackles extend up to mid zone. There is no peripheral oedema. A chest x-ray shows right middle and lower lobe consolidation with a small effusion. His SMART-COP score is calculated by the registrar including systolic blood pressure 88 mmHg, multilobar involvement, low albumin, respiratory rate 32, tachycardia 122, and confusion. He has had peripheral intravenous access established and 2 sets of blood cultures and a sputum sample have been taken.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 122/min, BP 88/56 mmHg, RR 32/min, SpO2 91% room air, temperature 39.1 °C
data_table.Examination: Bronchial breath sounds right base extending to mid zone with reduced expansion; small right pleural effusion; capillary refill 3 seconds; abbreviated mental test score 8 of 10
data_table.Investigations: WCC 18.4 x10^9/L with neutrophilia, CRP 312 mg/L (<5), urea 12.6 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), albumin 28 g/L (35-50), lactate 3.6 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); SMART-COP score 6 (very high); chest x-ray right middle/lower lobe consolidation with small effusion; blood cultures and sputum sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical intravenous antibiotic regimen to commence now?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g 6-hourly and intravenous doxycycline 100 mg 12-hourly until microbiological results return and severity is reassessed
options.rationale: This is the standard moderate severity AU regimen; with SMART-COP 6 (severe) the recommended Tx Guidelines pathway uses ceftriaxone plus azithromycin (or moxifloxacin monotherapy if beta-lactam allergic). (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily and intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily as empirical cover for severe community acquired pneumonia per Therapeutic Guidelines
options.rationale: SMART-COP 5 or higher is severe CAP; empirical IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily PLUS IV azithromycin 500 mg daily is the AU Therapeutic Guidelines first-line for severe CAP, covering S pneumoniae and atypical organisms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g 6-hourly and intravenous vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading dose as broad spectrum cover for severe pneumonia with possible MRSA
options.rationale: Pip-taz plus vancomycin is reserved for healthcare-associated or aspiration pneumonia or post-influenza pneumonia where Pseudomonas or MRSA are suspected; not standard CAP cover. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous moxifloxacin 400 mg daily as monotherapy targeting Streptococcus pneumoniae and atypical pathogens together with a single agent in severe community acquired pneumonia
options.rationale: Moxifloxacin monotherapy is the AU alternative ONLY for severe beta-lactam allergy; in non-allergic patients ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is preferred and has better antimicrobial stewardship. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral amoxicillin 1 g 8-hourly plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 5 days outpatient with telephone review in 48 hours from the GP for symptom progression
options.rationale: Oral outpatient therapy is the AU regimen for low-severity CAP (CRB-65 0 or SMART-COP 0-2); SMART-COP 6 is severe and requires IV antibiotics with admission and HDU/ICU review. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: SMART-COP severity tool (Systolic BP, Multilobar, Albumin, Respiratory rate, Tachycardia, Confusion, Oxygen, pH) stratifies CAP. A score of 0-2 indicates outpatient management with oral antibiotics; 3-4 indicates admission for moderate disease; 5 or higher indicates severe CAP requiring IV antibiotics, HDU/ICU consideration, and assessment for invasive ventilation or vasopressors. AU Therapeutic Guidelines first-line for severe CAP is ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, escalating to a wider regimen (add gentamicin or pip-taz) for septic shock, immunocompromise, or specific exposures. Moxifloxacin monotherapy is the alternative in severe beta-lactam allergy.
key_points: SMART-COP 5+ is severe CAP requiring IV antibiotics and HDU/ICU assessment
AU first-line severe CAP: ceftriaxone 1 g + azithromycin 500 mg IV daily
Moxifloxacin monotherapy only for severe beta-lactam allergy
Pip-taz plus vancomycin reserved for HAP, aspiration, post-influenza
Atypical organisms (Legionella, Mycoplasma) covered by macrolide
explanation.pearls: SMART-COP score of 5 or higher predicts a need for intensive respiratory or vasopressor support in CAP and triggers IV ceftriaxone PLUS IV azithromycin; the macrolide cover for Legionella is the change from moderate-severity therapy.

sources.label: TSANZ/ATS Guidelines for the Management of Community-Acquired Pneumonia

stem:
A 72-year-old man with stage 3a CKD, type 2 diabetes, and stable angina is admitted with new exertional chest pain. He is taking metformin 1 g twice daily, ramipril 10 mg daily, frusemide 40 mg daily, perindopril, atorvastatin, and a recent course of ibuprofen for back pain. Troponin is mildly elevated and he has been booked for invasive coronary angiography in the morning.

He is haemodynamically stable. He is on a low background of oxygen 2 L/min for slight hypoxia. The cardiology team have asked you to prepare him for the procedure. His baseline creatinine is 138 micromol/L and his estimated GFR is 42 mL/min/1.73m2. Last echocardiogram showed normal LV function. He has had no recent diarrhoea, vomiting, or oral intake change. The procedure is non-emergent and could be delayed 24 hours if clinically warranted to optimise his renal status before exposure to iodinated contrast.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78/min, BP 138/82 mmHg, RR 16/min, SpO2 96% on 2 L/min oxygen, temperature 36.7 °C
data_table.Examination: Mucous membranes moist, no oedema; capillary refill 2 seconds; no focal cardiac findings beyond mild gallop rhythm; no jugular venous distension
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, urea 9.6 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), creatinine 138 micromol/L (50-90), eGFR 42 mL/min/1.73m2; troponin I 78 ng/L (<14, normal less than 14); haemoglobin 124 g/L; HbA1c 7.8% (5.6-6.4%)

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate prophylactic intervention to reduce his risk of contrast-induced acute kidney injury?

options.text: Intravenous isotonic 0.9% sodium chloride at 1 mL/kg/hour for 12 hours pre-procedure and 12 hours post-procedure with monitoring of fluid status and urine output
options.rationale: Isotonic IV crystalloid pre- and post-contrast is the only AU-recommended pharmacological prophylaxis with consistent evidence; KHA-CARI and KDIGO recommend 1 mL/kg/hour for 12 hours pre- and 12 hours post-procedure. (Source: KHA-CARI Guideline: Use of Contrast Agents in Patients with CKD; KDIGO AKI)
source_refs: KHA-CARI Guideline: Use of Contrast Agents in Patients with CKD

options.text: Oral N-acetylcysteine 600 mg twice daily for 24 hours pre-procedure and 24 hours post-procedure as a pharmacological prophylaxis for contrast-induced acute kidney injury
options.rationale: The PRESERVE trial (NEJM 2018) showed no benefit from N-acetylcysteine for contrast-induced AKI prevention versus placebo; AU and international guidelines no longer recommend it. (Source: PRESERVE trial; KDIGO AKI)

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 154 mmol/L at 3 mL/kg/hour for 1 hour pre-procedure and 1 mL/kg/hour for 6 hours post-procedure for renal protection against contrast nephropathy
options.rationale: PRESERVE trial also showed no benefit from sodium bicarbonate over isotonic saline; the simpler regimen of 0.9% saline is now standard. (Source: PRESERVE trial; KDIGO AKI)

options.text: Withhold metformin for 48 hours pre-procedure and 48 hours post-procedure to reduce the risk of lactic acidosis associated with metformin retention after iodinated contrast exposure
options.rationale: Withholding metformin reduces lactic acidosis risk (separate concern from CIN) but does NOT prevent contrast-induced acute kidney injury; standard practice is to withhold metformin in eGFR less than 30 OR check creatinine 48-72 h post-contrast in moderate CKD. (Source: AMH)

options.text: Pre-procedure furosemide 20 mg intravenously and mannitol 100 mL of 20% solution to maintain urine output during the procedure and post-procedure to reduce contrast nephropathy
options.rationale: Forced diuresis with furosemide and mannitol INCREASES contrast-induced AKI risk by reducing intravascular volume; isotonic hydration alone is the only proven prophylactic intervention. (Source: KDIGO AKI)

explanation.summary: Contrast-induced acute kidney injury (CI-AKI) risk rises with CKD, diabetes, heart failure, advanced age, hypovolaemia, repeat contrast exposure, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs at high doses, and high-volume or hyperosmolar contrast. KDIGO and KHA-CARI recommend isotonic saline IV (1 mL/kg/hour for 12 hours pre- and 12 hours post-contrast) as the only evidence-based pharmacological prophylaxis. The PRESERVE trial definitively refuted N-acetylcysteine and sodium bicarbonate. Adjuncts include: minimise contrast volume, use iso-osmolar or low-osmolar contrast, stop nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides), and hold metformin if eGFR less than 30 (or recheck creatinine 48-72 h post-contrast at moderate CKD). Statins have a small protective effect.
key_points: Isotonic saline 1 mL/kg/hour for 12h pre- and 12h post-contrast
PRESERVE trial: no benefit from N-acetylcysteine or bicarbonate
Stop nephrotoxins (NSAIDs) pre-procedure
Withhold metformin only for lactic acidosis concern, not CIN prevention
Forced diuresis worsens CIN risk
explanation.pearls: Isotonic 0.9% saline 1 mL/kg/hour for 12 hours pre- and 12 hours post-contrast is the only proven CIN prophylaxis; PRESERVE trial 2018 ended the use of N-acetylcysteine and sodium bicarbonate.

sources.label: KHA-CARI Guideline: Use of Contrast Agents in Patients with CKD

subtopic_detail: Adrenal crisis precipitated by intercurrent illness
stem:
A 41-year-old man with primary adrenal insufficiency (autoimmune Addison disease, diagnosed 6 years ago) attends a metropolitan emergency department brought in by his wife. He has had 2 days of fever, profuse vomiting, and watery diarrhoea after a barbecue. He stopped his oral hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone 36 hours ago because of the vomiting. He has lost approximately 4 kg in body weight over this period and now feels too weak to stand.

On arrival he is lethargic but rousable. His mucous membranes are dry, capillary refill is 4 seconds, and he has flat neck veins on examination. There is a faint diffuse hyperpigmentation of the buccal mucosa and palmar creases. There is no abdominal tenderness or peritonism. He has known hypothyroidism on thyroxine 100 mcg daily. His usual hydrocortisone dose is 15 mg morning and 5 mg afternoon. He carries an emergency hydrocortisone vial but has not used it. He has not had any recent steroid dose adjustment.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 132/min, BP 84/52 mmHg, RR 24/min, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 38.4 °C
data_table.Examination: Lethargic, dry mucous membranes, flat neck veins, capillary refill 4 seconds; buccal and palmar crease hyperpigmentation; abdomen soft non-tender; no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 122 mmol/L, potassium 6.0 mmol/L, urea 14.8 mmol/L (2.5-7.5), creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 88); venous blood gas pH 7.30, bicarbonate 16 mmol/L, lactate 3.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); venous glucose 3.2 mmol/L; cortisol pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate single best immediate intervention?

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus immediately followed by 200 mg over 24 hours by continuous infusion or 50 mg 6-hourly with intravenous 0.9% saline resuscitation
options.rationale: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus is the single most important intervention in adrenal crisis; do not wait for cortisol results. Saline 1 L over 1 hour for hypovolaemia; dextrose for hypoglycaemia; treat precipitant. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis and Treatment of Primary Adrenal Insufficiency; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency

options.text: Intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg now to provide glucocorticoid replacement and allow the planned short synacthen test to remain interpretable for diagnostic confirmation
options.rationale: Dexamethasone is preferred when the diagnosis is uncertain to preserve cortisol assay; this patient has known established Addison disease so hydrocortisone is the correct agent and starts within minutes. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency

options.text: Intravenous fludrocortisone equivalent 1 mg orally or via nasogastric tube alongside aggressive fluid resuscitation with intravenous 0.9% saline at 1 L over the first hour
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is not required acutely because high-dose hydrocortisone (>50 mg/day) has sufficient mineralocorticoid activity; oral fludrocortisone is added when daily steroid drops below 50 mg. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency

options.text: Intravenous calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL slow push for hyperkalaemia and then insulin-dextrose to shift potassium followed by intravenous hydrocortisone replacement at standard maintenance dose
options.rationale: Hyperkalaemia in adrenal crisis resolves with cortisol replacement and saline; calcium gluconate is only indicated if ECG changes present. Hydrocortisone bolus is the priority and corrects the underlying cause. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency

options.text: Take blood and urine cultures and commence intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g empirically as the most likely cause of his decompensation given the fever and gastrointestinal infection symptoms today
options.rationale: Source-control and empirical antibiotics are appropriate but the immediate priority is glucocorticoid replacement; sepsis without cortisol replacement in Addison disease is rapidly fatal. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a medical emergency precipitated by infection, gastroenteritis (vomiting prevents oral steroid absorption), trauma, surgery, or sudden cessation of glucocorticoid. Classical presentation: hypotension, dehydration, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, fever, abdominal pain. Treatment is hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus immediately, followed by 200 mg over 24 hours (or 50 mg every 6 hours), plus IV 0.9% saline 1 L over 1 hour for hypovolaemia, dextrose for hypoglycaemia, treat precipitant, and continue at stress dose for 24-48 hours before titrating down. Mineralocorticoid (fludrocortisone) is added when daily glucocorticoid drops below 50 mg because hydrocortisone has intrinsic mineralocorticoid activity at high doses. Education on sick-day rules (double oral dose for febrile illness, IM hydrocortisone 100 mg for vomiting) is the cornerstone of prevention.
key_points: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus is the priority intervention
Followed by 200 mg/24 h infusion or 50 mg IV 6-hourly
Saline 1 L over 1 hour for hypovolaemia, dextrose for hypoglycaemia
Fludrocortisone added only when daily steroid is below 50 mg
Sick-day rules: double oral dose for fever, IM hydrocortisone for vomiting
explanation.pearls: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV is the immediate priority in adrenal crisis; mineralocorticoid (fludrocortisone) is only added when total daily hydrocortisone drops below 50 mg because high-dose hydrocortisone has sufficient mineralocorticoid activity at the kidney.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency

subtopic_detail: Sgarbossa criteria in chest pain with new LBBB
stem:
A 64-year-old woman with hypertension and dyslipidaemia presents to a regional emergency department by ambulance with 80 minutes of severe central chest pain radiating to her left jaw and arm. She is sweaty and nauseated. There is no syncope and no cyanosis. She has a baseline ECG from 18 months ago in her electronic record which showed sinus rhythm with a normal QRS axis and no bundle branch block.

On arrival she is alert but in distress with the pain. Her bedside ECG shows sinus rhythm with new left bundle branch block; in V1-V3 there is 3 mm concordant ST elevation, in lead III there is 2 mm discordant ST elevation, and in V6 there is 5 mm discordant ST depression. Her chest is clear; cardiovascular examination is otherwise unremarkable. There is no peripheral oedema. A point of care troponin returns at 22 ng/L (less than 14). The nearest PCI-capable centre is 80 minutes by road. She has been given aspirin 300 mg orally and clopidogrel 600 mg orally in the ambulance.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96/min, BP 142/86 mmHg, RR 22/min, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Pain at rest, diaphoretic; chest clear, dual heart sounds with soft S4 gallop; no peripheral oedema; capillary refill 2 seconds; carotid pulses equal and full
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus rhythm with new LBBB, V1-V3 with 3 mm concordant ST elevation, lead III with 2 mm discordant ST elevation, V6 with 5 mm discordant ST depression; troponin I 22 ng/L (<14); haemoglobin 134 g/L; chest x-ray clear; baseline ECG (18 months ago) sinus rhythm no BBB

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Repeat the ECG in 30 minutes after analgesia and another point of care troponin and only escalate to reperfusion therapy if the second troponin returns elevated above the threshold
options.rationale: Waiting for serial troponin or repeat ECG in a STEMI-equivalent loses myocardium; positive Sgarbossa criteria with new LBBB warrant immediate reperfusion. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guideline 2016)

options.text: Arrange direct transfer to the nearest percutaneous coronary intervention capable centre for primary PCI within 120 minutes from first medical contact regardless of the LBBB ECG findings
options.rationale: Primary PCI is preferred when transfer time is under 90-120 minutes from first medical contact; with 80 minutes transfer plus angiography prep time the total exceeds the 120 minute window and thrombolysis is preferred. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guideline 2016)

options.text: Commence intravenous heparin 60 units/kg loading and 12 units/kg/hour infusion plus high-dose statin pending serial 3 hour troponin and admit to the coronary care unit for medical management
options.rationale: Treating this as NSTEMI ignores positive Sgarbossa with new LBBB; classifying it as a STEMI-equivalent is the standard of care and time-to-reperfusion drives outcome. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guideline 2016)

options.text: Administer thrombolysis with tenecteplase based on weight and reassess for transfer to a PCI-capable centre if symptoms persist or ECG fails to improve within 60 to 90 minutes
options.rationale: Modified Sgarbossa criteria are positive (concordant ST elevation 1 mm or more, OR concordant ST depression 1 mm or more in V1-V3, OR excessive discordant ST elevation); new LBBB plus positive Sgarbossa with 80 minute PCI transfer is a STEMI equivalent and requires thrombolysis. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Acute Coronary Syndromes 2016; Sgarbossa criteria)

options.text: Administer intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion and intravenous morphine for pain relief and observe the ECG response while transferring her to the cardiology ward for further evaluation
options.rationale: Analgesia and GTN are appropriate adjuncts but do not address the time-critical reperfusion need; symptomatic management without reperfusion is a major error in suspected STEMI. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guideline 2016)

explanation.summary: New left bundle branch block in the setting of chest pain is not automatically a STEMI equivalent; the modified Sgarbossa criteria (Smith) identify which patients have acute coronary occlusion. Positive criteria are: (1) concordant ST elevation 1 mm or more in any lead; (2) concordant ST depression 1 mm or more in V1, V2, or V3; (3) discordant ST elevation with proportionally excessive elevation (ST/S ratio of -0.25 or worse). Any one positive feature classifies as STEMI equivalent. Reperfusion strategy in Australia: primary PCI if first medical contact to balloon time is 90-120 minutes or less; otherwise fibrinolysis with tenecteplase, then transfer for rescue PCI if no resolution in 60-90 minutes (pharmaco-invasive strategy). Time-to-reperfusion is the dominant predictor of outcome.
key_points: New LBBB is not automatically a STEMI equivalent
Modified Sgarbossa criteria identify acute coronary occlusion in LBBB
Concordant ST elevation 1 mm or more is the most specific criterion
Reperfusion: primary PCI if under 120 min, otherwise thrombolysis plus transfer
Pharmaco-invasive strategy: thrombolysis then rescue PCI if no resolution
explanation.pearls: Modified Sgarbossa criteria - concordant ST elevation 1 mm or more in any lead is the most specific criterion (over 90%) for acute coronary occlusion in new LBBB; this is the key discriminator that drives the reperfusion decision.

stem:
A 27-year-old woman presents to a metropolitan emergency department 26 hours after the start of a staggered paracetamol ingestion. She began taking the tablets at 6 pm yesterday and continued at intervals over an 11-hour period, finishing at 5 am today. She has taken her own count of 24 x 500 mg tablets (total 12 g over 11 hours). She has been crying and nauseated since the morning. She drinks heavily on weekends, around 6 standard drinks per night, and takes regular oral contraceptive pill.

She is alert and oriented. She has mild right upper quadrant tenderness but no peritonism. She is haemodynamically stable. Bedside venous blood gas shows a mild metabolic acidosis. She has no other co-ingestants on history; urine drug screen is pending. She admits to ongoing suicidal ideation. The toxicology service has been contacted by phone. Mental health team have been notified. Her weight is 65 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, BP 118/74 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.8 °C
data_table.Examination: Alert oriented; mild right upper quadrant tenderness; no peritonism; no asterixis, no jaundice; abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Paracetamol level 95 mg/L (taken on arrival); ALT 1280 U/L (<35), AST 1140 U/L, INR 2.1, creatinine 88 micromol/L, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L, lactate 3.2 mmol/L (0.5-2.2); venous blood gas pH 7.32; urine bhCG negative; weight 65 kg

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Do not start acetylcysteine because the paracetamol nomogram cannot be applied to staggered ingestions and the level falls below the standard 4 hour treatment line cut off
options.rationale: The nomogram does not apply to staggered ingestion but acetylcysteine is started anyway if the cumulative dose exceeds 200 mg/kg or 10 g (whichever is less) in 24 hours OR if there are signs of hepatotoxicity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology; AU Paracetamol Poisoning Guideline 2020)

options.text: Arrange urgent liver transplantation assessment based on King's College Hospital criteria before commencing acetylcysteine to facilitate listing and avoid delay if she meets transplant criteria today
options.rationale: Acetylcysteine is started immediately; King's College criteria are reassessed at 48-72 hours and beyond, not before initial antidote. Acetylcysteine plus transplant referral run in parallel, not sequentially. (Source: AU Paracetamol Poisoning Guideline 2020)

options.text: Administer single dose oral activated charcoal 50 g and observe for 4 hours with repeat paracetamol level to plot on the nomogram before commencing further definitive antidotal treatment
options.rationale: Charcoal is only useful within 2 hours of acute ingestion; this presentation is 26 hours after the start of ingestion. Nomogram does not apply to staggered ingestion. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Discharge the patient with referral to community mental health team and the GP for further follow up since the paracetamol level of 95 mg/L is below the treatment threshold for acute single ingestion
options.rationale: Active hepatotoxicity (ALT 1280, INR 2.1) and metabolic acidosis (lactate 3.2, bicarbonate 18) indicate severe paracetamol toxicity in progress and discharge would be catastrophic. (Source: AU Paracetamol Poisoning Guideline 2020)

options.text: Commence intravenous acetylcysteine using the 2 bag regimen with 200 mg/kg over 4 hours then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours and refer to hepatology for King's College Hospital criteria assessment
options.rationale: Staggered ingestion exceeding 200 mg/kg in 24 hours plus evidence of hepatotoxicity (ALT 1280, INR 2.1) mandates IV acetylcysteine using the 2-bag regimen (200 mg/kg over 4 hours then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours); King's College criteria triage for liver transplantation. (Source: AU Paracetamol Poisoning Guideline 2020)

explanation.summary: Australian paracetamol poisoning guideline 2020 distinguishes acute single ingestion (use Rumack-Matthew nomogram from 4 hour level) from staggered ingestion (ingestion over more than 1 hour) and repeated supratherapeutic ingestion. Staggered ingestion thresholds: 200 mg/kg or 10 g (whichever is less) in 24 hours, or 150 mg/kg over 48 hours, or 100 mg/kg daily over 72 hours. The 2-bag IV acetylcysteine regimen (200 mg/kg over 4 hours then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours) has replaced the older 3-bag regimen due to fewer anaphylactoid reactions. Indications for continued infusion past 20 hours include rising ALT, INR over 2, lactic acidosis, or ongoing detectable paracetamol. King's College criteria (arterial pH less than 7.30 after fluid resuscitation; OR all of: PT over 100 seconds, creatinine over 300 micromol/L, grade 3-4 hepatic encephalopathy) trigger liver transplantation discussion.
key_points: Staggered paracetamol ingestion: do not use nomogram
Threshold: 200 mg/kg or 10 g in 24 hours plus hepatotoxic features
AU 2-bag IV acetylcysteine regimen replaces older 3-bag
Continued infusion if ALT rising, INR over 2, lactic acidosis, paracetamol detected
King's College criteria trigger transplant discussion
explanation.pearls: The 2-bag intravenous acetylcysteine regimen (200 mg/kg over 4 hours then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours) has replaced the older 3-bag regimen because it gives the same dose with fewer anaphylactoid reactions; AU practice since 2020.

subtopic_detail: Anticoagulation duration after first unprovoked PE
stem:
A 56-year-old previously well man was diagnosed with an unprovoked segmental pulmonary embolism three months ago after presenting with pleuritic chest pain and a CT pulmonary angiogram demonstrating filling defects in the right lower lobe segmental arteries. There was no recent surgery, hospitalisation, immobility, long-haul travel, malignancy, or hormonal therapy.

He was commenced on apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days, then 5 mg twice daily, and is now reviewed at the haematology clinic. He has had no bleeding, no recurrent symptoms, and tolerates the medication well. He has no family history of VTE. A thrombophilia screen was not performed. Renal function and platelet count are within normal limits. He asks how long he should continue treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: no calf swelling, lungs clear, no signs of recurrent VTE
data_table.Investigations: CTPA: right lower lobe segmental PE; FBC, UEC, LFTs within normal limits; no thrombophilia screen performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation plan from this review onwards?

options.text: Stop apixaban now; first unprovoked PE has reached the 3-month minimum duration
options.rationale: Three months is the minimum to treat the initial event but stopping after a first unprovoked PE carries approximately 10 percent recurrence in year 1 and 30 percent at 5 years; the question of extended therapy must be addressed. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Continue apixaban at 5 mg twice daily for a further 3 months only
options.rationale: A defined 6-month total is appropriate for provoked PE; first unprovoked PE warrants either stopping at 3 months or extending indefinitely at reduced dose, not an arbitrary 6-month duration. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Continue extended apixaban at 2.5 mg twice daily indefinitely given low bleed risk
options.rationale: After 3 to 6 months treatment-dose anticoagulation for first unprovoked PE in a patient with low bleed risk, current Australian and AMPLIFY-EXT trial guidance is extended apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily indefinitely, which roughly halves recurrence without substantially increasing major bleeding. (Source: THANZ; AMPLIFY-EXT trial)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Switch to warfarin with INR target 2 to 3 for extended secondary prevention regimen
options.rationale: Apixaban is non-inferior to warfarin for VTE prevention with less major bleeding; switching to warfarin would require INR monitoring without benefit. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Stop apixaban now and commence low-dose aspirin 100 mg daily for secondary prevention
options.rationale: Aspirin is inferior to DOAC for VTE recurrence prevention (WARFASA and ASPIRE trials showed approximately 35 percent reduction vs DOAC 80 percent), and is no longer preferred as extended VTE prophylaxis. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: First unprovoked PE requires a minimum 3 months of treatment-dose anticoagulation. The decision at 3 to 6 months is whether to stop or continue indefinitely at reduced dose. Current Australian (THANZ) guidance supports extended apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily indefinitely in patients with low bleed risk (HAS-BLED score less than 3, no anaemia, no recent bleeding), based on AMPLIFY-EXT trial showing reduction in recurrence without significant excess of major bleeding. Recurrence risk without extended therapy after first unprovoked PE is approximately 10 percent at 1 year and 30 percent at 5 years. Aspirin is inferior to DOACs for secondary prevention.
key_points: First unprovoked PE: minimum 3 months treatment dose
Extended therapy with apixaban 2.5 mg BD indefinitely halves recurrence (AMPLIFY-EXT)
Low bleed risk and ongoing tolerance favour extended therapy
Aspirin is inferior to DOAC for secondary VTE prevention
explanation.pearls: After 3 to 6 months treatment-dose apixaban for first unprovoked PE, continue apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily indefinitely if bleed risk is low (AMPLIFY-EXT).

sources.label: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

stem:
A 68-year-old postmenopausal woman is referred from primary care after a DEXA scan ordered for a fall demonstrated T-scores of -2.8 at the lumbar spine and -2.6 at the femoral neck. She had a minimal-trauma right wrist fracture six months ago when she slipped on wet pavement. Her FRAX 10-year hip fracture risk is calculated at 4 percent.

She takes no current medications, has no past gastrointestinal history, no malabsorption, and no malignancy. Renal function: creatinine 68 micromol/L, eGFR more than 90 mL/min/1.73 m2. Calcium and vitamin D were repleted three months ago and are within normal limits at 25-hydroxyvitamin D 78 nmol/L (more than 50). She has good dentition with no recent dental work or planned extractions. She can sit upright comfortably for 30 minutes after waking.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: no kyphosis, mild knee crepitus, no overt frailty features
data_table.Investigations: DEXA: T -2.8 spine, -2.6 femoral neck; FRAX hip 4%; creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90), eGFR >90; 25-OH-D 78 nmol/L (>50); no dental issues

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Calcium 600 mg with vitamin D 1000 IU daily and weight-bearing exercise only
options.rationale: Calcium, vitamin D, and exercise are necessary background therapy but do not alone reduce fracture risk in established osteoporosis with prior minimal-trauma fracture. Pharmacotherapy is indicated. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis prevention and management)

options.text: Raloxifene 60 mg daily orally with continuation of calcium and vitamin D background
options.rationale: Raloxifene reduces vertebral but not non-vertebral fracture risk and carries a VTE risk; it is not first-line for a 68-year-old with established osteoporosis and recent wrist fracture. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis prevention and management)

options.text: Teriparatide 20 microgram subcutaneously daily for severe osteoporosis treatment
options.rationale: Teriparatide is reserved by PBS for severe osteoporosis with multiple vertebral fractures or failure of antiresorptive therapy; she has not yet had a trial of first-line bisphosphonate. (Source: PBS criteria; RACGP Osteoporosis prevention and management)

options.text: Alendronate 70 mg orally weekly with calcium 600 mg and vitamin D 1000 IU daily
options.rationale: Weekly oral alendronate is the Australian first-line agent for postmenopausal osteoporosis in a patient who can sit upright for 30 minutes and has no upper GI contraindication. With background calcium and vitamin D it reduces vertebral, hip, and non-vertebral fracture risk. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis prevention and management; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously every six months instead of oral bisphosphonate
options.rationale: Denosumab is reserved as second-line when oral bisphosphonates are not tolerated or contraindicated (severe oesophageal disease, malabsorption, eGFR below 35) because of the rebound vertebral fracture risk if missed or stopped. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis prevention and management)

explanation.summary: First-line pharmacotherapy for postmenopausal osteoporosis in Australia is an oral bisphosphonate (alendronate 70 mg weekly or risedronate 35 mg weekly) with background calcium 1000 to 1300 mg daily and vitamin D sufficient to maintain 25-hydroxyvitamin D above 50 nmol/L. Denosumab 60 mg SC 6-monthly is second-line, reserved for intolerance to oral bisphosphonate (oesophagitis, dysphagia), eGFR less than 35, or malabsorption. Denosumab carries a meaningful rebound vertebral fracture risk if missed or stopped, requiring continuous adherence or transition to bisphosphonate before discontinuation. Zoledronic acid 5 mg IV annually is an alternative for those who cannot manage weekly dosing. Teriparatide is reserved for severe disease with multiple vertebral fractures or failure of first-line therapy.
key_points: First-line: weekly alendronate or risedronate plus calcium and vitamin D
Denosumab is second-line; rebound vertebral fracture risk after stopping
Zoledronic acid IV annually if oral bisphosphonate not tolerated or adherence concerns
Teriparatide reserved for severe disease or failure of first-line therapy
explanation.pearls: First-line osteoporosis: alendronate 70 mg weekly with calcium and vitamin D; denosumab 6-monthly is second-line because of vertebral rebound risk if missed.

subtopic_detail: First-line treatment for symptomatic Parkinson's disease
stem:
A 72-year-old retired carpenter has been seeing his GP over the past 12 months with a slowly progressive resting tremor of the right hand and difficulty initiating movements. His handwriting has become small and cramped and his wife has noted reduced facial expressivity. He has had two minor falls in the past month.

On examination he has a 4 Hz pill-rolling tremor at rest in the right hand that abolishes on movement, cogwheel rigidity in the right elbow, and bradykinesia on finger-tapping testing. His gait is shuffling with reduced arm swing on the right and his pull test is mildly impaired. His mood is euthymic, MMSE is 28/30, postural blood pressure shows no significant orthostatic drop, eye movements are full, and there are no cerebellar signs. He has been formally diagnosed with idiopathic Parkinson's disease by a neurologist and asks about starting treatment to keep working in his shed.

data_table.Vital signs: within normal limits
data_table.Examination: 4 Hz pill-rolling rest tremor right hand, cogwheel rigidity right elbow, bradykinesia, shuffling gait, MMSE 28/30, no orthostatic drop, no cerebellar signs
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain demonstrated mild generalised atrophy; DAT-SPECT not yet performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacological therapy?

options.text: Selegiline 5 mg daily orally as monotherapy to preserve dopaminergic neurons
options.rationale: MAO-B inhibitors provide modest symptomatic benefit but are less effective than levodopa for moderate motor symptoms in an older patient with functional impairment, and the neuroprotective claim is not established. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Amantadine 100 mg twice daily orally for resting tremor and bradykinesia symptoms
