options.rationale: Amantadine is primarily used for levodopa-induced dyskinesias and is not a robust first-line monotherapy for established motor symptoms in older patients. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Pramipexole 0.125 mg three times daily as dopamine-agonist-first regimen for tremor
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists carry higher rates of impulse control disorders, sleep attacks, hallucinations, and orthostatic hypotension, and are not preferred in patients over 70 because of these adverse effects. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Anticholinergic benztropine 1 mg twice daily oral therapy for resting tremor predominantly
options.rationale: Anticholinergics worsen cognition, urinary retention, constipation, and falls risk in older adults and should be avoided in patients over 70 with parkinsonism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Levodopa with carbidopa 50 mg / 12.5 mg three times daily, titrated to motor response
options.rationale: Levodopa combined with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor (carbidopa or benserazide) is the most effective antiparkinsonian agent and the preferred first-line therapy in older patients (over 65 to 70) where dopamine-agonist adverse effects predominate. Start low and titrate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; MDS Levodopa Recommendations)

explanation.summary: Initial pharmacotherapy in Parkinson's disease is informed by age, motor severity, and side-effect profile. In older patients (over 65 to 70) with functional motor impairment, levodopa combined with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor (carbidopa or benserazide) is the most effective and best-tolerated first-line agent. Dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole) provide adequate symptomatic relief in younger patients but carry higher rates of impulse control disorder, sleep attacks, hallucinations, and orthostatic hypotension; they are avoided as first line in older patients. Start levodopa low (50/12.5 mg three times daily) and titrate to balance motor benefit against the onset of motor fluctuations and dyskinesias.
key_points: Levodopa + decarboxylase inhibitor: first-line in older patients with motor impairment
Dopamine agonists in younger patients only because of older-age adverse effects
Anticholinergics avoided over 70 (falls, cognition, urinary retention)
Start low and titrate to symptomatic control and minimise dyskinesia
explanation.pearls: Start older Parkinson's patients on levodopa-carbidopa 50/12.5 mg three times daily and titrate; dopamine agonists carry higher impulse-control and orthostatic risk after 70.

subtopic_detail: Modified Duke criteria for definite infective endocarditis
stem:
A 64-year-old man with a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement 18 months ago presents with three weeks of low-grade fevers, anorexia, and night sweats. He had two recent dental cleanings without antibiotic prophylaxis. He takes apixaban 5 mg twice daily and atorvastatin.

On examination temperature is 38.2 degrees Celsius, pulse 96, blood pressure 116 by 68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 percent on room air. Cardiac auscultation reveals a soft early diastolic murmur not previously documented. Splinter haemorrhages are present in three nail beds. Two of three peripheral blood-culture sets drawn 12 hours apart grow Streptococcus mitis. Transthoracic echocardiogram is technically limited but suggests a small mobile echo-density on the aortic valve. Transoesophageal echocardiogram confirms a 9 mm vegetation on the prosthetic aortic valve with mild aortic regurgitation.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, BP 116/68, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 38.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: soft new early diastolic murmur, splinter haemorrhages in 3 nail beds, no Janeway lesions, no Osler nodes
data_table.Investigations: blood cultures: 2 of 3 sets grow S. mitis; TOE: 9 mm vegetation aortic prosthetic valve with mild AR; CRP 78 mg/L (<5); WCC 13.5 x10^9/L (4-11)

lead_in: What is the most accurate diagnostic classification of this case?

options.text: Definite IE on the basis of two major criteria (positive blood cultures plus echocardiographic evidence)
options.rationale: Two sets of blood cultures positive for a typical IE organism (viridans group streptococcus) plus echocardiographic evidence of vegetation on a prosthetic valve constitute two Duke major criteria, which alone make definite IE. (Source: Modified Duke Criteria 2023; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Possible IE; needs one further blood culture set to upgrade to definite IE diagnosis
options.rationale: Two of three positive culture sets with a typical organism already satisfies the major criterion (persistent bacteraemia with typical organism), particularly with prosthetic valve involvement. Further cultures are valuable but the diagnosis is already definite. (Source: Modified Duke Criteria 2023)

options.text: Rejected IE because only two of three blood-culture sets are positive for typical organism
options.rationale: Rejected IE requires a firm alternative diagnosis or resolution of symptoms with 4 days or less of antibiotics; this case meets the major criteria for definite IE. (Source: Modified Duke Criteria 2023)

options.text: Definite IE on basis of one major plus three minor criteria from this case alone
options.rationale: While he does meet some minor criteria (fever, vascular phenomena via splinters, prosthetic valve as predisposing factor), the strongest classification is two majors (cultures plus echocardiogram) which by itself reaches definite. (Source: Modified Duke Criteria 2023)

options.text: Possible IE; PET-CT should be added before commencing empirical antibiotics on suspicion
options.rationale: PET-CT (an imaging modality added to the 2023 modified Duke criteria for prosthetic valves more than 3 months post-implant) is helpful when echo is equivocal but is not required when echo and cultures already satisfy major criteria. (Source: Modified Duke Criteria 2023)

explanation.summary: The modified Duke criteria (2023 update) classify suspected infective endocarditis as definite, possible, or rejected. Two major criteria, OR one major plus three minor, OR five minor support definite IE. Major criteria: (a) typical IE organism from two separate cultures OR persistent bacteraemia with any organism OR single positive culture for Coxiella burnetii or phase I IgG titre at least 1:800; (b) imaging evidence of endocardial involvement (echocardiographic vegetation, abscess, prosthetic dehiscence, or PET-CT abnormal uptake on prosthetic valve more than 3 months post-implant). Minor criteria: predisposing condition, fever 38 degrees or more, vascular phenomena, immunological phenomena, microbiology that does not meet major. Vegetation on a prosthetic valve with two positive culture sets meets two majors and is definite IE.
key_points: Definite IE: 2 major OR 1 major + 3 minor OR 5 minor criteria
Major: typical organism in 2 cultures + echo or PET-CT evidence on prosthetic valve
PET-CT added in 2023 for prosthetic valves more than 3 months post-implant
Empirical antibiotics started after cultures, not deferred for PET-CT
explanation.pearls: Two positive cultures for typical organism plus echo vegetation on prosthetic valve equals definite IE by modified Duke 2023; PET-CT is added imaging only when echo is equivocal.

subtopic_detail: Initial investigation of suspected Cushing's syndrome
stem:
A 44-year-old woman presents with 14 months of progressive central weight gain (10 kg), facial rounding, easy bruising, proximal weakness climbing stairs, and new hypertension diagnosed three months ago (current BP 162 by 98 mmHg on amlodipine 5 mg daily). She also reports oligomenorrhoea over the past year.

On examination BMI is 33 with truncal adiposity, dorsocervical fullness, abdominal striae more than 1 cm wide and purplish in colour, and proximal weakness on sit-to-stand testing. She takes no exogenous glucocorticoids, no inhaled corticosteroids, no topical steroids, and no other medications other than amlodipine. Fasting glucose is 7.1 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), HbA1c 47 mmol/mol (less than 42), and potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0). She drinks 2 standard drinks of wine per week and does not work shifts.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 162/98 mmHg, otherwise within normal limits
data_table.Examination: BMI 33 with truncal adiposity, dorsocervical fullness, wide purplish abdominal striae, proximal weakness
data_table.Investigations: fasting glucose 7.1 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), HbA1c 47 mmol/mol (<42), potassium 3.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); no exogenous glucocorticoid exposure

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line diagnostic test?

options.text: Random morning serum cortisol level taken at 0800 in the outpatient pathology clinic
options.rationale: A single random morning cortisol shows substantial overlap between Cushing's and non-Cushing's states because of episodic secretion and stress reactivity, and is not a screening test for Cushing's syndrome. (Source: ESE Cushing's Guideline; RACGP Endocrinology)

options.text: Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test with 0800 cortisol the next morning
options.rationale: An overnight 1 mg DST (1 mg dexamethasone at 23:00 with serum cortisol measured 08:00 next morning) is one of three first-line screening tests endorsed by the Endocrine Society. A failure to suppress cortisol to less than 50 nmol/L is abnormal and prompts further investigation. (Source: ESE Cushing's Syndrome Guideline)

options.text: Plasma ACTH measurement at 0900 to distinguish ACTH-dependent from independent disease
options.rationale: ACTH is used after diagnosis is confirmed to determine the source (pituitary versus ectopic versus adrenal), not as the initial screening test for Cushing's syndrome itself. (Source: ESE Cushing's Syndrome Guideline)

options.text: MRI pituitary with gadolinium to look for a microadenoma at the corticotroph site
options.rationale: Imaging the pituitary before establishing Cushing's syndrome generates incidentaloma noise (10 percent of normal adults have pituitary lesions on MRI) and does not constitute screening. (Source: ESE Cushing's Syndrome Guideline)

options.text: Random plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio with concurrent serum potassium replacement
options.rationale: ARR screens for primary aldosteronism, not Cushing's syndrome. Although hypokalaemia is present, the clinical phenotype here is overwhelmingly Cushing's and screening should target that diagnosis. (Source: ESE Cushing's Syndrome Guideline)

explanation.summary: First-line screening for Cushing's syndrome uses one of three tests (Endocrine Society Guideline): 24-hour urinary free cortisol (two collections), late-night salivary cortisol (two samples on different nights), or overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test. The 1 mg DST is taken at 23:00 with cortisol measured at 08:00 next morning; a failure to suppress to less than 50 nmol/L is abnormal. If one test is abnormal, perform a second different test to confirm. Once Cushing's is confirmed biochemically, ACTH measurement determines whether ACTH-dependent (raised) or independent (suppressed), and imaging (pituitary MRI or adrenal CT) follows accordingly.
key_points: First-line screen: 24-h UFC, late-night salivary cortisol, OR overnight 1 mg DST
1 mg DST: dexamethasone at 23:00, cortisol next morning at 08:00, target less than 50 nmol/L
Confirm with a second different test before proceeding
ACTH and imaging come AFTER biochemical confirmation, not before
explanation.pearls: Cushing's screening: overnight 1 mg DST suppresses 08:00 cortisol to less than 50 nmol/L if normal; ACTH and pituitary MRI follow biochemical confirmation, not precede it.

subtopic_detail: Acute uncomplicated type B aortic dissection
stem:
A 62-year-old man with a 30-year history of poorly controlled hypertension presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of severe interscapular pain that began three hours ago while sitting at his desk. The pain is described as a tearing sensation. He took his usual amlodipine and irbesartan this morning.

On examination he is in obvious discomfort. Pulse 92 (regular), blood pressure 196 by 112 mmHg in the right arm and 188 by 108 mmHg in the left arm, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. Bilateral radial pulses are present and equal. Cardiac auscultation reveals no murmur, with normal first and second heart sounds. Abdominal examination is unremarkable, peripheral pulses are present in both lower limbs, and neurological examination is normal. CT angiography of the aorta shows an intimal flap commencing distal to the left subclavian artery and extending to the level of the renal arteries without branch-vessel compromise.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP right 196/112 mmHg left 188/108 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: equal radial pulses, no murmur, peripheral pulses present, no neurological deficit
data_table.Investigations: CTA aorta: intimal flap from distal to L subclavian to renal arteries; no branch-vessel compromise; troponin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate haemodynamic management?

options.text: Intravenous nitroprusside infusion titrated rapidly to systolic BP under 120 mmHg
options.rationale: Starting a pure vasodilator first causes reflex tachycardia which raises shear stress (dP/dt) on the aortic wall and risks dissection extension. Beta blockade must precede vasodilator therapy. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases Guideline; eTG: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Intravenous loop diuretic furosemide 40 mg with morphine 5 mg for analgesia
options.rationale: Diuresis is not the issue here and morphine alone is inadequate; the priority is rate and pressure control with beta blockade to reduce aortic wall stress. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous labetalol infusion titrated to heart rate 60 and SBP 100 to 120 mmHg
options.rationale: Uncomplicated type B aortic dissection (no branch-vessel compromise, no rupture, no rapidly expanding aorta) is managed medically. The priority is reducing aortic wall shear stress with IV beta-blockade first (labetalol or esmolol) to heart rate around 60 and systolic blood pressure 100 to 120 mmHg, with adjunct vasodilator (nitroprusside or GTN) added if pressure target not met. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases Guideline; eTG: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Immediate transfer to operating theatre for endovascular stent graft repair (TEVAR)
options.rationale: TEVAR is indicated for COMPLICATED type B (malperfusion, rupture, rapidly expanding aneurysm, refractory pain) or for those who fail medical therapy. Uncomplicated type B is medically managed first. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases Guideline)

options.text: Immediate cardiothoracic surgical consult for ascending aorta surgical replacement repair
options.rationale: This is a type B dissection (distal to the left subclavian artery), not type A. Surgical replacement is for type A dissections, which involve the ascending aorta and risk cardiac tamponade. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases Guideline)

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection management depends on Stanford classification. Type A (involves ascending aorta) requires emergent surgical repair due to risk of cardiac tamponade, aortic regurgitation, and coronary occlusion. Type B (distal to left subclavian only) is medically managed if uncomplicated, with IV beta-blockade first (labetalol 20 mg bolus then infusion titrated, OR esmolol infusion) to target heart rate around 60 and SBP 100 to 120 mmHg. Vasodilator (sodium nitroprusside or glyceryl trinitrate) is added only after rate is controlled, to prevent reflex tachycardia raising shear stress. Complicated type B (malperfusion, rupture, rapid expansion, refractory pain) requires TEVAR or surgery.
key_points: Type A dissection: emergent surgery (ascending aorta involved)
Type B uncomplicated: medical management with IV beta blockade FIRST
Targets: heart rate around 60, SBP 100 to 120 mmHg
Vasodilator added only after rate control to avoid reflex tachycardia
explanation.pearls: Uncomplicated type B aortic dissection: IV labetalol or esmolol first to HR 60 and SBP 100 to 120 mmHg; only then add vasodilator to avoid reflex tachycardia raising aortic shear stress.

subtopic_detail: Pituitary apoplexy with visual loss and hypopituitarism
stem:
A 56-year-old man with a known 2 cm non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma (diagnosed 4 years ago, on watchful waiting) presents to the emergency department with sudden onset of severe retro-orbital headache 90 minutes ago, followed by nausea, vomiting, and progressive loss of vision in the temporal fields of both eyes. He also reports double vision when looking laterally.

On examination he is alert but distressed. Pulse 58, blood pressure 86 by 54 mmHg lying flat, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 35.8 degrees Celsius. He has bilateral temporal field defects on confrontation, left lateral rectus weakness, and a sluggish pupillary response on the left. Neck is supple. Bedside glucose is 3.0 mmol/L (3.5-7.7). Serum sodium is 128 mmol/L (135-145). His regular medications include atorvastatin and irbesartan, no glucocorticoids. He has not been unwell otherwise.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 58, BP 86/54 lying flat, RR 22, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 35.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: alert, bilateral temporal field defects, left lateral rectus weakness, sluggish left pupil, neck supple
data_table.Investigations: bedside glucose 3.0 mmol/L (3.5-7.7), sodium 128 mmol/L (135-145), known 2 cm non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma 4 years ago

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management priority?

options.text: Urgent neurosurgical consult and transfer for transsphenoidal decompression first
options.rationale: Surgical decompression is the definitive treatment but is delayed by minutes-to-hours of imaging and theatre availability. Untreated adrenal insufficiency in this window causes cardiovascular collapse and death; hydrocortisone goes first. (Source: ESE Pituitary Apoplexy Guideline)

options.text: MRI pituitary with contrast to confirm apoplexy before any pharmacological treatment
options.rationale: Waiting for imaging confirmation before stress-dose steroid risks adrenal crisis in the imaging suite. The diagnosis is strongly suspected on clinical grounds (known macroadenoma plus thunderclap headache plus visual loss plus cranial nerve palsy plus hypotension plus hyponatraemia) and treatment is empiric. (Source: ESE Pituitary Apoplexy Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous 3 percent hypertonic saline 100 mL bolus for hyponatraemia correction first
options.rationale: The hyponatraemia here is secondary to glucocorticoid deficiency and resolves with hydrocortisone replacement plus isotonic saline. Hypertonic saline is not the first or appropriate intervention. (Source: ESE Pituitary Apoplexy Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous mannitol 1 g/kg over 20 minutes to reduce intracranial pressure first
options.rationale: Mannitol may have a role in raised ICP but does not address the underlying adrenal insufficiency, and aggressive osmotic diuresis in a hypotensive hypovolaemic patient worsens haemodynamics. (Source: ESE Pituitary Apoplexy Guideline)

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg stat, IV saline, then urgent neurosurgical referral and MRI
options.rationale: Pituitary apoplexy with hypotension, hyponatraemia, and hypoglycaemia indicates acute hypoadrenalism. Stress-dose hydrocortisone 100 mg IV must precede imaging and surgery to prevent cardiovascular collapse. Then urgent MRI confirms diagnosis and neurosurgery decides on decompression timing. (Source: ESE Pituitary Apoplexy Guideline; AMH)

explanation.summary: Pituitary apoplexy is haemorrhage or infarction within a pituitary tumour. Classic presentation is sudden severe retro-orbital headache, visual loss (chiasmal compression causes bitemporal hemianopia), cranial nerve III/IV/VI palsies (cavernous sinus extension), nausea, vomiting, and acute hypopituitarism with hypoadrenalism (hypotension, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia). Immediate management is stress-dose hydrocortisone 100 mg IV BEFORE any imaging or surgery to prevent cardiovascular collapse. Resuscitate with IV saline, treat hypoglycaemia, then urgent MRI to confirm and neurosurgical referral. Surgery (transsphenoidal decompression) is indicated within 7 days for severe visual loss or rapid deterioration; conservative management with steroids alone is reasonable for those with stable mild visual changes.
key_points: Pituitary apoplexy triad: thunderclap headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia
Acute hypoadrenalism causes hypotension, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia
Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV BEFORE imaging or surgery to prevent crisis
Surgery within 7 days for severe visual loss or rapid deterioration
explanation.pearls: Pituitary apoplexy: give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV before MRI or theatre to prevent adrenal crisis; transsphenoidal decompression within 7 days for severe visual loss.

subtopic_detail: Necrotising soft tissue infection diagnosis and urgent intervention
stem:
A 59-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on metformin presents to the emergency department with a 36-hour history of rapidly worsening pain in his right thigh, three days after a minor scratch from gardening. The pain is now described as out of proportion to what he can see on the skin surface.

On examination he is pale, with pulse 132, blood pressure 90 by 58 mmHg, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 38.8 degrees Celsius. There is a 15 cm area of dusky, mottled skin over the anterior thigh with bullous changes at one edge, exquisite tenderness extending well beyond the visible erythema, and crepitus on palpation. Plain X-ray of the thigh shows scattered subcutaneous gas. Bloods: WCC 22 x10^9/L (4-11), CRP 240 mg/L (less than 5), creatinine 168 micromol/L (45-90), sodium 131 mmol/L (135-145), glucose 14 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), haemoglobin 116 g/L (130-170), lactate 4.8 mmol/L (less than 2). The calculated LRINEC score is 9.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132, BP 90/58, RR 28, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 38.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: 15 cm dusky mottled skin with bullae, exquisite tenderness beyond erythema, crepitus on palpation, pale and unwell
data_table.Investigations: X-ray thigh: scattered subcutaneous gas; WCC 22 x10^9/L (4-11), CRP 240 mg/L (<5), creatinine 168 micromol/L (45-90), sodium 131 mmol/L (135-145), glucose 14 mmol/L (3.0-5.4), Hb 116 g/L (130-170), lactate 4.8 mmol/L (<2); LRINEC score 9

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate priority?

options.text: Urgent surgical debridement in operating theatre with broad-spectrum antibiotics
options.rationale: Necrotising soft tissue infection (LRINEC at least 8 high probability, subcutaneous gas, crepitus, bullae, pain out of proportion, septic shock) requires urgent operative debridement within hours. Time to surgery is the single biggest determinant of mortality. Empirical antibiotics (meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin) accompany but do not replace surgery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; ANZBA Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection)
source_refs: ANZBA Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection Guidelines

options.text: MRI of the right thigh urgently to confirm necrotising fasciitis before theatre
options.rationale: MRI may add diagnostic certainty in equivocal cases but the clinical and biochemical picture here is unambiguous; waiting for MRI delays definitive surgery by hours and worsens mortality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Empirical IV flucloxacillin 2 g six hourly and reassess clinically in two hours of observation
options.rationale: Flucloxacillin alone does not cover the polymicrobial flora (Streptococcus pyogenes, anaerobes, Gram-negative rods) typical of type I necrotising fasciitis. Watchful waiting in any necrotising infection costs lives. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy referral as primary intervention before surgical debridement
options.rationale: HBO has an adjunctive role in some institutions but never replaces or precedes surgical debridement. Time-to-surgery dominates mortality in necrotising fasciitis above all else. (Source: ANZBA Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection Guidelines)
source_refs: ANZBA Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection Guidelines

options.text: Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation with crystalloid 30 mL/kg targeting MAP at least 65 mmHg first
options.rationale: Fluid resuscitation begins in parallel and is essential, but it does not address the source which is necrotic tissue that must be excised. Without source control, sepsis progresses despite optimal fluid management. (Source: ANZBA Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection Guidelines)
source_refs: ANZBA Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection Guidelines

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection (necrotising fasciitis, gas gangrene, Fournier gangrene) is a surgical emergency. Clinical hallmarks are pain out of proportion to skin findings, rapid progression over hours, dusky or mottled skin, bullae, crepitus, anaesthesia over the affected area, and systemic toxicity. The LRINEC score (CRP, WCC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, glucose) supports diagnosis: 6 or more intermediate probability, 8 or more high probability. Plain X-ray or CT may show subcutaneous gas. The single most important intervention is urgent surgical debridement within 6 hours; every hour of delay increases mortality. Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics (meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin for toxin suppression) accompany but do not replace surgery. Resuscitation, source control, and ICU support run in parallel.
key_points: LRINEC 6 to 7 intermediate, 8 or more high probability of necrotising fasciitis
Time to surgical debridement is the dominant mortality determinant
Empirical: meropenem + vancomycin + clindamycin (toxin suppression)
Bullae, crepitus, pain out of proportion, subcutaneous gas are late signs
explanation.pearls: Necrotising fasciitis with LRINEC of 8 or more plus subcutaneous gas: surgical debridement within 6 hours dominates mortality; meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin accompany but do not replace surgery.

sources.label: ANZBA Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection Guidelines

stem:
A 34-year-old non-pregnant woman presents to the emergency department with two days of fevers, rigors, and right-sided loin pain on a background of dysuria and frequency for four days. She is otherwise well, has no allergies, has no urinary tract abnormalities, and is not catheterised. She is sexually active with a male partner and uses condoms; she had a uncomplicated cystitis 14 months ago treated with trimethoprim.

On examination she is unwell but not septic. There is marked right costovertebral angle tenderness. The abdomen is otherwise soft. She is tolerating oral fluids and food.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 102 /min, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 38.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: right costovertebral angle tenderness, soft abdomen, no peritonism
data_table.Investigations: urine dipstick: leukocytes 3+, nitrites positive, blood 1+; FBC WCC 14.6 x10^9/L; CRP 88 mg/L; creatinine 78 micromol/L; lactate 1.8 mmol/L; urine culture and blood cultures sent

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic?

options.text: Oral ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 7 days at home
options.rationale: Oral ciprofloxacin is reserved for mild pyelonephritis suitable for outpatient management. Significant fever, rigors, and raised inflammatory markers warrant initial IV therapy and observation under Therapeutic Guidelines. Fluoroquinolone resistance in E. coli is also a regional issue. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg once-daily plus IV amoxicillin 2 g six hourly
options.rationale: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic recommends IV gentamicin plus amoxicillin (or ampicillin) as first-line empirical therapy for moderate to severe acute pyelonephritis in non-pregnant adults requiring admission. Gentamicin covers gram-negative uropathogens including most E. coli; amoxicillin extends cover for enterococci. Step-down to oral guided by culture and sensitivity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Oral trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 14 days as outpatient therapy
options.rationale: Trimethoprim is appropriate for uncomplicated lower UTI when local resistance is low. It does not provide adequate parenteral cover for pyelonephritis and oral monotherapy is insufficient at this severity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: IV vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading then 15 mg/kg twelve hourly
options.rationale: Vancomycin targets gram-positive organisms (MRSA, enterococci) and does not cover the dominant gram-negative uropathogens. It is not an empirical choice for pyelonephritis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: IV meropenem 1 g eight hourly as the empirical first-line agent
options.rationale: Meropenem is reserved for severe sepsis with risk factors for multi-drug resistance, ESBL exposure, or failure of first-line. Routine first-line use drives carbapenem resistance and is not Therapeutic Guidelines first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Acute pyelonephritis in non-pregnant adults requiring admission is empirically treated with IV gentamicin (5 to 7 mg/kg once-daily, calculated by ideal body weight) plus IV amoxicillin 2 g six hourly per Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic. Mild pyelonephritis suitable for outpatient management can be treated with oral ciprofloxacin or amoxicillin-clavulanate guided by local resistance. Always send urine and blood cultures before antibiotics. Step-down to a culture-directed oral agent for a total 10 to 14 day course. Consider imaging (CT or US) if no improvement at 48 to 72 hours or if anatomic abnormalities are suspected.
key_points: Moderate to severe pyelonephritis: IV gentamicin once-daily plus IV amoxicillin first-line
Mild outpatient pyelonephritis: oral ciprofloxacin or amoxicillin-clavulanate
Always urine and blood cultures before antibiotics; step-down to oral by sensitivity
Imaging at 48 to 72 hours if no improvement to exclude complications
explanation.pearls: Adult acute pyelonephritis (admission): IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg once-daily plus IV amoxicillin 2 g six hourly per Therapeutic Guidelines. Step-down to culture-directed oral for total 10 to 14 days. Image if no improvement at 48 to 72 hours.

stem:
A 68-year-old man with COPD reviews at your respiratory clinic. He has a 50 pack-year history (quit 4 years ago), GOLD group B disease, FEV1 56% predicted post-bronchodilator, and has been on tiotropium 18 micrograms daily for two years. In the past year he has had three moderate exacerbations requiring oral prednisolone and antibiotics, none requiring hospital admission. His mMRC dyspnoea grade is 3.

His blood eosinophil count is 380 cells per microlitre on a recent FBC. He has had no pneumonias. He uses his short-acting salbutamol inhaler about four times a week. He is on optimal non-pharmacological therapy (pulmonary rehabilitation completed, influenza and pneumococcal vaccines up to date, smoking cessation maintained).

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 84 /min, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: barrel chest, reduced air entry bilaterally, no wheeze at rest, no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: FEV1/FVC 0.58 post-bronchodilator; FEV1 56% predicted; blood eosinophils 380 cells per microlitre

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in inhaled therapy?

options.text: Add oral azithromycin 250 mg three times weekly as long-term prophylaxis
options.rationale: Long-term macrolide prophylaxis is considered for frequent exacerbators on optimal inhaled therapy including triple inhaler; it is not the next step before escalating inhalers. Cardiac and hearing screening are required. (Source: GOLD 2024; COPD-X)

options.text: Add a LABA to the LAMA but defer ICS until further exacerbations
options.rationale: LAMA plus LABA (no ICS) is appropriate if eosinophils are below 100 cells per microlitre and exacerbations are infrequent. With eosinophils 380 and three exacerbations in a year, ICS is indicated under GOLD and COPD-X. (Source: GOLD 2024; COPD-X)

options.text: Escalate to a LAMA plus LABA plus inhaled corticosteroid triple inhaler
options.rationale: GOLD 2024 and Lung Foundation Australia recommend escalating to triple therapy (LAMA plus LABA plus ICS) for patients with two or more moderate exacerbations or one hospitalisation per year despite LAMA monotherapy, particularly when blood eosinophils are 300 cells per microlitre or higher. ICS efficacy is greatest in this eosinophilic phenotype. (Source: GOLD 2024 Strategy; COPD-X Australian Guidelines)

options.text: Add oral theophylline 200 mg twice daily and review symptoms in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic window and modest bronchodilator effect; it is reserved for refractory cases when inhaled options are exhausted. (Source: GOLD 2024; COPD-X)

options.text: Stop tiotropium and switch to inhaled corticosteroid monotherapy
options.rationale: ICS monotherapy in COPD is inferior to LAMA monotherapy and increases pneumonia risk. Stopping the LAMA is harmful. (Source: GOLD 2024; COPD-X)

explanation.summary: GOLD 2024 and Lung Foundation Australia's COPD-X guideline use exacerbation history and eosinophil count to direct ICS use. Patients with two or more moderate exacerbations or one hospitalisation per year on LAMA or LABA monotherapy should escalate to LAMA plus LABA, with ICS added if eosinophils are 300 cells per microlitre or higher (or 100 to 300 with frequent exacerbations). Triple therapy in a single inhaler improves adherence. After 3 to 6 months of triple therapy, ICS can be considered for withdrawal if no exacerbations and eosinophils remain low; long-term azithromycin is added for ongoing frequent exacerbators despite triple therapy.
key_points: Two or more moderate exacerbations per year on LAMA: escalate to LAMA plus LABA plus ICS if eosinophils 300 or higher
ICS benefit is greatest at eosinophils 300 cells per microlitre or higher
Long-term azithromycin reserved for frequent exacerbators despite triple inhaler
ICS monotherapy is not used in COPD; pneumonia risk and inferior outcomes
explanation.pearls: GOLD/COPD-X COPD escalation: two or more exacerbations on LAMA, escalate to LAMA+LABA+ICS especially if eosinophils 300 cells per microlitre or higher. Long-term azithromycin only for frequent exacerbators on triple therapy. ICS monotherapy is not used in COPD.

stem:
A 78-year-old woman is seen in your general practice with a new diagnosis of persistent atrial fibrillation, picked up on routine ECG when she presented with palpitations. She has hypertension on perindopril and amlodipine, type 2 diabetes on metformin, and chronic kidney disease stage 3a (eGFR 52 mL/min per 1.73 m^2). She has never had a stroke or TIA. She lives independently and has no falls history.

Her CHA2DS2-VA score is 4 (hypertension, age 75 or over, diabetes, female sex). HAS-BLED is 1 (hypertension). She has no contraindications to oral anticoagulation. She is rate-controlled on metoprolol 50 mg twice daily and has chosen a rate-control strategy after counselling.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 78 /min, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: irregularly irregular pulse, no carotid bruits, no peripheral oedema, no signs of heart failure
data_table.Investigations: creatinine 102 micromol/L (45 to 90); eGFR 52 mL/min per 1.73 m^2; FBC and LFT within normal limits; ECG confirms AF rate 78

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulant choice?

options.text: Dabigatran 150 mg twice daily orally for stroke prevention
options.rationale: Dabigatran is highly renally cleared (80%) and is dose-adjusted in CKD. While usable here, apixaban is preferred in moderate CKD due to lower renal dependence and better bleeding profile in elderly patients. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ Atrial Fibrillation Guidelines

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg daily as antiplatelet stroke prevention monotherapy
options.rationale: Aspirin is no longer recommended for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation. It has minimal benefit and similar bleeding risk to anticoagulants. NHFA/CSANZ explicitly removes aspirin from AF stroke prevention. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ Atrial Fibrillation Guidelines

options.text: Warfarin titrated to a therapeutic INR of 2.0 to 3.0
options.rationale: Warfarin is acceptable when DOACs are contraindicated, but DOACs (particularly apixaban) are preferred first-line in this setting given non-inferior efficacy, lower intracranial haemorrhage, and no INR monitoring. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ Atrial Fibrillation Guidelines

options.text: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily orally indefinitely for stroke prevention
options.rationale: Apixaban is the preferred DOAC in moderate CKD (eGFR 30 to 50) under NHFA/CSANZ AF guidance because of its lower renal clearance (about 27%) and a strong real-world safety profile. Standard dose 5 mg twice daily applies; dose reduction to 2.5 mg twice daily requires two of: age 80 or over, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 micromol/L or higher. She meets none. (Source: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ Atrial Fibrillation Guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ Atrial Fibrillation Guidelines

options.text: Left atrial appendage closure with a Watchman device alone
options.rationale: LAA closure is reserved for patients with contraindications to long-term oral anticoagulation. She has no contraindications and tolerates oral therapy. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ Atrial Fibrillation Guidelines

explanation.summary: The NHFA/CSANZ Atrial Fibrillation Guidelines recommend oral anticoagulation for non-valvular AF when the CHA2DS2-VA score is 2 or higher. DOACs are preferred over warfarin in non-valvular AF for non-inferior efficacy, lower intracranial haemorrhage, and no INR monitoring. Apixaban is the preferred DOAC in moderate CKD (eGFR 30 to 50). Apixaban dose reduction (2.5 mg twice daily) requires two of: age 80 or over, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 micromol/L or higher. Aspirin is no longer recommended for AF stroke prevention; LAA closure is reserved for those with anticoagulation contraindications.
key_points: CHA2DS2-VA 2 or higher: oral anticoagulation indicated; DOAC preferred over warfarin
Apixaban is preferred in moderate CKD (eGFR 30 to 50)
Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily if two of: age 80 or over, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 or higher
Aspirin is removed from AF stroke prevention; LAA closure if anticoagulation contraindicated
explanation.pearls: AF stroke prevention NHFA/CSANZ: CHA2DS2-VA 2 or higher gets a DOAC, preferably apixaban in moderate CKD (eGFR 30 to 50). Reduce apixaban to 2.5 mg twice daily if two of: age 80 or over, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 or higher.

sources.label: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ Atrial Fibrillation Guidelines

stem:
A 72-year-old man with chronic kidney disease stage 4 is brought to the emergency department feeling weak and lethargic. His usual medications include perindopril, spironolactone, and atorvastatin. He had gastroenteritis with diarrhoea for three days and has been off food and water but kept taking his usual medications. He is alert and oriented but mildly confused.

His ECG shows peaked T waves in the precordial leads, a PR interval of 240 ms, and a QRS duration of 116 ms. He has no chest pain. He has not yet been catheterised.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 56 /min, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: mildly dehydrated, no peripheral oedema, no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: potassium 7.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0); sodium 138 mmol/L; bicarbonate 14 mmol/L; creatinine 380 micromol/L (baseline 220); pH 7.28; ECG: peaked T waves, PR 240 ms, QRS 116 ms

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Urgent haemodialysis booking without further pharmacological intervention
options.rationale: Dialysis is the definitive treatment for refractory hyperkalaemia in CKD but takes time to set up. Pharmacological bridging with calcium gluconate then insulin-dextrose and salbutamol is started while dialysis is being arranged. (Source: KHA Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: IV actrapid insulin 10 units in 50 mL of 50% dextrose over 15 minutes
options.rationale: Insulin-dextrose lowers serum potassium by intracellular shift over 30 to 60 minutes but does not stabilise the myocardium acutely. With ECG changes, calcium gluconate comes first to protect against arrhythmia while waiting for shift therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology; KHA)

options.text: Oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate (resonium) 30 g now and repeat in 4 hours
options.rationale: Cation-exchange resins act over hours and do not address acute arrhythmia risk. They are adjunctive for ongoing potassium load, not immediate. (Source: KHA Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: IV furosemide 80 mg as a bolus to drive renal potassium loss
options.rationale: Loop diuretics increase renal potassium excretion but require adequate renal function and time. With CKD stage 4, AKI on top, and dehydration, the response is limited and slow. Cardiac protection is the priority. (Source: KHA Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: IV calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL over 10 minutes for cardiac membrane stabilisation
options.rationale: ECG changes (peaked T waves, prolonged PR, widened QRS) in the setting of hyperkalaemia mandate immediate cardiac membrane stabilisation with IV calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL over 10 minutes. Calcium does not lower potassium but reduces myocardial excitability and arrhythmia risk within minutes. Insulin-dextrose and salbutamol then drive potassium intracellularly; definitive removal (diuretics, dialysis) follows. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology; KHA Hyperkalaemia)

explanation.summary: Acute hyperkalaemia with ECG changes is a medical emergency. The Kidney Health Australia stepwise approach is: immediate IV calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL over 10 minutes for membrane stabilisation, then intracellular shift therapy (IV insulin 10 units with dextrose 25 g; nebulised salbutamol 10 to 20 mg; sodium bicarbonate if acidotic), then definitive removal (diuretics if responsive, cation-exchange resins, or haemodialysis). The offending medications (ACE inhibitor, spironolactone) are held. Recheck potassium and ECG at 30 minutes; calcium gluconate can be repeated.
key_points: Calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL over 10 minutes for cardiac membrane stabilisation
Insulin-dextrose, salbutamol nebs, bicarbonate (if acidotic) drive intracellular shift
Diuretics, resins, or dialysis for definitive removal
Hold ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and potassium-sparing diuretics
explanation.pearls: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes: IV calcium gluconate 10% 10 mL over 10 minutes for membrane stabilisation FIRST, then insulin-dextrose plus nebulised salbutamol for shift, then diuretics/resin/dialysis for removal. Hold ACEi, ARBs, spironolactone.

stem:
A 56-year-old man with type 2 diabetes attends the emergency department late at night with worsening left lower leg pain over 18 hours. He gave himself a small cut while gardening yesterday. The pain is now out of proportion to the small wound and he is reluctant to move his foot. He has had rigors at home and one episode of vomiting.

On examination there is a 1 cm puncture wound on the calf with surrounding erythema. The skin overlying the lateral calf is dusky purple in one area and tender well beyond the visible margin of erythema. There are no crepitations on palpation; an early plain film shows no gas. He is unwell-looking and rigoring on the trolley.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 122 /min, blood pressure 98/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 /min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 39.0 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: pain out of proportion, dusky discolouration of skin lateral calf, tenderness beyond erythema margin, no crepitations
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.4 x10^9/L; haemoglobin 130 g/L (130 to 170); sodium 132 mmol/L; creatinine 142 micromol/L (baseline 80); CRP 240 mg/L; glucose 18.4 mmol/L; lactate 4.8 mmol/L; LRINEC score 9

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent surgical consultation for immediate operative debridement after blood cultures and IV antibiotics
options.rationale: Pain out of proportion, dusky skin, tenderness beyond erythema, septic physiology, and LRINEC of 9 (high risk, more than 6) make necrotising fasciitis the working diagnosis. Survival depends on time to surgical debridement, which is the definitive treatment. Empirical IV antibiotics (meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin under Therapeutic Guidelines) and resuscitation are given concurrently. CT or MRI must not delay theatre. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Mark the erythema with a marker pen and review in 4 hours on IV flucloxacillin
options.rationale: Outlining cellulitis and watching is appropriate for uncomplicated cellulitis without sepsis or red flags. The features here mandate operative assessment, not observation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: CT with contrast of the leg before any surgical referral to confirm the diagnosis
options.rationale: Imaging supports diagnosis but must not delay theatre when clinical suspicion is high. CT or MRI may show gas or fascial fluid but a normal scan does not exclude necrotising fasciitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy in addition to IV piperacillin-tazobactam, deferring surgery
options.rationale: Hyperbaric oxygen is an adjunct considered only after surgical debridement. It does not replace operative source control. Piperacillin-tazobactam alone misses the clindamycin role in suppressing exotoxin production. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Trial of IV flucloxacillin 2 g six hourly for 24 hours and reassess for debridement
options.rationale: Monotherapy with flucloxacillin and observation in the setting of suspected necrotising fasciitis delays definitive care and increases mortality. The patient needs immediate broad-spectrum cover and theatre. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency with mortality strongly correlated with time to debridement. Clinical clues are pain out of proportion to skin findings, dusky or purpura-like skin, crepitations, tenderness beyond erythema, rapid progression, and systemic toxicity (septic shock, AKI). The LRINEC score uses CRP, WCC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, and glucose; a score of 6 or higher is high risk and 8 or higher is very high risk. Empirical antibiotics in Australia are meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin (clindamycin for exotoxin suppression in group A streptococcal cases). Imaging must not delay theatre.
key_points: Time to surgical debridement is the strongest mortality determinant
Empirical antibiotics: meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin
LRINEC 6 or higher is high risk; 8 or higher is very high risk
Imaging must not delay theatre
explanation.pearls: Necrotising fasciitis: immediate surgical debridement plus IV meropenem + vancomycin + clindamycin (clindamycin for exotoxin suppression). LRINEC 6 or higher is high risk. Do not delay theatre for imaging.

stem:
A 64-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance with sudden-onset severe breathlessness and one episode of syncope at home 30 minutes ago. She returned from a long-haul flight three days ago. She has no past medical history of bleeding, no recent surgery, and is not on anticoagulants.

On arrival she is pale, cool peripherally, and clammy. The right ventricle is felt heaving on palpation of the lower sternum. Bedside echocardiography shows a dilated and hypokinetic right ventricle with septal flattening. CT pulmonary angiogram demonstrates bilateral central filling defects. There is no evidence of intracranial pathology on CT brain and no history of recent stroke, surgery, or bleeding.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 132 /min, blood pressure 78/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 /min, SpO2 88% on 15 L non-rebreather, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: cool peripheries, prominent neck veins, loud P2, no calf swelling, GCS 15
data_table.Investigations: troponin I 220 ng/L (less than 14); BNP 1400 pg/mL; lactate 4.2 mmol/L; CTPA: bilateral central PE; echocardiography: dilated hypokinetic RV

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Emergent surgical pulmonary embolectomy as the first-line reperfusion strategy
options.rationale: Surgical embolectomy is reserved for patients with contraindications to thrombolysis or failed thrombolysis, and where cardiac surgical capability is on-site. Systemic thrombolysis remains first-line where not contraindicated. (Source: ESC PE Guidelines)
source_refs: ESC Guidelines for Acute Pulmonary Embolism

options.text: Therapeutic enoxaparin 1.5 mg/kg subcutaneously once daily and observe
options.rationale: Therapeutic enoxaparin alone is appropriate for non-massive PE. With shock and RV failure, the patient needs reperfusion therapy; anticoagulation alone has high mortality. (Source: ESC PE Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
source_refs: ESC Guidelines for Acute Pulmonary Embolism

options.text: Apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily for outpatient management
options.rationale: DOAC monotherapy is appropriate for intermediate-low or low-risk PE in haemodynamically stable patients suitable for outpatient care. Shock and RV dysfunction exclude this pathway. (Source: ESC PE Guidelines)
source_refs: ESC Guidelines for Acute Pulmonary Embolism

options.text: IV alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours alongside resuscitation and unfractionated heparin
options.rationale: Massive (high-risk) pulmonary embolism with sustained hypotension and right heart dysfunction has high short-term mortality. Australian and ESC guidelines recommend systemic thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours, or 0.6 mg/kg over 15 minutes in cardiac arrest) when there are no absolute contraindications. Catheter-directed thrombolysis is an alternative in centres where it is available. (Source: ESC Guidelines for Acute Pulmonary Embolism; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
source_refs: ESC Guidelines for Acute Pulmonary Embolism

options.text: Inferior vena cava filter insertion before starting any anticoagulation
options.rationale: IVC filters are considered when anticoagulation is absolutely contraindicated or when recurrent PE occurs despite anticoagulation. They do not address the existing clot burden and provide no haemodynamic benefit. (Source: ESC PE Guidelines)
source_refs: ESC Guidelines for Acute Pulmonary Embolism

explanation.summary: Massive (high-risk) pulmonary embolism is defined by sustained hypotension (systolic BP under 90 mmHg for at least 15 minutes or needing vasopressors) or shock not from another cause. Mortality without reperfusion is high. ESC and Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular recommend systemic thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours, or a weight-based bolus during cardiac arrest) with unfractionated heparin if there are no absolute contraindications (active intracranial pathology, recent ischaemic stroke, active bleeding). Catheter-directed thrombolysis and surgical embolectomy are alternatives. Anticoagulation alone is insufficient.
key_points: Massive PE: shock or sustained hypotension warrants reperfusion therapy
Alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours plus unfractionated heparin is the standard regimen
Catheter-directed thrombolysis is an alternative where available
Surgical embolectomy if thrombolysis contraindicated or failed
explanation.pearls: Massive PE with shock: IV alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours plus unfractionated heparin if no absolute contraindication. Catheter-directed thrombolysis or surgical embolectomy when contraindications or failure. Anticoagulation alone is insufficient.

sources.label: ESC Guidelines for Acute Pulmonary Embolism

stem:
A 42-year-old woman with autoimmune Addison's disease is brought to the emergency department by ambulance with vomiting, abdominal pain, lethargy, and confusion. She has been on hydrocortisone 20 mg in the morning and 10 mg at lunchtime with fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily for 8 years. She has had a viral gastroenteritis for two days and stopped her hydrocortisone yesterday because she could not keep tablets down.

She is drowsy on arrival and disoriented to time and place. Her abdomen is diffusely tender without peritonism. She has been given 1 L of IV 0.9% sodium chloride en route. The medical registrar is at the bedside.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 124 /min, blood pressure 84/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: drowsy, dehydrated, abdomen mildly tender without peritonism, hyperpigmentation of buccal mucosa
data_table.Investigations: sodium 126 mmol/L (135 to 145); potassium 5.8 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0); glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.9 to 5.4); urea 12 mmol/L; creatinine 110 micromol/L (45 to 90)

lead_in: What is the single best immediate management step?

options.text: Oral hydrocortisone 20 mg stat once her vomiting has fully settled
options.rationale: Oral hydrocortisone is inappropriate in a vomiting drowsy patient; absorption is unreliable and the patient cannot keep it down. IV is the route in crisis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: IV dexamethasone 4 mg as a single dose while awaiting cortisol and ACTH results
options.rationale: Dexamethasone is used when diagnostic short Synacthen testing is planned and cortisol assay must not be confounded, in patients without an established diagnosis. In an established Addison's patient with a clear crisis, hydrocortisone is preferred for its mineralocorticoid activity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg as a bolus then 200 mg per 24 hours as a continuous infusion
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis is a life-threatening glucocorticoid deficiency state. Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology and the Endocrine Society direct immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus, then 200 mg per 24 hours as a continuous infusion (or 50 mg six hourly), plus IV fluid resuscitation and dextrose for hypoglycaemia. Bolus hydrocortisone at this dose has sufficient mineralocorticoid effect; separate fludrocortisone is unnecessary acutely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology; Endocrine Society Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline)

options.text: IV fludrocortisone 200 micrograms with IV 0.9% sodium chloride bolus
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is not available as an IV preparation in Australia. Hydrocortisone at high dose provides mineralocorticoid activity that adequately covers the acute phase. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Withhold steroids until a short Synacthen test confirms adrenal insufficiency
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis is treated empirically. Withholding glucocorticoid pending diagnostic testing in an established or suspected crisis is associated with mortality. Diagnostic testing is performed later, on stable dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis presents with hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, and altered mental status, typically precipitated by a stress event (infection, surgery, trauma) in a patient with adrenal insufficiency. Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology directs immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus followed by 200 mg per 24 hours by continuous infusion (or 50 mg six hourly), IV crystalloid resuscitation (1 L of 0.9% sodium chloride in the first hour, then guided by haemodynamics), and IV dextrose for hypoglycaemia. Always treat empirically; diagnostic short Synacthen testing waits for stability. Sick-day rules and emergency hydrocortisone injection kits prevent crises in known patients.
key_points: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 200 mg per 24 hours by continuous infusion (or 50 mg six hourly)
IV 0.9% sodium chloride resuscitation; IV dextrose for hypoglycaemia
Empirical treatment; do not wait for short Synacthen testing in crisis
Sick-day rules and emergency injection kit prevent crisis in known patients
explanation.pearls: Adrenal crisis: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 200 mg per 24 hours by infusion (or 50 mg six hourly). IV 0.9% saline resuscitation and IV dextrose for hypoglycaemia. Empirical treatment; do not wait for Synacthen testing.

stem:
A 58-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by ambulance with one hour of central crushing chest pain radiating to the jaw. He has hypertension and is a current smoker. Paramedics gave him aspirin 300 mg, oxygen, and sublingual GTN with one episode of profound hypotension after the GTN; his BP recovered with a 500 mL saline bolus.

On arrival he is pale and clammy but alert. The ECG shows 2 mm ST elevation in leads II, III, and aVF with reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL. A right-sided V4R lead shows 1.5 mm ST elevation. There is no murmur. Chest is clear and the JVP is elevated. Primary PCI is available on-site within 30 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 56 /min, blood pressure 92/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 /min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: elevated JVP, clear chest, no peripheral oedema, no murmurs
data_table.Investigations: ECG: 2 mm ST elevation II/III/aVF with reciprocal depression I/aVL; V4R 1.5 mm ST elevation; troponin I 380 ng/L (less than 14); chest film clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: IV 0.9% sodium chloride 500 mL bolus and prepare for primary PCI
options.rationale: Inferior STEMI with right-sided V4R elevation indicates right ventricular involvement. RV infarcts are preload-dependent: nitrates and morphine are AVOIDED because they reduce preload and cause hypotension. Fluid loading restores RV output. Primary PCI within 90 minutes is the reperfusion strategy of choice. (Source: CSANZ Acute Coronary Syndrome Guidelines)

options.text: IV glyceryl trinitrate infusion starting at 5 micrograms per minute
options.rationale: Nitrates are contraindicated in RV infarction because they drop preload to the already volume-dependent right ventricle and can precipitate hypotension and cardiogenic shock. The first GTN dose already caused profound hypotension; further GTN would worsen this. (Source: CSANZ ACS Guidelines)

options.text: IV furosemide 40 mg now to offload the right ventricle today
options.rationale: Diuresis worsens RV infarct shock by reducing preload further. Furosemide is appropriate for LV failure with pulmonary oedema, which is not present here. (Source: CSANZ ACS Guidelines)

options.text: IV metoprolol 5 mg now before transfer to the cardiac catheter lab
options.rationale: Beta-blockers are deferred in haemodynamically unstable inferior STEMI, particularly with bradycardia and RV infarction, due to risk of cardiogenic shock and worsening AV block. They are introduced once stable. (Source: CSANZ ACS Guidelines)

options.text: Fibrinolysis with tenecteplase as the primary reperfusion strategy
options.rationale: Primary PCI is preferred over fibrinolysis when available within 90 minutes of first medical contact. Fibrinolysis is reserved for centres without timely access to PCI. (Source: CSANZ ACS Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Inferior STEMI carries a 30 to 50% risk of right ventricular involvement, especially when the proximal RCA is occluded. V4R lead with ST elevation of 1 mm or more confirms RV involvement. The right ventricle is preload-dependent, so RV infarction creates pseudo-cardiogenic shock that responds to fluid loading. Nitrates, morphine, and diuretics are avoided because they reduce preload. Primary PCI within 90 minutes of first medical contact is the reperfusion strategy of choice; fibrinolysis only if PCI not accessible within 120 minutes. Bradycardia and AV block are common in inferior infarcts and may need atropine or temporary pacing.
key_points: RV infarction is preload-dependent: load fluid, avoid nitrates, morphine, and diuretics
V4R ST elevation 1 mm or more confirms RV involvement
Primary PCI within 90 minutes is preferred over fibrinolysis
Bradycardia and AV block are common; atropine or temporary pacing as needed
explanation.pearls: Inferior STEMI with V4R ST elevation: RV infarct is preload-dependent. Fluid load, AVOID nitrates/morphine/diuretics, refer for primary PCI within 90 minutes. Be ready for bradyarrhythmia.

subtopic_detail: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura - avoid platelet transfusion
stem:
A 38-year-old previously well woman presents to the emergency department with 4 days of fatigue, headache, and a petechial rash over her shins. She also describes intermittent visual disturbance for the last 24 hours. She has no recent infections, no medications, and no family history of bleeding.

Full blood count shows haemoglobin 78 g/L, platelets 12 x 10^9/L, and white cells 7.6 x 10^9/L. Blood film shows numerous schistocytes (5 to 8 per high power field), polychromasia, and no blasts. LDH is 1280 U/L (less than 250), bilirubin 38 micromol/L (less than 20), haptoglobin under 0.1 g/L, creatinine 142 micromol/L (baseline unknown but eGFR estimated 42). Direct antiglobulin test is negative. Coagulation profile is within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse 102 /min, blood pressure 134/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: alert, oriented but mildly confused on detailed history, petechiae over shins, no organomegaly, no lymphadenopathy, no focal neurology, fundoscopy normal
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 78 g/L (115-160), platelets 12 x10^9/L (150-450), schistocytes on film 5-8 per high power field, LDH 1280 U/L (under 250), haptoglobin under 0.1 g/L (0.3-2.0), DAT negative, creatinine 142 micromol/L (45-90), coagulation profile normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Discuss immediate plasma exchange with the haematology team and avoid platelet transfusion despite the platelet count
options.rationale: Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia plus thrombocytopenia in the absence of an alternative explanation is thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura until proven otherwise. PLASMIC score is high. Plasma exchange is the definitive treatment because it removes the inhibitor and replaces ADAMTS13. Platelet transfusion is associated with worse outcomes (thrombosis) and is reserved for life-threatening bleeding. (Source: ISTH guidelines for TTP; BSH guidelines for thrombotic microangiopathies)

options.text: Transfuse a single adult dose of platelets to raise the platelet count above 50 x 10^9/L before any other intervention
options.rationale: Platelet transfusion in suspected TTP can precipitate microvascular thrombosis (stroke, myocardial infarction, mesenteric ischaemia) and is associated with worse outcomes. Reserve for major or life-threatening bleeding. (Source: ISTH guidelines for TTP)

options.text: Commence empirical intravenous ceftriaxone plus metronidazole for presumed sepsis-related microangiopathy syndromes
options.rationale: There is no clinical evidence of sepsis (no fever beyond mild, no focal source, normal lactate, normal coagulation). Treating as sepsis delays plasma exchange in TTP. (Source: ISTH guidelines for TTP)

options.text: Commence high-dose oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily as sole therapy and review response at the haematology ward round
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are an adjunct to plasma exchange (often combined with caplacizumab and rituximab) but monotherapy delays definitive treatment. Plasma exchange is the upstream intervention. (Source: ISTH guidelines for TTP)

options.text: Transfuse fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg as a substitute for plasma exchange while the exchange room is being prepared
options.rationale: FFP infusion is a temporising measure when plasma exchange cannot be initiated immediately, but it does not replace exchange. The question stem indicates haematology is available and the next step is to initiate exchange, not infuse FFP indefinitely. (Source: ISTH guidelines for TTP)

explanation.summary: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is suggested by microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (schistocytes, raised LDH, low haptoglobin, DAT-negative anaemia), thrombocytopenia, with or without neurology, renal impairment, or fever, in the absence of an alternative explanation. Plasma exchange is the definitive treatment and is initiated urgently. Platelet transfusion is associated with worse outcomes and is reserved for major bleeding only.
key_points: TTP pentad (now non-mandatory): MAHA, thrombocytopenia, neurology, renal impairment, fever.
PLASMIC score predicts severe ADAMTS13 deficiency.
Plasma exchange is first-line; FFP is a bridge if exchange is delayed.
Avoid platelet transfusion except for major bleeding.
explanation.pearls: TTP demands urgent plasma exchange; platelet transfusion is associated with worse outcomes because it fuels microvascular thrombosis, so reserve transfusion for life-threatening bleeding.

stem:
A 62-year-old man with a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement four months ago is admitted to a tertiary cardiology unit with two weeks of fevers, night sweats, and unintentional weight loss of 3 kg. He had a dental extraction six weeks ago without antibiotic prophylaxis. He has no penicillin allergy and no intravenous drug use.

On examination he is alert but unwell-appearing. He has new conjunctival petechiae and three small painless lesions on the palms (Janeway lesions). Auscultation reveals an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge with a soft heart sound at the base. Capillary return is two seconds. Three separate sets of blood cultures over two hours have been collected. Transthoracic echocardiogram shows a 9 mm vegetation on the aortic prosthesis with moderate aortic regurgitation but no abscess. His vital signs are below.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 102, blood pressure 124/64, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 38.9 degrees
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 102 g/L, white cells 14.2 x10^9/L, CRP 162 mg/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, three sets of blood cultures pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g every 4 hours plus gentamicin 1 mg/kg every 8 hours for empirical native valve cover
options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin is appropriate for empirical native valve endocarditis with subacute presentation but does not cover methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus or coagulase negative staphylococci, both of which are common in early prosthetic valve endocarditis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 4 hours as monotherapy targeting methicillin sensitive staphylococcus aureus only
options.rationale: Flucloxacillin covers methicillin sensitive Staphylococcus aureus but misses MRSA, coagulase negative staphylococci, and lacks biofilm penetration appropriate for prosthetic valve endocarditis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin 25 mg/kg load then 15 to 20 mg/kg twice daily, gentamicin 1 mg/kg every 8 hours, plus rifampicin
options.rationale: Prosthetic valve endocarditis under 12 months from surgery is treated empirically as for staphylococci including MRSA, with vancomycin plus gentamicin plus rifampicin to penetrate biofilm. Rifampicin is added once stable on vancomycin/gentamicin for biofilm activity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily plus oral doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for empirical Q fever endocarditis cover
options.rationale: Q fever endocarditis is unusual outside livestock contact and typically presents with culture negative endocarditis; empirical cover for the common pathogens of prosthetic valve endocarditis is the priority while serology is pending. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 8 hours as broad spectrum empirical cover until culture results return
options.rationale: Piperacillin-tazobactam is appropriate for nosocomial sepsis but does not cover MRSA or coagulase negative staphylococci which dominate early prosthetic valve endocarditis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE) within 12 months of surgery is dominated by Staphylococcus aureus and coagulase negative staphylococci, often methicillin resistant, with biofilm formation on the prosthesis. Australian empirical therapy is vancomycin plus gentamicin plus rifampicin. Late PVE (over 12 months) and native valve endocarditis follow a different empirical regimen (benzylpenicillin plus flucloxacillin plus gentamicin). Surgery is indicated for heart failure, uncontrolled infection, large vegetation greater than 10 mm with embolism, perivalvular abscess, or fungal endocarditis.
key_points: Early PVE (< 12 months): vancomycin + gentamicin + rifampicin
Late PVE and native valve: benzylpenicillin + flucloxacillin + gentamicin
Modified Duke criteria for diagnosis
TOE more sensitive than TTE; mandatory for PVE
Surgical indications: heart failure, uncontrolled infection, abscess, large vegetation with embolism
explanation.pearls: Rifampicin must NEVER be started before two negative blood cultures on vancomycin or daptomycin - introducing rifampicin into a high inoculum staphylococcal bacteraemia rapidly selects rifampicin-resistant mutants and renders the biofilm-active drug useless.

stem:
A 24-year-old male medical student presents to a metropolitan emergency department six hours after a hollow-bore needlestick injury sustained while clearing a sharps container. The source patient is a 38-year-old man known to be living with HIV; his most recent viral load three months ago was reported as undetectable on bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide and his HIV physician has been contactable.

The needle had visible fresh blood and entered the dorsum of the student's left hand to a depth of around 3 mm with active bleeding. The student washed the wound under running water and the injury was reported within 10 minutes. His baseline HIV serology, hepatitis B surface antibody (vaccinated, anti-HBs 240), hepatitis C antibody, and pregnancy considerations are not applicable. He has no current medications.

data_table.Investigations: source patient HIV viral load undetectable 3 months ago, source patient hepatitis B surface antigen negative, source patient hepatitis C antibody negative, student baseline HIV serology pending, anti-HBs 240 mIU/mL (>10 protective), student hepatitis C antibody pending, full blood count and renal function within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step regarding HIV post exposure prophylaxis?

options.text: Reassure that the source undetectable viral load makes PEP unnecessary and arrange follow up serology at 6 weeks and 3 months
options.rationale: Undetectable viral load on treatment for at least six months strongly reduces transmission risk but the ASHM guideline still recommends offering PEP for high risk percutaneous needlestick exposures unless source recent viral load is documented undetectable AND adherence is verified. Documented adherence requires a more recent check than three months. (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines)

options.text: Commence 5 days of bictegravir, emtricitabine, and tenofovir alafenamide and review at day 5 to decide whether to continue
options.rationale: PEP duration is 28 days as a fixed course; truncated regimens have not been shown to prevent infection. The chosen regimen is also not the ASHM first line PEP combination. (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines)

options.text: Commence 28 days of zidovudine plus lamivudine as a two drug regimen following older Australian and overseas guidance
options.rationale: Two drug PEP is no longer standard; three drug regimens are preferred for high risk percutaneous exposures because of improved tolerability and resistance profile. Zidovudine is also no longer first line in Australian PEP regimens. (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines)

options.text: Commence 28 days of tenofovir 245 mg, emtricitabine 200 mg, and raltegravir 400 mg twice daily within 72 hours of exposure
options.rationale: Hollow bore percutaneous injury with visible blood from a known HIV positive source meets ASHM high risk criteria. Three drug PEP is recommended: tenofovir/emtricitabine backbone plus an integrase inhibitor (raltegravir or dolutegravir) for 28 days, starting within 72 hours (sooner is better; pharmacokinetic effect drops sharply after 48 to 72 hours). (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines)

options.text: Defer PEP pending source patient viral load on the same day and start only if the result is detectable above 200 copies
options.rationale: Waiting for results delays PEP initiation past the highly time sensitive window. PEP is started immediately and discontinued if the source is later confirmed HIV negative or genuinely undetectable with documented adherence. (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines)

explanation.summary: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) in Australia follows ASHM guidelines. High risk exposures (percutaneous injury with hollow needle and visible blood from a known HIV source, receptive anal intercourse with HIV positive source) warrant three drug PEP for 28 days within 72 hours; tenofovir/emtricitabine plus an integrase inhibitor (raltegravir or dolutegravir) is the preferred backbone. Baseline HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, syphilis, and pregnancy testing where applicable are arranged. Follow up HIV serology at 6 weeks and 3 months (4th generation antigen-antibody) confirms or excludes seroconversion. Counselling on safer sex and abstinence from blood donation until cleared is essential.
key_points: Start PEP within 72 hours (earlier the better), continue for 28 days
Three drug regimen: tenofovir + emtricitabine + integrase inhibitor (raltegravir or dolutegravir)
Baseline HIV, hepatitis B and C, syphilis, pregnancy test where applicable
Follow up 4th generation HIV serology at 6 weeks and 3 months
Discontinue PEP if source confirmed HIV negative or genuinely durably undetectable
explanation.pearls: Source virological suppression (durable undetectable on ART for at least 6 months with documented adherence) reduces sexual transmission risk to effectively zero (U=U) but for high risk percutaneous needlestick the residual uncertainty about source adherence usually still warrants PEP unless real-time viral load can be confirmed.

stem:
A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 9.4 percent on metformin and gliclazide) presents to a regional emergency department with 36 hours of progressive right calf pain and swelling after he caught his ankle on a fence post. The redness is now spreading rapidly above the knee. He says the pain is severe, much worse than the appearance suggests.

On examination he is unwell-appearing with rigors. The right calf is erythematous extending above the knee with a 12 cm patch of dusky purple skin, two small superficial blisters, and exquisite tenderness extending well beyond the visible margin of erythema. Sensation is reduced over part of the dusky area, and there is no crepitus. Vital signs are below. Bedside investigations are obtained.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 124, blood pressure 102/62, respiratory rate 24, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 124 g/L, white cells 22.4 x10^9/L, sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), glucose 17.4 mmol/L, creatinine 162 micromol/L, CRP 286 mg/L (<5), venous lactate 4.2 mmol/L, LRINEC score 9, plain radiograph of leg without subcutaneous gas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Mark the leading edge of erythema, admit for intravenous flucloxacillin 2 g every 6 hours, and review the leg in 12 hours
options.rationale: LRINEC score of 9 (high probability necrotising fasciitis), pain out of proportion, dusky skin with blistering, and systemic features mandate urgent surgical exploration and broad spectrum antibiotics. Monitoring and narrow spectrum therapy alone is inadequate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Administer high dose intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg as the first intervention before surgical exploration of the leg
options.rationale: IVIG is an adjunct for streptococcal toxic shock syndrome where supported, used after source control and broad spectrum antibiotics, not as the first intervention. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Commence intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.8 g every 4 hours alone and arrange magnetic resonance imaging before any surgery
options.rationale: MRI delays definitive treatment and necrotising fasciitis is a clinical diagnosis supported by surgical exploration. Benzylpenicillin alone is inadequate empirical cover. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Apply hyperbaric oxygen therapy as the primary treatment without immediate surgical debridement by the on call surgical team
options.rationale: Hyperbaric oxygen is adjunctive (where available) after surgical debridement, not a substitute for it. Delay risks rapid progression and mortality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Take blood cultures, give intravenous meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin, and arrange urgent surgical debridement
options.rationale: LRINEC 6 or more raises the probability of necrotising fasciitis to greater than 50 percent and clinical features here (pain out of proportion, dusky/bullous skin, sodium 132, lactate 4.2, CRP 286) all support the diagnosis. Empirical broad spectrum coverage including a beta lactam (meropenem or piperacillin-tazobactam), vancomycin for MRSA, and clindamycin for toxin suppression is standard, with simultaneous surgical debridement. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection is a surgical emergency with mortality 25 to 35 percent. The LRINEC score (CRP, white cells, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, glucose) stratifies probability but does not replace clinical judgement; pain out of proportion, dusky discoloration, bullae, crepitus, and rapidly spreading erythema are red flags.
