Treatment is simultaneous urgent surgical debridement with empirical broad spectrum antibiotics (meropenem or piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin plus clindamycin for toxin suppression). IVIG is considered for streptococcal toxic shock syndrome.
key_points: Pain out of proportion to appearance is the classical early sign
LRINEC 6 or more: > 50 percent probability of necrotising fasciitis
Empirical: meropenem (or piperacillin-tazobactam) + vancomycin + clindamycin
Urgent surgical debridement is the cornerstone
Clindamycin added for toxin suppression in streptococcal disease
explanation.pearls: Clindamycin 600 mg IV every 8 hours suppresses streptococcal exotoxin production and continues for at least 48 hours even after surgical source control - the antitoxin benefit is independent of cell wall activity.

stem:
A 64-year-old man with longstanding hypertension and bicuspid aortic valve known to a cardiologist presents to a regional emergency department with two hours of sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the interscapular area and now to the right loin. He says the pain was maximal at onset. He has not had recent trauma and has not used cocaine. He has had no syncope. He is a non-smoker.

On examination he is diaphoretic and frightened. The right radial pulse is weak; the left is normal. Right and left blood pressures differ by 28 mmHg. There is an early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge that he says is new (last cardiology echo six months ago noted aortic regurgitation graded 'trivial'). There is no focal neurology, no abdominal tenderness, and palpable femoral pulses bilaterally. There is no clinical pneumothorax. ECG shows sinus tachycardia without ischaemic changes.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 102, blood pressure 188/96 right arm and 160/82 left arm, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia, troponin within normal limits, D-dimer 6.2 mg/L (<0.5), chest radiograph mediastinal widening, point of care echo dilated ascending aorta with intimal flap

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous esmolol infusion targeting heart rate 60 to 80 and systolic blood pressure 100 to 120, with immediate CT angiography
options.rationale: Type A aortic dissection (ascending aorta involvement on echo, mediastinal widening, asymmetric pulses, new diastolic murmur) is a surgical emergency. Pre-operative care targets heart rate first with esmolol or labetalol to reduce shear stress (dP/dt), then vasodilator if needed for blood pressure. CT aortic angiography confirms anatomy and guides surgical planning. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases Guidelines)

options.text: Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion at 50 micrograms per minute to lower blood pressure as the priority intervention
options.rationale: Vasodilators alone increase reflex tachycardia and shear stress on the aorta, which can extend the dissection. Heart rate is controlled with a beta blocker first before adding a vasodilator. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases Guidelines)

options.text: Intravenous heparin 80 units/kg bolus then infusion for presumed pulmonary embolus given the markedly elevated D-dimer
options.rationale: Anticoagulation is contraindicated and catastrophic in aortic dissection; the elevated D-dimer reflects the dissection itself, not pulmonary embolism. CTA must precede any anticoagulation when dissection is suspected. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases Guidelines)

options.text: Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg with morphine 5 mg intravenously and admit for cardiac telemetry observation overnight
options.rationale: Sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated in hypertensive emergencies because of unpredictable hypotension. Observation without surgical referral for type A dissection has greater than 50 percent mortality at 48 hours. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases Guidelines)

options.text: Intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg over 90 minutes for suspected ST elevation myocardial infarction
options.rationale: Thrombolysis in aortic dissection causes catastrophic haemorrhage. The ECG here shows no ischaemic changes and the clinical picture is dissection, not infarct. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection is classified by Stanford as type A (ascending aorta or arch, always surgical) or type B (descending aorta, usually medical unless complicated by malperfusion, rupture, or persistent pain). Pre-operative management targets dP/dt: heart rate first to 60 to 80 with esmolol or labetalol, then blood pressure to systolic 100 to 120 with vasodilator if needed. CT aortic angiography is the imaging gold standard; transoesophageal echocardiography is an alternative in unstable patients. Mortality is 1 to 2 percent per hour untreated for type A. Predisposing factors include hypertension, bicuspid aortic valve, Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes, family history, and stimulant use.
key_points: Stanford A (ascending): surgical emergency, 1 to 2 percent mortality per hour untreated
Stanford B (descending): medical unless complicated
Heart rate first (esmolol/labetalol) target 60 to 80, then BP target 100 to 120 systolic
Vasodilators alone are dangerous (reflex tachycardia)
CT aortic angiography is the imaging gold standard
explanation.pearls: Untreated Stanford A aortic dissection mortality rises by 1 to 2 percent per hour for the first 48 hours - the 'time is aorta' window is similar in magnitude to STEMI 'time is muscle' but the intervention is operative repair rather than reperfusion.

stem:
A 36-year-old man is brought to the resuscitation bay of a major trauma centre 15 minutes after a high-speed motorcycle collision. He has bilateral femoral shaft fractures with active bleeding from the right thigh stump (a traumatic above-knee amputation), an open pelvic fracture, and a haemoperitoneum on focused ultrasound (FAST positive). He has had 1 unit of group O red cells from the trauma fridge en route.

On arrival he is alert but confused and pale. Pulse rate 142, blood pressure 76/48, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 92 percent on 10 L oxygen via Hudson mask, temperature 35.4 degrees. Two large bore intravenous cannulae are in. The Code Crimson team has been activated. Initial bloods are returning. The trauma team consultant asks you to coordinate the haematology side of the resuscitation.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 142, blood pressure 76/48, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 92 percent on 10 L oxygen, temperature 35.4 degrees
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 64 g/L, platelets 122 x10^9/L, INR 1.4, fibrinogen 1.2 g/L (2 to 4), lactate 6.8 mmol/L, base excess negative 8, ionised calcium 0.92 mmol/L (1.10 to 1.30), ROTEM EXTEM CT 95 sec (38 to 79) and FIBTEM A10 6 mm (>10), shock index 1.9

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give recombinant factor VII 90 micrograms/kg as the primary intervention to control bleeding before any other product
options.rationale: Recombinant factor VIIa is not first line; it is a rescue agent considered after ratio-balanced transfusion, fibrinogen replacement, surgical control, and correction of acidosis/hypocalcaemia. Routine use has not improved mortality and may increase thrombosis. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Protocol)

options.text: Transfuse two units of packed red cells, then reassess clinical status and laboratory results before further blood products
options.rationale: Sequential reassessment under-resuscitates in established trauma induced coagulopathy and risks worsening the acidosis-hypothermia-coagulopathy triad. Activation of the massive transfusion protocol is required when there are signs of ongoing significant bleeding. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Protocol)

options.text: Give 2 L of crystalloid resuscitation before any blood products to restore peripheral perfusion and blood pressure
options.rationale: Crystalloid resuscitation in major haemorrhage dilutes clotting factors, worsens acidosis, increases bleeding, and is contraindicated as the primary resuscitation fluid. Damage control resuscitation prioritises blood products. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Protocol)

options.text: Activate the massive transfusion protocol at a 1:1:1 ratio with intravenous tranexamic acid, cryoprecipitate, and calcium
options.rationale: Trauma induced coagulopathy with hypothermia, acidosis, ionised hypocalcaemia, and low fibrinogen (Code Crimson criteria) needs simultaneous correction. The Australian National Blood Authority massive transfusion protocol uses balanced 1:1:1 ratios, TXA within 3 hours, calcium replacement to maintain ionised calcium > 1.1, and goal-directed fibrinogen replacement to keep fibrinogen above 1.5 to 2 g/L (or FIBTEM A10 > 7 mm). (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Protocol)

options.text: Defer tranexamic acid and rely on the trauma surgeon to achieve operative haemostasis before any antifibrinolytic agent
options.rationale: CRASH-2 trial showed tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of trauma reduces all-cause mortality (number needed to treat about 67) and death from bleeding (NNT about 121). Delaying TXA beyond 3 hours loses the benefit and may increase thrombosis. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Protocol)

explanation.summary: Massive transfusion in trauma is guided by the National Blood Authority criteria: anticipated requirement of 4 or more units of packed red cells in one hour, or ongoing major bleeding with haemodynamic instability. Australian protocols use balanced 1:1:1 ratios (packed red cells, FFP, platelets), TXA within 3 hours (CRASH-2), goal-directed fibrinogen replacement (cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate, target above 1.5 to 2 g/L), calcium supplementation (ionised calcium > 1.1), prevention of hypothermia, and concurrent surgical or interventional radiology source control. ROTEM or thromboelastography guides component therapy.
key_points: Activate MTP for anticipated 4+ units packed red cells in 1 hour or ongoing major bleeding
1:1:1 ratio (RBC:FFP:platelets) until ROTEM/TEG guidance available
TXA 1 g IV bolus + 1 g over 8 hours, within 3 hours of injury (CRASH-2)
Fibrinogen target > 1.5 to 2 g/L (cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate)
Ionised calcium > 1.1 mmol/L; avoid hypothermia and acidosis
explanation.pearls: Every unit of citrated packed red cells lowers ionised calcium - after 4 units, give 10 mL of 10 percent calcium gluconate (or 10 mL of 10 percent calcium chloride via central access) to keep ionised calcium above 1.1 mmol/L and preserve clotting cascade function.

stem:
A 52-year-old woman with poorly adherent hypertension (intermittent perindopril and amlodipine over years) is brought to the emergency department with a 12 hour history of a generalised throbbing headache, two episodes of vomiting, and progressive blurred vision. She has noticed a yellow tinge to lights and difficulty reading texts. There is no focal weakness, no chest pain, and no dyspnoea.

On examination she is alert but uncomfortable. The optic discs are bilaterally swollen with retinal haemorrhages and cotton wool spots. Auscultation reveals mild bibasal crackles without overt fluid overload. Cardiac auscultation is normal. There is no abdominal aortic mass, no carotid bruit, and no focal neurology. Vital signs and bedside investigations are below.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 92, blood pressure 232/138, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 96 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees
data_table.Investigations: 12 lead ECG sinus rhythm with voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy, troponin within normal limits, urinalysis blood 2+ protein 2+, creatinine 132 micromol/L (baseline 92), CT brain within normal limits, chest radiograph mild pulmonary venous congestion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her blood pressure in the first hour?

options.text: Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion at 50 micrograms/min targeting a blood pressure under 140/90 within thirty minutes
options.rationale: Rapid reduction to under 140/90 within 30 minutes risks cerebral and coronary hypoperfusion in chronically hypertensive patients whose autoregulation has shifted. The target is a controlled 20 to 25 percent fall over the first hour. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg and admit for cardiac telemetry observation with reassessment of blood pressure overnight
options.rationale: Sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated in hypertensive emergency because of unpredictable hypotension, reflex tachycardia, and risk of ischaemic stroke. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Intravenous labetalol infusion targeting mean arterial pressure reduction of about 20 percent over the first 60 minutes
options.rationale: Hypertensive emergency (severe hypertension plus end organ damage: papilloedema/retinopathy, acute kidney injury, mild pulmonary venous congestion) requires controlled lowering. Australian and ESC guidance limits initial mean arterial pressure reduction to 20 to 25 percent in the first hour and to around 160/100 over 2 to 6 hours to avoid cerebral hypoperfusion. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Restart perindopril 5 mg and amlodipine 10 mg orally and review blood pressure response in twenty four hours' time
options.rationale: Oral therapy alone is too slow for hypertensive emergency with end organ damage. Intravenous therapy with continuous monitoring is required for at least the first 24 hours. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Intravenous hydralazine 20 mg bolus repeated every 30 minutes targeting diastolic blood pressure under 70 mmHg today
options.rationale: Hydralazine causes unpredictable hypotension and reflex tachycardia, and the target diastolic of under 70 risks coronary hypoperfusion in left ventricular hypertrophy. Labetalol or a nicardipine/clevidipine infusion are preferred where available. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Hypertensive emergency is severe hypertension (typically systolic above 180 or diastolic above 120 mmHg) plus end organ damage (hypertensive encephalopathy, retinopathy with papilloedema, acute kidney injury, acute pulmonary oedema, aortic dissection, acute coronary syndrome, eclampsia). Australian guidance is to reduce mean arterial pressure by 20 to 25 percent over the first hour, then to about 160/100 over 2 to 6 hours, then gradually to normal over 24 to 48 hours. Specific situations have specific targets (aortic dissection systolic under 120, acute ischaemic stroke under 185/110 if thrombolysis, eclampsia under 160/110). First line agents are intravenous labetalol, nicardipine, or clevidipine; glyceryl trinitrate when pulmonary oedema or ACS dominates.
key_points: Hypertensive emergency = severe HT + end organ damage
Target 20 to 25 percent MAP reduction in first hour
Avoid sublingual nifedipine and rapid normalisation
Labetalol, nicardipine, clevidipine are first line
Specific targets: aortic dissection systolic < 120; stroke < 185/110 if thrombolysis; eclampsia < 160/110
explanation.pearls: In hypertensive emergency without aortic dissection, lowering mean arterial pressure below 20 to 25 percent of the presenting value in the first hour can cross the autoregulation lower limit (typically 60 to 70 mmHg MAP in normotensives but shifted up by 20 to 30 mmHg in chronic hypertensives) and precipitate watershed ischaemic stroke.

subtopic_detail: Adrenal insufficiency and perioperative steroid cover
stem:
A 58-year-old woman with autoimmune primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) for 15 years on hydrocortisone 20 mg morning, 10 mg lunch, and fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily is scheduled for an open Hartmann procedure for diverticular perforation under general anaesthesia. She arrives in the ED via ambulance hypotensive after one day of vomiting, fever, and abdominal pain. She missed her morning hydrocortisone today.

On arrival she is drowsy and pale. Capillary blood glucose 3.2 mmol/L. Pulse rate 132, blood pressure 78/48, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 96 percent on 4 L oxygen via nasal prongs, temperature 38.4 degrees. The abdomen is rigid with rebound tenderness. CT shows free intraperitoneal air and free fluid consistent with perforated diverticulitis. The surgical team plans theatre as soon as she is stabilised. Bloods are below.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 132, blood pressure 78/48, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 96 percent on 4 L oxygen, temperature 38.4 degrees
data_table.Investigations: sodium 128 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 5.4 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), urea 12.4 mmol/L, creatinine 142 micromol/L, glucose 3.2 mmol/L, lactate 4.2 mmol/L, white cells 22.4 x10^9/L, haemoglobin 124 g/L, CT free intraperitoneal air, blood cultures pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 200 mg over 24 hours, saline resuscitation, antibiotics, and proceed to theatre
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis precipitated by sepsis and surgical illness needs immediate parenteral hydrocortisone (100 mg IV bolus then 200 mg over 24 hours by infusion or 50 mg six hourly), aggressive fluid resuscitation, glucose correction, treatment of the precipitant (broad spectrum antibiotics, surgical source control), and continuation of stress dose hydrocortisone perioperatively. Mineralocorticoid replacement is unnecessary at hydrocortisone doses above 50 mg/day because of cross-binding. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Double her usual oral hydrocortisone dose, give intravenous fluids, and proceed to theatre once vital signs improve
options.rationale: Oral therapy is inadequate during vomiting, sepsis, and impending major surgery; absorption is unreliable and underdosing precipitates further crisis. Parenteral stress dose hydrocortisone is mandatory. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg as the steroid of choice in adrenal crisis given its longer half life than hydrocortisone
options.rationale: Dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity and is reserved for the diagnostic phase (does not interfere with cortisol assays). Hydrocortisone is preferred for treatment because it provides both glucocorticoid and at high doses sufficient mineralocorticoid activity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Withhold steroids until a random cortisol level can be measured and a short Synacthen test arranged through endocrine
options.rationale: Diagnosis is already established (15 year history of Addison disease). Withholding hydrocortisone for repeat testing during a life threatening crisis is dangerous and unnecessary. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Intravenous fludrocortisone 200 micrograms as the priority before hydrocortisone for mineralocorticoid replacement now
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is only available orally and has no role during acute crisis; hydrocortisone at stress doses provides adequate mineralocorticoid activity. The acute priority is intravenous hydrocortisone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a medical emergency with mortality 6 to 15 percent in known Addison disease, precipitated by intercurrent illness, surgery, missed doses, or new corticosteroid antagonists. Immediate management is intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 200 mg over 24 hours (infusion or divided 50 mg six hourly), 1 L 0.9 percent saline in the first hour, glucose correction, identification and treatment of the precipitant, and continuation of stress dose steroids until clinical recovery. Major surgery requires 100 mg pre-induction, then 200 mg over 24 hours; minor surgery requires double the usual dose for 24 hours. Mineralocorticoid replacement (fludrocortisone) resumes only when hydrocortisone falls below 50 mg/day.
key_points: Diagnose adrenal crisis on clinical grounds; do not delay treatment for testing in established disease
Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus then 200 mg over 24 hours (infusion or 50 mg six hourly)
1 L 0.9 percent saline in first hour; correct glucose with dextrose if hypoglycaemic
Major surgery: 100 mg pre-induction, 200 mg/24 h until oral intake
Fludrocortisone unnecessary while hydrocortisone > 50 mg/day
explanation.pearls: Australian Addison Disease emergency cards specify an intramuscular hydrocortisone 100 mg dose kept by the patient for self administration before transfer to hospital - the time-critical step that prevents death during gastroenteritis when oral steroids cannot be absorbed.

subtopic_detail: Acute hyperkalaemia in chronic kidney disease
stem:
A 65-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease stage 4 (baseline eGFR 22) presents to a metropolitan emergency department with one day of generalised weakness and palpitations. His regular medications include ramipril 10 mg daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, and atorvastatin 40 mg at night.

On examination he is alert with proximal muscle weakness limiting hip flexion. He is normotensive and not in fluid overload. ECG shows tall peaked T waves throughout the praecordial leads without QRS widening or P wave loss. Cardiac monitor confirms sinus rhythm. He has not had any vomiting, no recent gastroenteritis, no recent radiocontrast, and no over-the-counter medication changes. He took his usual morning dose of medications. He has no history of cardiac arrhythmia and no implanted device.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 78, blood pressure 142/86, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees
data_table.Investigations: potassium 7.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), sodium 136 mmol/L (135-145), bicarbonate 18 mmol/L (22-28), creatinine 280 micromol/L (60-110), urea 22 mmol/L (3-8), eGFR 18 mL/min/1.73 m squared, glucose 8.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate sequence of management?

options.text: 10 percent calcium chloride 10 mL intravenously over 10 minutes then repeat urea and electrolytes at 30 minutes for trend assessment
options.rationale: Calcium chloride is more vesicant than calcium gluconate; gluconate is preferred for peripheral administration. Calcium also protects the myocardium but does not lower potassium, so further intracellular shift agents are required. (Source: KHA Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate 30 g orally and recheck the serum potassium in 4 hours for trend before any further intervention
options.rationale: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate has slow onset (hours) and limited evidence; it is not appropriate as monotherapy in severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes. (Source: KHA Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Soluble insulin 10 units intravenously with 50 mL of 50 percent dextrose intravenously over 30 minutes and observe for hypoglycaemia thereafter
options.rationale: Insulin-dextrose is essential to shift potassium intracellularly but does not address myocardial protection or remove potassium. Calcium gluconate is given first for myocardial stabilisation. (Source: KHA Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent intravenously over 2 minutes, then insulin-dextrose and salbutamol nebuliser, and cease ramipril and spironolactone
options.rationale: Severe hyperkalaemia (potassium 6.5 or more) with ECG changes requires immediate calcium gluconate for myocardial stabilisation, then potassium-shifting therapy (insulin-dextrose and salbutamol nebuliser), and removal of offending drugs (ACE inhibitor and potassium-sparing diuretic). Definitive removal is via diuresis, resin, or dialysis. (Source: KHA Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Sodium bicarbonate 50 mmol intravenously over 5 minutes and arrange urgent haemodialysis with the on-call renal team for definitive treatment
options.rationale: Sodium bicarbonate has modest potassium-lowering effect and is reserved for severe metabolic acidosis. Haemodialysis is definitive but is preceded by myocardial stabilisation and pharmacological potassium shift. (Source: KHA Hyperkalaemia)

explanation.summary: Severe hyperkalaemia (potassium 6.5 or more) or any hyperkalaemia with ECG changes is treated in the order: calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent intravenous over 2 minutes for myocardial stabilisation, insulin 10 units with 50 mL of 50 percent dextrose for intracellular shift, salbutamol 10 to 20 mg nebulised as additional shift, removal of offending drugs (ACE inhibitor, ARB, potassium-sparing diuretic, NSAID), and definitive removal via diuresis, gut binders, or dialysis.
key_points: Severe hyperkalaemia: K >= 6.5 or any K with ECG changes
Sequence: stabilise myocardium, shift intracellular, then remove
Calcium gluconate 10 mL 10% IV over 2 min (peripheral preferred)
Insulin 10 units + 50 mL 50% dextrose IV; salbutamol 10-20 mg nebulised
Stop ACE inhibitor, ARB, potassium-sparing diuretic, NSAID
explanation.pearls: Calcium gluconate stabilises the myocardium within 2 to 3 minutes of administration and lasts 30 to 60 minutes, but does not lower potassium - the shift and removal steps must still follow.

subtopic_detail: Adult DKA initial fluid and insulin
stem:
A 25-year-old man with type 1 diabetes mellitus presents to a metropolitan emergency department with 24 hours of vomiting, polyuria, and progressive lethargy following several days of viral upper respiratory illness. He has stopped his usual insulin glargine 20 units at night and his rapid-acting insulin doses for the past 24 hours because of vomiting and concerns about hypoglycaemia.

On examination he is alert with dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, and slow capillary return at three seconds. There is acetone on his breath and his respiration is deep and slow. He has no fever, no abdominal tenderness, and no localising signs of infection. His weight is 75 kg today. He has no chronic complications of diabetes and his HbA1c three months ago was 7.6 percent. There is no recent travel and no chest pain.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 130, blood pressure 110/70, respiratory rate 28, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees
data_table.Investigations: venous gas pH 7.05, bicarbonate 7 mmol/L (22-28), glucose 32 mmol/L, beta-hydroxybutyrate 6.0 mmol/L, sodium 134 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 4.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.0), creatinine 110 micromol/L (60-110), urea 9 mmol/L (3-8)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first hour of fluid and insulin management?

options.text: 1 litre 0.9 percent saline as a rapid bolus over 30 minutes then maintenance at 100 mL/hour without potassium replacement initially in the first hour
options.rationale: Maintenance-only fluids after a single bolus undertreat the typical 5 to 8 litre deficit of adult DKA. Aggressive replacement is required, although tailored to age and comorbidity. (Source: APEG and ADS Adult DKA Guidelines)
source_refs: APEG and ADS Adult DKA Guidelines

options.text: Insulin infusion 0.1 units/kg/hour immediately without prior fluid resuscitation and crystalloid only added once the potassium falls below 4.0 mmol/L
options.rationale: Insulin should follow fluid resuscitation by 15 to 30 minutes; insulin without volume expansion risks worsening hypotension and cerebral oedema. (Source: APEG and ADS Adult DKA Guidelines)
source_refs: APEG and ADS Adult DKA Guidelines

options.text: 0.9 percent saline 1 L bolus over one hour with intramuscular insulin 10 units every 4 hours and oral potassium supplementation 2 grams daily
options.rationale: Intramuscular insulin is unreliable in DKA because of poor peripheral perfusion; a continuous intravenous insulin infusion is required after fluid resuscitation. (Source: APEG and ADS Adult DKA Guidelines)
source_refs: APEG and ADS Adult DKA Guidelines

options.text: 5 percent dextrose 1 L at 100 mL/hour and rapid-acting subcutaneous insulin 10 units stat with repeat doses every 2 hours guided by capillary glucose
options.rationale: Dextrose is added only once blood glucose falls below 14 mmol/L to allow ongoing insulin infusion without hypoglycaemia; it is not first-line fluid in early DKA. (Source: APEG and ADS Adult DKA Guidelines)
source_refs: APEG and ADS Adult DKA Guidelines

options.text: 0.9 percent saline 500 mL bolus over 15 to 30 minutes, reassess, then 250 to 500 mL/hour with insulin infusion 0.1 units/kg/hour started after fluids are flowing
options.rationale: Adult DKA initial management: rapid crystalloid bolus to restore intravascular volume, then ongoing replacement at 250 to 500 mL/hour, with intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour commenced after fluids are running and potassium has been measured. Add potassium when serum K is below 5.5 mmol/L. (Source: APEG and ADS Adult DKA Guidelines)
source_refs: APEG and ADS Adult DKA Guidelines

explanation.summary: Adult DKA management is fluid first (0.9 percent saline 500 mL to 1 L over 15 to 30 minutes followed by 250 to 500 mL per hour) then intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour. Add potassium chloride when serum potassium falls below 5.5 mmol/L because total body potassium is depleted despite normal or high initial serum levels. Switch to 5 percent dextrose with saline once blood glucose falls below 14 mmol/L to allow ongoing insulin while resolving ketoacidosis. Identify and treat the precipitant.
key_points: Fluid bolus 500 mL to 1 L 0.9 percent saline over 15-30 min
Ongoing replacement 250-500 mL/hour for total deficit 5-8 L
Insulin infusion 0.1 units/kg/hour after fluids running
Add potassium when serum K < 5.5 mmol/L
Switch to dextrose when glucose < 14 mmol/L
explanation.pearls: Continue the long-acting basal insulin alongside the insulin infusion to avoid rebound DKA when the infusion is stopped, and overlap subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin with the infusion by 1 to 2 hours during transition.

sources.label: APEG and ADS Adult DKA Guidelines

stem:
A 30-year-old woman with a long-standing history of asthma presents to a metropolitan emergency department with worsening shortness of breath over the past four hours. She is on long-acting beta-agonist and corticosteroid inhaler maintenance therapy. She has not had a hospital admission in the last 12 months but has needed three short oral prednisolone courses in the same period.

On arrival she is talking in single words, sitting upright with shoulder elevation. She has audible wheeze with use of accessory muscles. She has received three back-to-back salbutamol nebulisers (5 mg each) and one ipratropium nebuliser (500 micrograms) in the first 30 minutes. Peak expiratory flow is 35 percent of her best (380 L/min recorded six months ago). She has not yet received corticosteroid. She has no chest pain and no fever. Smoke detector activated cooking on her stove this morning.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 132, blood pressure 128/82, respiratory rate 36, SpO2 91 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees
data_table.Investigations: venous gas pH 7.36, pCO2 38 mmHg, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L, chest radiograph hyperinflated lung fields without consolidation or pneumothorax

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes plus intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg, continuous nebulised salbutamol, and senior medical review
options.rationale: Severe asthma exacerbation with peak flow under 50 percent, SpO2 under 92 percent on air, and inadequate response to back-to-back beta-agonist gets intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes plus systemic corticosteroid (intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg or oral prednisolone 50 mg) and continuous nebulised salbutamol, with senior review. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 0.5 mg of 1:1000 solution into the deltoid muscle and intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g for empirical antibacterial cover
options.rationale: Intramuscular adrenaline is reserved for anaphylaxis or peri-arrest asthma where conventional therapy has failed; antibiotics are not routine for asthma exacerbation without a bacterial trigger. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Intravenous aminophylline loading dose 5 mg/kg over 30 minutes followed by a continuous infusion at 0.5 mg/kg/hour for ongoing bronchodilation
options.rationale: Aminophylline has narrow therapeutic index and is reserved for severe exacerbations refractory to standard therapy; it is not the next step after first-line salbutamol and ipratropium. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Immediate endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation in the emergency department resuscitation bay with paralysis and sedation
options.rationale: Intubation is reserved for impending or actual respiratory arrest with falling conscious state, rising carbon dioxide despite maximum therapy, or exhaustion; this patient still has trial of medical therapy remaining. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

options.text: Heliox 70:30 helium-oxygen mixture by face mask as primary bronchodilator with continued back-to-back salbutamol nebulisers without further escalation
options.rationale: Heliox is an adjunct in selected centres for refractory cases; the evidence base is limited and it is not the next step in standard escalation in Australia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

explanation.summary: Severe and life-threatening asthma exacerbation is treated with oxygen titrated to SpO2 93 to 95 percent, repeated nebulised salbutamol (with ipratropium for severe exacerbations), systemic corticosteroid (oral prednisolone 50 mg or intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg), and intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes when peak flow remains below 50 percent. Refractory cases escalate to aminophylline, salbutamol infusion, heliox, non-invasive ventilation, or intubation under senior care.
key_points: Severe: PEF < 50 percent, talking words, accessory muscles, HR > 110
Life-threatening: silent chest, SpO2 < 92, exhaustion, normal-rising CO2
Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 20 min when first-line therapy fails
Systemic corticosteroid: prednisolone 50 mg oral or hydrocortisone 200 mg IV
Watch CO2 - rising indicates exhaustion and need for ventilatory support
explanation.pearls: A normal or rising carbon dioxide in a severe asthma exacerbation is a red flag indicating exhaustion and imminent respiratory failure - escalate to senior care and consider intubation rather than continuing the medical ladder.

subtopic_detail: Pulmonary embolism Wells score and imaging strategy
stem:
A 72-year-old woman is reviewed on the orthopaedic ward on day 4 after an elective right total knee replacement. She is taking enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneous prophylaxis. She has had four hours of sudden onset shortness of breath and right-sided pleuritic chest pain.

On examination she is mildly distressed with mild right calf swelling but no overt deep vein thrombosis signs. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations are otherwise unremarkable with normal heart sounds and clear chest. Wells score is calculated: PE more likely than alternative diagnosis (3), HR over 100 (1.5), surgery in last 4 weeks (1.5), no haemoptysis, no malignancy, no previous PE; total score 6 (high probability). The on-call radiologist has called the intern to ask whether a D-dimer is required before CTPA is performed.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 110, blood pressure 124/74, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 94 percent on room air, temperature 37.0 degrees
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia rate 110 without S1Q3T3, chest radiograph clear lung fields without effusion or wedge, troponin within normal limits

lead_in: Which imaging strategy is most appropriate?

options.text: Wait for D-dimer result with age-adjusted threshold of 0.72 mg/L (age multiplied by 0.01) and perform CTPA only if above this threshold to limit ionising radiation
options.rationale: Age-adjusted D-dimer is for ruling out PE in low or moderate clinical probability patients. With a Wells score above 4 the pretest probability is too high for D-dimer to safely rule out PE. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: PE)

options.text: Proceed directly to CT pulmonary angiogram without D-dimer because PE likely (Wells > 4) requires imaging-based exclusion regardless of D-dimer result
options.rationale: Wells > 4 (PE likely) skips D-dimer because of inadequate negative predictive value at high pretest probability. CTPA is the first-line imaging in Australia and is required to rule in or out PE. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Perform ventilation-perfusion scan instead of CT pulmonary angiogram given the moderate-to-high pretest probability and current chronic kidney disease concerns
options.rationale: V/Q scan is reserved for renal impairment with low risk of indeterminate scan (clear chest radiograph, young patient) or for contrast allergy; CTPA is first-line in adults without contraindication. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Commence empirical therapeutic enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcutaneously twice daily and arrange outpatient follow-up at the haematology day unit in 48 hours
options.rationale: Empirical therapeutic anticoagulation can bridge a delay to imaging but does not replace definitive imaging. Outpatient management of suspected PE in a postoperative patient without confirmation is unsafe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Perform bilateral lower limb compression Doppler ultrasound as initial test and treat only if a deep vein thrombosis is identified on the affected operative limb
options.rationale: Lower limb Doppler is a reasonable adjunct (positive Doppler with high pretest probability can avoid CTPA) but is not the primary test in a high probability patient who can have CTPA. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: The two-tier Wells score for PE stratifies pretest probability as PE likely (over 4 points) or unlikely (4 or fewer). PE likely proceeds directly to CT pulmonary angiogram; PE unlikely has D-dimer with age-adjusted threshold (age multiplied by 10 ng/mL above 50 years, i.e. 0.72 mg/L FEU at 72) and only requires CTPA if D-dimer is above threshold. CTPA is first-line imaging in Australia; V/Q scan is reserved for contrast allergy or significant renal impairment with normal chest radiograph.
key_points: Wells > 4: PE likely, proceed direct to CTPA
Wells <= 4: D-dimer first with age-adjusted threshold over 50 years
Age-adjusted D-dimer threshold: age x 10 ng/mL (or x 0.01 if mg/L FEU)
CTPA is first-line imaging; V/Q for contrast allergy or significant CKD
Lower limb Doppler can confirm DVT and avoid CTPA in high probability cases
explanation.pearls: Age-adjusted D-dimer uses the formula (age in years multiplied by 10 ng/mL FEU) above age 50 - this raises the threshold from a fixed 500 to around 720 at age 72 and avoids unnecessary CTPA in older patients with PE unlikely Wells.

subtopic_detail: SIADH versus cerebral salt wasting after SAH
stem:
A 58-year-old woman is on day 7 after surgical clipping of an anterior communicating artery aneurysm following a subarachnoid haemorrhage. Her serum sodium has fallen from 138 to 124 mmol/L over the past 24 hours. She is mildly drowsy. There has been no new neurological deficit on examination this morning.

Nursing observation shows polyuria of 4 litres over the previous 24 hours. On bedside review her mucous membranes are dry, jugular venous pressure is not visible, and capillary return is two seconds. Her body weight has fallen from 68 kg yesterday to 66 kg today. She is on regular enteral feeds via nasogastric tube providing 1500 mL daily and intravenous 0.9 percent saline at 80 mL/hour. She has had no vomiting and no diarrhoea.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 100, blood pressure 110/65, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees
data_table.Investigations: serum sodium 124 mmol/L (135-145), serum osmolality 258 mosm/kg (275-295), urine sodium 80 mmol/L, urine osmolality 580 mosm/kg, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, weight reduction 2 kg over 24 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Fluid restrict to 800 mL daily, withhold intravenous saline, and arrange demeclocycline 600 mg twice daily for refractory disease over the next 48 hours
options.rationale: The picture is volume-contracted (weight loss, dry mucous membranes, polyuria) rather than euvolaemic, making cerebral salt wasting more likely than SIADH. Fluid restriction would worsen cerebral perfusion. (Source: Australian Stroke Foundation Guidelines)

options.text: Administer 3 percent hypertonic saline 100 mL bolus then continuous infusion at 50 mL/hour and aim for a sodium rise of 10 mmol/L over the next 12 hours
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizures, coma). Rapid correction risks central pontine myelinolysis. The current sodium is amenable to careful isotonic replacement. (Source: Australian Stroke Foundation Guidelines)

options.text: 0.9 percent saline 1 L over 1 hour then 200 mL/hour, target sodium rise of 6 to 8 mmol/L over 24 hours, salt tablets 6 g daily if hyponatraemia persists
options.rationale: Cerebral salt wasting after subarachnoid haemorrhage is treated with isotonic saline replacement and salt loading, with the goal of restoring intravascular volume and sodium without exceeding 8 to 10 mmol/L rise per 24 hours (central pontine myelinolysis risk). Fluid restriction is contraindicated in cerebral salt wasting because it worsens cerebral perfusion. (Source: Australian Stroke Foundation Guidelines)

options.text: Demeclocycline 600 mg twice daily as a vasopressin receptor antagonist to allow free water excretion and restore serum sodium gradually toward normal range
options.rationale: Demeclocycline blocks vasopressin action and would worsen polyuria and hypovolaemia in cerebral salt wasting. It is also slow to act and rarely used in acute care. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Tolvaptan 15 mg daily as a vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist with strict fluid restriction to 1 litre per day and daily sodium monitoring on the ward
options.rationale: Tolvaptan is used in euvolaemic or hypervolaemic hyponatraemia (SIADH, heart failure) and is dangerous in hypovolaemic hyponatraemia such as cerebral salt wasting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Hyponatraemia after subarachnoid haemorrhage is most commonly SIADH (euvolaemic, normal urine output) or cerebral salt wasting (hypovolaemic, high urine output, weight loss). Volume status is the key discriminator since urinary sodium and osmolality overlap. Cerebral salt wasting is treated with isotonic saline replacement plus salt loading; SIADH is treated with fluid restriction and tolvaptan if severe. Correction rate is limited to 8 to 10 mmol/L per 24 hours to avoid central pontine myelinolysis.
key_points: SIADH: euvolaemic, normal weight, treat with fluid restriction
CSW: hypovolaemic, weight loss, polyuria, treat with isotonic saline + salt
Both can have urine sodium > 40 and urine osmolality > 100
Maximum correction 8-10 mmol/L per 24 hours to avoid CPM
Hypertonic saline only for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia
explanation.pearls: Weight loss and polyuria differentiate cerebral salt wasting from SIADH after subarachnoid haemorrhage; the management diverges sharply (fluid replacement vs restriction) so getting the diagnosis right matters more than any single laboratory value.

subtopic_detail: Stanford type A aortic dissection acute management
stem:
A 58-year-old man with long-standing poorly controlled hypertension presents to a metropolitan emergency department with sudden severe central chest pain radiating to the interscapular region. The pain reached maximum intensity within seconds and has been steady for two hours.

On examination he is in distress. There is a difference between his blood pressure measurements in the right arm and left arm of 40 mmHg. He has a soft early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. The chest is clear and the heart sounds are otherwise normal. Chest radiograph demonstrates a widened mediastinum measuring 9 cm. CT angiogram of the aorta has confirmed a Stanford type A dissection extending from the aortic root through the arch into the descending thoracic aorta. There is no malperfusion of major branch vessels reported. The cardiothoracic team are aware.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 96, blood pressure right arm 180/100, blood pressure left arm 140/85, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees
data_table.Investigations: 12-lead ECG sinus rhythm without ST changes, troponin within normal limits, chest radiograph widened mediastinum, CT angiogram Stanford type A dissection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous labetalol infusion targeting systolic blood pressure below 120 and admit to coronary care for ongoing medical management with antihypertensive review
options.rationale: Coronary care admission and medical management alone are appropriate for uncomplicated type B dissection. Type A is a surgical emergency. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Aspirin 300 mg, clopidogrel 600 mg, atorvastatin 80 mg, and admit to coronary care for management of likely non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome
options.rationale: Antiplatelets are contraindicated in aortic dissection; this is dissection, not acute coronary syndrome, despite an overlapping presentation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Intravenous labetalol with intravenous nitroprusside as second-line vasodilator and book elective cardiothoracic surgery in 24 to 48 hours after optimisation
options.rationale: Type A dissection is a surgical emergency with mortality rising 1 to 2 percent per hour without operation. Elective delay is contraindicated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Intravenous labetalol infusion targeting heart rate below 60 and systolic blood pressure below 120, opioid analgesia, and immediate cardiothoracic surgery referral for emergency repair
options.rationale: Type A dissection is a surgical emergency requiring immediate cardiothoracic repair. Pre-operative goals are heart rate under 60 (beta-blocker first to reduce wall stress before any vasodilator) and systolic blood pressure under 120, plus analgesia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Therapeutic heparin infusion and admit to intensive care for monitoring of haemodynamics and trends in renal function and creatinine over 24 hours
options.rationale: Anticoagulation is contraindicated in aortic dissection because it worsens the dissection and any bleeding into the pericardium or pleura. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Stanford type A aortic dissection involves the ascending aorta and is a surgical emergency with mortality rising at 1 to 2 percent per hour without operation. Initial medical therapy targets heart rate under 60 (beta-blocker first to reduce dP/dt and wall stress) and systolic blood pressure under 120, plus opioid analgesia. Beta-blocker must precede any vasodilator (nitroprusside) because vasodilator-induced reflex tachycardia would worsen dissection. Antiplatelets and anticoagulants are contraindicated. Type B is medical first line unless complicated.
key_points: Type A: ascending aorta, surgical emergency, mortality 1-2 percent per hour
Type B: descending aorta beyond left subclavian, medical first line
Pre-op: HR < 60, SBP < 120, beta-blocker before vasodilator
Antiplatelets and anticoagulants contraindicated
Blood pressure differential > 20 mmHg and widened mediastinum are classical signs
explanation.pearls: Beta-blocker before vasodilator in aortic dissection: nitroprusside alone causes reflex tachycardia that increases the shear stress (dP/dt) on the dissection flap and propagates the tear.

stem:
A 65-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus presents to a metropolitan emergency department with 24 hours of erythema and severe pain in the left thigh after a minor garden scratch. He describes the pain as far worse than the appearance suggests and is unable to bear weight on the affected leg.

On examination he is septic-appearing but alert. The left thigh shows ill-defined erythema extending from the knee to the upper thigh with marked tenderness but no obvious blistering, no clear demarcation, and no crepitus on palpation. The skin surface looks deceptively mild compared with the pain. The general surgical registrar reviews and is reluctant to operate on grounds of insufficient skin signs, suggesting observation and reassessment in 6 hours with empirical antibiotics. The microbiology registrar has been called by the team.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 110, blood pressure 130/80, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 38.4 degrees
data_table.Investigations: white cells 19.0 x10^9/L (4-11), haemoglobin 132 g/L (130-180), sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 110 micromol/L (60-110), glucose 14 mmol/L, CRP 220 mg/L (<5), lactate 2.8 mmol/L, LRINEC score 8 (CRP 4 + WCC 1 + Hb 0 + Na 2 + creatinine 0 + glucose 1)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g daily and observe with reassessment of the leg appearance and inflammatory markers in six hours of close monitoring
options.rationale: LRINEC 8 with pain out of proportion and septic appearance in a diabetic patient is high probability necrotising fasciitis; six-hour observation risks mortality given the documented 9 percent per hour rise in death rate with delayed surgery. (Source: ASID Skin and Soft Tissue Infections)
source_refs: ASID Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

options.text: MRI lower limb with contrast to confirm necrotising fasciitis based on fascial enhancement and fluid collections before booking the operating theatre
options.rationale: MRI may show fascial thickening but is not sensitive enough to rule out necrotising fasciitis and the time to scan delays surgical exploration which is the diagnostic gold standard. (Source: ASID Skin and Soft Tissue Infections)
source_refs: ASID Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

options.text: Punch biopsy of skin sent for frozen section histopathology to confirm fascial necrosis before surgical decision-making is made by the consultant
options.rationale: Frozen section biopsy of skin alone misses subfascial disease and adds a delay; intraoperative finger test on surgical exploration is the diagnostic gold standard. (Source: ASID Skin and Soft Tissue Infections)
source_refs: ASID Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

options.text: Bedside ultrasound looking for fascial thickening and subcutaneous fluid then targeted incisional biopsy if those features are seen on the ultrasound
options.rationale: Bedside ultrasound has poor sensitivity for necrotising fasciitis and a normal scan does not exclude the diagnosis; pursuit of imaging delays definitive surgical exploration. (Source: ASID Skin and Soft Tissue Infections)
source_refs: ASID Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

options.text: Urgent operating theatre for surgical exploration and aggressive debridement with intravenous meropenem, clindamycin, and vancomycin broad spectrum cover
options.rationale: LRINEC 8 in a diabetic patient with pain out of proportion and septic features is high probability necrotising fasciitis. The skin signs lag behind subcutaneous disease and a low threshold for surgical exploration is the standard of care. Empirical antibiotics include broad gram-negative cover (meropenem), antitoxin (clindamycin for streptococcal and clostridial), and gram-positive cover including MRSA (vancomycin). (Source: ASID Skin and Soft Tissue Infections)
source_refs: ASID Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis carries 25 to 35 percent mortality even with prompt surgery and approaches 100 percent without it. Skin signs lag behind subcutaneous disease, so pain out of proportion to appearance and systemic toxicity should prompt operative exploration regardless of how the skin looks. LRINEC 8 or more is high risk (PPV around 65 percent) but a lower score does not rule out the diagnosis. Empirical antibiotics are broad spectrum: meropenem (or piperacillin-tazobactam) plus clindamycin for antitoxin effect plus vancomycin for MRSA, then narrowed on culture.
key_points: LRINEC >= 8: high probability; LRINEC < 6 does not rule out
Pain out of proportion + sepsis + diabetes: low threshold to operate
Imaging delays surgery and adds little; the finger test at operation is gold standard
Empirical antibiotics: meropenem + clindamycin + vancomycin
Mortality rises around 9 percent per hour of surgical delay
explanation.pearls: Clindamycin is included in necrotising fasciitis cover for its antitoxin effect rather than its antibacterial spectrum: it switches off streptococcal exotoxin and clostridial toxin production through ribosomal inhibition even when the patient is already on a broader gram-positive agent.

sources.label: ASID Skin and Soft Tissue Infections

subtopic_detail: Hyperkalaemia in CKD with competing guideline cutoffs
stem:
A 68-year-old man with CKD stage 4 (baseline eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73 m^2) presents to the emergency department with worsening fatigue and palpitations. He takes perindopril 8 mg, spironolactone 25 mg, and metformin 500 mg BD, all unchanged for 6 months. His last potassium 4 weeks ago was 5.1 mmol/L. The treating intern has already given him 10 mL of 10 per cent calcium gluconate IV and salbutamol 20 mg via nebuliser, with a repeat ECG pending and a venous gas drawn.

The man is alert, has chest discomfort rated 3 out of 10, and has had no syncope. He has had no missed dialysis (he is pre-dialysis under the renal team and is on a low-potassium diet).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 56 bpm regular, BP 142/86 mmHg, RR 16, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 7.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.0); sodium 138; bicarbonate 16; eGFR 18 mL/min/1.73 m^2; creatinine 280 micromol/L (baseline 220); pH 7.28 on VBG; ECG sinus bradycardia 54 bpm with tall peaked T waves V2-V5, PR interval 220 ms, QRS 110 ms (was 90 ms at baseline)
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 8 mg daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, metformin 500 mg BD

lead_in: Following the initial calcium and salbutamol, what is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence intravenous insulin 10 units in 50 mL of 50 per cent dextrose over 20 minutes with paired blood glucose at 30 and 60 minutes, repeat ECG, and concurrently contact the nephrology team for emergency haemodialysis
options.rationale: Hyperkalaemia of 7.4 mmol/L with ECG changes beyond peaked T waves (PR prolongation, QRS widening from 90 to 110 ms) is life-threatening and requires both ongoing shifting therapy AND definitive removal of potassium. Insulin-dextrose is the second-line shifting agent after calcium and salbutamol; calcium stabilises the myocardium but does NOT lower potassium. Salbutamol shifts potassium intracellularly by approximately 0.5 to 1.0 mmol/L for 2 to 6 hours. The CKD stage 4 (eGFR 18) means the kidney cannot excrete the potassium load and the patient will rebound; emergency haemodialysis is the definitive removal therapy and should be arranged concurrently, not after the medical management has failed. (Source: KHA-CARI: Acute Kidney Injury and Hyperkalaemia; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology; Australian Resuscitation Council guideline 11.5.1)

options.text: Commence intravenous sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol over 60 minutes with paired blood gas at 30 and 60 minutes, monitor calcium and sodium, and recheck potassium at 60 minutes
options.rationale: Sodium bicarbonate has a small and variable effect on potassium shift and is not recommended as routine first-line shifting therapy in AU guidelines; its role is limited to severe metabolic acidosis with concurrent hyperkalaemia where the acidosis is the dominant contributor. The pH of 7.28 is mild-moderate and the dominant issue is the potassium of 7.4 with ECG changes. Insulin-dextrose plus emergency dialysis is the AU pathway. (Source: KHA-CARI: Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Administer sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Resonium) 30 g orally now and 15 g 4-hourly with sorbitol, with repeat potassium at 6 hours and rectal Resonium if the patient cannot tolerate oral
options.rationale: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate is slow-acting (4 to 6 hours), has limited evidence for emergency hyperkalaemia, and carries a risk of intestinal necrosis (particularly with sorbitol). The Therapeutic Goods Administration has issued warnings; AU practice now favours patiromer or zirconium cyclosilicate for chronic management. In acute life-threatening hyperkalaemia with ECG changes, Resonium is NOT the next step. (Source: KHA-CARI: Hyperkalaemia; Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Cease perindopril and spironolactone, repeat potassium at 6 hours, ensure low-potassium diet, and arrange outpatient nephrology review within 1 week
options.rationale: Stopping the offending medications is appropriate as part of the management but is not sufficient when potassium is 7.4 with ECG changes; the patient needs ongoing shifting therapy and emergency dialysis or other definitive removal. Outpatient review in 1 week does not address acute hyperkalaemia. (Source: KHA-CARI: Hyperkalaemia)

options.text: Repeat the calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 per cent IV over 10 minutes, repeat the salbutamol 20 mg nebuliser, and re-check ECG and potassium in 30 minutes before further escalation
options.rationale: Repeating calcium is appropriate if ECG changes persist (every 30 to 60 minutes), but calcium does NOT lower potassium - it only stabilises the myocardium. Repeating salbutamol can add a further 0.3 to 0.5 mmol/L drop. Neither addresses the underlying need to remove potassium from the body in a patient with eGFR 18. Insulin-dextrose plus dialysis activation is the next step. (Source: KHA-CARI: Hyperkalaemia)

explanation.summary: This is life-threatening hyperkalaemia (potassium 7.4 mmol/L with PR prolongation and QRS widening beyond peaked T waves) in CKD stage 4. The AU pathway is concurrent: stabilise myocardium (calcium), shift potassium intracellularly (salbutamol then insulin-dextrose), and definitively remove potassium (haemodialysis when eGFR cannot excrete the load). The candidate must NOT confuse calcium and salbutamol with potassium-lowering definitive therapy; both are bridges only. The disconfirming finding is the QRS widening from 90 to 110 ms, indicating progression beyond first-degree changes and the need for both ongoing shifting and definitive removal. Competing guideline cutoffs (KDIGO international vs KHA-CARI Australian) on dialysis indications are similar but the AU framing emphasises early renal team activation in CKD stage 4 with acute hyperkalaemia rather than waiting for a fixed potassium threshold. In context, every acute hyperkalaemia with ECG changes in CKD requires concurrent action on three fronts (stabilise, shift, remove) and an immediate dialysis decision rather than a sequential pathway.
key_points: Calcium stabilises myocardium; does NOT lower potassium.
Salbutamol and insulin-dextrose are temporising shifting agents (0.5 to 1.0 mmol/L drop, 2 to 6 hour effect).
Definitive removal requires kidneys, gut binders (slow, chronic), or dialysis (acute, fast).
Sodium polystyrene sulfonate is slow and carries intestinal necrosis risk; not for emergency use.
QRS widening beyond peaked T waves is a sign of progression and an indication for emergency dialysis activation.
explanation.pearls: In acute hyperkalaemia with ECG changes in CKD stage 4 or 5, call the renal team for emergency dialysis concurrently with insulin-dextrose - do not wait for medical management to fail.
